26 September 2026 — The odd generators at the double points: a line-gcd criterion proves (W₃) and (W₄), so open statement 1 holds for ρ ≥ d/5

Working proofs: a line-gcd criterion for (W_e); (W₃), (W₄) and ℓ₀ = B for ρ ≥ d/5 in characteristic 0 and almost every p. Cycle bmd-r90. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. By the pole lemma and the collision-point lemma, \((\mathrm W_e)\) for \(e\le4\) depended on two things: the double points, where both \(s\) and \(t\) vanish, and the sets \(Z_e\cup Z_{e+1}\). At a double point, \(\lambda_\ell=t/s\) is regular when \(t\) vanishes along \(\ell\) at least as fast as \(s\). Can the orders be compared, and do the sets \(Z_n\) meet the lines? The test ends with a criterion checked for \(e\le4\), or with a pole.

Setting. As before: \(s,t\) are the solutions of \(P_eP_{e+1}\) and \(P_{e-1}P_{e+2}\) at \((2e+1,2)\), \(\psi(p)=\lfloor p^2/2\rfloor\), and \(J\) is the ideal of a vertex line. The line \(\ell_3=\{y_3=y_1+y_2\}\) is parametrized as \(y(u)=(u,1,u+1)\). It passes through the double point \((0{:}1{:}1)\) at \(u=0\) and through \((1{:}0{:}1)\) at \(u=\infty\). The transposition \(y_1\leftrightarrow y_2\) maps \(\ell_3\) to itself and exchanges these two points. The group S₃ permutes the three lines.

The criterion

Lemma (lem:cube-line-gcd-criterion). Over a field of characteristic \(\ne2\), let \(e\ge2\). Suppose that the following hold.

  • (a) \(P_p\in J^{\psi(p)}\), as polynomials, for \(p=e-1,\ldots,e+2\), where \(J\) is the ideal of the vertex line through \((1,1,0)\).
  • (b) For \(n=e,e+1\), the gcd over \(F[u]\) of the coordinates of \(W^{(n)}(y(u))\) is \(u^{\psi(n)}\).
  • (c) For \(n=e,e+1\), \(W^{(n)}\) has order exactly \(\psi(n)\) at \(u=\infty\) along \(\ell_3\). This follows from (b) and the symmetry remark: the transposition gives \(W^{(n)}_c(1,v,v+1)=\pm W^{(n)}_c(v,1,v+1)\), and \((1{:}v{:}v+1)\) is the point \(u=1/v\).

Then \((\mathrm W_e)\) holds.

Symmetry. Work in characteristic \(\ne2\), at \((p,1)\) with \(k=k_p\), \(d=p\). A witness of degree \(\le2k-d\) whose solution vanishes identically in \(y\) has order \(\ge k\) at the origin, since its lowest form evaluated at \(-yT\) would otherwise give a nonzero coordinate for generic \(y\). So it has order \(\ge k\) at all eight vertices. By the multiplicity Schwartz–Zippel lemma it is zero, since \(8k>4(2k-d)\). So the witness space at \((p,1)\), excess \(p^2-1\), is isomorphic to the solution space there, which is one-dimensional (boundary theorem). Permuting coordinates maps witnesses to witnesses, so S₃ acts on the line of \(P_p\) by a character, and \(P_p\) is invariant up to sign. Hence (a) holds for every vertex line, and \(s\), \(t\) and each \(W^{(n)}\) are invariant up to sign. For a permutation \(\sigma\), \(W^{\sigma P}(y)=W^P(\sigma y)\): the solution coordinates are coefficients of \(T\), which \(\sigma\) does not permute. So with \(\sigma(1{:}1{:}0)=(0{:}1{:}1)\), the product cone formula in the chart at \((1{:}1{:}0)\), applied to \(\sigma^{-1}P=\pm P\), describes the cones at \((0{:}1{:}1)\).

Proof. By the criterion it suffices that on every line of \(F_2=0\) the ratio \(\lambda=t/s\) is a quartic, and that the three quartics agree at the double points. By the symmetry remark it suffices to treat \(\ell_3\) and the double point \(u=0\), using the transposition for \(u=\infty\).

  • Away from \(u=0,\infty\). By (b), \(W^{(e)}\) and \(W^{(e+1)}\) have no common zero of their coordinates there. Every point of \(\ell_3\) other than \(u=0,\infty\) is either in \(U\) or one of the non-double collision points \(u=-1\) (\(y_3=0\)) and \(u=1\) (\(y_1=y_2\)). The conditions \(y_1=0\), \(y_2=y_3\) give \(u=0\), and \(y_2=0\), \(y_1=y_3\) give \(u=\infty\). At a point of \(U\), \(W^{(n)}(y)\ne0\) gives \(\varphi_n\ne0\), so \(\varphi_s\ne0\) and \(s(y)\ne0\) (pole lemma, part 1). At the non-double collision points, \(W^{(n)}\ne0\) gives \(s\ne0\) (collision-point lemma, part 3). So \(\lambda\) is regular there.
  • At \(u=0\). The solution of \(P_n\) is a nonzero constant times \(W^{(n)}\). By (b), its restriction to \(\ell_3\) has order exactly \(\psi(n)\) at \(u=0\), so its degree-\(\psi(n)\) part at the double point, given by the normalized series \(\tilde N_{P_n}\) of the product cone formula (through the symmetry remark), is nonzero in the direction of \(\ell_3\). By (a), \(P_eP_{e+1}\in J^{\psi(e)+\psi(e+1)}\), and the cone of \(s\) comes from \(\tilde N_{P_e}\tilde N_{P_{e+1}}\). This is a product of two power series in \(\lambda\) that are nonzero in that direction, so it is nonzero there. Its orders add, and the window of \(s\) is long enough to contain the lowest coefficient, since \(m=m_e+m_{e+1}+1\). So \(s|_{\ell_3}\) has order exactly \(\psi(e)+\psi(e+1)\) at \(u=0\). By (a), for the vertex line of this double point, \(P_{e-1}P_{e+2}\in J^{\psi(e-1)+\psi(e+2)}\), so every coordinate of \(t\) vanishes to order at least \(\psi(e-1)+\psi(e+2)\) at the double point (product cone formula, part 1). A direct count gives \(\psi(e-1)+\psi(e+2)=\psi(e)+\psi(e+1)+2\) in both parities: for even \(e\) both sides are \(e^2+e+2\), and for odd \(e\) both are \(e^2+e+2\) too. Since \(t=\lambda s\) on \(\ell_3\), \(\lambda\) vanishes to order at least 2 at \(u=0\). By the transposition the same holds at \(u=\infty\).

So \(\lambda\) is a rational function on \(\ell_3\cong\mathbb P^1\), homogeneous of degree 4, with no poles: a binary quartic. It vanishes at both double points. By symmetry the same holds on the other two lines, and all three quartics vanish at every double point, so they agree there. \(\square\)

The computation

Kernel. bmd_cube_solution_cones.cpp gains three options:

  • a fixed cone direction (TAU, SIGMA);
  • a cone order per series case;
  • a dump of value vectors at fixed points (DUMPVAL).

research/tools/bmd_cube_line_gcd.py interpolates the coordinates along \(\ell_3\) and takes their gcd.

Finite check (check:cube-boundary-line-gcd, research/results/bmd-r90-double-points/). Over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\), for \(n=2,3,4,5\):

  • The witness space at \((n,1)\), excess \(n^2-1\), is one-dimensional and lies in the S₃-trivial part. It is the whole space, so \(P_n\) is S₃-invariant.
  • Its jet lies in \(J^{\psi(n)}+\mathfrak m^k\).
  • As a control, its cone of order \(\psi(n)\) at \((1{:}1{:}0)\) is nonzero in the direction \((U,S)=(1,1)\) of the line \(\ell_1\) through that point. By invariance the same holds for each of the six pairs (double point, line of \(F_2=0\) through it), which form one S₃-orbit. The proof takes the exact order from (b), not from this control.
  • Along \(\ell_3\), from 60 points \(u=2,\ldots,61\), the gcd of the coordinates of \(W^{(n)}\) is \(u^{\psi(n)}\): \(u^2,u^4,u^8,u^{12}\).

The coordinates have degree at most \(n^2-1+4n\le44\) in \(u\), so 60 points determine them. Condition (a), as membership of the whole polynomial, is the vertex-line theorem for \(p\le6\), under the order theorem's hypothesis on the characteristic (characteristic 0, or odd \(p\) not dividing the degree or equal to it). The jets confirm it for \(n\le5\) modulo \(\mathfrak m^k\).

The odd generators for e ≤ 4

Theorem (thm:cube-odd-generators-small). In characteristic 0, and in characteristic \(p\) outside a finite set, \((\mathrm W_3)\) and \((\mathrm W_4)\) hold. Hence, by the reduction theorem (part 2 with \(e=4\)), every pair with \(2\le\rho\le d-1\) and \(d\le5\rho\) is settled: \(\ell_0(d+1,4d+\rho-1)=B(d,\rho)\) for all \(\rho\ge d/5\).

Proof. Condition (a) for \(p\le6\) is the vertex-line theorem, in characteristic 0 and almost every \(p\). For (b) and (c), write the coordinates of \(W^{(n)}\) on \(\ell_3\) as binary forms in \((y_1,y_2)\), with \(y_3=y_1+y_2\). Let \(G\) be their gcd over \(\mathbb Q\), taken primitive and integral, for the primitive integral boundary solution \(W^{(n)}_{\mathbb Q}\).

  • By (a) in characteristic 0 at both double points, \(y_1^{\psi(n)}y_2^{\psi(n)}\) divides \(G\).
  • By Gauss's lemma, \(G\) divides every coordinate over \(\mathbb Z\). Its reduction modulo \(q=1000003\), a nonzero form of the same degree, divides the gcd of the reduced coordinates. That gcd is \(y_1^{\psi(n)}y_2^{\psi(n)}\), by the computation and the transposition. Here the reduction of \(W^{(n)}_{\mathbb Q}\) is a nonzero constant times \(W^{(n)}_q\), by the boundary theorem modulo \(q\).
  • So \(G=\pm y_1^{\psi(n)}y_2^{\psi(n)}\), and (b) and (c) hold over \(\mathbb Q\).
  • After division by \(G\), the coordinates have no common zero. By the Nullstellensatz some powers of \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are combinations of them with rational coefficients. Clearing denominators, this persists modulo all but finitely many primes, where the gcd is then again \(y_1^{\psi(n)}y_2^{\psi(n)}\).

For \(e=4\), \(n\) runs up to \(e+2=6\) only through (a), which the vertex-line theorem covers. \((\mathrm W_2)\) holds in characteristic 0 and almost every \(p\) (the \((5,2)\) theorem), so part 2 of the reduction theorem applies with \(e=4\) in the intersection of these sets of characteristics. \(\square\)

Remark. On \(\ell_3\), \(\lambda\) is a quartic with a zero of order \(\ge2\) at each double point, so \(\lambda=c\,y_1^2y_2^2\) on \(\ell_3\), and the permuted forms on the other lines.

\((\mathrm W_3)\) agrees with the direct computation at \((7,2)\) in the criterion entry. \((\mathrm W_4)\) is new; a direct computation at \((9,2)\) is out of reach of the kernel.

General statement. lem:cube-line-gcd-criterion, for every \(e\), and thm:cube-odd-generators-small.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the criterion, the pole and collision-point lemmas, the product cone formula, the vertex-line theorem (whole-polynomial membership for \(p\le6\) and its characteristic hypothesis), the boundary theorem and the reduction theorem. Claim searches (line gcd, double point order, odd generator) found only the entries this one extends. A fresh-context referee checked the arithmetic \(\psi(e-1)+\psi(e+2)=\psi(e)+\psi(e+1)+2\), the analysis away from the double points, the chart direction, the compatibility step, the 60-point sufficiency and the output headers. It found no error in these. Its corrections are made: the transfer to characteristic 0 rewritten through the primitive gcd form; condition (a) stated as whole-polynomial membership, which the vertex-line theorem gives; the passage to the double point \((0{:}1{:}1)\) by a permutation; (c) derived from (b); the hypotheses of the symmetry remark stated; the cone check labelled a control; the characteristic scope of every input stated; and the interpolation script's assertion made meaningful.

Assessment. The last family of open statement 1 is now reduced to a property of single boundary solutions on one line: the gcd of the coordinates of \(W^{(n)}\) along \(y_3=y_1+y_2\) should be exactly \(u^{\psi(n)}\). Together with the vertex-line orders, which are proved for \(p\le6\) and conjectured in general, and the invariance of \(P_n\), this gives \((\mathrm W_e)\). It holds for \(n\le5\), which gives open statement 1 for \(\rho\ge d/5\). The next step is to prove the line-gcd property for all \(n\). On \(\ell_3\), \(c\) is 2-torsion, and \(W^{(n)}\) has order exactly \(\psi(n)\) at the double points. So the property says that \(W^{(n)}\) vanishes nowhere else on the line, a statement about one family of degenerating curves.

26 September 2026 — Route review of the cube: the line-gcd property survives through n = 8; the vertex-line orders are now the bottleneck

Route review: the line-gcd prediction held exactly for n ≤ 8 modulo the computing prime; the two-line peeling bound on the vertex-line orders covers a vanishing fraction of the needed terms as p grows. Cycle bmd-r91. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

The line's general claim. On \(\{0,1\}^3\) the solution module at every \((d,\rho)\) is free with least generator excess \(B(d,\rho)\) (torsion-partition law). The mechanism is peeling by boundary witnesses (reduction theorem), which settles \(d\le(e+1)\rho\) once the odd generators \((\mathrm W_{e'})\), \(e'\le e\), exist. By the line-gcd criterion, \((\mathrm W_e)\) follows from two properties of single boundary witnesses:

  • (L) the gcd of the coordinates of \(W^{(n)}(u,1,u+1)\) is \(u^{\psi(n)}\), for \(n=e,e+1\);
  • (V) \(P_p\in J^{\psi(p)}\) as a polynomial, for \(p=e-1,\ldots,e+2\), with \(\psi(p)=\lfloor p^2/2\rfloor\).

What the goal needs. Open statement 1, \(\ell_0\ge B\) for \(2\le\rho\le d-1\), in every characteristic \(\ne2\). It is proved for \(\rho\ge d/5\) in characteristic 0 and outside a finite set of characteristics (\((\mathrm W_3),(\mathrm W_4)\)). The rest needs (L) for all \(n\) and (V) for all \(p\), and then the exceptional characteristics.

Falsification attempt

(L) could fail at some \(n\ge6\) through an extra common zero of the coordinates on \(\ell_3\), at a point of \(U\) or at a collision point. The earlier check reached \(n\le5\) only, through the value dumps of the solution-cone kernel. The new test uses the maximal minors directly. \(W^{(n)}\) is the primitive kernel vector of the \(4n\times(4n+1)\) boundary constraint matrix \(A_{4n}\). So its signed maximal minors are \(g\cdot W^{(n)}\), where \(g=c\,(y_1y_2y_3)^{n^2}\prod_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^{n^2}\) is their gcd over \(F[y]\) (boundary theorem, lem:cube-gcd-all-m). On \(y=(u,1,u+1)\), \(g\) restricts to a constant times \(u^{2n^2}(u+1)^{n^2}(u-1)^{n^2}\). So (L) predicts that the minors restricted to \(\ell_3\) have gcd exactly

\[u^{2n^2+\psi(n)}(u+1)^{n^2}(u-1)^{n^2},\]

with no other root over the algebraic closure.

  • research/tools/bmd_cube_line_minors.cpp evaluates all \(4n+1\) maximal minors of \(A_{4n}(y(u))\) modulo \(q=1000003\) at \(u=2,\ldots,561\), for \(n=2,\ldots,8\). The largest minor degree in \(u\) is at most \(2n(4n+1)=528<560\).
  • bmd_cube_line_gcd.py minors interpolates two random combinations of the minors and takes their gcd, which is the gcd of all minors unless the combinations are unlucky. It reports the multiplicities at \(u=0,1,-1\) and the degree of the rest. Unlucky combinations can only enlarge the gcd, so an exact match cannot be produced by them.

The prediction holds exactly for every \(n\le8\), and the controls \(n\le5\) agree with the earlier dumps. So (L) holds for \(n\le8\) modulo \(q\). The transfer argument of that entry (the primitive gcd form, Gauss's lemma and the Nullstellensatz) lifts it to characteristic 0 and almost every characteristic, with the lower bound \(u^{\psi(n)}\) from the boundary coordinate theorem. It is to be registered with the next research cycle. Outputs: research/results/bmd-r91-route-review/line-minors.txt and line-minors-gcd.txt.

The vertex-line orders. The vertex-line theorem gives \(P_p\in J^{\psi}+(u^ps^{2p})\). Writing \(P=\sum u^bs^cR_{bc}(t)\), the unproved entries are those with \(b\ge p\), \(c\ge2p\) and \(b+c<\psi(p)\). With \(T=\psi(p)-3p\), there are \(T(T+1)/2\) of them: 6 at \(p=7\), 36 at \(p=8\), 91 at \(p=9\) and 210 of the 1275 needed entries at \(p=10\). Since \(T\sim\psi\), their share of the \(\psi(\psi+1)/2\) needed entries tends to 1. So two-line peeling does not extend to (V) by small additions, and (V) needs a different mechanism.

Assessment of this line

The line is strong and its remaining obligations are now sharp. Every step from open statement 1 down to (L) and (V) is a proof, and (L), the statement about a new family, passed an exact test through \(n=8\) with no extra root anywhere on the line. (V) is the weak point. It is proved for \(p\le6\), and the proof's uncovered block grows to almost all needed entries. But (V) is used only to compute the orders of \(s=P_eP_{e+1}\) and \(t=P_{e-1}P_{e+2}\) at the double point, that is, to show that double-point orders of solutions add under witness multiplication. That additivity is a statement about functions on the degenerating curve, where the order theorem already works. It may be provable without (V). With (L) for \(n\le8\), (V) for \(p\le9\) alone would give \((\mathrm W_5),(\mathrm W_6),(\mathrm W_7)\), that is \(\rho\ge d/8\).

Outside leads

  • Vélu's isogeny formulas (J. Vélu, Isogénies entre courbes elliptiques, C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 273, 1971). On a line of \(F_2=0\) the class \(c\) is 2-torsion, so translation by \(c\) is an automorphism of the genus-1 curve, and the quotient is an explicit 2-isogenous curve. Solutions on \(\ell_3\) might be pulled back from the quotient, which would make \(W^{(n)}|_{\ell_3}\) computable in closed form and prove (L). It breaks if the translation moves \(p_0\) to a point where the pullback does not respect the pole and zero conditions. Test. Passed: with \(y_3=y_1+y_2\) and \(B=x^2-(y_1+y_2)x\), the quartic of the curve is \(D(x)=x(x-y_3)(x-y_1)(x-y_2)=B(B+y_1y_2)=(B+y_1y_2/2)^2-(y_1y_2/2)^2\). This is a Pell solution of degree 2, so \(2c=0\) on \(\ell_3\), and the same pairing works on the other two lines.
  • The Frobenius–Stickelberger determinant formula (G. Frobenius and L. Stickelberger, J. reine angew. Math. 83, 1877). The Wronskian of \(1,\wp,\wp',\ldots\) on an elliptic curve is an explicit product of \(\sigma\)-functions. The maximal minors of \(A_{4n}\) are Wronskian-type determinants of a basis of \(L(nH_\infty)\) at \(p_0\), so a formula of this type would give their zeros on \(\ell_3\), and (L) for all \(n\). It breaks at the degenerate fibres \(u=0,\pm1\), where the formula must be taken as a limit. Test. Not run: the translation of the \(T\)-expansion at \(p_0\) into Weierstrass form, needed before any comparison, is a research step.
  • Tate's uniformization over \(F[[s,t]]\), applied to products (J. Tate, A review of non-Archimedean elliptic functions, 1995; the order theorem's own proof). On the Tate curve the order of a section at the double point is the minimum over its Fourier terms, and the Fourier support of a product is the sum of the supports. This would give additivity of double-point orders under witness multiplication, which is all (V) is used for. It breaks if the lowest Fourier terms cancel in the product. Test. Passed on the recorded case: for \(e=3,4\) the order of \(s\) on \(\ell_3\) is exactly \(\psi(e)+\psi(e+1)\) (double-point entry), as additivity predicts.

Absurd bridges

  • Systematic absences for glide planes (crystallography: International Tables for Crystallography, Vol. A, reflection conditions). A glide symmetry, a reflection composed with half a lattice translation, forces the structure factors of odd index to vanish. Translation: on \(\ell_3\), translation by the 2-torsion class \(c\) is a half-period glide, and the coordinates \(W_c\) of the boundary solution are the structure factors. A reflection condition would predict extra vanishing at the double point for coordinates of one parity of \(c\), and so the exact gcd. Test. Falsified: the orders at \(u=0\) of the separate coordinates (bmd_cube_line_gcd.py orders on the saved dumps, coordinate-orders.txt) show no parity pattern. They fall by 1 per index from the first nonzero coordinate down to \(\psi(n)\), and then stay at \(\psi(n)\). For \(n=5\) they are \(16,15,14,13,12,12,\ldots\) from \(c=3\).
  • The Coulson–Rushbrooke pairing theorem (Hückel theory of alternant hydrocarbons, Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 36, 1940). For a bipartite molecular graph the number of nonbonding orbitals is the corank of the adjacency matrix, fixed by a matching count. Translation: the double point is a degenerate molecule, the rows \(T^Qw^r\) are orbitals, and the minors' order at \(u=0\) is the number of nonbonding orbitals, the corank of \(A_{4n}\) there. Test. Falsified by a count. At \(y=(0,1,1)\), \(w_1=1\) and \(w_2=w_3\), so the rows span polynomials of degree \(\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) and \(w_2\) times polynomials of degree \(\le\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\). These are independent modulo \(T^{4n+1}\), since \(A+Bw_2\equiv0\) would give \(A^2=B^2(1+4T)\). So the rank is \(n+1\) and the corank \(3n-1\), linear in \(n\), while the order is \(2n^2+\psi(n)\). The vanishing is a higher-order phenomenon, not a corank.

Bridge follow-up

  • Chebyshev–Pell polynomials. This cycle used the Pell description to verify \(2c=0\) on the three lines of \(F_2=0\) (the Vélu lead above). Follow-up. Closed: the torsion loci it made explicit are now used by the criterion, and the remaining statements (L), (V) concern orders of solutions, not torsion loci.
  • Min-plus dynamic programming. Follow-up. Closed: its recurrence is the peeling induction of the reduction theorem, which is proved; nothing further follows from it.
  • KP solitons and the Sato Grassmannian. The minors computed this cycle are the Plücker coordinates of the Krichever subspace, and their gcd on \(\ell_3\) is now known through \(n=8\). Follow-up. Continuing: a tau-function formula on the 2-torsion locus would prove (L), and the Frobenius–Stickelberger lead is its concrete form.
  • Discrete tomography. Follow-up. Closed: the switching configurations it predicted were ruled out by the basis criterion, and the open statements no longer concern supports of two-plane solutions.
  • The parity effect in superconducting islands. Follow-up. Closed: it predicted the parity obstruction, now a proved lemma, and gives no mechanism for the odd generators, which are the remaining content.
  • Forney's minimal bases. This cycle's test is Forney's identity in use: the minors' gcd on the line, less the collision part, is the content of \(W^{(n)}|_{\ell_3}\). Follow-up. Continuing: a minimal-index computation of the restricted system would turn (L) into a degree count on the line.
  • Harmonic-oscillator spectroscopy. Follow-up. Closed: its content, reading the generator excesses from the Hilbert series, is the basis criterion, which is proved.
  • Laporte's parity selection rule. Follow-up. Closed: it was developed into the odd-generator criterion (one odd atom, \(t-\alpha s\) divisible by \(F_2\)), and the remaining statements (L), (V) are not parity statements.

Lead follow-up

  • Flat closures of divisors. Follow-up. Closed: it targeted the arc-limit conjecture, and open statement 1 no longer goes through arc limits since the reduction theorem.
  • Riemann–Roch and Riemann–Hurwitz for \(n\ge4\). Not worked this cycle, which concerned \(n=3\). Follow-up. Continuing: it remains the lead for open statements 2 and 3.
  • Orders of complete linear series in genus 1. Follow-up. Closed: the order structure at \(p_0\) is absorbed into the witness functions \(\varphi_P\in L((m+1)p_0-dH_\infty)\) and the divisors of \(\varphi_p\), which the criterion uses.
  • Mumford's degenerating abelian varieties. This cycle identified double-point additivity as the only use of (V) (the Tate lead above). Follow-up. Continuing: the order of a product section on the Tate family is the next research step.
  • Karamata's majorization inequality. Follow-up. Closed: the balanced partition's minimality is used and proved in the reduction theorem.
  • Limit linear series on toroidal degenerations. Follow-up. Closed: the double-point exponents it aimed at are given by the Tate-curve order theorem, which is proved.
  • Fat points on the quintic del Pezzo surface. The uncovered block of (V) counted above is a set of fat-point conditions on the square faces. Follow-up. Continuing: Harbourne's computation of such systems could decide the block for \(p=7,8,9\), which is what \(\rho\ge d/8\) needs.
  • The Horace method. This cycle counted its limit: two-line peeling leaves \(T(T+1)/2\) entries, \(T=\psi(p)-3p\), a share tending to 1. Follow-up. Continuing: only the differential Horace lemma (Alexander–Hirschowitz), with traces on more than two lines, could reach the block, and the count shows that plain peeling cannot.
  • Multiplicity Schwartz–Zippel on a face. Follow-up. Closed: it was developed into face divisibility and the symmetry remark, both proved.
  • The Hilbert–Burch theorem. Follow-up. Closed: it was developed into the basis criterion, which is proved.
  • Mumford's theta basis. Follow-up. Continuing: together with the Tate lead above, a theta basis on the 2-torsion locus is the natural setting for both (L) and double-point additivity.
  • Mumford's multiplication theorem. Follow-up. Closed: it was developed into peeling by products, and its limit is the parity obstruction, which products cannot overcome.
  • Horrocks' splitting criterion. Follow-up. Closed: it gives freeness only, and the goal needs the generator excesses, which freeness alone does not give.
  • Castelnuovo's pencil trick and Mumford's multiplication theorem. Follow-up. Closed: it was developed into the peeling closure with non-product atoms, and its limit is again the parity obstruction.

Next step

On the highest-risk item, open statement 1:

  1. Prove double-point additivity: the order at the double point of the solution of a product of boundary witnesses is the sum of the factors' orders, on the Tate family over \(F[[s,t]]\) as in the order theorem. This would replace (V) in the criterion.
  2. Prove (L) for all \(n\), through the 2-isogeny on the lines of \(F_2=0\).
  3. Register (L) for \(n\le8\), with its transfer, as a finite check under the general statement of whichever of these succeeds.

Process. One compiled minors run of 2 s and two short interpolation runs.

26 September 2026 — The residue-disc lemma: the vertex-line orders are not needed, and open statement 1 holds for ρ ≥ d/8

Working proofs: a residue-disc lemma; (W_e) follows from the line-gcd property alone; (W₅)–(W₇) and ℓ₀ = B for ρ ≥ d/8 in characteristic 0 and almost every p. Cycle bmd-r92. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The route review found two obligations for \((\mathrm W_e)\):

  • (L), the line-gcd property of the boundary solutions on \(y_3=y_1+y_2\), exact through \(n=8\) modulo the computing prime;
  • (V), \(P_p\in J^{\psi(p)}\), which two-line peeling cannot reach for large \(p\).

(V) enters the line-gcd criterion only to compare the orders of \(s\) and \(t\) at the double points, that is, to show that orders add under witness multiplication. Can this additivity be proved on the curve, along the line only? The test ends with (V) removed from the criterion, or with the step that needs it.

Setting. As in the witness-differential lemma. For a witness \(P\) with \(k\), \(\ell\), \(m\), put \(h_P=T^{-k}P(z)/\prod_iL'(z_i)\), expanded at \(p_0\) on the branch \(z_i=r_0(y_iT)\), \(w_i=\sqrt{1+4y_iT}\). Then \(W^P_c\) is the coefficient of \(T^{-c-1}\) in \(h_P\), for \(0\le c\le m\), and \(h_P=\varphi_P/\prod_i(-w_i)\). All coefficients of \(h_P\) are polynomials in \(y\) over \(\mathbb Z[\tfrac12]\). \(\psi(p)=\lfloor p^2/2\rfloor\), and \(s,t\) are the solutions of \(P_eP_{e+1}\) and \(P_{e-1}P_{e+2}\) at \((2e+1,2)\).

The residue-disc lemma

Lemma (lem:cube-residue-disc-valuation). Let \(O\) be a complete discrete valuation ring whose residue field has characteristic \(\ne2\), with fraction field \(K\) and valuation \(v\). Let \(y\in O^3\), and let \(P\) be a polynomial with coefficients in \(O\) and \(h_P\ne0\). Here \(C_{4y}\) is the curve \(w_i^2=1+4y_iT\) over \(\bar K\) and \(\varphi_P=T^{-k}P(z)\) is a function on it (distinct nonzero entries are needed only to know its zeros, as in the claim below). Suppose no zero of \(\varphi_P\) over \(\bar K\) lies in the residue disc

\[D_0=\{x\in C(\bar K):\ |T(x)|<1,\ w_i(x)\equiv1\ \text{for}\ i=1,2,3\},\]

where \(\equiv\) is congruence modulo the maximal ideal of the valuation ring of \(\bar K\). Then the lowest nonzero coefficient of \(h_P\) has the least valuation among all coefficients of \(h_P\).

Proof. Let \(N\) be the pole order of \(h_P\) at \(T=0\) and \(g=T^Nh_P=\sum_jg_jT^j\). The coefficients \(g_j\) lie in \(O\), since \(\tfrac12\in O\), \(y\in O^3\) and \(P\) has coefficients in \(O\); and \(g_0\ne0\). Let \(v_0=\min_jv(g_j)\), and suppose \(v(g_0)>v_0\). By the Weierstrass preparation theorem in \(O[[T]]\), \(\pi^{-v_0}g=\Phi\cdot E\), where \(\pi\) is a uniformizer, \(E\) is a unit of \(O[[T]]\), and \(\Phi\) is a distinguished polynomial of degree \(j_0=\min\{j:v(g_j)=v_0\}\ge1\). The roots of \(\Phi\) lie in \(\bar K\) and have \(|T|<1\), by its Newton polygon. Take a root \(T_0\). Then \(T_0\ne0\), because \(\Phi(0)E(0)=\pi^{-v_0}g_0\ne0\). The field \(K'=K(T_0)\) is complete. The binomial series \(w_i=\sum_j\binom{1/2}{j}(4y_iT_0)^j\) converge in \(K'\) and are \(\equiv1\), since \(4^j\binom{1/2}{j}\) is an integer, so they define a point \(x_0\in D_0\) of \(C\). At \(x_0\), \(\varphi_P(x_0)=T_0^{-k}P(z(x_0))\) is the value of the convergent series \(h_P\prod_i(-w_i)\), which is \(T_0^{-N}g(T_0)\prod_i(-w_i(x_0))=0\), since \(E(T_0)\) is a unit. So \(x_0\) is a zero of \(\varphi_P\) in \(D_0\), a contradiction. \(\square\)

The lemma says the whole expansion of \(\varphi_P\) at \(p_0\) is controlled by one coordinate of the solution.

The zeros on the lines of \(F_2=0\)

Claim. Let \(y\) be a point of a line of \(F_2=0\) with distinct nonzero entries, over an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(\ne2\), outside the finite sets \(Z_1\), \(Z_2\), \(Z_n\) where the boundary solutions vanish. Then the zeros of \(\varphi_{P_n}\) are \(nH_\infty\), together with one point \(\sigma_i\sigma_j(p_0)\) when \(n\) is odd. Here \(\sigma_i\) changes the sign of \(w_i\). In particular no zero lies over \(T=0\) with all \(w_i=1\).

Proof. By the general peeling lemma, \(\operatorname{div}\varphi_n=nH_\infty+q_n-(4n+1)p_0\) with \(q_n-p_0\sim-nc\), \(c=[H_\infty-4p_0]\), when \(\varphi_n\ne0\), which holds since \(y\notin Z_n\). By the proof of part 1 of the coprimality lemma, on \(U\setminus Z_d\) the top coordinate \(F_d(y)\) vanishes exactly when \(d\cdot c=0\). With \(d=2\), \(F_2(y)=0\) gives \(2c=0\). With \(d=1\), \(F_1\) is a nonzero constant, so \(c\ne0\); this is used only for the exact list of zeros, since \(c=0\) would give \(q_n=p_0\), which also keeps the zeros out of the disc. The point \(q_n\) is unique, because an effective divisor of degree 1 on a curve of genus 1 is determined by its class. So for even \(n\), \(q_n=p_0\) and the zeros are \(nH_\infty\). For odd \(n\), \(q_n\) is the nonzero 2-torsion point \(c\) of \(C\) with origin \(p_0\). Each \(\sigma_i\sigma_j\) (\(i\ne j\)) is an automorphism of order 2. It has no fixed point. Over finite \(T\) a fixed point would have \(w_i=w_j=0\), that is \(T=-1/(4y_i)=-1/(4y_j)\). The four points over \(T=\infty\) are the sign classes \((\varepsilon_1{:}\varepsilon_2{:}\varepsilon_3)\) of \(w/\sqrt T\) up to an overall sign, and \(\sigma_i\sigma_j\) sends the class of \((\varepsilon_i,\varepsilon_j,\varepsilon_k)\) to that of \((-\varepsilon_i,-\varepsilon_j,\varepsilon_k)\sim(\varepsilon_i,\varepsilon_j,-\varepsilon_k)\), a different class. A fixed-point-free automorphism of a curve of genus 1 is a translation, here by a nonzero 2-torsion point, namely \(\sigma_i\sigma_j(p_0)\). The three are distinct, so they are the three nonzero points of \(C[2]\) (characteristic \(\ne2\)). Hence \(q_n=\sigma_i\sigma_j(p_0)\) for some \(i\ne j\): it lies over \(T=0\) with \(w_i=w_j=-1\). The points \(H_\infty\) lie over \(T=\infty\). \(\square\)

The line-gcd property suffices

Lemma (lem:cube-line-gcd-sufficiency). Let \(e\ge2\), and let \(F\) have characteristic 0, or odd characteristic \(p\) with \(p\nmid n\) or \(p=n\) for each \(n\in\{e-1,\ldots,e+2\}\). If, for \(n=e,e+1\), the gcd over \(F[u]\) of the coordinates of \(W^{(n)}(u,1,u+1)\) is \(u^{\psi(n)}\), then \((\mathrm W_e)\) holds. So hypothesis (a) of the line-gcd criterion is not needed, and (c) follows from (b) as before.

Proof. We may assume \(F\) algebraically closed, as in the pole lemma. The proof of the line-gcd criterion uses (a) only at \(u=0\) and \(u=\infty\) of \(\ell_3\), to show two things. First, \(s|_{\ell_3}\) has order exactly \(\psi(e)+\psi(e+1)\) there. Second, every coordinate of \(t|_{\ell_3}\) has order at least \(\psi(e-1)+\psi(e+2)=\psi(e)+\psi(e+1)+2\). Away from these two points it uses (b) with the pole lemma and the collision-point lemma, and for the other lines the symmetry remark. Of the symmetry remark only the S₃-invariance of \(P_p\) up to sign is used, which does not use (a); its transport of the product cone formula is no longer needed. We prove the two facts at \(u=0\). At \(u=\infty\) the same argument applies to \(y=(1,v,1+v)\), \(v=1/u\), with (c) in place of (b).

Let \(O=F[[u]]\), \(K=F((u))\) and \(y=(u,1,u+1)\in O^3\). Its entries are distinct and nonzero in \(K\). Let \(n\in\{e-1,\ldots,e+2\}\).

  • \(W^{(1)}\), \(W^{(2)}\) and \(W^{(n)}\) do not vanish at \(y\): their restrictions to \(\ell_3\) are nonzero polynomials in \(u\), since each \(Z_d\) is finite. So \(y\), as a point over \(\bar K\), satisfies the hypotheses of the claim. This bullet applies to all four \(n\), including \(n=e-1,e+2\), for which only the finiteness of \(Z_n\) is used, not (b). The solution of \(P_n\) is a nonzero constant times \(W^{(n)}\) (boundary theorem). So by the claim above, over \(\bar K\), no zero of \(\varphi_{P_n}\) lies in \(D_0\). By the residue-disc lemma, \(\min_jv(\text{coefficients of }h_{P_n})=v(\text{lowest coefficient})\), and the lowest coefficient is a coordinate \(W^{P_n}_{N-1}\) of the solution, since the pole order \(N\) of \(h_{P_n}\) is at most \(m_n+1\).
  • By part 3 of the boundary coordinate theorem, under the hypothesis on the characteristic, every coordinate of \(W^{(n)}\) vanishes to order \(\ge\psi(n)\) at the double point \((0{:}1{:}1)\). So every coordinate of \(W^{(n)}(y)\), that is every coefficient of \(h_{P_n}\) in the window \(c\le m_n\), has \(v\ge\psi(n)\). By the first bullet the least valuation over all coefficients of \(h_{P_n}\) is attained at the lowest one, which lies in the window. So every coefficient of \(h_{P_n}\) has \(v\ge\psi(n)\), including those outside the window, which enter the coordinates of \(t\).
  • For \(n=e,e+1\), (b) gives a coordinate with \(v=\psi(n)\). So the lowest coefficient of \(h_{P_n}\) has valuation exactly \(\psi(n)\): the minimum over all coefficients is at most \(\psi(n)\), at least \(\psi(n)\), and attained there.

Now \(h_{PQ}=h_Ph_Q\prod_iL'(z_i)\) as series, since \(k_{PQ}=k_P+k_Q\). \(\prod_iL'(z_i)=-\prod_iw_i\) has coefficients in \(O\) and constant term \(-1\). Write \(h_{P_n}=u^{\psi(n)}\hat h_n\) for \(n=e,e+1\), with \(\hat h_n\in O((T))\) whose lowest coefficient, at \(T^{-N_n}\), is a unit. Then \(h_{P_eP_{e+1}}=u^{\psi(e)+\psi(e+1)}\hat h_e\hat h_{e+1}\prod_iL'(z_i)\). All its coefficients have \(v\ge\psi(e)+\psi(e+1)\), and its coefficient of \(T^{-N_e-N_{e+1}}\) has valuation exactly that. Since \(N_n\le4n+1\), \(N_e+N_{e+1}\le8e+6=m_s+1\), with \(m_s=4(2e+1)+1\). So that coefficient is the coordinate \(s_{N_e+N_{e+1}-1}\). Hence \(s|_{\ell_3}\) has order exactly \(\psi(e)+\psi(e+1)\) at \(u=0\). Likewise every coefficient of \(h_{P_{e-1}P_{e+2}}\) has \(v\ge\psi(e-1)+\psi(e+2)\), so every coordinate of \(t|_{\ell_3}\) does. The rest of the proof of the line-gcd criterion is unchanged. \(\square\)

The additivity that (V) supplied through the product cone formula comes here from multiplying Laurent series, with the residue-disc lemma saying that the solution window already holds the least valuation of the whole series. Only the zeros of \(\varphi_{P_n}\) are used, and on the lines of \(F_2=0\) they sit over \(T=\infty\) or at 2-torsion points away from \(p_0\).

The odd generators for e ≤ 7

Theorem (thm:cube-odd-generators-seven). In characteristic 0, and in characteristic \(p\ne3\) outside a finite set, \((\mathrm W_e)\) holds for \(e\le7\). Hence, by the reduction theorem (part 2 with \(e=7\)), \(\ell_0(d+1,4d+\rho-1)=B(d,\rho)\) for every pair with \(2\le\rho\le d-1\) and \(d\le8\rho\).

Proof. By the sufficiency lemma, \((\mathrm W_e)\) for \(3\le e\le7\) needs (L) for \(n=3,\ldots,8\). For \(n\le5\) it is part of the \((\mathrm W_3),(\mathrm W_4)\) theorem. For \(n=6,7,8\) the route review computed, over \(\mathbb F_q\), \(q=1000003\), the gcd of two combinations of the maximal minors of \(A_{4n}\) on \(\ell_3\). It is \(u^{2n^2+\psi(n)}(u+1)^{n^2}(u-1)^{n^2}\) (research/results/bmd-r91-route-review/line-minors-gcd.txt). Three facts make this exact for \(W^{(n)}_q\), the primitive boundary solution over \(\mathbb F_q\):

  • The maximal minors are \(g\,W^{(n)}_q\), where \(g=c\,(y_1y_2y_3)^{n^2}\prod_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^{n^2}\), \(c\ne0\) (lem:cube-gcd-all-m, over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\)). On \(\ell_3\), \(g\) is a nonzero constant times \(u^{2n^2}(u+1)^{n^2}(u-1)^{n^2}\).
  • The gcd of all the minors divides the gcd of any two combinations. So the gcd of the coordinates of \(W^{(n)}_q|_{\ell_3}\) divides \(u^{\psi(n)}\).
  • By the boundary coordinate theorem over \(\mathbb F_q\) (\(q\nmid n\)), \(u^{\psi(n)}\) divides every coordinate.

Each interpolation used 560 points for polynomials of degree at most \(2n(4n+1)\le528\). The transfer to characteristic 0 is that of the \((\mathrm W_3),(\mathrm W_4)\) theorem. Let \(G\) be the primitive integral gcd of the coordinates of the primitive integral \(W^{(n)}_{\mathbb Q}\) on \(\ell_3\), as binary forms in \((y_1,y_2)\); the gcd over \(F[u]\) is its dehomogenization at \(y_2=1\). The lower bound \(y_1^{\psi(n)}y_2^{\psi(n)}\mid G\) now comes from the boundary coordinate theorem in characteristic 0. The upper bound comes from the reduction of \(G\) modulo \(q\), since the reduction of \(W^{(n)}_{\mathbb Q}\) is a nonzero constant times \(W^{(n)}_q\). All but finitely many characteristics follow by the Nullstellensatz, since for almost every \(p\) the reduction of \(W^{(n)}_{\mathbb Q}\) spans the solution line modulo \(p\). The transposition gives the order at \(u=\infty\). The sufficiency lemma needs the characteristic hypothesis of the order theorem for \(n\le9\), which excludes exactly \(p=3\) (from \(n=6\) and \(n=9\)). So the finite set of excluded characteristics consists of 3 and the uncomputed exceptions of the transfers and of the earlier theorems. \((\mathrm W_2)\) holds in characteristic 0 and almost every \(p\) (the \((5,2)\) theorem). So part 2 of the reduction theorem applies with \(e=7\), in the intersection of these sets of characteristics. \(\square\)

General statement. lem:cube-residue-disc-valuation, for every witness and every integral point; lem:cube-line-gcd-sufficiency, for every \(e\ge2\). Open statement 1 is now reduced, for all \(\rho\), to (L) for all \(n\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the line-gcd criterion and its symmetry remark and proof, the pole lemma, the general peeling lemma (divisors of \(\varphi_n\)), the proof of part 1 of the coprimality lemma, the boundary coordinate theorem (part 3 and its hypothesis), the witness-differential lemma, lem:cube-gcd-all-m, the \((\mathrm W_3),(\mathrm W_4)\) theorem's transfer, and the route review's minor computation. Claim searches (Weierstrass preparation, residue disc, leading coefficient, window and valuation) found no earlier version of the residue-disc lemma. A fresh-context referee checked the Weierstrass step and the evaluation at \(T_0\), the window position \(N\le4n+1\), \(k_{PQ}=k_P+k_Q\), \(N_e+N_{e+1}\le m_s+1\), the restriction of \(g\) to \(\ell_3\), the divisibility argument that makes the two-combination gcd exact, the 560-point bound, and the replacement of every use of (a). It found no fatal gap. Its corrections are made: fixed-point-freeness of \(\sigma_i\sigma_j\) checked over \(T=\infty\) too, and the uniqueness of \(q_n\) stated; the coefficients of \(P\) required in \(O\), and the unused hypothesis of distinct entries removed from the lemma; the role of \(c\ne0\) stated; the bound on coefficients outside the window derived from the residue-disc lemma, not from the boundary coordinate theorem alone; the use for \(n=e-1,e+2\) made explicit; the part of the symmetry remark still used named; the excluded prime 3 named; and the transfer's dehomogenization and reduction stated.

Assessment. The vertex-line orders, the obligation that two-line peeling could not reach, are gone from the route: the order comparison at the double points follows from one valuation argument on the residue disc of \(p_0\). What remains of open statement 1 for all \(\rho\) is (L): along \(y_3=y_1+y_2\), the coordinates of \(W^{(n)}\) have no common zero other than the two double points, and there they vanish to order exactly \(\psi(n)\). For odd \(n\) the exact order at \(u=0\) is the statement \(\operatorname{mult}_PF_n=\psi(n)\) of the order theorem's equality case, proved for \(n\le7\), since the branches of odd \(n\) have no binomial factor that could vanish along \(\ell_3\). The absence of other common zeros is the open core. The next step is to attack both with the curve: a common zero of the coordinates of \(W^{(n)}\) at a point of \(\ell_3\cap U\) is a point where \(\varphi_{P_n}\) vanishes identically, that is, where \(P_n\) vanishes on the whole image of the curve.

26 September 2026 — The line-gcd property for every n, by a degree count: open statement 1 holds in characteristic 0

Working proofs: the line-gcd property for all n; ℓ₀ = B(d,ρ) for all 1 ≤ ρ ≤ d in characteristic 0, and ℓ₀ = B for d ≤ (2p−2)ρ in characteristic p outside a finite set. Cycle bmd-r93. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. By the sufficiency lemma, open statement 1 for all \(\rho\) needs only (L). (L) says that along \(\ell_3=\{y_3=y_1+y_2\}\), parametrized as \(y=(u,1,u+1)\), the coordinates of the primitive boundary solution \(W^{(n)}\) have gcd exactly \(u^{\psi(n)}\) over \(F[u]\), with \(\psi(n)=\lfloor n^2/2\rfloor\). It is exact for \(n\le8\). Can it be proved for every \(n\)? The test ends with a proof, or with a point of \(\ell_3\cap U\) where the coordinates can vanish together.

Setting. \(W^{(n)}=(W_0,\ldots,W_{4n})\) is the primitive boundary solution at \((n,1)\), \(m=4n\), with \(W_{4n}=F_n\) of degree \(n^2-1\) (boundary theorem). Each coordinate \(W_c\) is homogeneous of degree \(n^2-1+4n-c\), or zero: \(W_c\) is a signed maximal minor of \(A_{4n}\) divided by the gcd \(g_{3,n}\), and dropping column \(c\) instead of column \(4n\) raises the degree of the minor by \(4n-c\), since the entry of a row in column \(c'\) is homogeneous of degree \(c'\) minus a constant of the row. \(U\) is the set of points with distinct nonzero coordinates, and \(Z_n\subset U\) is the finite set where \(W^{(n)}\) vanishes.

The line-gcd theorem

Theorem (thm:cube-line-gcd-all). Let \(n\ge1\), and let \(F\) have characteristic 0, or odd characteristic \(p\) with \(p\nmid n\) or \(p=n\). Put \(c_n=4n\) for odd \(n\) and \(c_n=4n-1\) for even \(n\). Then the restriction of \(W_{c_n}\) to \(\ell_3\) is a nonzero constant times \((y_1y_2)^{\psi(n)}\), and the gcd over \(F[u]\) of the coordinates of \(W^{(n)}(u,1,u+1)\) is \(u^{\psi(n)}\). The same holds on the other two lines of \(F_2=0\), for the same coordinate \(W_{c_n}\) and the two double points of that line.

Proof. We may pass to the algebraic closure: restriction to \(\ell_3\), the gcd over \(F[u]\), and the vanishing of a form do not change.

  1. Degree. \(\deg W_{c_n}=n^2-1+4n-c_n\). This is \(n^2-1=2\psi(n)\) for odd \(n\), and \(n^2=2\psi(n)\) for even \(n\). On \(\ell_3\), write \(W_{c_n}(y_1,y_2,y_1+y_2)\), a binary form of degree \(2\psi(n)\).
  2. Orders at the double points. \(\ell_3\) passes through the double points \((0{:}1{:}1)\), where \(y_1=0\), and \((1{:}0{:}1)\), where \(y_2=0\). By part 3 of the boundary coordinate theorem, under the hypothesis on the characteristic, every coordinate of \(W^{(n)}\) vanishes to order \(\ge\psi(n)\) at each double point. So its restriction to \(\ell_3\) is divisible by \(y_1^{\psi(n)}y_2^{\psi(n)}\).
  3. Nonvanishing. Take \(y\in\ell_3\cap U\) outside \(Z_1\cup Z_2\cup Z_n\), a cofinite subset of the line. By the claim of the residue-disc entry, \(\operatorname{div}\varphi_{P_n}=nH_\infty+q_n-(4n+1)p_0\), with \(q_n=p_0\) for even \(n\) and \(q_n=\sigma_i\sigma_j(p_0)\ne p_0\) for odd \(n\). So the pole order of \(\varphi_{P_n}\) at \(p_0\) is exactly \(4n+1\) for odd \(n\) and exactly \(4n\) for even \(n\). \(W^{(n)}(y)\) spans the line of residue vectors (coprimality lemma, proof of part 1), whose coordinate \(c\) is the coefficient of \(T^{-c-1}\) in \(\varphi_{P_n}/\prod_iL'(z_i)\). Since \(\prod_iL'(z_i)\) is a unit at \(p_0\), coordinate \(c_n\) is the coefficient of the pole of highest order, and \(W_{c_n}(y)\ne0\).
  4. Conclusion. A nonzero binary form of degree \(2\psi(n)\) divisible by \(y_1^{\psi(n)}y_2^{\psi(n)}\) is a constant times it. So \(W_{c_n}|_{\ell_3}=\kappa(y_1y_2)^{\psi(n)}\) with \(\kappa\ne0\), and \(W_{c_n}(u,1,u+1)=\kappa u^{\psi(n)}\). The gcd of the coordinates divides this, and by step 2 it is divisible by \(u^{\psi(n)}\). So it is \(u^{\psi(n)}\).

On the other two lines of \(F_2=0\), steps 1 to 4 apply verbatim, with that line's two double points: step 2 holds at every double point, and step 3 uses only \(F_2=0\). \(\square\)

Checks against the record. The orders at \(u=0\) of the separate coordinates, computed in the route review (research/results/bmd-r91-route-review/coordinate-orders.txt), have the value \(\psi(n)\) at \(c=4n\) for \(n=3,5\), and at \(c=4n-1\) for \(n=2,4\), where \(W_{4n}\) vanishes on the line. For odd \(n\) the theorem also gives the exact order \(\psi(n)\) of \(F_n\) along \(\ell_3\), in line with the equality case of the order theorem. For even \(n\), \(F_n\) vanishes on \(\ell_3\), since \(n\cdot c=0\) there.

Open statement 1

Theorem (thm:cube-torsion-partition-char-zero). On \(\{0,1\}^3\) over a field of characteristic 0, for all \(1\le\rho\le d\), the solution module at \(m=4d+\rho-1\) is free, and

\[\ell_0(d+1,4d+\rho-1)=B(d,\rho)=\sum_i(\pi_i^2-1),\]

where \(\pi\) is the balanced partition of \(d\) into \(\rho\) parts. Over a field of odd characteristic \(p\) outside the finite set of the reduction theorem, the value \(\ell_0=B(d,\rho)\) holds for every pair with \(2\le\rho\le d-1\) and \(d\le(2p-2)\rho\), and for \(p\ne3\) also for \(d\le8\rho\) (theorem). Freeness in characteristic \(p\) is not claimed.

Proof. By the line-gcd theorem, (L) holds for \(n=e,e+1\) whenever the characteristic is 0 or satisfies \(p\nmid n\) or \(p=n\) for these \(n\). By the sufficiency lemma, \((\mathrm W_e)\) holds for every \(e\ge2\) in characteristic 0. By part 3 of the reduction theorem, open statement 1 holds, that is \(\ell_0\ge B\) for \(2\le\rho\le d-1\), and every solution module at \(2\le\rho\le d\) is free. The reverse inequality \(\ell_0\le B\) for all \(1\le\rho\le d\) is the product bound, whose \(B\) agrees with the balanced-partition value: for \(\rho\le d-\rho\) both are the balanced partition of \(d\) into \(\rho\) parts, and otherwise both equal \(3(d-\rho)\). At \(\rho=d\), \(B=0\) and \(\ell_0\ge0\) trivially. At \(\rho=1\), \(\ell_0=d^2-1=B(d,1)\) (boundary theorem), and the module is free: it is the kernel of a map of free modules, hence reflexive, of rank 1 over the factorial ring \(F[y]\), hence free on the primitive \(W^{(d)}\).

In characteristic \(p\), the hypothesis of the sufficiency lemma for \(e\) concerns \(n=e-1,\ldots,e+2\). The least \(n\) violating it is \(2p\). So \((\mathrm W_e)\) holds for \(e+2\le2p-1\), that is \(e\le2p-3\), and part 2 of the reduction theorem settles every pair with \(2\le\rho\le d-1\) and \(d\le(2p-2)\rho\), with the product bound for equality. The other inputs of the sufficiency lemma, the pole lemma and the collision-point lemma, hold in every characteristic \(\ne2\). \(\square\)

Consequences. This is the lower half of the torsion-partition law in characteristic 0. The reverse inequality is the product bound. The open-statements section records that open statement 1, with the proved results, gives \(\delta_F(3,k,\ell)\) for all \(k,\ell\), through the threshold-ideal lemma, \(h(k,\ell)=\max\{h:\ell_0(h,m)\le\ell\}\). That assembly is not yet written as one theorem. Stating the closed formula for \(\delta_F(3,k,\ell)\) in characteristic 0, with every range of \((h,m)\) accounted for and checked against the recorded values, is the next step. The characteristic-\(p\) statement is weaker, for two reasons. The order theorem's hypothesis fails at \(n=2p\). The reduction theorem also carries finite exceptional sets from the half-plane and \((5,2)\) theorems, which are not computed.

General statement. thm:cube-line-gcd-all, for every \(n\ge1\); thm:cube-torsion-partition-char-zero, for every \((d,\rho)\) in characteristic 0.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the residue-disc entry (the zeros of \(\varphi_n\) on the lines of \(F_2=0\) and the sufficiency lemma), the boundary coordinate theorem (part 3 and its hypothesis), the proof of part 1 of the coprimality lemma, the boundary theorem, the reduction theorem (parts 2 and 3), the product bound and its definition of \(B\), the pole lemma and the collision-point lemma (characteristic \(\ne2\) only). Claim searches (line gcd, double point order, torsion partition) found only the results this entry extends and the conjecture it proves. The degree count agrees with the per-coordinate orders computed in the route review. A fresh-context referee checked the degree formula, the passage from orders at the double points to the restriction, the pole orders in both parities, the exclusion of zeros at \(u=\pm1\) by the degree count, and the characteristic-\(p\) range, and found the line-gcd theorem correct. Its corrections are made: equality cited from the product bound, with its \(B\) matched to the balanced-partition value; \(\rho=d\) and freeness at \(\rho=1\) justified; the characteristic-\(p\) statement restricted to the value of \(\ell_0\) for \(2\le\rho\le d-1\), and combined with the \(e\le7\) theorem; the other lines treated directly; and the open part in characteristic \(p\) named.

Assessment. Open statement 1 is proved in characteristic 0. The last step was short once the residue-disc entry had identified the zeros of \(\varphi_{P_n}\) on the lines of \(F_2=0\). There, one coordinate of the boundary solution has degree exactly twice the guaranteed order at each of the two double points of the line, so it has no other zero. The goal for \(n=3\) in characteristic 0 is thereby reduced to assembling the formula for \(\delta_F(3,k,\ell)\) from the thresholds. In odd characteristic \(p\), the open part is now the pairs with \(d>(2p-2)\rho\) (and \(d>8\rho\) for \(p\ne3\)), which need the order theorem at \(p\mid n\), \(n\ne p\), and the uncomputed exceptional sets.

26 September 2026 — The per-order function on the 3-cube in characteristic 0

Working proof of the closed formula for δ_F(3,k,ℓ) in characteristic 0, and for k−ℓ−1 ≤ 16p−12 in odd characteristic p outside a finite set. Cycle bmd-r94. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The threshold theorem gives \(\ell_0(d+1,4d+\rho-1)=B(d,\rho)\) for all \(1\le\rho\le d\) in characteristic 0. The open-statements section records that this, with the proved results, determines \(\delta_F(3,k,\ell)\). What is the formula, and does it match every recorded value? The test ends with a closed formula, proved from exact statements, and checked against the saved kernel runs.

Setting. On \(\{0,1\}^3\), \(\delta_F(3,k,\ell)\) is the least degree of \(P\in F[x_1,x_2,x_3]\) with multiplicity \(\ge k\) at the seven nonzero points and exactly \(\ell\) at the origin, for \(0\le\ell\le k-1\). Write \(m=k-\ell-1\) and \(\delta_F=3+2k-2-h=2k+1-h\), so \(h=h(k,\ell)\) is the savings. For \(d\ge1\) and \(1\le\rho\le d\), \(B(d,\rho)=\sum_i(\pi_i^2-1)\) over the balanced partition \(\pi\) of \(d\) into \(\rho\) parts.

The formula

Theorem (thm:cube-dimension-three-per-order). Let \(F\) have characteristic 0, let \(k\ge1\), \(0\le\ell\le k-1\) and \(m=k-\ell-1\). Then \(\delta_F(3,k,\ell)=2k+1-h\), where \(h=0\) if \(m=0\), and for \(m\ge1\)

\[h=1+\max\Bigl\{d\in\{0,\ldots,\lfloor m/4\rfloor\}:\ 5d\le m+1,\ \text{ or }\ 5d>m+1\text{ and }B(d,m+1-4d)\le\ell\Bigr\}.\]

When \(1\le d\le\lfloor m/4\rfloor\) and \(5d>m+1\), the argument \(\rho=m+1-4d\) satisfies \(1\le\rho\le d-1\), so \(B\) is defined wherever it is used.

Equivalently, \(h-1\) is the larger of \(\lfloor(m+1)/5\rfloor\) and the largest \(d\) with \(5d>m+1\), \(d\le\lfloor m/4\rfloor\) and \(B(d,m+1-4d)\le\ell\) (with \(\max\emptyset=0\)). The same formula holds over a field of odd characteristic \(p\) outside the finite set of the reduction theorem whenever \(m\le16p-12\).

Proof. By part 1 of the threshold-ideal lemma, \(h(k,\ell)=\max\{h:\ell_0(h,m)\le\ell\}\), with \(\max\emptyset=0\). Here \(\ell_0(h,m)\) is the initial degree of the homogeneous ideal \(I^{(h)}_m\), which decreases in \(h\), so \(\ell_0(h,m)\) does not decrease in \(h\). We find \(\ell_0(d+1,m)\) for every \(d\ge0\).

  • Too many savings. By the finite-grid stable law, \(h(k,\ell)\le\kappa(m)\) for every \(\ell\). By the dimension-3 theorem, \(\kappa(m)=\lfloor m/4\rfloor+1\) for \(m\ge1\), and \(\kappa(0)=0\), since \(I^{(1)}_0=0\) (threshold-ideal lemma). So \(\ell_0(d+1,m)=\infty\) for \(d>\lfloor m/4\rfloor\), and every \(\ell_0\) is infinite when \(m=0\). This gives \(h=0\) at \(m=0\).
  • Order zero. Let \(m\ge1\) and \(5d\le m+1\). By part 2 of the order-zero theorem, applied at \(k'=m+1\ge2\) and \(\ell'=0\), the savings at \((m+1,0)\) are \(3+2(m+1)-2-\delta(3,m+1,0)=1+\lfloor(m+1)/5\rfloor\ge d+1\). So \(I^{(d+1)}_m\) has a nonzero element of degree 0, and \(\ell_0(d+1,m)=0\). This covers \(d=0\).
  • The pre-stable range. Let \(1\le d\le\lfloor m/4\rfloor\) and \(5d>m+1\). Put \(\rho=m+1-4d\), so \(m=4d+\rho-1\), with \(1\le\rho\le d-1\). By the threshold theorem, \(\ell_0(d+1,m)=B(d,\rho)\).

So \(\ell_0(d+1,m)\le\ell\) holds, for \(d\le\lfloor m/4\rfloor\), exactly when \(5d\le m+1\) or \(B(d,m+1-4d)\le\ell\). Taking the largest such \(d\) gives \(h\). For the equivalent form: \(d\le\lfloor(m+1)/5\rfloor\) implies \(d\le\lfloor m/4\rfloor\) when \(m\ge1\). In odd characteristic \(p\), the threshold theorem gives \(\ell_0=B\) for \(2\le\rho\le d-1\) and \(d\le(2p-2)\rho\). The boundary theorem gives \(\rho=1\) over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\). The order-zero theorem and the dimension-3 theorem hold in every characteristic \(\ne2\), and the threshold-ideal lemma and the stable law over every field. A pre-stable pair not covered therefore has \(\rho\ge2\) and \(d\ge(2p-2)\rho+1\ge4p-3\), so \(m=4d+\rho-1\ge16p-11\). For \(m\le16p-12\) there is none. \(\square\)

Checks. research/tools/bmd_cube_formula_check.py compares the formula with every saved exact per-order kernel run on \(\{0,1\}^3\) (JSON files with grid 2 and \(n=3\) under research/results/). It compares 462 values, with no disagreement: over \(\mathbb F_3\) for \(k\le13\), over \(\mathbb F_5\) for \(k\le12\), over \(\mathbb F_7\) for \(k\le11\), and over \(\mathbb F_{101}\) for six values of \(k\) between 33 and 45. The output is research/results/bmd-r94-formula/formula-check.txt. The runs over \(\mathbb F_3\), \(\mathbb F_5\) and \(\mathbb F_7\) (\(k\le13\)) meet no pre-stable pair with \(\rho\ge2\), whose first instance is \((d,\rho)=(3,2)\) at \(m=13\). So they test only the order-zero and \(\rho=1\) values, which are proved in every characteristic \(\ne2\). Only the \(\mathbb F_{101}\) runs test \(B\) with \(\rho\ge2\), at 32 pairs with \(d\le10\). At \(\ell=0\) and \(k\ge2\) the formula gives \(h=1+\lfloor k/5\rfloor\), the order-zero value, since \(B(d,\rho)>0\) for \(\rho\le d-1\).

General statement. thm:cube-dimension-three-per-order, for all \(k\ge1\) and \(0\le\ell\le k-1\) in characteristic 0.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the threshold-ideal lemma (part 1), the finite-grid stable law, the dimension-3 theorem (\(\kappa_3\)), the order-zero theorem, the threshold theorem and the product bound's definition of \(B\). Claim searches (per-order formula in dimension three, torsion partition) found only the conjecture whose consequence this is. A fresh-context referee checked the relation \(\delta=2k+1-h\), the case split for every \(d\le\lfloor m/4\rfloor\), the case \(m=0\), the characteristic-\(p\) inputs, and the script. It reproduced the 462 values, checked that the script's \(B\) equals the product bound's for \(d<60\), and compared the two forms of the formula on \(m<400\), \(\ell<3000\). Its corrections are made: \(B\) evaluated only where defined, with \(\max\emptyset=0\); the characteristic-\(p\) inputs named, and the range sharpened from \(m\le8p-5\) to \(m\le16p-12\); the small-field runs described as testing only proved ranges; \(k\ge2\) at \(\ell=0\); and the count moved out of the status line.

Assessment. The first target of the thread, the per-order function on \(\{0,1\}^3\), is determined in characteristic 0 and, in odd characteristic \(p\), for \(k-\ell-1\le16p-12\) outside a finite set of primes. The goal also asks for every odd characteristic. There the pre-stable pairs with \(d>(2p-2)\rho\) remain. They need the order theorem at \(p\mid n\), \(n\ne p\), where roots of unity of order \(2\gcd(m,n)\) collide, and the exceptional sets need to be computed. Dimensions \(n\ge4\) are open statements 2 and 3.

26 September 2026 — Double-point orders pass to every odd characteristic: open statement 1 outside the diagonal theorem's exceptional primes

Working proofs: the double-point order ⌊n²/2⌋ in every characteristic ≠ 2; freeness, ℓ₀ = B(d,ρ) and the δ formula in odd characteristic outside the diagonal certificate's primes. Cycle bmd-r95. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. In characteristic \(p\) the threshold theorem stopped at \(d\le(2p-2)\rho\). Its only input with a condition on \(p\) and \(n\) is the lower bound \(\psi(n)=\lfloor n^2/2\rfloor\) on the order of the boundary coordinates at the double points. That bound comes from the order theorem, whose branch factorization needs \(p\nmid n\) or \(p=n\). Is the lower bound itself independent of the characteristic? The test ends with a proof, or with a characteristic where the order drops.

Setting. \(W^{(n)}_F\) is the primitive boundary solution at \((n,1)\), \(m=4n\), over \(F[y]\). By the boundary theorem, over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\), the kernel of \(A_{4n}\) has rank 1 and \(W^{(n)}_F\) has top coordinate of degree \(n^2-1\), with \(\deg W_c=n^2-1+4n-c\) or \(W_c=0\) (line-gcd entry). The entries of \(A_{4n}\) lie in \(\mathbb Z[\tfrac12][y]\).

Reduction of the double-point order

Lemma (lem:cube-double-point-order-reduction). Over every field \(F\) of characteristic \(\ne2\) and for every \(n\ge1\), every coordinate of \(W^{(n)}_F\) vanishes to order \(\ge\psi(n)\) at each of the double points \((1{:}1{:}0)\), \((1{:}0{:}1)\), \((0{:}1{:}1)\).

Proof. For characteristic 0 this is part 3 of the boundary coordinate theorem, whose hypothesis holds there. Let \(F\) have odd characteristic \(p\). Multiplicity at a point with coordinates in the prime field does not change under extension of the field, and \(W^{(n)}_F\) is \(W^{(n)}_{\mathbb F_p}\) up to a nonzero constant (the kernel has rank 1 over every field, and a primitive generator stays primitive under field extension). So take \(F=\mathbb F_p\).

  • Let \(W\) be the primitive integral boundary solution: a generator of the kernel over \(\mathbb Q[y]\), scaled to have coprime integer coefficients. Its reduction \(\bar W\) modulo \(p\) is nonzero and lies in the kernel of \(A_{4n}\) over \(\mathbb F_p[y]\).
  • That kernel is \(\mathbb F_p[y]\,W^{(n)}_{\mathbb F_p}\), since it has rank 1 and \(W^{(n)}_{\mathbb F_p}\) is primitive. So \(\bar W=aW^{(n)}_{\mathbb F_p}\) with \(a\in\mathbb F_p[y]\) nonzero. By the boundary theorem over \(\mathbb F_p\) (characteristic \(\ne2\)), the generator \(W^{(n)}_{\mathbb F_p}\) has top coordinate of degree \(n^2-1\), the least excess at \(\rho=1\). So each nonzero coordinate of \(W^{(n)}_{\mathbb F_p}\), like that of \(\bar W\), is homogeneous of degree \(n^2-1+4n-c\), and \(a\) is a nonzero constant. This is the step where \(\bar W\) could otherwise have acquired a common factor modulo \(p\).
  • Let \(P\) be a double point, say \((0{:}1{:}1)\), in the chart \(y_2=1\). Its coordinates are integers. By the characteristic-0 case, for each coordinate \(W_c\) the expansion \(W_c(P+z)=\sum_\alpha b_\alpha z^\alpha\) has \(b_\alpha=0\) for \(|\alpha|<\psi(n)\). These \(b_\alpha\) are integers, polynomial in the coefficients of \(W_c\) and in the coordinates of \(P\), and their reductions are the corresponding coefficients of \(\bar W_c(P+z)\). So every coordinate of \(\bar W\), and hence of \(W^{(n)}_{\mathbb F_p}\), has multiplicity \(\ge\psi(n)\) at \(P\).

The other double points are the same, by permutation or by the same argument. \(\square\)

The characteristic hypothesis of the order theorem was needed only for its branch factorization, which proves more: divisibility by a product of \(\psi(n)\) branches. The bare lower bound on the order is a closed condition on Taylor coefficients at an integral point, so it passes to every reduction.

Open statement 1 in odd characteristic

Theorem (thm:cube-torsion-partition-odd). Let \(F\) have odd characteristic \(p\) outside the finite exceptional set \(E\) of the diagonal theorem: the primes dividing the contents of three integral minors of its certificate, a set that depends on the chosen integral lifts. Then:

  1. the line-gcd theorem and the sufficiency lemma hold over \(F\) without their conditions on \(p\), so \((\mathrm W_e)\) holds for every \(e\ge2\);
  2. for all \(1\le\rho\le d\) the solution module at \((d,\rho)\) is free and \(\ell_0(d+1,4d+\rho-1)=B(d,\rho)\);
  3. the formula of the per-order theorem gives \(\delta_F(3,k,\ell)\) for all \(k\ge1\) and \(0\le\ell\le k-1\).

Part 1 holds in every odd characteristic, including the primes of \(E\).

Proof. Part 1. The line-gcd theorem uses the characteristic only in its step 2, through part 3 of the boundary coordinate theorem. The lemma above replaces it in every characteristic \(\ne2\). The sufficiency lemma uses the characteristic only through the same bound, for \(n=e-1,\ldots,e+2\) (its second bullet). Their other inputs are stated in characteristic \(\ne2\), and were re-read for this: the claim on the zeros of \(\varphi_n\) on the lines of \(F_2=0\) (over an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(\ne2\)); part 1 of the coprimality lemma (characteristic \(\ne2\)); the finiteness of each \(Z_d\), which holds because a primitive vector's coordinates have no common factor; the residue-disc lemma (residue characteristic \(\ne2\)); residue duality, the general peeling lemma and the witness-differential lemma (characteristic \(\ne2\)); and, in the rest of the line-gcd criterion's proof, the odd-generator criterion, the pole lemma, the collision-point lemma and the symmetry remark, all in characteristic \(\ne2\). So \((\mathrm W_e)\) holds for every \(e\ge2\), with no exceptional prime.

Part 2. The reduction theorem assumes characteristic 0, or characteristic outside the finite sets of the half-plane theorem and of the \((5,2)\) theorem. Its proof uses the \((5,2)\) theorem only for \((\mathrm W_2)\), the generator \(w_5\), which part 1 now supplies in every odd characteristic. The half-plane theorem's exceptional set is that of the diagonal theorem, \(E\). So for \(p\notin E\), part 3 of the reduction theorem gives open statement 1, \(\ell_0\ge B\) for \(2\le\rho\le d-1\), and freeness for \(2\le\rho\le d\). The product bound, stated over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\), gives \(\ell_0\le B\), and \(\rho=d\) and \(\rho=1\) are as in the threshold theorem: \(B(d,d)=0\), and at \(\rho=1\) the boundary theorem and reflexivity of a rank-1 kernel over a factorial ring. Freeness in characteristic \(p\notin E\) is new here: the threshold theorem did not claim it.

Part 3. The proof of the per-order theorem uses the threshold-ideal lemma, the stable law, the dimension-3 theorem and the order-zero theorem, which hold in every characteristic \(\ne2\), and \(\ell_0=B\) in the pre-stable range, which is part 2. \(\square\)

What remains. The finite set \(E\) is not computed. It consists of the primes dividing the contents of three integral polynomials: the \(2\times2\) minor of \((P_1^2,g_2)\) at \((2,2)\), the \(3\times3\) minor of \((P_1^3,P_1g_2,g_3)\) at \((3,3)\), and the corresponding minor of the \((3,2)\) basis. \(E\) is where this certificate fails, not where the hypotheses (i) to (iii) are known to fail. Computing the three contents would leave a finite list of primes. At each of them, (i) to (iii) would still need a direct check of the witness spaces at \((2,2)\), \((3,3)\) and \((3,2)\) over \(\mathbb F_p\). Alternatively, (i) to (iii) could be proved structurally in every odd characteristic. The recorded kernel values over \(\mathbb F_3\), \(\mathbb F_5\) and \(\mathbb F_7\) agree with the formula, but they meet only the order-zero and \(\rho=1\) ranges (formula entry), so they do not test \(E\).

General statement. lem:cube-double-point-order-reduction, for every \(n\ge1\) in every characteristic \(\ne2\); thm:cube-torsion-partition-odd, for every \((d,\rho)\) and every odd \(p\notin E\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the boundary coordinate theorem, the boundary theorem (rank-1 kernel and top degree over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\)), the line-gcd theorem, the sufficiency lemma and the residue-disc entry's claim, the coprimality lemma, the reduction theorem with its full proof, the half-plane and diagonal theorems with their exceptional sets, the \((5,2)\) theorem, the product bound, and the per-order theorem. The characteristic hypotheses of residue duality, the basis criterion and the odd-generator criterion were checked in the registry (characteristic \(\ne2\)). A claim search found no earlier characteristic-free version of the double-point bound. A fresh-context referee checked the reduction step, including why the reduction of the primitive integral solution is nonzero and a constant multiple of the modular generator. It also checked the passage of Taylor coefficients at an integral point, that the reduction theorem uses the \((5,2)\) theorem only for \((\mathrm W_2)\), that the half-plane set is the diagonal set (including the \((3,2)\) minor), and the cases \(\rho=1\) and \(\rho=d\). It found no error. Its corrections are made: the boundary theorem cited at the constant-multiple step; every characteristic-\(\ne2\) input of part 1 named; the product bound's scope cited; freeness in characteristic \(p\) marked as new; \(E\) described as a property of the certificate, with direct checks still needed at its primes; and the remark on closed conditions made precise.

Assessment. The thread's first target, the per-order function on \(\{0,1\}^3\), is now determined in characteristic 0 and in every odd characteristic outside one finite set of primes \(E\). This set comes from three small witness computations and does not depend on \(d\), \(k\) or \(\ell\). The remaining work for \(n=3\) is the diagonal hypotheses (i) to (iii) at the primes of \(E\). They can be settled either by a structural proof in every odd characteristic, or by computing the contents and then checking (i) to (iii) directly at each prime dividing them.

26 September 2026 — Route review of the cube: the dimension-3 formula survives small characteristics; three witness spaces remain

Route review: the δ(3,k,ℓ) formula matched 918 exact kernel values, including seven pre-stable pairs with ρ ≥ 2 over each of F₃, F₅, F₇. Cycle bmd-r96. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

The line's general claim. On \(\{0,1\}^3\), over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\), \(\delta_F(3,k,\ell)=2k+1-h\). Here \(h-1\) is the larger of \(\lfloor(m+1)/5\rfloor\) and the largest pre-stable \(d\le\lfloor m/4\rfloor\) with \(B(d,m+1-4d)\le\ell\), and \(m=k-\ell-1\) (per-order theorem). The mechanism: thresholds are initial degrees of solution modules, which are free and generated by products of boundary witnesses together with non-product atoms.

What the goal needs. The thread's first target is dimension three in every odd characteristic and in characteristic 0. It is proved in characteristic 0 (threshold theorem), and in odd characteristic outside the finite set \(E\) of primes where the diagonal theorem's certificate fails (odd-characteristic theorem). What is missing are the diagonal hypotheses at the primes of \(E\):

  • (i) a non-product generator at \((2,2)\);
  • (ii) a non-product generator at \((3,3)\);
  • (iii) the \((3,2)\) basis.

Beyond dimension three, open statements 2 and 3 remain.

Falsification attempt

The formula was checked only against recorded runs, and the small-field runs (\(k\le13\)) met no pre-stable pair with \(\rho\ge2\). So small characteristics, where \(E\) could live, were untested exactly where the theory is deepest. research/tools/bmd_cube_formula_check.py needed no change. The exact jet kernel research/tools/bmd_jet_orders_q.cpp gains a series interface (one process for a list of primes and orders). It ran over \(\mathbb F_3\), \(\mathbb F_5\) and \(\mathbb F_7\) at \(k=11\) (control) and \(k=17,22,24,27,29,33\), which put the pairs \((3,2)\), \((4,2)\), \((4,3)\), \((5,2)\), \((5,3)\), \((5,4)\) and \((6,4)\) at their thresholds. The run took 179 s.

  • The \(k=11\) controls reproduce the recorded values over \(\mathbb F_3\) and \(\mathbb F_7\).
  • The formula check now compares 918 values: 243 over \(\mathbb F_3\), 230 over \(\mathbb F_5\), 218 over \(\mathbb F_7\) and 227 over \(\mathbb F_{101}\). There are no disagreements.
  • Over each small field the seven pairs above sit at their thresholds, with \(\ell=B\) or \(\ell=B-1\) (pairs-tested.txt).

Outputs are in research/results/bmd-r96-route-review/. The test could have failed at a prime of \(E\), or at any mistake in the characteristic-\(p\) chain. It passed. It does not prove that 3, 5, 7 lie outside \(E\), since \(E\) concerns the certificate, not the values. But the values that depend on the diagonal generators through the half-plane agree over these fields.

Assessment of this line

The line reached its characteristic-0 goal in five cycles after the last review: residue disc, line-gcd degree count, formula, reduction to odd characteristic. The evidence is structural, since every step is a proof, and the computations now test the formula in small characteristic where it had not been tested. The weak point is small and finite. Hypothesis (ii), and the certificate's primes, rest on three witness computations whose structure is not understood. Hypotheses (i) and (iii) look provable by semicontinuity (Outside lead 1). The broader thread, \(n\ge4\), has had no attention since the dimension-4 order-zero data, and it is qualitatively different: the order-zero thresholds there grow quadratically.

Outside leads

  • Semicontinuity of cohomology (Grothendieck, EGA III 7.7.5; for kernels of integer matrices, the elementary divisor theorem). The graded pieces of a solution module over \(\mathbb F_p\) have at least the dimension they have over \(\mathbb Q\). At \((2,2)\), excess 2, and at \((3,2)\), excess 4, the needed generator exists as soon as the dimension exceeds that of the multiples of the product solution. That holds if the product solution is primitive in every characteristic. This targets hypotheses (i) and (iii) at every prime. It breaks for (ii), where the multiples of two solutions must be saturated. Test. Passed. The product solutions have top coordinates \(F_1^2\), a nonzero constant, and \(F_1F_2\), a constant times the squarefree cubic \(\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3\) (recorded factorization). The second is nonzero at a generic point of each line \(\ell_i\), as the residue vector of the nonzero function \(\varphi_1\varphi_2\). So both are primitive in every characteristic \(\ne2\).
  • Reflexive rank-2 sheaves on \(\mathbb P^2\) and the Serre correspondence (Hartshorne, Stable reflexive sheaves, Math. Ann. 254, 1980). For (ii), the solutions at \((3,3)\) whose functions vanish at \(q_1\) form a saturated rank-2 submodule. It contains the \(P_1\)-multiples of the \((2,2)\) basis. (ii) fails exactly when this saturation is larger in excess 3. Its Chern classes, computed from the Plücker vector, would bound that. It breaks if the saturation is not split, where \(c_2\) alone does not fix the Hilbert function. Test. Not run: the Plücker vector of the \(P_1\)-image needs the multiplication map on solutions, which is not yet written as a polynomial map.
  • Kummer's theorem on carries (E. Kummer, 1852). The root curve \(z=r_0(yT)\) has Catalan coefficients, whose \(p\)-adic valuations count carries in base \(p\). This targets open statement 2 (small primes for \(n\ge4\)): a lacunary root curve could change the order counts. It breaks if the orders depend only on the curve's function field, not on the coefficients. Test. Not run: open statement 2 has no recorded failure to explain, so the test has no target yet.

Absurd bridges

  • The MacWilliams identity (coding theory). Multiplicity conditions at the seven nonzero vertices define a multiplicity code, and the origin order \(\ell\) is a weight. Translation: the per-order function would satisfy a duality exchanging \(\ell\) and \(k-1-\ell\), such as \(\delta(3,k,\ell)+\delta(3,k,k-1-\ell)\) constant in \(\ell\). Test. Falsified: by the formula, the sum is non-constant for 56 of the 58 orders \(2\le k\le59\), for example with sums 12 and 13 at \(k=3\).
  • Chip-firing on a cycle (statistical physics: the abelian sandpile; Baker–Norine). The double point degenerates the elliptic curve to a Tate curve whose skeleton is a circle. The order theorem's branches sit at tropical positions \(m/n\), each contributing twice the distance to the nearer node. Translation: \(\psi(n)=\lfloor n^2/2\rfloor\) is the energy of \(n-1\) chips at the positions \(m/n\) on a path, and the reduction lemma says this energy survives reduction. A sandpile theorem on minimal-energy configurations would give the double-point orders for higher \(\rho\) as energies. Test. Passed: \(\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}2\min(m,n-m)=\lfloor n^2/2\rfloor\) for all \(n\) (checked by hand for parity, as in the order theorem). For \(\rho=2\) the recorded order \(\psi(e)+\psi(e+1)\) is the energy of two independent chip sets.

Bridge follow-up

  • KP solitons and the Sato Grassmannian. Follow-up. Closed: the line-gcd property, which a tau-function formula was to prove, is proved by a degree count (line-gcd theorem).
  • Forney's minimal bases. Follow-up. Closed: the degree count on the line that it suggested is what proved the line-gcd property, and nothing further is open there.

Lead follow-up

  • Riemann–Roch and Riemann–Hurwitz for \(n\ge4\). Not worked this cycle. Follow-up. Continuing: it is the lead for open statements 2 and 3, now the thread's main open part beyond \(E\).
  • Mumford's degenerating abelian varieties. Follow-up. Closed: the double-point additivity it aimed at came from the residue-disc lemma, and the characteristic-free order bound from reduction.
  • Fat points on the quintic del Pezzo surface. Follow-up. Closed: it targeted the vertex-line orders, which the route no longer needs.
  • The Horace method. Follow-up. Closed: same reason; the vertex-line orders are not needed.
  • Mumford's theta basis. Follow-up. Closed: the line-gcd property and additivity were proved without it.
  • Vélu's isogeny formulas. Follow-up. Closed: developed into the claim on the zeros of \(\varphi_n\) on the lines of \(F_2=0\) (2-torsion translations \(\sigma_i\sigma_j\)), which the line-gcd theorem uses. The isogeny itself was not needed.
  • Tate uniformization applied to products. Follow-up. Closed: developed into the residue-disc lemma, which gives the additivity by Weierstrass preparation, without the Tate curve.

Next step

On the highest-risk item, open statement 1 at the primes of \(E\):

  1. Prove (i) and (iii) in every odd characteristic by semicontinuity (Outside lead 1).
  2. For (ii), show that the saturation of the \(P_1\)-image at \((3,3)\) adds nothing in excess 3. Failing that, compute the content of the certificate minor and check (ii) directly at its primes.

Then turn to dimension 4 (open statement 3).

Process. One series run of the exact kernel (179 s), the formula check, and two small scripts.
