26 September 2026 — The diagonal hypotheses hold in every odd characteristic: the per-order function on the 3-cube over every field of characteristic ≠ 2

Working proof, with an exact certificate: the diagonal theorem in every odd characteristic, hence ℓ₀ = B and the δ(3,k,ℓ) formula over every field of characteristic ≠ 2. Cycle bmd-r97. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The odd-characteristic theorem proves the per-order function on \(\{0,1\}^3\) in odd characteristic outside a finite set \(E\), the primes where the diagonal theorem's certificate fails. Can \(E\) be emptied, by a certificate that covers every odd prime at once? The test ends with a proof for every odd prime, or with a prime where a hypothesis fails.

Setting. The diagonal theorem assumes, over \(F\):

  • (i) a witness solution \(g_2\) of excess 2 at \((2,2)\), not in \(F(y)P_1^2\);
  • (ii) a witness solution \(g_3\) of excess 3 at \((3,3)\), not in the \(F(y)\)-span of \(P_1^3\) and \(P_1g_2\);
  • (iii) a free module at \((3,2)\) on witness solutions of excesses 3 and 4.

\(K_{d,\rho}=\ker A_m\), \(m=4d+\rho-1\), is the solution module over \(F[y]\), of rank \(\rho\) over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\), since the gcd of the maximal minors of \(A_m\) is nonzero (lem:cube-gcd-all-m). The script builds the rows from \(w_i=\sqrt{1+4y_iT}=\sum_j\binom{1/2}{j}4^jy_i^jT^j\), whose coefficients are integers, rather than from the root curve \(z_i=r_0(y_iT)=(1-w_i)/2\). The row set \(\{T^Qw^r:2Q+|r|\le d\}\) is closed under lowering \(r\), so it spans the same \(\mathbb Z[\tfrac12]\)-module as \(\{T^Qz^r\}\), and the kernel is the same in characteristic \(\ne2\). A rerun with the \(z_i\) gave identical excesses and contents. With the \(w_i\), the entries of \(A_m\) are integers times monomials. The map is graded, with source degrees \(c\) and target degrees \(Q\).

The certificate

Theorem (thm:cube-diagonal-every-odd). Over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\):

  • \(K_{2,2}\) is free on generators of excesses \(0,2\);
  • \(K_{3,2}\) is free on generators of excesses \(3,4\);
  • \(K_{3,3}\) is free on generators of excesses \(0,2,3\).

Hence hypotheses (i) to (iii) hold, and the diagonal theorem, with its corollary, holds in every characteristic \(\ne2\).

Proof. The script research/tools/bmd_cube_basis_content.m2 (Macaulay2) builds the graded map \(A_m\) and computes minimal generators of its kernel. The output is research/results/bmd-r97-diagonal-certificate/basis-content.txt.

  • Over \(\mathbb Q\). For \((2,2)\), \((3,2)\), \((3,3)\) the kernel has \(\rho\) minimal generators, of excesses \(\{0,2\}\), \(\{3,4\}\), \(\{0,2,3\}\), which sum to \(N(d,\rho)=d^2-1-\binom\rho2\) (2, 7, 5). The script scales each to a primitive integral vector and computes the content of the \(\rho\times\rho\) minors: \(150=2\cdot3\cdot5^2\), \(25=5^2\), and \(168750=2\cdot3^3\cdot5^5\). Their only odd prime factors are 3 and 5.
  • Odd \(p\ne3,5\). The integral generators reduce to solutions over \(\mathbb F_p\), since \(A_m\) is integral. Their minors are not all zero modulo \(p\), because \(p\) does not divide the content. So they are \(\rho\) independent solutions over \(\mathbb F_p(y)\) with excess sum \(N(d,\rho)\). By the basis criterion (characteristic \(\ne2\)), they are a basis of \(K_{d,\rho}\) over \(\mathbb F_p\).
  • \(p=3,5\), and 7 as a control. Over \(\mathbb Z/p\) the script computes minimal generators directly: \(\rho\) generators with the same excesses in each case. A module of rank \(\rho\) generated by \(\rho\) elements is free on them.
  • Characteristic 0 and extensions. Freeness and the generator degrees of a graded kernel do not change under extension of the base field. So the statements pass from \(\mathbb Q\) and \(\mathbb F_p\) to every field of that characteristic.

From freeness to the hypotheses:

  • (iii): the basis \((b_3,b_4)\) at \((3,2)\) has excesses 3 and 4. The excess-3 part is \(F\,b_3\), so the solution of \(P_1P_2\) is a nonzero multiple of \(b_3\), and \(b_3\) has nonzero top coordinate.
  • (i): the excess-0 part of \(K_{2,2}\) is spanned by one basis element, of which the solution \(s_0\) of \(P_1^2\) is a nonzero multiple. So the excess-2 basis element \(g\) is not in \(F(y)s_0\).
  • (ii): at \((3,3)\) the excess-0 part is spanned by the solution \(s_1\) of \(P_1^3\). The solution \(t\) of \(P_1g_2\) is a witness solution of excess 2 (witness-differential lemma, part 3, characteristic \(\ne2\)). It is not in \(F(y)s_1\). At a generic \(y\in U\), residue duality is injective (characteristic \(\ne2\)), and \(\varphi_{P_1g_2}=\varphi_1\varphi_{g_2}\), \(\varphi_{P_1^3}=\varphi_1^3\). So \(t(y)\in F\,s_1(y)\) would give \(\varphi_{g_2}\in F\varphi_1^2\), since \(\varphi_1\ne0\) in the function field, and then \(g_2(y)\in F\,s_0(y)\), which fails at generic \(y\) by (i). The excess-2 part is the \(F[y]_2\)-multiples of \(s_1\) plus the basis element \(b_2\), so \(t=fs_1+\gamma b_2\) with \(\gamma\ne0\), and \((s_1,t,b_3)\) is again a basis. Hence \(b_3\) is not in the \(F(y)\)-span of \(s_1\) and \(t\).

The product solutions are nonzero over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\). The top coordinate of a product witness solution is, up to sign, the product of the top coordinates of its factors (lowest parts multiply, product bound entry). By the boundary theorem over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\), \(F_1\) is a nonzero constant and \(F_2\) a nonzero cubic. So \(s_0\), \(s_1\) and the solution of \(P_1P_2\) have top coordinates \(\pm F_1^2\), \(\pm F_1^3\), \(\pm F_1F_2\), all nonzero. In (i) and (ii) the new basis element is replaced by itself plus a form times \(s_0\) or \(s_1\), chosen so that its top coordinate is nonzero. The change of basis is unitriangular, so the result is again a basis with the same excesses. By part 1 of the threshold-ideal lemma (any field), a homogeneous solution with nonzero top coordinate comes from a witness. \(\square\)

The 3-cube over every field

Theorem (thm:cube-dimension-three-every-field). Over every field \(F\) of characteristic \(\ne2\):

  • for all \(1\le\rho\le d\) the solution module at \((d,\rho)\) is free and \(\ell_0(d+1,4d+\rho-1)=B(d,\rho)\);
  • for all \(k\ge1\) and \(0\le\ell\le k-1\), with \(m=k-\ell-1\), \(\delta_F(3,k,\ell)=2k+1-h\), where \(h=0\) if \(m=0\). Otherwise \(h-1\) is the larger of \(\lfloor(m+1)/5\rfloor\) and the largest \(d\le\lfloor m/4\rfloor\) with \(5d>m+1\) and \(B(d,m+1-4d)\le\ell\), or 0 if there is none.

Proof. Characteristic 0 is the per-order theorem. In odd characteristic, the odd-characteristic theorem proves both statements outside the exceptional set of the diagonal theorem. That set \(E\) was defined by the earlier certificate of the diagonal theorem's corollary, and the odd-characteristic theorem uses \(p\notin E\) only to obtain (i) to (iii). The new certificate gives (i) to (iii) for every odd \(p\), so it replaces that condition. The half-plane theorem's exceptional set is that of the diagonal theorem, and the reduction theorem's is that of the half-plane theorem once \((\mathrm W_2)\) holds (odd-characteristic theorem, part 1). \(\square\)

Checks. The theorem agrees with all 918 recorded exact kernel values over \(\mathbb F_3\), \(\mathbb F_5\), \(\mathbb F_7\) and \(\mathbb F_{101}\) (route review), and with the direct generator computations over \(\mathbb Z/3\), \(\mathbb Z/5\), \(\mathbb Z/7\) above. The rational generator excesses reproduce the diagonal theorem's recorded bases.

General statement. thm:cube-dimension-three-every-field, for all \(k,\ell\) over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\); thm:cube-diagonal-every-odd, the three base cases in every characteristic \(\ne2\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the diagonal theorem (hypotheses and corollary), the basis criterion, the half-plane theorem, the odd-characteristic theorem, the threshold-ideal lemma, the gcd lemma, the boundary theorem and the witness-differential lemma. Claim searches (diagonal generator, certificate, exceptional characteristic) found only the diagonal theorem and the characteristic-independence conjecture this settles for \(n=3\). A fresh-context referee checked several things. It checked the content logic and the rank-\(\rho\) freeness argument over \(\mathbb Z/p\), the row count \(4d\), and the grading and excess formula, including the passing homogeneity assertion. It reran the script with the root curve \(z_i\) in place of \(w_i\), with identical output, and over \(\mathbb Z/11\), which also agrees. It also checked the deduction of (i) to (iii) and the passage of the corollary and the half-plane theorem to every odd \(p\). It found no mathematical error. Its corrections are made: the \(w\)-rows explained; the independence in (ii) derived from characteristic-\(\ne2\) lemmas; the nonvanishing of the product solutions sourced; the unitriangular basis change stated; the replacement of \(E\) made explicit; and the factor 2 set aside.

Assessment. The thread's first target is reached: the per-order function on \(\{0,1\}^3\) is determined over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\). The last step was a finite certificate. The contents of three small integral bases have only the odd prime factors 3 and 5, and those two primes were checked directly. Semicontinuity alone would not have covered (ii), which needed the saturation of the \(P_1\)-image. The thread's goal continues with dimensions \(n\ge4\) (open statements 2 and 3).

26 September 2026 — Dimension 4: the first pre-stable thresholds, and a line bound that is exact only in dimension 3

Working proof of a line lower bound on thresholds for every n; finite check of ℓ₀(3,13) = 12 on {0,1}⁴ over F₃₂₀₀₃. Cycle bmd-r98. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. With dimension 3 solved (theorem), open statement 3 asks for the pre-stable thresholds \(\ell_0(h,m)\) for \(n\ge4\). No conjectured formula exists, and the only data are the boundary values \(\ell_0(d+1,8d-4)=0,15,55,115,195\) for \(d\le5\) and the order-zero thresholds \(m=5,19,39\) (check). What are the thresholds for savings 3, at \(12\le m\le18\), and does the dimension-3 structure (free modules, excess sums, products) persist? The test ends with the values, or with the structural feature that fails.

Setting. On \(\{0,1\}^4\), \(N_{2,4}(d)=8d-4\) for \(d\ge2\), so savings \(d+1\) need \(m\ge8d-4\) (stable law). By the threshold-ideal lemma, \(\ell_0(h,m)\) is the initial degree of the ideal \(I^{(h)}_m\) of top coordinates of the kernel of \(A_m\) (rows \(T^Qz^r\), \(2Q+|r|\le h-1\)). A homogeneous solution of excess \(\ell\) has \(W_c\) of degree \(\ell+m-c\).

The line bound

Lemma (lem:cube-line-threshold-bound). On \(\{0,1\}^n\) over any field, let \(L\) be a line \(y=au+bv\), and let \(I_L\) be the ideal of top coordinates of the kernel of \(A_m(au+bv)\) over \(F[u,v]\). If some element of \(I^{(h)}_m\) of degree \(\ell_0(h,m)\) does not vanish identically on \(L\), as for a generic line, then \(\operatorname{indeg}I_L\le\ell_0(h,m)\).

Proof. Let \(W\) be a homogeneous solution of excess \(\ell_0\) with \(W_m|_L\ne0\). Substituting \(y=au+bv\) commutes with the linear system, so \(W(au+bv)\) is a solution over \(F[u,v]\), homogeneous of the same excess. Its top coordinate \(W_m|_L\) is a nonzero element of \(I_L\) of degree \(\ell_0\). \(\square\)

On a line the kernel is a free module over \(F[u,v]\), and its minimal generators are computed quickly. Equality needs more. Suppose the global module is free, \(A_m\) keeps its generic rank on \(L\), the line misses the curve where the primitive Plücker coordinates vanish together, and the lemma's non-vanishing hypothesis holds. Then the restricted basis spans a saturated submodule of full rank of the line kernel, hence all of it, and the bound is an equality.

Computations

research/tools/bmd_cube_thresholds_m2.m2 (Macaulay2, over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\)) builds the graded map \(A_m\) and computes minimal generators of its kernel: globally, on a random line, or globally up to a given excess (syz with a degree limit, which returns every syzygy of degree at most the limit). Outputs are in research/results/bmd-r98-dimension-four/.

  • Control, \(n=3\). Globally for \(d=3\), and on the line for \(d=3,4\), the thresholds are \(8,3,0\) and \(15,6,3,0\), which is \(B(d,\rho)\). The generator excesses are those of the dimension-3 theorem, for example \(\{0,2,3,4\}\) at \((d,m)=(4,19)\). On these cases the line is exact in dimension 3.
  • \(n=4\), \(d=2\), on the line. For \(m=12,\ldots,18\) the line thresholds are \(15,7,4,2,1,0,0\), with generator excesses \(\{15\}\), \(\{7,7\}\), \(\{4,4,4\}\), \(\{2,2,2,3\}\), \(\{1^5\}\), \(\{0^6\}\), \(\{-1^6,0\}\). At \(m=17,18\) the line shows excess 0 and even negative excess. The global thresholds there are at least 1, since the order-zero threshold for savings 3 is \(m=19\).
  • \(n=4\), \(d=2\), globally. At \(m=12\) (rank 1) the global run did not finish within 5 minutes; the value 15 there is the recorded boundary check (check:cube-boundary-gcd-degrees), also a line computation. At \(m=13\) (rank 2) there is no solution of excess \(\le8\), and up to excess 15 the syzygies have excesses \(12,13,14,14,15\), with a nonzero top coordinate at excess 12. So \(\ell_0(3,13)=12\) over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), above the line value 7. The run took 428 s of wall time (Macaulay2 reports 617 s of CPU time).

Finite check (check:cube-dimension-four-thresholds). On \(\{0,1\}^4\) over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\):

  • \(\ell_0(3,13)=12\);
  • the line values 4, 2, 1 at \(m=14,15,16\), which are lower bounds for \(\ell_0(3,m)\) for every line outside a proper closed set (the lemma's hypothesis), not certified for the seeded line;
  • in dimension 3, agreement with \(B(d,\rho)\) globally for \(d=3\), and on the line for \(d\le4\).

What changes in dimension 4. At \(m=13\) the line splitting is \((7,7)\), while no global solution has excess below 12. If the global module were free, a line missing the Plücker locus, a curve in \(\mathbb P^3\) that a generic line avoids, would carry the global excesses. So, for the random line used, the module at \(m=13\) is not free. The line computation does not certify that this line is generic, so this is strong evidence rather than a proof. A certificate would be more than two minimal generators of the module in excess \(\le15\). The degree-limited output is not necessarily minimal, so its five columns alone do not prove this. The dimension-3 route rested on freeness (the basis criterion), and it does not carry over. The recorded boundary values fit \(\ell_0(d+1,8d-4)=10d^2-10d-5\) for \(2\le d\le5\) (four values, no mechanism).

General statement. lem:cube-line-threshold-bound, for every \(n\), \(h\), \(m\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the threshold-ideal lemma (part 1), the stable law, and the recorded dimension-4 boundary and order-zero checks. A fresh-context referee checked several things: the lemma, the script's excess formula and threshold rule, and the degree-limit semantics, by a small dimension-3 test in which the degree-limited syzygies were exactly the minimal generators up to each limit. It also checked every quoted number against the saved outputs. Its corrections are made: the runtime source, the global control restricted to \(d=3\), the line bounds stated with the lemma's hypothesis, the extra hypotheses of the equality statement, the non-freeness bound corrected to 12 with the certificate that would settle it, an unsupported sentence on products cut, and a label clarified. The computations were validated against dimension 3, where every value is proved. The degree-limited runs certify the absence of solutions below the limit, since the syzygies returned include every one up to the limit. Process: the first global run for dimension 4 timed out after 20 minutes without output. Macaulay2 buffered its output, which the script now flushes per case. A later series was refused by the run guard after four argument lists. The remaining values need one series invocation with per-case limits.

Assessment. Dimension 4 is structurally different. The thresholds fall from 15 at \(m=12\) to 12 at \(m=13\), a first step of 3, where the analogous dimension-3 steps from the boundary are larger (15 to 6 at \(d=4\)). The modules appear non-free, and the line method, exact in dimension 3, is only a lower bound. The next step is to finish the \(d=2\) row (\(m=14\) to \(18\)) in one run, and then to look for the mechanism. Candidates are the genus-5 curve's torsion loci replacing \(B\), and syzygies of the non-free modules.

26 September 2026 — Route review of the cube after dimension 3: the savings-3 row in dimension 4 falls in pairs

Route review: ℓ₀(3,m) on {0,1}⁴ over F₃₂₀₀₃ is 15, 12, 11, 6, 5, 2, 2, 0 for m = 12,…,19; dimension-3 structure fails, and the next step is the threshold generators themselves. Cycle bmd-r99. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

The line's general claim. The per-order function on \(\{0,1\}^n\) in characteristic \(\ne2\) is determined by the thresholds \(\ell_0(h,m)\), the initial degrees of the threshold ideals (threshold-ideal lemma). In dimension 3 they are the torsion-partition values \(B(d,\rho)\) over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\) (theorem). The claim to establish is an analogous law for \(n\ge4\).

What the goal needs. Open statement 3 (the pre-stable thresholds for \(n\ge4\)), and open statement 2 (small primes for \(n\ge4\)). No formula is conjectured for either.

Falsification attempt

The dimension-3 route predicts free modules, line splittings equal to the global excesses, and thresholds that drop fast from the boundary (for \(d=4\): \(15,6,3,0\)). The savings-3 row in dimension 4 tests all three. research/tools/bmd_cube_thresholds_m2.m2 gains an incremental mode. It raises the excess limit on one cached Gröbner computation and stops at the first excess with a syzygy of nonzero top coordinate. It also counts minimal generators up to that excess. Over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\) (research/results/bmd-r99-route-review/):

\(m\)1213141516171819
rank12345678
\(\ell_0(3,m)\)15121165220
line value15742100–

The value at 12 is the recorded boundary check, and the value 0 at 19 is the recorded order-zero threshold. The values at 13 are from the dimension-4 entry. The values at 14 to 18 are new: at each, no syzygy exists below the stated excess. At \(m=14\) there are 3 minimal generators of excess 11, and at \(m=16\) and \(18\) there are 3, all with nonzero top coordinate at 16 and two of three at 18. The runs took 258 s for \(m=14\) and 111 s for \(m=15\) to \(18\) (CPU).

The test falsifies the dimension-3 picture. The thresholds fall slowly and in pairs, \((12,11)\), \((6,5)\), \((2,2)\), not like \(B\). The line values are strict lower bounds at every \(m\) from 13 to 18. Writing \(j=19-m\), the even values fit \(\ell_0=i(i+1)\) for \(j=2i\le6\) (0, 2, 6, 12). That is a fit through four points, not a law.

Assessment of this line

The line's first target is complete, over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\), with a verified chain of proofs. The second phase, dimension 4, has just started. It is weak in mechanism: every tool that proved dimension 3 fails there, or is untested. That includes freeness and the basis criterion, the genus-1 curve with its torsion points, peeling by products (which lose two savings in dimension 4), and the line method. The evidence is one row of eight values in one characteristic. More rows will be expensive: the \(d=3\) row has thresholds up to 55, and Gröbner cost grows about 1.8-fold per excess. So the next step must find structure in the data already at hand, not add rows.

Outside leads

  • Castelnuovo's bound and the theta divisor of a genus-5 curve (Arbarello–Cornalba–Griffiths–Harris, Geometry of Algebraic Curves I, Ch. III). In dimension 3 the thresholds came from torsion loci of an elliptic curve. In dimension 4 the curve \(w_i^2=1+4y_iT\) has genus 5. The analogue of \(d\cdot c=0\) is the vanishing of \(h^0\) of a line bundle, a theta-divisor condition, whose degree would give the boundary thresholds \(15,55,115,195\). This targets open statement 3. It breaks if the loci are not reduced. Test. Passed (arithmetic): the genus is \(1+2^{n-2}(n-3)=5\), and the boundary values fit \(10d^2-10d-5\), quadratic in \(d\) as the degree of a pulled-back theta divisor must be.
  • The Buchsbaum–Eisenbud acyclicity criterion (Eisenbud, Commutative Algebra, Thm. 20.9). The dimension-4 solution modules are not free. Their minimal free resolutions, whose Betti numbers the incremental runs begin to show, would say how far from free they are, and whether the excess-sum inequality of the basis criterion survives. This targets the mechanism of the slow drop. It breaks if the resolutions are long. Test. Passed (weak): at \(m=13\) the two least generators have excess sum \(12+13=25\), above the line splitting sum 14, as the inequality requires.
  • Factorization of the threshold generators (the dimension-3 lowest parts: \(L_2\) and \(L_2^2\) in the torsion-partition entry). In dimension 3 the degree-\(\ell_0\) part of the threshold ideal was spanned by products of torsion loci. In dimension 4 the degree-2 generators at \(m=17,18\) and the degree-5 ones at \(m=16\) can be factored directly. This targets open statement 3. It breaks if they are irreducible. Test. Not run: the generators were not saved by this run; the next cycle computes and factors them.

Absurd bridges

  • Wei's monotonicity of generalized Hamming weights (coding theory: V. Wei, IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 37, 1991). Translation: the thresholds \(\ell_0(3,m)\), read backwards in \(m\), would be a weight hierarchy of a code built from the multiplicity conditions, and Wei's theorem would make them strictly monotone. Test. Falsified: \(\ell_0(3,17)=\ell_0(3,18)=2\).
  • Odd–even staggering of nuclear binding energies (nuclear physics: Bohr–Mottelson, Nuclear Structure I, pairing). Translation: \(j=19-m\) is a particle number and \(\ell_0\) an energy. Pairing makes the second difference \(\Delta(j)=\ell_0(j)-\tfrac12(\ell_0(j-1)+\ell_0(j+1))\) alternate in sign. A pairing theorem would explain the pairs. Test. Passed: \(\Delta(1),\ldots,\Delta(6)=1,-1.5,1,-2,2,-1\) alternate in sign.

Bridge follow-up

  • Chip-firing on a cycle. Not worked this cycle. Follow-up. Continuing: in dimension 4 the degeneration skeleton is a graph of genus 5, and the paired thresholds might be chip energies on it. That is a candidate reading of the odd–even staggering found above.

Lead follow-up

  • Riemann–Roch and Riemann–Hurwitz for \(n\ge4\). Used this cycle for the genus-5 lead above. Follow-up. Continuing: it now carries open statement 3.
  • Semicontinuity. Follow-up. Closed: the diagonal hypotheses it targeted were proved in every odd characteristic by an exact content certificate (theorem), which also covers (ii), beyond semicontinuity's reach.

Next step

On the highest-risk item, open statement 3: compute the threshold generators of the savings-3 row (degree 2 at \(m=17,18\), degree 5 at \(m=16\), degree 6 at \(m=15\)) and factor them. Also test whether they are \(S_4\)-invariant up to sign, and whether they vanish on the collision loci or on new loci. In dimension 3 this step revealed the torsion structure behind \(B\).

Process. Two Macaulay2 runs (258 s and 111 s CPU), one series invocation for \(m=15\) to \(18\).

26 September 2026 — Dimension 4: below order zero the threshold ideal starts with one symmetric quadric

Finite check of the savings-3 threshold generators on {0,1}⁴ over F₃₂₀₀₃, and a conjecture that one symmetric quadric generates at the step below order zero for every d. Cycle bmd-r100. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The route review found the savings-3 row \(\ell_0(3,m)=15,12,11,6,5,2,2,0\) for \(m=12,\ldots,19\) on \(\{0,1\}^4\). In dimension 3 the threshold generators were products of torsion loci (\(L_2\), \(L_2^2\)) (torsion-partition entry). What are they in dimension 4? The test ends with their factorizations, and with a prediction that can fail at the next \(d\).

Setting. As in the dimension-4 entry. The degree-\(\ell_0\) part of the threshold ideal \(I^{(3)}_m\) is spanned by the top coordinates of the syzygies of excess \(\ell_0\). The incremental mode of research/tools/bmd_cube_thresholds_m2.m2 now prints them factored.

The generators

Over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\) (research/results/bmd-r100-dimension-four-generators/factored-generators.txt):

  • \(m=17\) and \(m=18\), \(\ell_0=2\): every threshold generator (one at 17, two at 18) is a scalar multiple of the same quadric, \(y_1^2+y_2^2+y_3^2+y_4^2+16001\sum_{i<j}y_iy_j\). Since \(2\cdot16001\equiv-1\), this is \(-\tfrac12\) times \[Q=\sum_{i<j}y_iy_j-2\sum_iy_i^2.\] It is irreducible and \(S_4\)-invariant.
  • \(m=16\), \(\ell_0=5\): three generators, each an irreducible quintic, with symmetric coefficient patterns.
  • \(m=15\), \(\ell_0=6\): one generator, an irreducible sextic.

Finite check (check:cube-dimension-four-generators). The factorizations above, over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), at \(m=15,\ldots,18\) for savings 3 on \(\{0,1\}^4\).

A conjecture

In dimension 3, one step below order zero, the threshold is \(B(d,d-1)=3\) for every \(d\ge2\) (near-diagonal family), and its generator is \(L_2\), the locus where the point \(2c_1\) has order 2. The dimension-4 row shows the same kind of structure: a single invariant form, independent of \(m\) on the last two steps. The analogue is the following.

Conjecture (conj:cube-dimension-four-quadric). On \(\{0,1\}^4\), in characteristic 0 and large characteristic, for every \(d\ge2\), let \(M(d)\) be the least \(m\) with \(\ell_0(d+1,m)=0\) (\(M=19,39\) for \(d=2,3\), order-zero check). Then \(\ell_0(d+1,M(d)-1)=2\), and the degree-2 part of the threshold ideal there is spanned by \(Q=\sum_{i<j}y_iy_j-2\sum_iy_i^2\).

The conjecture predicts \(\ell_0(4,38)=2\) with generator \(Q\). The test at \(d=3\), \(m=38\) ran out of time: the Gröbner computation did not finish its first excess step in 15 minutes. Deciding it needs a kernel that works degree by degree, restricted to \(S_4\)-invariant solutions. At excess 2 the unknowns of the plain system number about \(1.4\cdot10^5\), about 24 times fewer with the symmetry.

General statement. conj:cube-dimension-four-quadric, for every \(d\ge2\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the dimension-4 entry and the route review (script, excess rule), and the dimension-3 torsion-partition entry (lowest parts). The factorizations are Macaulay2's, over the computing field. The identification of 16001 with \(-\tfrac12\) was checked by hand. No new proof is claimed, so no reviewer pass was run. The conjecture is stated from one row, with its falsifying test named.

Assessment. The first structural datum in dimension 4 is a single symmetric quadric at the steps just below order zero, in the place where dimension 3 has its 2-torsion cubic. What locus it cuts out on the genus-5 curve is the question that could lead to a mechanism. The immediate obstacle is computational: Gröbner bases in four variables fail beyond \(m\approx18\).

26 September 2026 — A symmetric kernel for the threshold ideals: the quadric reappears at d = 3 in dimension 4

Working proof of the reduction to invariant solutions; finite check: on {0,1}⁴ at m = 38 the invariant part of the savings-4 threshold ideal starts with the quadric Q in degree 2, as conjectured for the invariant part. Cycle bmd-r101. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The quadric conjecture predicts \(\ell_0(4,38)=2\) on \(\{0,1\}^4\), with the degree-2 part of the threshold ideal spanned by \(Q=\sum_{i<j}y_iy_j-2\sum_iy_i^2\). The Gröbner computation did not reach \(m=38\). Can the symmetry of the system make the test feasible? The test ends with the invariant degree-\(\le2\) part of \(I^{(4)}_{38}\), which either contains \(Q\) or refutes the conjecture.

Setting. As in the dimension-4 entry: rows \((Q,r)\), \(r\in\{0,1\}^n\), \(2Q+|r|\le d\), with \(A_{(Q,r),c}(y)\) the coefficient of \(T^c\) in \(T^Q\prod_{r_i=1}w_i\), \(w_i=\sqrt{1+4y_iT}\). A homogeneous solution of excess \(\ell\) has \(W_c\) of degree \(\ell+m-c\), and \(I^{(h)}_m\) is the ideal of top coordinates \(W_m\).

Invariant solutions

Lemma (lem:cube-symmetric-reduction). On \(\{0,1\}^n\) over a field \(F\), \(S_n\) acts on the solutions by \((\sigma W)_c(y)=W_c(\sigma^{-1}y)\), preserving excess. So \(I^{(h)}_m\) is \(S_n\)-stable. If \(n!\) is invertible in \(F\), the \(S_n\)-invariant elements of \(I^{(h)}_m\) of degree \(\ell\) are exactly the top coordinates of the \(S_n\)-invariant solutions of excess \(\ell\). In particular \(I^{(h)}_m\) has a nonzero element of degree 0 if and only if an invariant solution of excess 0 has nonzero top coordinate.

Proof. Write \((\sigma y)_i=y_{\sigma^{-1}(i)}\) and \((\sigma r)_i=r_{\sigma^{-1}(i)}\). \(A_{(Q,r),c}\) depends only on the \(y_i\) with \(r_i=1\), and symmetrically, so \(A_{(Q,r),c}(\sigma^{-1}y)=A_{(Q,\sigma r),c}(y)\). Hence the equation of row \((Q,\sigma r)\) for \(\sigma W\), \(\sum_cA_{(Q,\sigma r),c}(y)W_c(\sigma^{-1}y)=\sum_cA_{(Q,r),c}(\sigma^{-1}y)W_c(\sigma^{-1}y)\), is the equation of row \((Q,r)\) for \(W\) at \(\sigma^{-1}y\). So \(\sigma W\) is a solution, with top coordinate \(W_m\circ\sigma^{-1}\) and the same degrees. If \(f\in I\) is invariant and \(f=W_m\), the average \(\frac1{n!}\sum_\sigma\sigma W\) is an invariant solution with top coordinate \(f\). Conversely, an invariant solution has an invariant top coordinate. The degree-0 part of \(I\) is a space of constants, which is invariant. \(\square\)

The kernel. research/tools/bmd_cube_symmetric_solutions.cpp (FLINT, \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), where \(4!\) is invertible) computes the invariant solutions of a given excess.

  • The unknowns are the coefficients of \(W_c=\sum_\lambda x_{c,\lambda}m_\lambda\) in the monomial symmetric functions.
  • There is one row \((Q,1^s0^{n-s})\) per \(S_n\)-orbit of rows. Its polynomial is invariant under \(S_s\times S_{n-s}\), so its coefficients are taken at one monomial per orbit of that group.
  • Since \(A_{(Q,r),c}=\sum_{|j|=c-Q}\prod_{i\le s}C_{j_i}y_i^{j_i}\) involves only \(y_1,\ldots,y_s\), the coefficient of \(y^\alpha\) in \(A\,m_\lambda\) is \(\sum_j\prod C_{j_i}\) over the \(j\) with \(\operatorname{sort}(\alpha-(j,0))=\lambda\).

At \(m=38\) the systems have about \(10^4\) rows and \(6\)–\(7\cdot10^3\) columns, against about \(1.4\cdot10^5\) unknowns without the symmetry.

Results

One run (research/results/bmd-r101-symmetric-kernel/symmetric-solutions.txt, 127 s):

  • Control, dimension 3, \((d,m)=(3,13)\). No invariant solution of excess 2. At excess 3 the invariant top coordinate is \(m_{111}-\tfrac12m_{21}+\tfrac12m_3=-\tfrac12L_2\), where \(L_2=\prod_i(e_1-2y_i)=-m_3+m_{21}-2m_{111}\) is the 2-torsion cubic. This matches \(\ell_0(4,13)=B(3,2)=3\) and the recorded lowest part.
  • Control, dimension 4, \(d=2\). At \(m=17,18\) there is no invariant top coordinate of excess 1, and at excess 2 the invariant top coordinate is \(m_{11}-2m_2=Q\). At \(m=15\) there is none at excess 5 and one at excess 6. This matches the Gröbner results of the route review and the factorizations.
  • Test, dimension 4, \(d=3\), \(m=38\). At excess 0 there is no invariant solution. At excess 1 there are 5 invariant solutions, all with top coordinate 0. At excess 2 there are 21 invariant solutions, whose top coordinates span the line of \(m_{11}-2m_2=Q\).

Finite check (check:cube-quadric-d3). On \(\{0,1\}^4\) over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), for savings 4 at \(m=38\):

  • \(Q\in I^{(4)}_{38}\), so \(\ell_0(4,38)\le2\);
  • by the lemma, \(I^{(4)}_{38}\) has no element of degree 0, so \(\ell_0(4,38)\ge1\);
  • its invariant part in degree 2 is the line of \(Q\), and it has no invariant element of degree 1.

So, over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), \(\ell_0(4,38)\in\{1,2\}\), and the invariant degree-2 part of the threshold ideal is the line of \(Q\). Two things remain open. The value 1 remains possible only through a copy of the standard representation of \(S_4\) among the linear forms of \(I\). The conjecture's claim that \(Q\) spans the whole degree-2 part also needs the non-trivial \(S_4\)-isotypic components of the quadrics in \(I\) to vanish. Both need solutions invariant under a smaller group, a larger system. So this is a partial test.

Field. The lower bound \(\ell_0(4,38)\ge1\) transfers to characteristic 0 and to all but finitely many characteristics, since the rational invariant system at excess 0 has rank at least its rank modulo 32003, which is full. The statements \(Q\in I\) and the span of the invariant quadrics are established only over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\): no rational lift was computed.

General statement. lem:cube-symmetric-reduction, for every \(n\), \(h\), \(m\) in characteristic 0 or \(p>n\); the tested claim is conj:cube-dimension-four-quadric.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the threshold-ideal lemma, the dimension-4 and quadric entries, and the torsion-partition entry's \(L_2\). The kernel was validated on three independent references: the dimension-3 cubic \(L_2\) (converted to the \(m_\lambda\) basis by hand), the Gröbner thresholds and generators at \(m=15,17,18\), and the absence of excess-1 tops at \(m=17,18\). The lemma is the standard Reynolds-operator argument. A fresh-context referee checked several things. It checked the lemma, including the index convention now stated, and the kernel: orbit representatives, the monomial-coefficient formula, the \(C_j\) recurrence, the column blocks, the reading of the top coordinates, and the inclusion of rows with \(Q>0\). It also checked the conversion of \(L_2\) and the residues \(16001=-\tfrac12\), \(16002=\tfrac12\), \(32001=-2\). It found no error. Its corrections are made: the explicit convention in the proof, the scope of the check limited to the invariant part and called a partial test, and the field of each conclusion.

Assessment. The quadric conjecture passed a partial test: the same invariant quadric appears one step below order zero at \(d=3\), where nothing forced it. The non-invariant parts in degrees 1 and 2 remain untested. Together with the dimension-3 cubic \(L_2\) in the same position, this points to a torsion-type locus on the genus-5 curve, which is the next thing to identify. The symmetric kernel is fast, a minute where Gröbner bases failed. It makes rows at larger \(d\) feasible, and with a stabilizer-invariant version, the excess-1 question at \(m=38\).

26 September 2026 — The threshold ideals are symmetric in the n+1 branch points, which explains the quadric and the 2-torsion cubic

Working proof: every threshold ideal on {0,1}ⁿ is stable under S_{n+1} permuting the branch points 0, y₁, …, y_n; corollary: ℓ₀(4,38) = 2 on {0,1}⁴ over F₃₂₀₀₃. Cycle bmd-r102. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The threshold generators found so far are the 2-torsion cubic \(L_2\) at \((3,13)\) in dimension 3 (torsion-partition entry), and the quadric \(Q=\sum_{i<j}y_iy_j-2\sum_iy_i^2\) in dimension 4 one step below order zero (quadric entry, symmetric kernel). Both are symmetric in more than the coordinates. Written in terms of the points \(r_0=0,r_1=y_1,\ldots,r_n=y_n\):

  • \(Q=-\tfrac12\sum_{0\le i<j\le4}(r_i-r_j)^2\);
  • \(L_2\) is the product over the three pairings \(\{0,y_i\},\{y_j,y_k\}\) of the difference of the pair sums.

Is there a symmetry of the whole problem permuting \(0,y_1,\ldots,y_n\)? The test ends with a proof, or with a threshold generator that breaks the symmetry.

Setting. Over a field \(F\) of characteristic \(\ne2\), let \(w_i=(1+4y_iT)^{1/2}\in F[y][[T]]\), with constant term 1. For \(d\ge0\), \(V_d(y)\) is the \(F[y]\)-span of \(T^Qw^r\), \(r\in\{0,1\}^n\), \(2Q+|r|\le d\). This spans the same module as the rows \(T^Qz^r\) of the threshold-ideal lemma, since \(z_i=(1-w_i)/2\) and the index set is closed under lowering \(r\). \(\mathrm{Sol}^{(d+1)}_m\) is the set of \(W\in F[y]^{m+1}\) with \(\sum_{c\le m}W_c[T^c]f=0\) for all \(f\in V_d(y)\). \(I^{(d+1)}_m\) is the ideal of top coordinates \(W_m\). A homogeneous solution of excess \(\ell\) has \(W_c\) of degree \(\ell+m-c\).

The symmetry theorem

Theorem (thm:cube-branch-point-symmetry). Let \(\psi(y)=(y_1,\,y_1-y_2,\,\ldots,\,y_1-y_n)\), a linear involution. For every \(d,m\) and every homogeneous solution \(W\) of excess \(\ell\), there is a homogeneous solution \(W''\) of excess \(\ell\) with \(W''_m=\pm W_m\circ\psi\). Hence \(I^{(d+1)}_m\circ\psi=I^{(d+1)}_m\). Together with the coordinate permutations (symmetric reduction), the threshold ideals are stable under the group generated by \(S_n\) and \(\psi\). Since they are homogeneous, they are also stable under \(-1\). Let \(S_{n+1}\) act on \(y\) as on the positions of the points \(r_0=0,r_1=y_1,\ldots,r_n=y_n\), relabelled and translated so that the point labelled 0 is at 0; this is the reflection representation. Then the threshold ideals are \(S_{n+1}\)-stable. For \(n\ge2\) the group generated by \(S_n\) and \(\psi\) is \(S_{n+1}\times\{\pm1\}\).

Proof. Let \(\tau=-T/(1+4y_1T)\in F[y_1][[T]]\). Substitution \(T\mapsto\tau\) is an automorphism \(\varphi^*\) of \(F[y][[T]]\), since \(\tau=-T+O(T^2)\). It is an involution: substituting \(\tau\) into \(-\tau/(1+4y_1\tau)\) gives \(T\). Put \(\bar w_i=(1+4\psi(y)_iT)^{1/2}\). Since \[1+4y_i\tau=\frac{1+4(y_1-y_i)T}{1+4y_1T}\ (i\ge2),\qquad 1+4y_1\tau=\frac1{1+4y_1T},\] and square roots with constant term 1 are unique, \(\varphi^*w_i=\bar w_i/\bar w_1\) for \(i\ge2\), and \(\varphi^*w_1=1/\bar w_1\). So, with \(e=d-2Q-|r|\ge0\), \[\varphi^*(T^Qw^r)=\bar w_1^{-d}\cdot(-1)^QT^Q\,(1+4\psi(y)_1T)^{\lfloor e/2\rfloor}\,\bar w_1^{\,e-2\lfloor e/2\rfloor}\prod_{i\ge2,\,r_i=1}\bar w_i,\] using \(\bar w_1^{-2Q-|r|}=\bar w_1^{-d}\bar w_1^{e}\). The second factor is an \(F[y]\)-combination of the \(T^{Q'}\bar w^{r'}\) with \(2Q'+|r'|\le2Q+2\lfloor e/2\rfloor+(e\bmod2)+|r|-r_1\le d\). So \(\varphi^*V_d(y)\subseteq\bar w_1^{-d}V_d(\psi(y))\). Applying the same with \(\psi(y)\) in place of \(y\), and using that \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are involutions, gives equality.

On coefficients, write \(\hat f=([T^c]f)_{c\le m}\). Then \(\widehat{\varphi^*f}=U\hat f\) and \(\widehat{\bar w_1^dg}=V\hat g\), with \(U,V\) lower triangular. They have diagonals \((-1)^c\) and 1, and entries \(U_{c,j},V_{c,j}\in F[y_1]\) homogeneous of degree \(c-j\). Terms of order above \(m\) never reach order \(\le m\). Let \(M=VU\). As \(f\) runs over \(V_d(y)\), \(M\hat f\) runs over the windows of \(V_d(\psi(y))\). So \(W\) solves the system at \(y\) if and only if \(W'=(M^{-1})^{\mathsf T}W\) solves it with parameters \(\psi(y)\). \((M^{-1})^{\mathsf T}\) is upper triangular with diagonal \(\pm1\) and entries homogeneous of degree \(c-j\) in \(y_1\). So \(W'\) is polynomial, has the same excess, and \(W'_m=\pm W_m\). Finally \(W''=W'\circ\psi\) solves the system at \(\psi(\psi(y))=y\), with \(W''_m=\pm W_m\circ\psi\). Since \(\psi\) is linear and invertible, \(I\circ\psi\subseteq I\) with degrees preserved, and equality follows by applying it twice.

For the group: the threshold ideals are homogeneous, since the solution module is graded by excess and \(W_m\) has degree \(\ell\), so they are stable under \(-1\). The transposition \(s_{01}\) of \(r_0\) and \(r_1\), in the reflection representation, is \(y\mapsto(-y_1,y_2-y_1,\ldots,y_n-y_1)\), the map \(x\mapsto x-y_1\) on the points, followed by relabelling. So \(\psi=-s_{01}\), corresponding to the reflection \(x\mapsto y_1-x\). Hence the ideals are stable under \(s_{01}\) and under \(S_n\) (the transpositions \(s_{ij}\), \(i,j\ge1\)), which generate \(S_{n+1}\). For \(n\ge2\), \(\psi s_{12}\psi=s_{02}\) shows that \(\langle S_n,\psi\rangle\) contains \(S_{n+1}\), and hence \(-1\). \(\square\)

Geometrically, \(T\mapsto\tau\) is the Möbius map of the \(T\)-line fixing \(T=0\) (so \(p_0\)) and exchanging \(T=\infty\) with the branch point \(T=-1/(4y_1)\). The divisors \(H_\infty\) and \(H_1\) over them are linearly equivalent, since \(\operatorname{div}w_1=H_1-H_\infty\). So \(L(dH_\infty)\) goes to \(w_1^{-d}L(dH_\infty)\), which is the unit factor \(\bar w_1^{-d}\) above.

Consequences

  • Dimension 3. In characteristic 0 or \(p>3\), the invariants of \(S_4\) on the reflection representation have degrees 2, 3, 4. The unique invariant cubic is the third power sum of the centred points, proportional to the \(x\)-coefficient of the depressed quartic with roots \(0,y_1,y_2,y_3\). That coefficient is proportional to \(L_2\). So the degree-3 threshold generator at \((3,13)\) is the invariant cubic, and the dimension-3 theorem's thresholds are carried by \(S_4\)-stable ideals.
  • Dimension 4. Over a field of characteristic 0 or greater than 5, the quadrics on the reflection representation \(R\) of \(S_5\) decompose as \(\operatorname{Sym}^2R=\mathbf1\oplus R\oplus[3,2]\). The invariant line is spanned by \(\sum_{i<j}(r_i-r_j)^2=-2Q\). The linear forms are \(R\) itself, which is irreducible.

Corollary (cor:cube-quadric-threshold-d3). On \(\{0,1\}^4\) over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\):

  • \(\ell_0(4,38)=2\);
  • \(\ell_0(3,17)=\ell_0(3,18)=2\);
  • in each case the degree-2 part of the threshold ideal is the line of \(Q\), plus possibly a copy of \([3,2]\), which the \(S_4\)-invariant computation cannot see.

Proof. By the theorem, \(I_1\) is an \(S_5\)-subrepresentation of the linear forms \(R\), so \(I_1=0\) or \(I_1=R\). \(R\) restricted to \(S_4\) contains the invariant form \(y_1+\cdots+y_4\). The symmetric kernel found no invariant solution of excess 1 with nonzero top coordinate at \(m=38\), nor at \(m=17,18\). By the symmetric reduction, \(I_1\) has no nonzero \(S_4\)-invariant element, so \(I_1=0\). Then \(I_0=0\) too, since \(1\in I\) would give \(y_1\in I\). Also \(Q\in I_2\) (same run), so \(\ell_0=2\). In \(I_2\), a copy of \(R\) would add an \(S_4\)-invariant quadric independent of \(Q\): \(R\) restricted to \(S_4\) contains the trivial representation, and \(\mathbf1\) and \(R\) are different isotypic components. The computation shows the invariant part of \(I_2\) is one-dimensional. \([3,2]\) restricted to \(S_4\) is \([3,1]\oplus[2,2]\), with no invariant vector. \(\square\)

So the quadric conjecture at \(d=2,3\) reduces, over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), to the absence of a \([3,2]\) component in \(I_2\). Where \(I_2\) is one-dimensional, its spanning quadric must be \(Q\), because the only \(S_5\)-semi-invariant quadric is the invariant one.

General statement. thm:cube-branch-point-symmetry, for every \(n,d,m\) over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the threshold-ideal lemma (the system and \(I\)), the symmetric reduction and the symmetric kernel's data, and the torsion-partition entry's \(L_2\). A claim search (symmetry, branch points, Möbius, reparametrization) found no earlier version. A fresh-context referee checked the proof and found it correct. It checked the Möbius formulas and the involution, the row identity with the degree count \(2Q'+|r'|\le d-r_1\), and the reverse inclusion. It checked the triangular coefficient maps, the truncation, the step \(W'=(M^{-1})^{\mathsf T}W\) with \(W'_m=(-1)^mW_m\), and homogeneity, all as identities in \(F[y][[T]]\). It verified \(L_2\circ\psi=-L_2\) exactly, and checked the \(S_5\) representation theory and the corollary's logic. Its corrections are made. The group statement is fixed: \(\psi=-s_{01}\), so \(\langle S_n,\psi\rangle=S_{n+1}\times\{\pm1\}\). Homogeneity gives the \(S_{n+1}\)-stability, degree 0 is excluded in the corollary, and the characteristic scope of the dimension-3 invariant theory is stated. No hypothesis is unused: characteristic \(\ne2\) enters through \(w_i\) and \(z_i\).

Assessment. The threshold ideals have a hidden \(S_{n+1}\) symmetry: \(H_\infty\) is one of \(n+1\) interchangeable branch fibres of the curve \(w_i^2=1+4y_iT\). That explains why the first threshold generators are the low-degree invariants of \(S_{n+1}\): the cubic \(L_2\) for \(n=3\), and the quadric \(Q\) for \(n=4\). For dimension 4 it turns the search for the threshold ideals into representation theory of \(S_5\) on polynomials in the reflection representation, together with the curve's torsion loci. The next step is to ask which \(S_5\)-representations occur in \(I^{(h)}_m\) in each degree. The symmetric kernel, run for each isotypic component, can answer this at the tested \((d,m)\). That may give the dimension-4 thresholds without Gröbner bases.

26 September 2026 — In characteristic 0 the collision exponents at the boundary are exact in every dimension, and any other factor of the gcd is doubled in the determinant

Working proof in characteristic 0: along each collision divisor, g_{n,d} and Δ_{n,d} have exponent E_n(d) for all n, d; any other prime factor of g divides Δ twice. On {0,1}⁴, ℓ₀(d+1, 8d−4) = 10d²−10d−5 − deg of the rest of g. Cycle bmd-r103. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. Open statement 3 asks for the pre-stable thresholds in dimension \(n\ge4\). At the \(\kappa\)-boundary \(m=N=N_{2,n}(d)\) the threshold-ideal lemma (Part 2) gives \(\ell_0(d+1,N)=\deg\Delta_{n,d}-\deg g_{n,d}\), where \(g_{n,d}\) is the gcd of the maximal minors of the \(N\times(N+1)\) constraint matrix. For \(n=4\) the line computations give \(\ell_0=0,15,55,115,195\) for \(d\le5\), rigorously only over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\) (boundary theorem entry, "Every dimension"). Two implications are missing for every \(d\):

  1. the collision exponent \(v_D(g_{n,d})\) equals \(E_n(d)\). The collision limit lemma proves this only for \(m\ge2^{n-1}d\), and \(N<2^{n-1}d\) for \(n\ge4\);
  2. \(g_{n,d}\) has no prime factor other than the collision forms. The genus-1 argument of the proposition has no analogue for \(n\ge4\).

The test ends with a proof of either implication, or with the obstruction that blocks it. This cycle develops the Riemann–Roch lead on the fibre curve for \(n\ge4\) (route review 6, lead 2), through the Wronskian of \(V_d\) on that curve.

Setting. \(F\) is a field of characteristic 0. For \(a\in F^n\) and \(r\in\{0,1\}^n\), \(w_i=(1+a_iT)^{1/2}\) and \(w^r=\prod_{r_i=1}w_i\) in \(F[a][[T]]\). A degree vector is \(\nu=(\nu_r)_{r\in\{0,1\}^n}\) with integers \(\nu_r\ge-1\), and \(N_\nu=\sum_r(\nu_r+1)\ge1\). Put \(V_\nu(a)=\bigoplus_rw^r\,F[T]_{\le\nu_r}\) (the summand is 0 when \(\nu_r=-1\)), and let \(\Delta_\nu(a)\) be the \(N_\nu\times N_\nu\) determinant of the coefficients of \(T^0,\ldots,T^{N_\nu-1}\) in the \(T^jw^r\) (\(0\le j\le\nu_r\)). Its entries lie in \(\mathbb Z[\tfrac12][a]\). For \(\nu_r=\lfloor(d-|r|)/2\rfloor\) this is \(\Delta^w_{n,d}=\pm2^e\Delta_{n,d}(a/4)\) (Hermite–Padé form, Part 3). The collision divisors are the \(\binom{n+1}2\) hyperplanes \(y_i=0\) and \(y_i=y_j\), and \(E_n(d)=\sum_P(d-e(P))\) over the basis elements \(P=T^Qz^{r'}\) of \(V_{n-1,d-1}\), of weight \(e(P)=2Q+|r'|\).

The generic normality lemma

Lemma (lem:cube-generic-normality). For every \(n\ge1\) and every degree vector \(\nu\), \(\Delta_\nu\ne0\) in \(\mathbb Z[\tfrac12][a]\). Equivalently, over every field of characteristic 0 and for \(a\) outside a hypersurface, the orders at \(T=0\) of \(V_\nu(a)\) are exactly \(0,\ldots,N_\nu-1\). For each fixed \(\nu\), the same holds over every field whose characteristic is odd and outside a finite set of primes, namely those dividing every coefficient of \(\Delta_\nu\).

In the language of the Hermite–Padé form, every multi-index is normal for the system \(\{w^r\}\) at generic centres, in characteristic 0. The case \(\nu_r=\lfloor(d-|r|)/2\rfloor\) is the characteristic-0 theorem, and the proof is the same.

Proof. Work over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\), and take \(a\) with distinct nonzero entries. The curve \(C_a:w_i^2=1+a_iT\) is irreducible, and the \(w^r\) are a basis of its function field over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}(T)\), by Kummer theory (transport lemma). So the \(N=N_\nu\) functions \(f_{j,r}=T^jw^r\) are linearly independent over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\).

  • The Wronskian. Since \(dw_i/dT=a_i/(2w_i)\), the derivatives \(d^kf_{j,r}/dT^k\) are rational functions on \(C_a\). In characteristic 0 the Wronskian \(W=\det(d^kf_{j,r}/dT^k)_{0\le k<N}\) of independent functions is a nonzero rational function. Choose a point \(q\) with \(t=T(q)\) finite, \(1+a_it\ne0\) for all \(i\), and \(W\) regular and nonzero at \(q\).
  • Transport to \(q\). Put \(s=T-t\) and \(a'_i=a_i/(1+a_it)\). Near \(q\), \(w_i=w_i(q)\,(1+a'_is)^{1/2}\), where the square root has constant term 1: both sides square to \(1+a_iT\), and they agree at \(q\). Also \(T^j=\sum_{k\le j}\binom jkt^{j-k}s^k\). So the matrix of Taylor coefficients at \(q\) (orders \(0,\ldots,N-1\) in \(s\)) is \(B\,D\,H(a')\), where:
    • \(H(a')\) is the matrix whose determinant is \(\Delta_\nu(a')\);
    • \(D=\operatorname{diag}(w(q)^r)\) is invertible;
    • \(B\) is block lower unitriangular, one block for each \(r\).
  • Conclusion. \(W(q)=\prod_{k<N}k!\cdot\prod_rw(q)^{r(\nu_r+1)}\cdot\Delta_\nu(a')\). So \(\Delta_\nu(a')\ne0\), and \(\Delta_\nu\) is a nonzero polynomial. A nonzero polynomial over \(\mathbb Z[\tfrac12]\) stays nonzero modulo every odd prime except the finitely many dividing all its coefficients. The equivalence with the orders is Part 2 of the Hermite–Padé form: the space has \(N\) distinct orders, and these are \(0,\ldots,N-1\) exactly when no nonzero element has order \(\ge N\). \(\square\)

The collision exponents at the boundary

Theorem (thm:cube-boundary-collision-exponents). Let \(F\) have characteristic 0, \(n\ge2\), \(d\ge1\), \(N=N_{2,n}(d)\) and \(m\ge N-1\). Let \(A_m\) be the \(N\times(m+1)\) constraint matrix (the coefficients of \(T^0,\ldots,T^m\) in the \(T^Qz^r\), \(2Q+|r|\le d\)), and \(g_m\) the gcd of its maximal minors. So \(g_N=g_{n,d}\), and \(A_{N-1}\) is square with determinant \(\pm\Delta_{n,d}\). Then for each collision divisor \(D\):

  1. the nonzero elementary divisors of \(A_m\) over the local ring at \(D\) are exactly the \(d-e(P)\), for \(P\) running over the basis of \(V_{n-1,d-1}\);
  2. hence \(v_D(g_m)=v_D(\Delta_{n,d})=E_n(d)=\sum_{k=0}^{\min(n-1,d)}\binom{n-1}k\bigl\lfloor(d-k+1)^2/4\bigr\rfloor\);
  3. \(g_{n,d}=c\prod_D\ell_D^{\,E_n(d)}\cdot g^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}\), with \(c\ne0\) a constant, \(\ell_D\) the collision forms, and \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}\) prime to every collision form. So \[ \ell_0(d+1,N)=\deg\Delta_{n,d}-\tbinom{n+1}2E_n(d)-\deg g^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}. \] For \(n=4\) and \(d\ge2\): \(N=8d-4\), \(E_4(d)=d^2+(d-1)^2\), \(\deg\Delta_{4,d}=30d^2-30d+5\), and \[ \ell_0(d+1,8d-4)=10d^2-10d-5-\deg g^{\mathrm{nc}}_{4,d}. \]

For fixed \((n,d)\), parts 1 and 2 hold over every field of odd characteristic outside a finite set of primes. In odd characteristic \(p\), part 3 needs three things: the exponents of parts 1 and 2; the initial-segment law at \((n,d)\), which holds for \(p>2^{n-1}d\) (theorem); and \(p\nmid\mathrm{content}(\Delta_{n,d})\), so that the degree formula holds. Each excludes finitely many \(p\) for fixed \((n,d)\).

Proof. Take \(D:y_1=0\) first, in the setting of the collision limit lemma: \(F'=F(y_2,\ldots,y_n)\), \(O=F'[[\varepsilon]]\) with \(y_1=\varepsilon\), \(V=V_{n,d}\otimes O\), and \(\Lambda\) its full-series saturation.

  • The limit space. By parts 1 and 2 of that lemma, \(\Lambda\) has the \(O\)-basis consisting of the basis of \(V_{n-1,d}\) and the \(\varepsilon^{-(d-e(P))}L_P\), and \(\Lambda/\varepsilon\Lambda=U\), where \(U=U^{(n-1)}_d=\operatorname{span}_{F'}\{T^Qz^{r'}:Q+|r'|\le d\}\), of dimension \(N\). Since \(z^{r'}=\prod_{r'_i=1}(1-w_i)/2\) is triangular in the \(w^{r''}\), \(r''\le r'\), with unit diagonal \((-\tfrac12)^{|r'|}\), and the index set is closed under lowering \(r'\), we have \(U=V_\nu(4y_2,\ldots,4y_n)\) with \(\nu_{r'}=\max(d-|r'|,-1)\).
  • Normality of the limit. The \(4y_i\) (\(i\ge2\)) are algebraically independent over \(F\). By the lemma, \(\Delta_\nu(4y_2,\ldots,4y_n)\ne0\) in \(F'\). So the truncation \(U\to F'^{\,N}\) (coefficients of \(T^0,\ldots,T^{N-1}\)) is bijective, and every nonzero element of \(U\) has order \(\le N-1\le m\).
  • Saturation. Let \(\tau_m\) be the truncation modulo \(T^{m+1}\). The images modulo \(\varepsilon\) of the basis of \(\tau_m(\Lambda)\) are the truncations of a basis of \(U\), which are independent. So \(\tau_m\) is injective on \(\Lambda\), and \(\tau_m(\Lambda)\) is a direct summand of \(O^{m+1}\): a free submodule with a basis independent modulo the maximal ideal extends to a basis. Hence the elementary divisors of \(\tau_m(V)\subseteq O^{m+1}\) are those of \(\tau_m(V)\subseteq\tau_m(\Lambda)\), that is, of \(V\subseteq\Lambda\). By part 2 of the collision limit lemma, \(\Lambda/V\cong\bigoplus_PO/\varepsilon^{d-e(P)}\). This is the argument of that lemma's part 3, with the order bound \(N-1\) in place of \(2^{n-1}d\).
  • Valuations. The rows of \(A_m\) are the \(\tau_m\) of the basis of \(V\). So the sum of its elementary divisors, \(E_n(d)\), is \(v_{y_1}\) of the gcd of its maximal minors, computed in the discrete valuation ring \(F[y]_{(y_1)}\), whose completion is \(O\). For \(m=N-1\) the only maximal minor is \(\pm\Delta_{n,d}\).
  • Other collision divisors. The divisors \(y_i=0\) follow by permuting the variables. For \(y_i=y_j\), the Möbius transport of the boundary theorem writes \(A_m(a)=G\,\tilde A_m(\tilde a)\,H\), with \(G,H\) invertible over \(\mathbb Z[\tfrac12][a]\) and \(\tilde a\) an invertible linear change of \(a\) sending the divisor to \(\tilde a_1=0\). The column change \(H\) comes from the substitution \(T=\tilde T/(1-a_j\tilde T)\), which is triangular for the \(T\)-adic filtration, so this holds for every truncation \(m\). The Smith form over the local ring therefore transfers, as in the collision limit lemma.
  • The formula for \(E_n(d)\). Group the \(P=T^Qz^{r'}\) by \(k=|r'|\) and put \(\mu=d-k\). The inner sum is \(\sum_{0\le Q\le(\mu-1)/2}(\mu-2Q)=\lfloor(\mu+1)^2/4\rfloor\) for \(\mu\ge0\): for \(\mu=2b\) it is \(b(b+1)\), and for \(\mu=2b+1\) it is \((b+1)^2\).
  • Part 3. In characteristic 0 the initial-segment law holds at \((n,d)\) (theorem), so the threshold-ideal lemma (Part 2) gives \(\ell_0(d+1,N)=\deg\Delta_{n,d}-\deg g_{n,d}\). Here \(g_{n,d}\mid\Delta_{n,d}\ne0\), and by part 2 each collision form divides \(g_{n,d}\) exactly \(E_n(d)\) times. Every entry \((Q,r;c)\) of \(A\) is homogeneous of degree \(c-Q\), so \(\deg\Delta_{n,d}=\sum_{c<N}c-\sum Q\).
    • For \(n=4\), \(\sum_{c<N}c=(8d-4)(8d-5)/2=32d^2-36d+10\).
    • \(\sum Q=\sum_k\binom4kT(\lfloor(d-k)/2\rfloor)\) with \(T(x)=x(x+1)/2\). For \(d=2u\) this is \(T(u)+10T(u-1)+5T(u-2)\); for \(d=2u+1\) it is \(5T(u)+10T(u-1)+T(u-2)\). Both equal \(2d^2-6d+5\).
    • So \(\deg\Delta_{4,d}=30d^2-30d+5\). The four terms of \(E_4(d)\) sum to \(2d^2-2d+1\) for both parities, and \(30d^2-30d+5-10(2d^2-2d+1)=10d^2-10d-5\).

In odd characteristic \(p\), the argument needs only \(\Delta_\nu\not\equiv0\pmod p\) for the limit vector \(\nu\) above, which excludes finitely many \(p\) for each \((n,d)\). \(\square\)

Checks. For \(n=3\) the theorem gives \(E_3(d)=d^2\) and \(\deg\Delta_{3,d}-6E_3(d)=d^2-1\), which is the boundary theorem, there proved in every odd characteristic. For \(n=4\), \(E_4(d)=1,5,13,25,41\) (\(d\le5\)), the exponents found in both \(g\) and \(\Delta\) on the test lines over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\) (line computations). research/tools/bmd_cube_collision_counts.py (output research/results/bmd-r103-collision-exponents/counts.json) asserts four identities from the definitions:

  • the closed form of \(E_n(d)\), for \(2\le n\le7\) and \(d\le40\);
  • \(E_4(d)=d^2+(d-1)^2\);
  • \(\deg\Delta_{4,d}=30d^2-30d+5\);
  • the value \(10d^2-10d-5\).

This is arithmetic outside the proof. It also records \(\deg\Delta_{n,d}-\binom{n+1}2E_n(d)\) for \(n\le6\), \(d\le10\): 0, 45, 220, 540 for \(n=5\), and 0, 105, 665, 1960 for \(n=6\).

Other factors of the gcd are doubled

Proposition (prop:cube-extra-factors-double). Let \(F\) have characteristic 0, \(n\ge2\) and \(d\ge1\). Every prime factor \(\pi\) of \(g_{n,d}\) other than the collision forms satisfies \(\pi^2\mid\Delta_{n,d}\). Hence, if the part of \(\Delta_{n,d}\) prime to the collision forms is squarefree, then \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}=1\) and \(\ell_0(d+1,N)=\deg\Delta_{n,d}-\binom{n+1}2E_n(d)\). For \(n=4\) and \(d\ge2\) that value is \(10d^2-10d-5\).

Proof. Work over \(\overline F\) in the coordinates \(a=4y\), where \(\Delta^w_{n,d}(a)=\pm2^e\Delta_{n,d}(y)\). The gcd of the minors does not change under field extension. A prime \(\pi\in F[y]\) is squarefree over \(\overline F\), since it is separable in characteristic 0. Its prime factors over \(\overline F\) divide \(\Delta_{n,d}\), which has rational coefficients, so they are absolutely irreducible factors of \(\Delta_{n,d}\) and are defined over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\). If each of these distinct factors divides \(\Delta_{n,d}\) at least twice, then \(\pi^2\mid\Delta_{n,d}\). So it suffices to treat a prime \(\pi\in\overline{\mathbb Q}[a]\). Write \(\Delta^w_{n,d}=\pi^\mu R\) with \(\pi\nmid R\), let \(Z=V(\pi)\), and let \(X=\sum_ia_i^2\partial/\partial a_i\). Put \(\varphi_t(a)=(a_i/(1+a_it))_i\), the parameters of the transport lemma at the point \(T=t\); then \(\frac d{dt}\varphi_t(a)=-(\varphi_t(a)_i^2)_i\).

  • The Wronskian identity. Fix \(a^*\) with distinct nonzero entries, and let \(W\) be the Wronskian of the basis \(T^Qw^r\) of \(V_d(a^*)\) on \(C_{a^*}\). By the proof of the lemma, at every point \(q\) with \(t=T(q)\) and \(1+a^*_it\ne0\) (whether or not \(W(q)\ne0\)), \(W(q)\) is \(\Delta^w_{n,d}(\varphi_t(a^*))\) times a factor that is regular and nonzero near \(p_0\). \(T\) is a local parameter at \(p_0\), so \(\operatorname{ord}_{p_0}W=\operatorname{ord}_{t=0}\Delta^w_{n,d}(\varphi_t(a^*))\).
  • Weights. In characteristic 0, \(\operatorname{ord}_{p_0}W\) is the weight \(\sum_i(\varepsilon_i-i)\) of the orders \(\varepsilon_0<\cdots<\varepsilon_{N-1}\) of \(V_d(a^*)\) at \(p_0\). For a basis adapted to these orders, the lowest term of \(W\) is a nonzero multiple of \(\det(\varepsilon_j(\varepsilon_j-1)\cdots(\varepsilon_j-k+1))_{k,j}=\prod_{i<j}(\varepsilon_j-\varepsilon_i)\ne0\).
  • Points of \(Z\) have weight \(\ge2\). Let \(a^*\in Z\) have distinct nonzero entries. Then all maximal minors of \(A_N\) vanish at \(a^*\), so \(A_N(a^*)\) has rank \(
  • \(Z\) is not invariant under the flow. Suppose \(X\pi=h\pi\) for a polynomial \(h\). Take \(a^*\in Z\) with distinct nonzero entries; there is such a point, since \(Z\) is irreducible and not a collision hyperplane. Then \(u(t)=\pi(\varphi_t(a^*))\in\overline{\mathbb Q}[[t]]\) satisfies \(u'=-h(\varphi_t(a^*))\,u\) and \(u(0)=0\). Comparing coefficients, \(u=0\) in characteristic 0. So \(\Delta^w_{n,d}(\varphi_t(a^*))=0\) identically, and \(W\) vanishes to infinite order at \(p_0\). Then \(W=0\), contradicting the independence of the basis. Hence \(\pi\nmid X\pi\).
  • Conclusion. Choose \(a^*\in Z\) with distinct nonzero entries, \(R(a^*)\ne0\) and \((X\pi)(a^*)\ne0\). This is possible because \(Z\) is irreducible, \(Z\) is not a collision hyperplane, and \(R,X\pi\notin(\pi)\). Then \(\frac d{dt}\pi(\varphi_t(a^*))|_{t=0}=-(X\pi)(a^*)\ne0\), so \(\operatorname{ord}_{t=0}\Delta^w_{n,d}(\varphi_t(a^*))=\mu\). By the first three steps this order is at least 2, so \(\mu\ge2\). The final sentence is part 3 of the theorem with \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}=1\). \(\square\)

The proposition says more. A factor of \(\Delta_{n,d}\) prime to the collision forms, of multiplicity \(\mu\), is a divisor along which \(p_0\) has weight exactly \(\mu\) at a general point. It lies in \(g_{n,d}\) exactly when the top order there is at least \(N+1\). A simple factor is a divisor of simple Weierstrass points of \(V_d\) (orders \(0,\ldots,N-2,N\)), and these never enter \(g\).

What remains for the dimension-4 boundary. In characteristic 0, \(\ell_0(d+1,8d-4)=10d^2-10d-5\) for all \(d\ge2\) now reduces to one statement: \(g_{4,d}\) has no factor other than the collision forms. By the proposition, it suffices that the non-collision part of \(\Delta_{4,d}\), of degree \(10d^2-10d-5+\deg g^{\mathrm{nc}}_{4,d}\), is squarefree. For a fixed \(d\) this can be certified. By the theorem, \(\Delta_{4,d}=c'\prod_D\ell_D^{\,E_4(d)}\cdot\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\) over \(\mathbb Q\). Restrict to a line over \(\mathbb F_p\) with \(c'\not\equiv0\), divide by exactly \(\prod_D\ell_D|_L^{\,E_4(d)}\), and suppose the quotient is squarefree of full degree. The quotient is the reduction of \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\) on the line, and a square factor over \(\mathbb Q\) would reduce to a square factor there. So \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\) is then squarefree over \(\mathbb Q\), with no assumption about exponents mod \(p\). For all \(d\) the question is geometric. Does the locus of points of the fibre curves whose top order is at least \(N+1\) have codimension 2? The generic expectation is codimension 2, a Schubert condition of codimension 2 on the osculating flag. By the proposition, a divisorial component would have to be a divisor of Weierstrass points of weight at least 2.

General statement. lem:cube-generic-normality, for every \(n\ge1\) and every degree vector in characteristic 0. thm:cube-boundary-collision-exponents and prop:cube-extra-factors-double, for every \(n\ge2\) and \(d\ge1\) in characteristic 0.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the collision limit lemma and the collision-lifts lemma, the Hermite–Padé form, the transport lemma, the threshold-ideal lemma (Part 2), and the Möbius transport in the dimension-3 boundary theorem. Claim searches (Wronskian, generic perfect Hermite–Padé system, collision exponent, elementary divisors, saturation, boundary gcd) found the characteristic-0 theorem, which is the special case \(\nu_r=\lfloor(d-|r|)/2\rfloor\) of the lemma. They also found the collision limit lemma, whose part 3 the theorem extends from \(m\ge2^{n-1}d\) to \(m\ge N-1\). Nothing found implies the proposition. The arithmetic identities were asserted by script. A fresh-context referee checked every step and found no error that breaks a stated result. It checked the factorization \(B\,D\,H(a')\), the limit space as \(V_\nu\), the saturation, the transport at every truncation, both parities of \(E_n(d)\) and the closed forms against the output, and the Wronskian, weight, flow and transversality steps of the proposition. Its corrections are made: the passage from \(\overline F\) to \(F\); the three conditions for part 3 in odd characteristic; the exact division in the squarefreeness certificate; and the pointwise validity of the Wronskian identity. No hypothesis is unused. Characteristic 0 enters through the Wronskian and the division by \(k+1\), and \(d\ge2\) is needed for \(N_{2,4}(d)=8d-4\).

Assessment. One of the two missing implications for the dimension-4 boundary is proved in characteristic 0, for every \(d\) and in every dimension: the collision exponents of \(g_{n,d}\) and of \(\Delta_{n,d}\) are exactly \(E_n(d)\). The tool is small. The Wronskian argument that proved the initial-segment law works for every degree vector, so the degenerate limit systems along collisions are normal too. The other implication is reduced to squarefreeness of the non-collision part of \(\Delta_{n,d}\), which a line computation over one prime certifies for each fixed \(d\). The general form is a statement about higher Weierstrass points of \(V_d\) on the genus-5 curves. The lead on Riemann–Roch for the fibre curve gave the Wronskian and weight language for this; it did not give a codimension-2 argument. Odd characteristic remains open for \(n\ge4\) (open statement 2), since the ordinary Wronskian fails there.

26 September 2026 — The dimension-4 boundary thresholds are 10d² − 10d − 5 for 2 ≤ d ≤ 9 in characteristic 0: the determinant's other part is squarefree

Working proof in characteristic 0: ℓ₀(d+1, 8d−4) = 10d²−10d−5 on {0,1}⁴ for 2 ≤ d ≤ 9, and ℓ₀(d+1, N) = 45, 220, 540 on {0,1}⁵ for d = 2, 3, 4, from squarefreeness certificates. Cycle bmd-r104. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. By the collision-exponent theorem and the doubled-factor proposition, in characteristic 0 the boundary threshold \(\ell_0(d+1,N_{2,n}(d))\) equals \(\deg\Delta_{n,d}-\binom{n+1}2E_n(d)\) whenever the part of \(\Delta_{n,d}\) prime to the collision forms is squarefree. The previous entry described a certificate for that from one line over one prime. The missing implication for open statement 3 at the boundary is the absence of non-collision factors in \(g_{n,d}\). This cycle tests the stronger squarefreeness for \(n=4\) at every \(d\) the kernel reaches quickly, with \(n=3\) as a control and \(n=5\) as a test of the next dimension. A square factor would end the route through the proposition; squarefreeness at every tested \(d\) proves the threshold there.

The certificate

Kernel. research/tools/bmd_cube_delta_squarefree.cpp (FLINT) restricts \(y\) to the line \(y=u+tv\) over \(\mathbb F_p\), \(p=1000003\). It builds the \(N\times N\) matrix of the coefficients of \(T^0,\ldots,T^{N-1}\) in the \(T^Qz^r\) as polynomials in \(t\), and takes its determinant \(\Delta|_L\) with nmod_poly_mat_det. It then checks three conditions:

  1. \(\deg_t\Delta|_L\) equals the homogeneous degree \(\sum_{c<N}c-\sum Q\);
  2. the \(\binom{n+1}2\) collision roots on the line are distinct, and each is a root of multiplicity exactly \(E_n(d)\);
  3. the quotient \(R\) of \(\Delta|_L\) by \(\prod_D(t-t_D)^{E_n(d)}\) satisfies \(\gcd(R,R')=1\).

It also prints the degrees of the irreducible factors of \(R\) over \(\mathbb F_p\). The lines are the one used for the line computations (for \(n=4\)), and lines with the same kind of random coordinates for \(n=3\) and \(n=5\). The commands are in the output headers.

Why the three conditions certify. Over \(\mathbb Q\), \(\Delta_{n,d}=c'\prod_D\ell_D^{\,E_n(d)}\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\), by the collision-exponent theorem, with \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\in\mathbb Z[y]\) primitive and prime to the collision forms. The \(\ell_D\) are primitive too, so by Gauss's lemma \(c'=\pm\mathrm{content}(\Delta_{n,d})\in\mathbb Z\).

  • Condition 1 says that the top coefficient \(\Delta_{n,d}(v)\) of \(\Delta|_L\) is nonzero mod \(p\). So \(p\nmid c'\), and every factor of \(\Delta_{n,d}\) keeps its degree on \(L\) modulo \(p\).
  • \(\ell_D|_L\) is a nonzero constant times \(t-t_D\). So by condition 2, \(R\) is a nonzero constant times the reduction of \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}|_L\).
  • A factorization \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}=\pi^2\rho\) over \(\mathbb Q\) with \(\pi\) primitive and nonconstant (and homogeneous, as a factor of a homogeneous polynomial, so the leading \(t\)-coefficient of \(\pi|_L\) is \(\pi(v)\)) would give \(\bar\pi|_L^{\,2}\mid R\), with \(\deg\bar\pi|_L=\deg\pi\ge1\), since \(\pi(v)\) divides \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}(v)\), which is nonzero mod \(p\). Condition 3 excludes this.

Condition 2 is needed. The kernel removes the full multiplicity of each \(t-t_D\), so an extra root of \(\bar\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}|_L\) at \(t_D\) would be stripped before condition 3. Multiplicity exactly \(E_n(d)\) is what makes \(R\) the reduction of \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}|_L\).

Finite check (check:cube-boundary-squarefree). All certificates pass (research/results/bmd-r104-boundary-squarefree/):

  • \(n=4\), \(2\le d\le9\) (n4-d2-5.txt, n4-d6-9.txt). The degrees of \(\Delta|_L\) are 65, 185, 365, 605, 905, 1265, 1685, 2165. The collision multiplicities are \(E_4(d)=5,13,25,41,61,85,113,145\), and \(R\) has degree \(10d^2-10d-5=15,55,\ldots,715\) and is squarefree. At \(d=2\), \(R\) splits into irreducible factors of degrees 4, 2, 3, 3, 3 over \(\mathbb F_p\).
  • \(n=5\), \(2\le d\le4\) (n5-d2-4.txt): \(N=17,32,48\), \(E_5=6,18,38\), and \(R\) is squarefree of degree 45, 220, 540.
  • Control, \(n=3\), \(2\le d\le10\) (n3-d2-10.txt): \(E_3=d^2\), and \(R\) is squarefree of degree \(d^2-1\), as the boundary theorem requires for its degree. Its squarefreeness was not recorded before.

The \(n=4\) multiplicities and degrees for \(d\le5\) agree with the earlier kernel bmd_cube_boundary_minors.cpp, which interpolated all \(N+1\) minors by hand-written elimination. The two implementations are independent. The runs' times are in the session record of this cycle.

The thresholds

Corollary (cor:cube-dimension-four-boundary-thresholds). Over every field of characteristic 0:

  • on \(\{0,1\}^4\), \(g_{4,d}\) is a constant times \(\prod_D\ell_D^{\,d^2+(d-1)^2}\), and \(\ell_0(d+1,8d-4)=10d^2-10d-5\), for \(2\le d\le9\);
  • on \(\{0,1\}^5\), \(\ell_0(d+1,N_{2,5}(d))=45,220,540\) for \(d=2,3,4\).

For each such \((n,d)\) the same holds in all but finitely many characteristics; the exceptional primes are not computed.

Proof. By the finite check, the non-collision part of \(\Delta_{n,d}\) is squarefree over \(\mathbb Q\). The doubled-factor proposition then gives \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}=1\) and \(\ell_0=\deg\Delta_{n,d}-\binom{n+1}2E_n(d)\), whose values are recorded in research/results/bmd-r103-collision-exponents/counts.json. The value \(10d^2-10d-5\) is part 3 of the collision-exponent theorem. For the finitely many characteristics, fix \((n,d)\). The following hold for all but finitely many \(p\):

  • the initial-segment law holds (\(p>2^{n-1}d\));
  • \(p\nmid\mathrm{content}(\Delta_{n,d})\);
  • the gcd of the maximal minors over \(\mathbb F_p\) is the reduction of the primitive gcd \(g\in\mathbb Z[y]\). Write \(M_c=g\,M'_c\), with the \(M'_c\) coprime over \(\mathbb Q\). Choose integers \(\lambda_c\) so that \(h=\sum_{c<N}\lambda_cM'_c\) is coprime to \(f=M'_N\): each prime factor of \(f\) misses some \(M'_c\), so each excludes a proper subspace of \(\lambda\)'s. After an integral linear change of coordinates, \(f\) and \(h\) have constant leading coefficients in \(y_1\), and \(\mathrm{Res}_{y_1}(f,h)\in\mathbb Z[y_2,\ldots]\) is nonzero. Exclude the \(p\) dividing the change's determinant, those leading coefficients, or some fixed nonzero coefficient of the resultant. A common factor of \(\bar f\) and \(\bar h\) has positive \(y_1\)-degree, since a \(y_1\)-free factor would divide the constant leading coefficient. So it would make \(\mathrm{Res}_{y_1}(\bar f,\bar h)=\overline{\mathrm{Res}_{y_1}(f,h)}\) vanish, which the choice of \(p\) excludes. So \(\gcd_c\bar M_c=\bar g\), of degree \(\deg g\); since \(g\) is primitive, \(\bar g=\pm\prod_D\ell_D^{\,E_n(d)}\). \(\square\)

This proves the dimension-4 values 15, 55, 115, 195 found on lines, in characteristic 0, and extends them to \(d\le9\). The first dimension-4 entry noted that \(\ell_0(3,12)=15\) had not been computed globally; it is now proved.

Conjecture (conj:cube-boundary-squarefree). For every \(n\ge2\) and \(d\ge1\), the part of \(\Delta_{n,d}\) prime to the collision forms is squarefree in \(\mathbb Q[y]\). Hence, in characteristic 0, \(g_{n,d}=c\prod_D\ell_D^{\,E_n(d)}\) and \(\ell_0(d+1,N_{2,n}(d))=\deg\Delta_{n,d}-\binom{n+1}2E_n(d)\), which is \(10d^2-10d-5\) for \(n=4\), \(d\ge2\). Evidence: the finite check above (\(n=3\), \(d\le10\); \(n=4\), \(d\le9\); \(n=5\), \(d\le4\)). For \(n=3\) the threshold formula is already proved, by the genus-1 argument; the squarefreeness is not.

By the doubled-factor proposition, a simple non-collision factor of \(\Delta_{n,d}\) is a divisor along which \(p_0\) is a simple Weierstrass point of \(V_d\). So the conjecture says that, at a general point of each divisorial component of the Weierstrass locus of \(V_d\) on the family of fibre curves, \(p_0\) is a simple Weierstrass point. For the canonical series on a general curve of genus \(g\), a general Weierstrass point is simple; this is the kind of statement to look for, adapted to the \((\mathbb Z/2)^n\)-covers here. That is the next step on the general \(d\).

General statement. conj:cube-boundary-squarefree, for every \(n\ge2\) and \(d\ge1\) in characteristic 0. The certificates prove its instances listed in cor:cube-dimension-four-boundary-thresholds.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the collision-exponent theorem and the doubled-factor proposition of the previous entry, with their referee's certificate conditions. A claim search (squarefree, boundary, Weierstrass) found no earlier version of the conjecture. The kernel agrees with the independent minors kernel for \(n=4\), \(d\le5\). A fresh-context referee checked the kernel against the definitions, recomputed \(\Delta_{3,2}=-4\prod\ell_D^4\,(y_1-y_2-y_3)(y_1-y_2+y_3)(y_1+y_2-y_3)\) over \(\mathbb Q\) with sympy, and matched every number to the output files. It found nothing that breaks a stated result. Its corrections are made: condition 2 is needed (the kernel strips full multiplicities); \(c'\) is the content, by Gauss's lemma; homogeneity of \(\pi\); the resultant step made precise; an unsourced timing sentence removed; and divisorial components in the conjecture's reformulation.

Assessment. The first pre-stable thresholds in dimension 4 are proved, in characteristic 0: at the boundary \(m=8d-4\) the threshold is \(10d^2-10d-5\) for \(2\le d\le9\). The certificate is cheap: one determinant over \(\mathbb F_p[t]\) and one gcd per \(d\), under a minute for all runs. The general \(d\) now needs one statement, squarefreeness of the non-collision part of \(\Delta_{n,d}\), which is a statement about simple Weierstrass points. The boundary is one end of the pre-stable range. The thresholds between the boundary and order zero, where the solution modules are not free, remain the harder part of open statement 3.
