26 September 2026 — Route review of the cube after the dimension-4 boundary: the squarefreeness conjecture restricts to a genus-1 problem

Route review: the boundary gcd is settled in characteristic 0 up to squarefreeness; on a collision hyperplane Δ^nc_{4,d} restricts to ∏(y_i−y_j)^{2(d−1)²} times a squarefree part for d ≤ 9, so the conjecture may reduce to genus 1. Cycle bmd-r105. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

The line's general claim. The per-order function on \(\{0,1\}^n\) in characteristic \(\ne2\) is determined by the thresholds \(\ell_0(h,m)\), the initial degrees of the threshold ideals (threshold-ideal lemma). Dimension 3 is solved over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\) (theorem). For \(n\ge4\) the claim to establish is a law for the thresholds.

What the goal needs. Open statement 3, the pre-stable thresholds for \(n\ge4\): at the boundary \(m=N_{2,n}(d)\), in the middle range, and at order zero. Open statement 2, small primes for \(n\ge4\). Since the last review, the boundary has moved from data to proofs:

  • in characteristic 0 the collision exponents of \(g_{n,d}\) and \(\Delta_{n,d}\) are exactly \(E_n(d)\) for all \(n,d\) (theorem);
  • any other factor of \(g_{n,d}\) is doubled in \(\Delta_{n,d}\) (proposition);
  • certificates give \(\ell_0(d+1,8d-4)=10d^2-10d-5\) for \(2\le d\le9\) (corollary).

The boundary for every \(d\) now rests on one conjecture: the part of \(\Delta_{n,d}\) prime to the collision forms, \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}\), is squarefree (squarefreeness conjecture). The middle range and order zero have data (the savings-3 row, the quadric and the \(S_5\) symmetry) but no mechanism.

Falsification attempt

The conjecture says that at a general point of each divisorial component of the zero locus of \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\), \(p_0\) is a simple Weierstrass point of \(V_d\), with orders \(0,\ldots,N-2,N\). research/tools/bmd_cube_delta_squarefree.cpp gains two modes, and both tests ran on \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\) (research/results/bmd-r105-route-review/).

  • Orders at Weierstrass points (mode orders, orders-n4-d2-9.txt). On the line of the certificates, \(R\) (the restriction of \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}_{4,d}\)) has 7 roots in \(\mathbb F_p\) for \(d\le9\): two at \(d=4\), four at \(d=5\), one at \(d=9\). At each, the orders of \(V_d\) at \(p_0\) are exactly \(0,\ldots,N-2,N\), and the \(N\times(N+3)\) matrix has rank \(N\). The prediction could have failed at each root, with orders \(0,\ldots,N-2,N+1\) or a rank drop. It did not.
  • The collision limit (mode limit, limit-n3-d1-9.txt). Along \(y_1=0\) the saturated boundary lattice reduces to the limit space \(U^{(3)}_d=\operatorname{span}\{T^Qz^r:Q+|r|\le d\}\) in \(y_2,y_3,y_4\) (collision limit lemma). Its determinant \(\Delta_U\) is therefore, up to a constant, \(\Delta_{4,d}/y_1^{E_4(d)}\) restricted to \(y_1=0\): \[ \Delta_U=c\prod_{j\ge2}y_j^{\,2E_4(d)}\prod_{2\le i<j}(y_i-y_j)^{E_4(d)}\cdot\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}_{4,d}\big|_{y_1=0}. \] For \(1\le d\le9\) the kernel finds:
    • multiplicity exactly \(2E_4(d)\) at each \(y_j\), so \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}|_{y_1=0}\) is prime to the \(y_j\);
    • multiplicity \(E_4(d)+2(d-1)^2\) at each \(y_i-y_j\) (\(2,8,18,\ldots,128\) beyond \(E_4\));
    • a squarefree remaining part, of degree \(4d^2+2d-11\) for \(d\ge2\) (9, 31, 61, 99, 145, 199, 261, 331).
    So on a collision hyperplane, \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}_{4,d}\) restricts to \(\prod_{2\le i<j}(y_i-y_j)^{2(d-1)^2}\) times a squarefree polynomial prime to the collision forms of the hyperplane. The degrees add up: \(6(d-1)^2+4d^2+2d-11=10d^2-10d-5\).

Neither test refuted the conjecture. The second gives a route to it. Suppose \(\pi^2\mid\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}_{4,d}\) for a prime \(\pi\). Then \(\pi|_D^{\,2}\) divides the restriction for every collision hyperplane \(D\); by the \(S_5\) symmetry, all ten restrictions have the same shape. With the squarefree remainder, \(\pi|_D\) must be a product of the three double-double forms of \(D\) (the forms \(r_i-r_j\) on \(\{r_a=r_b\}\), with \(\{i,j\}\) disjoint from \(\{a,b\}\)), for every \(D\). A single linear form cannot do this: on \(D_{01}\) it must be \(r_2-r_3+c(r_0-r_1)\), and on \(D_{02}\) that forces \(c=-1\). But then on \(D_{03}\) it restricts to \(r_1+r_2-2r_0\), which is not such a product. The route therefore needs two statements for all \(d\):

  1. no prime \(\pi\) other than a collision form restricts, on every collision hyperplane, to a product of double-double forms;
  2. the remaining part of \(\Delta_U\) is squarefree.

The second concerns the limit space, which lives on the genus-1 curve \(w_2,w_3,w_4\), where dimension 3's torsion methods apply.

Assessment of this line

At the boundary, the line has become strong. Two general theorems and a proposition, all proved in characteristic 0 for every \(n\) and \(d\), reduce the dimension-4 boundary law to one conjecture. That conjecture is certified through \(d=9\), and it now has a concrete reduction to a genus-1 statement. The rest of open statement 3 is weak: the thresholds between the boundary and order zero, where the modules are not free, have one row of data and no mechanism, and order zero (5, 19, 39) has no formula. Open statement 2 has not moved: every new proof uses the Wronskian and needs characteristic 0 or large \(p\). The pattern of the last cycles is sound: each proved a general statement and used computation only to certify instances or test predictions.

Outside leads

  • General Weierstrass points are simple (Eisenbud–Harris, "Existence, decomposition, and limits of certain Weierstrass points", Invent. Math. 87, 1987; Cukierman, "Families of Weierstrass points", Duke Math. J. 58, 1989). For the canonical series on a general curve, a general point of each component of the Weierstrass locus is a simple Weierstrass point. The analogue for \(V_d=L(dH_\infty)\) on the family of \((\mathbb Z/2)^4\)-covers is exactly the squarefreeness conjecture. It breaks because the family is special, and the \(S_5\) and deck symmetries could force weight-2 points along a divisor. Test. Passed: all 7 rational roots found on the certificate line are simple Weierstrass points (orders \(0,\ldots,N-2,N\)).
  • Limit linear series along collisions (Eisenbud–Harris, "Limit linear series: basic theory", Invent. Math. 85, 1986). The collision limit lemma is a limit-linear-series computation, and restricting the Weierstrass locus to the boundary divisor is the standard route to its multiplicities. This targets the squarefreeness conjecture through the restriction pattern above. It breaks if the restriction has square factors not made of boundary forms. Test. Passed: for \(d\le9\) the restriction to \(y_1=0\) is \(\prod(y_i-y_j)^{2(d-1)^2}\) times a squarefree part; only double-double forms repeat.
  • The Plücker formula for the total Weierstrass weight (Arbarello–Cornalba–Griffiths–Harris, Geometry of Algebraic Curves I, Ch. I, exercise C). On one curve \(C_a\) the total weight of \(V_d\) is \(N\cdot8d+N(N-1)(g-1)\), with \(g=5\). The non-branch points contribute 16 times the number of roots in \(t\) of \(\Delta^w_{4,d}(a/(1+at))\), by the Wronskian identity of the proposition. The formula would give the ramification weights at the branch fibres, and hence a second count of \(\deg\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\). This targets the boundary degree and breaks if the branch weights are not computable. Test. Not run: the weights at the branch fibres, where \(T\) is not a local parameter, need their own local computation, which is not a cheap test.

Absurd bridges

  • The von Neumann–Wigner non-crossing rule (quantum mechanics: von Neumann and Wigner, Phys. Z. 30, 1929; molecular potential curves in chemistry). Translation: the orders of \(V_d\) at a moving point are "levels", a Weierstrass point is a crossing of level \(N-1\) with level \(N\), and a point with top order \(\ge N+1\) is a double crossing. The rule says that crossings not forced by symmetry have codimension equal to the number of conditions. So a double crossing would have codimension 2 in the parameters, which is the statement that \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}=1\). A symmetry-resolved version would say which symmetries (here \(S_5\) and the deck group) could force a divisor of double crossings. Test. Passed: along the certificate line no double crossing occurs for \(d\le9\), since every root of \(R\) is simple, and the rational ones are single crossings.
  • Weierstrass semigroups of algebraic-geometry codes (coding theory: the Feng–Rao bound, Høholdt–van Lint–Pellikaan, "Algebraic geometry codes", Handbook of Coding Theory, 1998). Translation: \(V_1=L(H_\infty)\) is the canonical series of the genus-5 curve \(C_a\). The one-point codes at \(p_0\) have designed distance governed by the Weierstrass semigroup of \(p_0\), which is ordinary exactly when \(p_0\) is not a canonical Weierstrass point. A theorem there would bound the minimum distance of the multiplicity codes behind the cube problem. Test. Passed: \(\Delta_{4,1}\) is a constant times the ten collision forms (line computations, rest 0 at \(d=1\)). So \(p_0\) is never a canonical Weierstrass point at distinct nonzero \(y\), and its semigroup is ordinary, with gaps \(1,\ldots,5\).

Bridge follow-up

  • Chip-firing on a cycle. Not worked this cycle. Follow-up. Continuing. The double-double exponent \(2(d-1)^2\) found here is another quadratic "energy" at a degeneration, of the kind chip-firing produced for the Tate curve. It is the next candidate for that reading.
  • Odd–even staggering. Not worked this cycle; no new savings-3 values were computed. Follow-up. Continuing: it still describes the only middle-range row.

Lead follow-up

  • Riemann–Roch and Riemann–Hurwitz for \(n\ge4\). Developed in the collision-exponent entry: \(V_d=L(dH_\infty)\) on the genus-5 curve, the Wronskian and Weierstrass weights, and the doubled-factor proposition. Follow-up. Developed.
  • Castelnuovo's bound and the theta divisor. Follow-up. Closed: the boundary values \(10d^2-10d-5\) came from exact collision exponents and simple Weierstrass points, not from a theta-divisor degree. The remaining question is squarefreeness, which the theta-divisor picture does not address.
  • Buchsbaum–Eisenbud acyclicity. Not worked this cycle. Follow-up. Continuing: it remains the tool for the non-free middle range.

Next step

On the highest-risk item, open statement 3 at the boundary, prove the squarefreeness conjecture through the restriction to a collision hyperplane. Four steps:

  1. State and prove the restriction identity \(\Delta_U=c\prod y_j^{2E}\prod(y_i-y_j)^E\,\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}|_{y_1=0}\) in every dimension.
  2. Prove that no prime other than a collision form restricts, on every collision hyperplane, to a product of double-double forms.
  3. Explain the exponent \(2(d-1)^2\) along the double-double strata.
  4. Prove that the non-collision part of \(\Delta_U\) is squarefree. \(U^{(3)}_d\) lives on the genus-1 curve, where the dimension-3 methods (torsion points, the residue disc) apply.

Steps 1 and 2 are algebra, and step 4 is a genus-1 statement. After that, the middle range needs a mechanism; the \(S_5\) decomposition of the threshold ideals is the recorded next attempt there.

26 September 2026 — The squarefreeness conjecture reduces to the collision limit: no surface meets every collision plane only in double-double lines

Working proof in characteristic 0: for n ≥ 4, Δ^nc_{n,d} is squarefree if, on one collision hyperplane, it restricts to double-double forms times a squarefree part; the proof is a plane-curve lemma on the complete quadrangle. Cycle bmd-r106. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The dimension-4 boundary law in characteristic 0 is equivalent, given the doubled-factor proposition, to squarefreeness of \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}\), the part of \(\Delta_{n,d}\) prime to the collision forms (squarefreeness conjecture). Route review 15 found that on \(y_1=0\), for \(d\le9\), \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}_{4,d}\) restricts to \(\prod(y_i-y_j)^{2(d-1)^2}\) times a squarefree part. It proposed a route: exclude a repeated prime whose restriction to every collision hyperplane consists of double-double forms, and reduce the rest to the collision limit. This cycle develops that lead (limit linear series along collisions, lead 2 of the review). The test ends with a proof of the exclusion for all \(d\), or with a surface that meets every collision plane only in double-double lines.

Setting. \(F\) has characteristic 0, and \(n\ge4\). Write the points as \(r_0=0\), \(r_i=y_i\), so the collision forms are the \(\binom{n+1}2\) differences \(r_a-r_b\), and \(D_{ab}=\{r_a=r_b\}\). On \(D_{ab}\) the restriction of a collision form \(r_x-r_y\) is of one of two kinds:

  • a triple form \(r_a-r_z\), when \(\{x,y\}\) meets \(\{a,b\}\);
  • a double-double form \(r_z-r_w\), when \(\{z,w\}\) is disjoint from \(\{a,b\}\).

\(U_d=U^{(n-1)}_d=\operatorname{span}\{T^Qz^r:Q+|r|\le d\}\) in the variables \(y_2,\ldots,y_n\) is the limit space along \(y_1=0\) (collision limit lemma). \(\Delta_U\) is the \(N\times N\) determinant of its coefficients of \(T^0,\ldots,T^{N-1}\), \(N=N_{2,n}(d)\), with rows in the order of the listed basis.

The quadrangle lemma

Lemma (lem:cube-quadrangle-diagonal). Let \(A_1,\ldots,A_4\) be points of \(\mathbb P^2\) in general position over a field of characteristic 0. Each of the six sides \(A_iA_j\) contains one diagonal point \(A_iA_j\cap A_kA_l\). Let \(\mu\ge1\), and let \(C\) be a form of degree \(\mu\) such that, on each side, \(C\) restricts to \(\kappa_{ij}\) times the \(\mu\)-th power of the linear form vanishing at that side's diagonal point, for constants \(\kappa_{ij}\). Then all \(\kappa_{ij}=0\). The same holds in characteristic \(p\) when \(p\nmid2\mu\).

So no curve of degree \(\mu\) meets each side of a complete quadrangle only at the side's diagonal point.

Proof. Take \(A_1=(1{:}0{:}0)\), \(A_2=(0{:}1{:}0)\), \(A_3=(0{:}0{:}1)\), \(A_4=(1{:}1{:}1)\). The sides, and the value of \(C\) on each, are:

  • \(z=0\): \(\kappa_1(x-y)^\mu\);
  • \(x=y\): \(\kappa_2z^\mu\);
  • \(y=0\): \(\kappa_3(x-z)^\mu\);
  • \(x=z\): \(\kappa_4y^\mu\);
  • \(x=0\): \(\kappa_5(y-z)^\mu\);
  • \(y=z\): \(\kappa_6x^\mu\).

The diagonal points are \((1{:}1{:}0)\), \((1{:}0{:}1)\) and \((0{:}1{:}1)\). Put \(f(u,z)=C(1,1+u,z)\), a polynomial of degree \(\le\mu\).

  • Its homogeneous part of degree \(\mu\) is \(C(0,u,z)=\kappa_5(u-z)^\mu\). So \(f=\kappa_5(u-z)^\mu+g\) with \(\deg g\le\mu-1\).
  • \(f(u,0)=\kappa_1(-u)^\mu\) and \(f(0,z)=\kappa_2z^\mu\) are homogeneous of degree \(\mu\). So \(g(u,0)=g(0,z)=0\), and \(g=uz\,h\) with \(\deg h\le\mu-3\) (\(h=0\) if \(\mu\le2\)).
  • \(f(u,1)=C(1,1+u,1)=\kappa_4(1+u)^\mu\). So \(u\,h(u,1)=\kappa_4(1+u)^\mu-\kappa_5(u-1)^\mu\), where the left side has degree \(\le\mu-2\) in \(u\). The coefficients of \(u^\mu\) and \(u^{\mu-1}\) on the right vanish: \(\kappa_4=\kappa_5\), and \(\mu(\kappa_4+\kappa_5)=0\). Hence \(2\mu\kappa_5=0\), so \(\kappa_5=\kappa_4=0\).
  • Then \(f=uz\,h\). Comparing the restrictions: \(\kappa_1=\kappa_2=0\); \(f(-1,z)=C(1,0,z)=\kappa_3(1-z)^\mu\) vanishes at \(z=0\), so \(\kappa_3=0\); and \(f(u,1+u)=C(1,1+u,1+u)=\kappa_6\) vanishes at \(u=0\), so \(\kappa_6=0\). \(\square\)

Check. research/tools/bmd_cube_quadrangle_local.py (sympy, exact) solves the linear system for the six-plane arrangement \(x_x=x_y\) in \(x_a,x_b,x_c,x_d\), modulo translation. For \(\mu\le7\) every solution has all \(\kappa=0\), and the solutions are the multiples of \(\prod(x_x-x_y)\) (from \(\mu=6\)). The output is in research/results/bmd-r106-double-double/quadrangle-mu1-7.txt.

No surface meets every collision plane only in double-double lines

Lemma (lem:cube-no-double-double-surface). Let \(n\ge3\), and let \(\pi\in F[y_1,\ldots,y_n]\) be homogeneous of positive degree. Then for some collision hyperplane \(D\), \(\pi|_D\) is not a nonzero constant times a product of double-double forms of \(D\).

Proof. Suppose that every \(\pi|_{D_{xy}}=\lambda_{xy}\prod(\text{double-double forms of }D_{xy})\) with \(\lambda_{xy}\ne0\). Since \(\pi\) is homogeneous of positive degree, \(\pi|_{D_{01}}\) has positive degree, so it contains a double-double factor, say \(r_2-r_3\) after relabelling. Take the stratum \(r_0=r_1=r_2=r_3\), and a point \(Q\) of it where the other \(r_e\) are distinct from each other and from the common value (for \(n=3\), \(Q=0\)). Then \(\pi|_{D_{01}}\) vanishes at \(Q\), so \(\pi(Q)=0\), and every restriction below has order \(\alpha_{xy}\ge1\) at \(Q\). This is where homogeneity and positive degree are used: \(1+\prod(\text{all collision forms})\) restricts to 1 on every collision hyperplane. Expand \(\pi\) in affine coordinates \(x\) centred at \(Q\), as \(\pi=\sum_kP_k\) with \(P_k\) homogeneous of degree \(k\).

  • Restrictions. Take \(\{x,y,z,w\}=\{0,1,2,3\}\). The double-double forms of \(D_{xy}\) that vanish at \(Q\) are exactly the multiples of \(r_z-r_w\); the forms \(r_z-r_e\), \(r_w-r_e\) and \(r_e-r_{e'}\) (with \(e,e'\ge4\)) are units near \(Q\). So near \(Q\), \(\pi|_{D_{xy}}=\lambda_{xy}(r_z-r_w)^{\alpha_{xy}}U_{xy}\), with \(U_{xy}(Q)\ne0\). Since \(D_{xy}\) passes through \(Q\), restriction commutes with taking homogeneous parts. So \(P_k|_{D_{xy}}=0\) for \(k<\alpha_{xy}\), and \(P_{\alpha_{xy}}|_{D_{xy}}=\lambda_{xy}U_{xy}(Q)(r_z-r_w)^{\alpha_{xy}}\).
  • The quadrangle. Let \(\mu=\min\alpha_{xy}\ge1\), and let \(T\) be a 3-dimensional affine subspace through \(Q\) transverse to the stratum, with coordinates \(r_0-r_3\), \(r_1-r_3\), \(r_2-r_3\). Each \(D_{xy}\) contains the stratum, so \(T\cap D_{xy}\) is the plane \(x_x=x_y\) of \(T\), and \((P_\mu|_T)|_{T\cap D_{xy}}=(P_\mu|_{D_{xy}})|_T=\kappa_{xy}(r_z-r_w)^\mu\). Here \(\kappa_{xy}=\lambda_{xy}U_{xy}(Q)\ne0\) where \(\alpha_{xy}=\mu\), and \(\kappa_{xy}=0\) otherwise. In \(\mathbb P(T)\cong\mathbb P^2\) the six planes form a complete quadrangle. Its vertices are the four triple lines \(r_x=r_y=r_z\), in general position. The diagonal point of the side \(D_{xy}\) is \(D_{xy}\cap D_{zw}\), where \(r_z-r_w\) vanishes.
  • Conclusion. The quadrangle lemma, applied to \(P_\mu|_T\), gives all \(\kappa_{xy}=0\). This contradicts \(\kappa_{xy}\ne0\) for a pair with \(\alpha_{xy}=\mu\). \(\square\)

Check. research/tools/bmd_cube_double_double_surfaces.py computes, for \(n=4\), the space of forms of degree \(3\mu\) whose restriction to each \(D_{ab}\) is a multiple of \((\prod\text{double-double forms})^\mu\). It is 0 for \(\mu=1,2\) (surfaces-mu1-2.txt). This is the special case in which every exponent equals \(\mu\).

The reduction

Theorem (thm:cube-squarefree-reduction). In characteristic 0, let \(n\ge4\) and \(d\ge1\).

  1. Restriction identity. \(\Delta_U=c\prod_{j\ge2}y_j^{\,2E_n(d)}\prod_{2\le i<j}(y_i-y_j)^{E_n(d)}\cdot\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}\big|_{y_1=0}\), with \(c\ne0\) a constant.
  2. Reduction. Suppose that \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}|_{y_1=0}\) is a product of double-double forms of \(D_{01}\) times a squarefree polynomial prime to all collision forms of \(D_{01}\). Equivalently, by part 1, suppose that \(\Delta_U\) has multiplicity exactly \(2E_n(d)\) along each \(y_j\), and that its part prime to the collision forms of \(y_2,\ldots,y_n\) is squarefree. Then \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}\) is squarefree. So \(g_{n,d}=c'\prod_D\ell_D^{\,E_n(d)}\), and \(\ell_0(d+1,N)=\deg\Delta_{n,d}-\binom{n+1}2E_n(d)\), which is \(10d^2-10d-5\) for \(n=4\) and \(d\ge2\).

Proof. Part 1. By the collision-lifts lemma and the collision limit lemma, the basis of \(V_{n,d}\) is unitriangular, over \(F[y]\), to the basis consisting of the basis \(b_i\) of \(V_{n-1,d}\) and the \(L_P\). The matrix of truncated expansions of \(\{b_i\}\cup\{y_1^{-(d-e(P))}L_P\}\) has polynomial entries. Indeed \(L_P=P\,\Psi_{d-e}(y_1T)\), and \(\Psi_{d-e}\) is divisible by \(U^{d-e}\). Call its determinant \(\Delta^+\). Then \(\Delta_{n,d}=\pm y_1^{E_n(d)}\Delta^+\) up to a constant. At \(y_1=0\), the rows reduce to the \(b_i\) and to \(\psi_{d-e}T^{d-e}P\), which are the listed basis of \(U_d\) up to nonzero constants and order. So \(\Delta^+|_{y_1=0}=c\,\Delta_U\). By the collision-exponent theorem, \(\Delta_{n,d}=c'\prod_D\ell_D^{\,E_n(d)}\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\). Dividing by \(y_1^{E_n(d)}\) and setting \(y_1=0\) sends:

  • \(y_j\) and \(y_1-y_j\) to \(\pm y_j\);
  • \(y_i-y_j\) (\(i,j\ge2\)) to itself.

This gives part 1. Here \(\Delta_U\ne0\) by the generic normality lemma, so \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}|_{y_1=0}\ne0\).

Part 2. The two forms of the hypothesis agree by part 1: \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}|_{y_1=0}\) has no factor \(y_j\), which is the triple form \(r_0-r_j\), exactly when the multiplicity is \(2E_n(d)\). The Möbius transport and the coordinate permutations come from permutations \(\sigma\) of the \(n+1\) points \(r_0,\ldots,r_n\) (symmetry theorem), acting on \(y\) linearly. By the transport in the boundary theorem, they change \(\Delta_{n,d}\) by a constant factor: the determinant of a transformation invertible over \(\mathbb Z[\tfrac12][a]\) is a unit there, hence a constant. They permute the collision forms, so \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\circ\sigma^{-1}=c_\sigma\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\). For a collision hyperplane \(D=\sigma(D_{01})\), this gives \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}|_D=c\,(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}|_{D_{01}})\circ\sigma^{-1}\). And \(\sigma\) sends the triple and double-double forms of \(D_{01}\) to forms of the same kind on \(D\). So the hypothesis holds on every collision hyperplane, with the double-double forms of \(D\).

Suppose \(\pi^2\mid\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\) with \(\pi\) prime. Then \(\pi\) is homogeneous of positive degree and not a collision form. For each \(D\), \(\pi|_D\ne0\) (\(\pi\) is not \(\ell_D\)), and \(\pi|_D^{\,2}\) divides \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}|_D\). An irreducible factor of \(\pi|_D\) that divides the squarefree part would divide it twice. So every irreducible factor of \(\pi|_D\) is a double-double form of \(D\), and \(\pi|_D\) is a nonzero constant times a product of such forms. This holds for every \(D\), which contradicts the lemma. So \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\) is squarefree, and the rest is the doubled-factor proposition. \(\square\)

Where the reduction stands. The hypothesis of part 2 is a statement about the limit space \(U^{(n-1)}_d\) alone, one dimension lower. For \(n=4\) that space lives on the genus-1 curve \(w_2,w_3,w_4\), and the review's computation over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\) (research/results/bmd-r105-route-review/limit-n3-d1-9.txt) certifies the hypothesis in characteristic 0 for \(d\le9\). On its line \(\Delta_U\) has full degree mod \(p\), multiplicity exactly \(2E_4(d)\) at each \(y_j\), and a squarefree remaining part of degree \(4d^2+2d-11\) (\(d\ge2\)). Over \(\mathbb Q\) the multiplicity at \(y_j\) is at least \(2E_4(d)\) by part 1, and at most its value mod \(p\) when the degree is preserved. The squarefree part lifts as in the certificate: a square factor over \(\mathbb Q\) would reduce to a square factor of full degree on the line. This recovers the certified range of the corollary by a second route, not new instances.

Conjecture (conj:cube-limit-determinant-squarefree). For every \(d\ge1\), in characteristic 0, \(\Delta_U\) for \(U^{(3)}_d\) (variables \(y_2,y_3,y_4\)) has multiplicity exactly \(2E_4(d)\) along each \(y_j\), and its part prime to the forms \(y_j\) and \(y_i-y_j\) is squarefree. By the theorem, this implies \(\ell_0(d+1,8d-4)=10d^2-10d-5\) on \(\{0,1\}^4\) for every \(d\ge2\) in characteristic 0. Evidence: \(d\le9\), certified modulo 1000003, which implies characteristic 0 as explained above.

By the Wronskian argument of the doubled-factor proposition, applied to \(U_d\), which is transported by the same translations, a non-collision factor of \(\Delta_U\) with multiplicity \(\mu\) is a divisor along which \(p_0\) has weight \(\mu\) for \(U_d\) on the genus-1 curve. So the conjecture again says that the generic Weierstrass points are simple, now for the degree-\(2d\) subspace \(U_d\subset L(2dH_\infty)\) of codimension 4 on an elliptic curve. There the dimension-3 methods apply: the group law, torsion, and the residue disc. The multiplicity along \(y_j\) is a second collision computation, a triple collision \(r_0=r_1=r_j\) of the original problem.

General statement. thm:cube-squarefree-reduction, for every \(n\ge4\) and \(d\ge1\) in characteristic 0, with lem:cube-no-double-double-surface for every \(n\ge4\) and lem:cube-quadrangle-diagonal for every \(\mu\). The open part is conj:cube-limit-determinant-squarefree.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the collision-lifts and collision limit lemmas, the collision-exponent theorem, the doubled-factor proposition, the generic normality lemma, and the review's limit data. Claim searches (double-double, quadrangle, diagonal point, squarefree, restriction) found no earlier version. The quadrangle lemma was checked by exact linear algebra for \(\mu\le7\), and the global surface condition for \(\mu\le2\). A fresh-context referee checked the quadrangle lemma, the slice and the quadrangle identification, both parts of the theorem, the degree identity and the conjecture's match with part 2. It found one gap: \(\mu=\min\alpha\) could be 0 at a badly chosen stratum. This is fixed by choosing the stratum through a double-double factor, so \(\pi(Q)=0\), and the role of homogeneity is now stated. Its other corrections are made: the lemma's hypotheses (positive-degree homogeneous; irreducibility and \(n\ge4\) unused, so the lemma is stated for \(n\ge3\)); \(s=y_1\); the transfer through permutations of the points, with the explicit composition; and why the data over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\) certify the hypothesis in characteristic 0.

Assessment. The route proposed by the review works, and its geometric half is proved for every \(d\). A repeated factor of \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\) could hide only in surfaces meeting every collision plane in double-double lines. The quadrangle lemma rules these out: no plane curve meets each side of a complete quadrangle only at its diagonal point. What remains is a statement about the collision limit, one dimension lower. For \(n=4\) it is a Weierstrass-point statement on an elliptic curve, where the dimension-3 tools apply. The next cycle attacks it: first the multiplicity \(2E_4(d)\) at the triple collisions, then the simple Weierstrass points of \(U_d\) through the group law.

26 September 2026 — Merging a square root: an exact valuation and leading coefficient for every degree vector, and the triple-collision multiplicity of the limit determinant

Working proof in characteristic 0: along a_n = 0, Δ_ν has valuation Σ(α+1)(β+1) and leading coefficient a multiple of Δ_ν′ with ν′ = α+β+1; so the limit determinant has multiplicity exactly 2E₄(d) at y_j = 0, half of the limit conjecture. Cycle bmd-r107. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. By the reduction theorem, the dimension-4 boundary law \(\ell_0(d+1,8d-4)=10d^2-10d-5\) for every \(d\) follows from the limit conjecture. Its two halves are:

  1. the determinant \(\Delta_U\) of \(U^{(3)}_d\) has multiplicity exactly \(2E_4(d)\) along each \(y_j\);
  2. its part prime to the collision forms is squarefree.

The first half is a triple collision \(r_0=r_1=r_j\) of the original problem. Can it be computed exactly for all \(d\), by degenerating \(U_d\) along \(y_4\to0\) as the collision limit lemma degenerated \(V_d\)? The test ends with the exact multiplicity, or with a limit system that is not normal. This develops the limit-linear-series lead of route review 15 (lead 2).

Setting. As in the generic normality lemma: \(F\) has characteristic 0, \(w_i=(1+a_iT)^{1/2}\), and a degree vector \(\nu=(\nu_r)_{r\in\{0,1\}^n}\) has \(\nu_r\ge-1\). Degree vectors given by formulas are clipped, \(\nu_r=\max(\cdot,-1)\), and so are \(\nu'\) below. \(V_\nu=\bigoplus_rw^rF[T]_{\le\nu_r}\), and \(\Delta_\nu(a)\in\mathbb Z[\tfrac12][a]\) is the \(N_\nu\times N_\nu\) determinant of the rows \(T^jw^r\). Write \(r=(r',r_n)\), \(\alpha_{r'}=\nu_{(r',0)}\) and \(\beta_{r'}=\nu_{(r',1)}\).

The confluence lemma

Lemma (lem:cube-confluence-valuation). Let \(F\) have characteristic 0, \(n\ge1\), and \(\nu\) a degree vector. Put \(\nu'_{r'}=\alpha_{r'}+\beta_{r'}+1\), a degree vector on \(\{0,1\}^{n-1}\), and \(e(\nu)=\sum_{r'}(\alpha_{r'}+1)(\beta_{r'}+1)\). Then:

  • \(a_n^{e(\nu)}\) exactly divides \(\Delta_\nu\);
  • \((\Delta_\nu/a_n^{e(\nu)})\big|_{a_n=0}=c\,\Delta_{\nu'}(a_1,\ldots,a_{n-1})\) for a constant \(c\in\mathbb Q^\times\) depending only on \(\nu\).

For \(n=1\), \(\Delta_{\nu'}\) is the constant determinant of \(1,T,\ldots,T^{\alpha+\beta+1}\).

One-variable normality. For integers \(\alpha,\beta\ge-1\), not both \(-1\), let \(S_{\alpha,\beta}=\{A+Bw:\deg A\le\alpha,\ \deg B\le\beta\}\) with \(w=(1+U)^{1/2}\). Then the orders at \(U=0\) of \(S_{\alpha,\beta}\) are exactly \(0,\ldots,\alpha+\beta+1\).

  • The space has dimension \(\alpha+\beta+2\), so it suffices to exclude a nonzero \(f=A+Bw\) of order \(\ge\alpha+\beta+2\).
  • If \(B=0\), then \(A\) has degree \(\le\alpha\) but order \(>\alpha\), so \(A=0\). If \(A=0\), then \(\operatorname{ord}f=\operatorname{ord}B\le\beta<\alpha+\beta+2\).
  • Otherwise, since \(w'=w/(2(1+U))\), the terms in \(w\) cancel in \[ R=(2(1+U)B'+B)f-2(1+U)Bf'=(2(1+U)B'+B)A-2(1+U)A'B. \] So \(R\) is a polynomial of degree \(\le\alpha+\beta\) and of order \(\ge\operatorname{ord}f-1\ge\alpha+\beta+1\). Hence \(R=0\), that is \((A/B)'/(A/B)=1/(2(1+U))\). In characteristic 0 this gives \((A/B)^2=\gamma(1+U)\) for a constant \(\gamma\), which is impossible since \(\gamma(1+U)\) has odd degree and so is not a square in \(F(U)\).

So \(S_{\alpha,\beta}\) has a basis \(f_0,\ldots,f_{\alpha+\beta+1}\) with \(f_k=U^k\varphi_k(U)\), \(\varphi_k\in F[[U]]\) and \(\varphi_k(0)\ne0\). The coefficients can be taken rational.

Proof of the lemma. Fix \(r'\), with \(\alpha=\alpha_{r'}\), \(\beta=\beta_{r'}\), and replace the rows \(T^jw^{r'}\) (\(j\le\alpha\)) and \(T^jw^{r'}w_n\) (\(j\le\beta\)) by \(g_k=w^{r'}f_k(a_nT)\) (\(k\le\alpha+\beta+1\)).

  • The change of rows. Write \(f_k=\sum_jA_{kj}U^j+\sum_jB_{kj}U^jw\), with \(w_n=w(a_nT)\). Then \(g_k=\sum_jA_{kj}a_n^j\,T^jw^{r'}+\sum_jB_{kj}a_n^j\,T^jw^{r'}w_n\). The matrix taking the old rows of the block to the \(g_k\) is \(M\operatorname{diag}(a_n^j)\), where \(M\) is the invertible rational matrix of the \(f_k\). Its determinant is \(\det M\cdot a_n^{\binom{\alpha+1}2+\binom{\beta+1}2}\).
  • Divisibility. \(g_k=a_n^k\,h_k\) with \(h_k=w^{r'}T^k\varphi_k(a_nT)\in\mathbb Q[a][[T]]\). The block of \(k\)'s contributes \(a_n^{\binom{\alpha+\beta+2}2}\).
  • Determinants. Let \(H^+\) be the matrix of the truncated \(h_k\), over all blocks. Then \[ \prod_{r'}\det M_{r'}\cdot a_n^{\sum_{r'}(\binom{\alpha+1}2+\binom{\beta+1}2)}\,\Delta_\nu=a_n^{\sum_{r'}\binom{\alpha+\beta+2}2}\det H^+. \] Since \(\binom{\alpha+\beta+2}2-\binom{\alpha+1}2-\binom{\beta+1}2=(\alpha+1)(\beta+1)\), this gives \(\Delta_\nu=c'a_n^{e(\nu)}\det H^+\).
  • The limit. At \(a_n=0\), \(h_k=\varphi_k(0)\,T^kw^{r'}\) for \(k=0,\ldots,\nu'_{r'}\). These are, up to nonzero constants, the rows of \(V_{\nu'}\). So \(\det H^+|_{a_n=0}=\pm\prod\varphi_k(0)\cdot\Delta_{\nu'}\).
  • Exactness. \(\Delta_{\nu'}\ne0\) by the generic normality lemma, so the valuation is exactly \(e(\nu)\). \(\square\)

Check. research/tools/bmd_cube_confluence_check.py (sympy, exact) computes \(\Delta_\nu\) for ten degree vectors on \(\{0,1\}^2\), at \(a_1=-5/11\). In each case the \(a_2\)-valuation equals \(e(\nu)\), and the leading coefficient is a nonzero rational multiple of \(\Delta_{\nu'}(a_1)\) (research/results/bmd-r107-confluence/check-n2.txt).

The lemma gives a second proof of the generic normality lemma, by induction on \(n\): \(\Delta_{\nu'}\ne0\) implies \(\Delta_\nu\ne0\). It also reproves \(v_{y_n}(\Delta_{n,d})=E_n(d)\) from the collision-exponent theorem. This covers only the square determinant, not the gcd \(g_m\), and only the divisors \(y_i=0\); the divisors \(y_i=y_j\) still need the transport. For \(\nu_r=\lfloor(d-|r|)/2\rfloor\) (clipped), the blocks with \(m=d-|r'|\ge0\) have \((\alpha,\beta)=(\lfloor m/2\rfloor,\lfloor(m-1)/2\rfloor)\), and the others are empty. So \(e(\nu)=\sum_{|r'|\le d}\lfloor(m+1)^2/4\rfloor=E_n(d)\), and \(\nu'_{r'}=\max(m,-1)\), which is \(U_d\).

The triple collisions of the limit

Corollary (cor:cube-limit-triple-multiplicity). In characteristic 0, for every \(d\ge1\) and \(j\in\{2,3,4\}\), the determinant \(\Delta_U\) of \(U^{(3)}_d\) has multiplicity exactly \(2E_4(d)=4d^2-4d+2\) along \(y_j\). Moreover \[ \Delta_U=c\,y_4^{\,2E_4(d)}\,\Delta^+_U,\qquad \Delta^+_U\big|_{y_4=0}=c'\,\Delta_{\nu'}(4y_2,4y_3),\qquad \nu'_{r'}=\max(2(d-|r'|),-1), \] a determinant on the genus-0 curve \(w_2,w_3\). So the first half of the limit conjecture holds for every \(d\).

Proof. \(U_d=V_\nu(4y_2,4y_3,4y_4)\) with \(\nu_r=d-|r|\), and its \(z\)-basis determinant is \(\Delta_\nu\) up to a power of 2 (reduction theorem, setting). The blocks along \(a_4=4y_4\) have \((\alpha,\beta)=(d-|r'|,\,d-|r'|-1)\), clipped at \(-1\): \(\beta=-1\) when \(|r'|=d\), and \((\alpha,\beta)=(-1,-1)\) when \(|r'|>d\), where \((\alpha+1)(\beta+1)=0=(d-k+1)(d-k)\). So \[ e(\nu)=\sum_{k=0}^{2}\binom2k(d-k+1)(d-k)=d(d+1)+2d(d-1)+(d-1)(d-2)=4d^2-4d+2=2E_4(d), \] using \(E_4(d)=d^2+(d-1)^2\) (collision-exponent theorem). The case \(d=1\) is included: there the last term is 0 and \(e=2\). Also \(\nu'_{r'}=\max(2(d-|r'|),-1)\); for example \(\nu'=(2,0,0,-1)\) at \(d=1\). The other \(y_j\) follow by permuting \(y_2,y_3,y_4\), which permutes the rows. \(\square\)

Check. The multiplicities \(2E_4(d)=10,26,50,82,122,170,226,290\) are those found at every \(y_j\) on the line of route review 15 (limit-n3-d1-9.txt), for \(d=2,\ldots,9\), and 2 at \(d=1\).

What remains. The second half of the limit conjecture: the part of \(\Delta_U\) prime to \(y_j\) and \(y_i-y_j\) is squarefree. The corollary identifies its restriction to the triple sides \(y_j=0\), up to powers of \(y_2\), \(y_3\) and \(y_2-y_3\): it is the non-collision part of \(\Delta_{\nu'}\) up to such powers, since the multiplicity of \(\Delta_U\) along \(y_2=y_3\) is not computed. Here \(\nu'\) is \(\nu'=(2d,2d-2,2d-2,2d-4)\), a Hermite–Padé determinant for \(1,w_2,w_3,w_2w_3\) on a conic. Applying the lemma once more, \(\Delta_{\nu'}\) has valuation \(\sum_k\binom1k(2d-2k+1)(2d-2k-1)\) at \(y_3=0\) for \(d\ge2\) (3 at \(d=1\), from the clipped vector), with leading coefficient a monomial in \(y_2\). The restriction argument of the reduction theorem now runs in \(\mathbb P^2\). There the six collision lines form a complete quadrangle whose sides are of two kinds: the triple sides \(y_j=0\) and the double-double sides \(y_i=y_j\).

  • If the non-collision part of \(\Delta_U\) restricts on every side to a power of the diagonal form times a squarefree part, then the quadrangle lemma excludes a repeated factor. A factor of degree \(\mu\) with that restriction is a curve meeting each side only at its diagonal point.
  • The triple sides alone do not suffice: the conic \(\sum y_j^2-2\sum_{i<j}y_iy_j\) meets each coordinate side only at its diagonal point, doubly.
  • The double-double sides need a confluence along \(y_i=y_j\) for \(U_d\), which is not a transport of \(U_d\) to itself. The Möbius change sends \(U_d\) to a different degree vector.

General statement. lem:cube-confluence-valuation, for every \(n\ge1\) and every degree vector in characteristic 0. cor:cube-limit-triple-multiplicity, for every \(d\ge1\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the generic normality lemma, the collision-exponent theorem, the reduction theorem and the limit conjecture, and the review's limit data. A claim search (confluence, merged square root, one-variable Padé normality, valuation, leading coefficient) found no earlier version. A fresh-context referee checked every step and found nothing that breaks a stated result. It also checked the lemma exactly with sympy for \(n=2\): for ten degree vectors, including entries \(-1\), and two values of \(a_1\), the \(a_2\)-valuation is \(e(\nu)\), and the leading coefficient is a fixed nonzero rational multiple of \(\Delta_{\nu'}(a_1)\). Its corrections are made: the order bound when \(\beta=-1\); the non-square \(\gamma(1+U)\); clipping of degree vectors, with the edge blocks at \(d=1\); the scope of the reproof (square determinant, divisors \(y_i=0\)); the range \(d\ge2\) of the valuation formula for \(\Delta_{\nu'}\); and the restriction to the triple sides, which holds only up to powers of \(y_2\), \(y_3\) and \(y_2-y_3\).

Assessment. The confluence lemma is the right general tool for these determinants. It gives the exact valuation along any merged branch point and identifies the leading coefficient, and it reproves both the generic normality lemma and the collision exponents in one line each. With it, the first half of the limit conjecture holds for every \(d\), and only squarefreeness of the non-collision part of \(\Delta_U\) remains. That part will need restrictions to both kinds of side, as the conic example shows. The next step is the double-double sides of \(U_d\), through the transported degree vector, and then the genus-0 determinant \(\Delta_{\nu'}\), whose non-collision part governs the triple sides.

26 September 2026 — Squarefreeness holds for monotone degree vectors and fails for others: the determinant family behind the dimension-4 boundary

Finite check: the non-collision part of Δ_ν is squarefree for all 194 monotone and 1093 of 1097 non-monotone degree vectors with n = 2, entries ≤ 4, and for 52 with n = 3; four non-monotone vectors have the factor (3a₁+a₂)³. Cycle bmd-r108. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The dimension-4 boundary law reduces, for every \(d\), to squarefreeness of the non-collision part of one determinant, \(\Delta_U\) (reduction theorem, triple multiplicity). The confluence lemma relates determinants of different degree vectors: \(\Delta_U\) restricts to \(\Delta_{\nu'}\) on genus 0. An induction on \(n\) would need squarefreeness for a whole family of degree vectors closed under confluence. Is the non-collision part of \(\Delta_\nu\) squarefree for every degree vector \(\nu\), or only for a subclass? The test ends with a class where every tested vector passes and outside which failures occur, or with a failure inside the cube's own vectors.

Setting. As in the generic normality lemma: \(V_\nu=\bigoplus_rw^rF[T]_{\le\nu_r}\) and \(\Delta_\nu(a)\). The collision forms are \(a_i\) and \(a_i-a_j\). Call \(\nu\) monotone if \(\nu_r\ge\nu_{r'}\) whenever \(r\le r'\) coordinatewise. Degree vectors have entries \(\ge-1\); the cube's vectors \(\lfloor(d-|r|)/2\rfloor\) and \(d-|r|\), both clipped at \(-1\), are monotone. Clipping matters: \(\lfloor(d-|r|)/2\rfloor\) falls below \(-1\) when \(d-|r|\le-3\).

Monotone vectors behave well in two ways.

  • Closed under confluence. If \(\nu\) is monotone, so is \(\nu'_{r'}=\nu_{(r',0)}+\nu_{(r',1)}+1\): for \(r'\le r''\) both summands decrease.
  • The \(z\)-basis. For monotone \(\nu\), \(V_\nu\) is spanned by \(T^jz^r\) (\(j\le\nu_r\)), since \(z^r\) is triangular in the \(w^{r'}\), \(r'\le r\).

The test

Kernel. research/tools/bmd_cube_nu_squarefree.cpp (FLINT) takes a list of degree vectors. For each, it computes \(\Delta_\nu\) in the \(w\)-basis along the line \(a=u+tv\) over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\) with nmod_poly_mat_det, and checks the full homogeneous degree. It removes each collision root with its full multiplicity, and tests the rest \(R\) with \(\gcd(R,R')\). research/tools/bmd_cube_nu_specs.py generates the lists, research/tools/bmd_cube_nu_tally.py tallies the outcomes by monotonicity, and research/tools/bmd_cube_nu_factor.py factors \(\Delta_\nu\) exactly over \(\mathbb Q\) (sympy) for \(n=2\).

Validation. For \(U_2\) and \(U_4\) (the \(n=3\) vectors \(d-|r|\)), the kernel reproduces the \(z\)-basis limit data of route review 15, from an independent implementation in the \(w\)-basis:

  • degrees 60 and 340;
  • collision multiplicities 10, 7 and 50, 43;
  • squarefree rests of degree 9 and 61.

The exact factorizations over \(\mathbb Q\) agree with the kernel on the four \(n=2\) vectors factored.

Finite check (check:cube-degree-vector-squarefree). Results are in research/results/bmd-r108-degree-vectors/.

  • \(n=2\), every \(\nu\in\{-1,\ldots,4\}^4\) with \(N\ge2\) (1291 vectors, squarefree-n2.txt). Every determinant has full degree. The rest is squarefree for all 194 monotone vectors and for 1093 of the 1097 non-monotone ones.
  • The four exceptions are \((3,0,1,1)\), \((3,3,4,1)\) and their images under exchanging \(a_1,a_2\), indexed \((\nu_{00},\nu_{10},\nu_{01},\nu_{11})\). Over \(\mathbb Q\) (factor-n2.txt):
    • \(\Delta_{(3,0,1,1)}=c\,a_1^8a_2^{10}(a_1-a_2)^7(3a_1+a_2)^3\);
    • \(\Delta_{(3,3,4,1)}\) has \((3a_1+a_2)^3\) times a squarefree cubic.
    For comparison, the monotone \((3,2,2,1)\) gives the simple factors \((a_1+3a_2)(3a_1+a_2)\).
  • \(n=3\) (52 vectors, squarefree-n3.txt): \(d-|r|\) and \(\lfloor(d-|r|)/2\rfloor\) for \(1\le d\le6\), and 40 random vectors in \(\{-1,\ldots,5\}^8\) (seed 108). All are squarefree: 13 monotone and 39 non-monotone.

A squarefree rest of full degree on one line over one prime certifies squarefreeness over \(\mathbb Q\) when the collision multiplicities modulo \(p\) equal those over \(\mathbb Q\), as in the boundary certificate. The multiplicities along \(a_i=0\) are known over \(\mathbb Q\) from the confluence lemma, and the kernel's \(a_i\) multiplicities equal \(e(\nu)\) for every tested vector and every \(i\) (2738 cases, checked by the referee). Only the multiplicities along \(a_i=a_j\) stay uncertified. So for general \(\nu\) these results are strong evidence, not certificates.

Refutation of the unrestricted statement. "The non-collision part of \(\Delta_\nu\) is squarefree for every degree vector" is false: \(\nu=(3,0,1,1)\) gives \((3a_1+a_2)^3\), exactly over \(\mathbb Q\). The branch points are \(x_i=-1/a_i\) and \(\infty\), and the marked point is \(T=0\). The factor is the configuration \(x_2=-x_1/3\), where, by the Wronskian argument of the doubled-factor proposition (which applies to every \(V_\nu\)), \(p_0\) has weight 3 for this non-monotone series at a general point of the factor: the flow is transversal there, since \(X(3a_1+a_2)=3a_1^2+a_2^2=12a_1^2\ne0\) on \(a_2=-3a_1\). Directly, at \(a=(1,-3)\) and \((2,-6)\) the orders at \(T=0\) are \(0,\ldots,6,8,10\), of weight 3, and at \((1,-5)\) the weight is 0 (referee's computation).

Conjecture (conj:cube-monotone-squarefree). In characteristic 0, for every \(n\ge1\) and every monotone degree vector \(\nu\), the part of \(\Delta_\nu\) prime to the collision forms is squarefree. For \(\nu=d-|r|\) with \(n=3\), together with the triple-multiplicity corollary, it gives the whole limit conjecture, and with the reduction theorem the dimension-4 boundary law for every \(d\). For \(\nu=\lfloor(d-|r|)/2\rfloor\) and every \(n\ge2\), \(d\ge1\), it is the boundary squarefreeness conjecture, since \(\Delta_\nu(4y)\) is the \(z\)-basis \(\Delta_{n,d}\) up to a sign and a power of 2. Evidence: the finite check.

Towards a proof by induction. Monotonicity is preserved by confluence, so \(\Delta_\nu|_{a_n=0}\) (after removing \(a_n^{e(\nu)}\)) is \(\Delta_{\nu'}\) with \(\nu'\) monotone, whose non-collision part is squarefree by induction. The reduction theorem's argument then needs two more ingredients:

  • the exact multiplicities of \(\Delta_\nu\) along the collision divisors, so that no triple form survives in the restriction;
  • the restrictions to the other collision divisors \(a_i=a_j\).

Those are Möbius transports. By the computation of the confluence entry for \(U_d\), we expect them to move monotone spaces to spaces with prescribed vanishing at a branch point. So the induction should run over a larger class of isotypic Riemann–Roch data: for each character \(r\), a pole order at \(\infty\) and vanishing orders at the \(n\) finite branch fibres. We expect this class to be closed under the \(S_{n+1}\) permutations of branch points and under confluence; neither closure is proved. A further care: a non-collision factor can restrict to a collision form, as \(3a_1+a_2\) becomes \(3a_1\) at \(a_2=0\). The next step is to set up that class, prove the confluence lemma for it, and find the condition replacing monotonicity.

General statement. conj:cube-monotone-squarefree, for every \(n\ge1\) and every monotone degree vector in characteristic 0. The finite check tests it, and refutes the unrestricted version.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the confluence lemma, the generic normality lemma, the reduction theorem and the limit data of route review 15. A claim search (degree vector, squarefree, monotone, Hermite–Padé) found no earlier version. A fresh-context referee checked the kernel against the definitions and every number against the output files. It found nothing that breaks a stated result. It confirmed independently that the \(a_i\) multiplicities equal \(e(\nu)\) in all 2738 cases, the weight 3 on the factor \(3a_1+a_2\), and \(x_2=-x_1/3\). Its corrections are made: clipping of the floor vectors; the certification status (only the \(a_i=a_j\) multiplicities uncertified); transversality for the weight; the precise relation of the conjecture to the limit and boundary conjectures; and the two closure properties marked as expectations.

Assessment. The squarefreeness behind the dimension-4 boundary is not a special property of the cube's vectors. It holds across all 207 monotone vectors tested, with \(n=2,3\), and fails only outside that class. So the right statement is about a natural family closed under confluence, and a proof by induction on the number of branch points is now the plan. The failure \((3a_1+a_2)^3\) shows that some structural hypothesis is necessary. Whether monotonicity is the right one, or only a sufficient shadow of a Riemann–Roch condition, is the next question.

26 September 2026 — Route review of the cube: the boundary rests on simple pluricanonical Weierstrass points of Humbert curves; the middle range is next

Route review: the monotone squarefreeness conjecture survives 1248 degree vectors at larger degree; for n = 4 it is a simple-Weierstrass-point statement for the d-canonical series of Humbert curves. Next: the middle range of dimension 4. Cycle bmd-r109. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

The line's general claim. The per-order function on \(\{0,1\}^n\) in characteristic \(\ne2\) is determined by the thresholds \(\ell_0(h,m)\), the initial degrees of the threshold ideals (threshold-ideal lemma). Dimension 3 is solved over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\). For \(n\ge4\) the claim to establish is a law for the thresholds.

What the goal needs. Open statement 3 for \(n\ge4\): the thresholds at the boundary \(m=N_{2,n}(d)\), in the middle range, and at order zero. Also open statement 2, small primes. Since route review 15, three cycles worked on the boundary:

  • the reduction theorem, with the quadrangle lemma, reduces the boundary law for all \(d\) to a statement about the collision limit;
  • the confluence lemma proves half of that statement for every \(d\) (corollary);
  • the remaining half became one case of a conjecture for all monotone degree vectors (monotone squarefreeness), which fails without monotonicity.

Falsification attempt

The monotone conjecture was pushed to larger degrees, with research/tools/bmd_cube_nu_monotone_specs.py and the kernel bmd_cube_nu_squarefree.cpp on the lines of the previous entry, over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\) (research/results/bmd-r109-route-review/).

  • \(n=2\), every monotone vector with entries in \(\{-1,\ldots,8\}\), 1208 vectors with \(N\) up to 36 (squarefree-mono-n2.txt). All have full degree and a squarefree non-collision part.
  • \(n=3\), 40 random monotone vectors with entries up to 4 and \(N\) up to 32 (seed 109, squarefree-mono-n3.txt). All squarefree.

With the previous entry, 1261 distinct monotone vectors have now been tested (1208 with \(n=2\), which include the earlier 194, and 53 with \(n=3\)), with no failure. The prediction could have failed at any of them, as it does for the non-monotone \((3,0,1,1)\).

The objects, named. For \(n=4\) the fibre curve \(C:w_i^2=1+4y_iT\) is a \((\mathbb Z/2)^4\)-cover of the line branched at five points: a classical Humbert curve, of genus 5. Its divisor \(H_\infty\) is canonical. Indeed \(V_1\subseteq L(H_\infty)\) has dimension \(N_{2,4}(1)=5=g\), and a divisor of degree \(8=2g-2\) with \(h^0=g\) is canonical by Riemann–Roch. For \(d\ge2\), \(V_d\subseteq L(dH_\infty)=H^0(\omega_C^{\otimes d})\), and both have dimension \(8d-4=(2d-1)(g-1)\). So \(V_d\) is the \(d\)-canonical series. By the doubled-factor proposition, the boundary squarefreeness conjecture for \(n=4\) says the following: for a general member of the family, the \(d\)-canonical Weierstrass points away from the ramification points are all simple. For a general curve of genus \(g\), the analogous statement underlies Cukierman and Fong's computation of the divisor of \(n\)-canonical Weierstrass points. The Humbert curves are a special 2-dimensional family in \(\mathcal M_5\), so that does not apply directly.

Assessment of this line

At the boundary the line is strong in its results and stuck at one lemma.

  • Proved in characteristic 0. For \(2\le d\le9\), \(\ell_0(d+1,8d-4)=10d^2-10d-5\), and the collision structure is known for every \(d\).
  • Reduced for every \(d\). What remains is one precise conjecture, with 1261 passing monotone vectors and a family closed under confluence.
  • Stuck. A proof needs an induction over a class of spaces closed under Möbius transports, not yet defined. It is a genuine Weierstrass-point problem, simplicity of pluricanonical Weierstrass points on a special family, where the general-curve theory does not apply.

The middle range, between the boundary and order zero, has had no cycle since the symmetry theorem. It is the larger part of the per-order function, and its modules are not free. That is now the higher-risk item. The next cycles should move there, and keep the boundary conjecture as a target for a Weierstrass-point source.

Outside leads

  • Higher Weierstrass points on the universal curve (Cukierman and Fong, as cited in Amini–Gierczak–Richman, arXiv 2303.07729; the primary source is not read). They compute the divisor of weight-1 \(n\)-canonical Weierstrass points in the universal curve. The same computation on the Humbert family, a surface in \(\mathcal M_5\) with its \(S_5\) action, would count the Weierstrass locus. Comparing it with \(\deg\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\) would test simplicity. This targets the boundary conjecture. It breaks if the restriction to the family acquires excess components. Test. Passed (identification): \(H_\infty\) is canonical and \(V_d=H^0(\omega_C^{\otimes d})\), with \(8d-4=(2d-1)(g-1)\) for \(d\ge2\), as shown above.
  • Wronskians of polynomial spaces and the Shapiro conjecture (Mukhin–Tarasov–Varchenko, Annals 170, 2009). For \(n=2\) the curve is rational, \(V_\nu\) becomes a space of polynomials in a uniformizer, and \(\Delta_\nu\) is its Wronskian evaluated along the family. The theorem controls spaces whose Wronskian has only real roots. This targets the monotone conjecture for \(n=2\). It breaks if the roots are not real. Test. Not run: as a separate test. The real-root test in the first bridge below decides applicability, and it shows non-real roots for 8 of 45 small monotone vectors. So the theorem does not apply to all of them directly.
  • Tropical Weierstrass points and their weights (Amini–Gierczak–Richman, arXiv 2303.07729). Limits of Weierstrass points in a degeneration carry weights on the tropical curve. The iterated confluence of the confluence lemma is a maximal degeneration of the Humbert curve. There the valuation along each merged branch point is known exactly, and simplicity could be read off the limit weights. This targets the monotone conjecture. It breaks if the limit weights do not separate points. Test. Not run: it needs the metric graph of the iterated degeneration and its divisor theory, which is not a cheap computation.

Absurd bridges

  • The Lee–Yang circle theorem (statistical mechanics: Lee and Yang, Phys. Rev. 87, 1952). Translation: the non-collision part of \(\Delta_\nu(1,x)\) (\(n=2\), \(x=a_2/a_1\)) is a partition function in the fugacity \(x\). A Lee–Yang-type theorem would put its zeros on a line or circle, and zeros localized on a real ray interlace and are simple. Test. Falsified: for the 45 monotone vectors with entries \(\le2\) and \(N\ge3\), computed exactly with sympy (research/tools/bmd_cube_nu_real_roots.py, real-roots-n2.txt), 8 have non-real roots, for example \((2,0,1,0)\) with a rest of degree 2 and no real root.
  • Level-spacing statistics of quantum chaos (Wigner surmise; Bohigas–Giannoni–Schmit, Phys. Rev. Lett. 52, 1984). Translation: the Weierstrass points on the curve \(C_a\), the roots in \(t\) of \(\Delta_\nu(a/(1+at))\), are the "spectrum" of the family. Level repulsion, a vanishing density of small spacings, is the statistical form of simplicity. A family with that statistics has no divisor of double points. Test. Not run: spacing statistics need real or complex roots of large degree over \(\mathbb C\), while the kernels compute over finite fields, and the floating-point determinants are ill-conditioned at these degrees.

Bridge follow-up

  • Chip-firing on a cycle. Not worked. Follow-up. Continuing: it now joins the tropical lead above, since both read the degeneration's skeleton.
  • Odd–even staggering. Not worked. Follow-up. Continuing: the middle range, where it applies, is the next target.
  • The non-crossing rule. Its content is now the monotone squarefreeness conjecture, tested on 1261 monotone vectors in this cycle and the last. Follow-up. Continuing.
  • Weierstrass semigroups of AG codes. Follow-up. Closed: it gave the ordinary canonical semigroup of \(p_0\), which is now part of the canonical identification above. The codes add no tool for the higher series \(V_d\).

Lead follow-up

  • Riemann–Roch and Riemann–Hurwitz for \(n\ge4\). Follow-up. Closed: it has given everything it can. \(V_d\) is the \(d\)-canonical series of the Humbert curve (above), the Wronskian weights came from it, and the open question is now simplicity, which Riemann–Roch does not decide.
  • Buchsbaum–Eisenbud acyclicity. Not worked. Follow-up. Continuing: it is the tool for the non-free middle range, the next target.
  • General Weierstrass points are simple. Developed into the Humbert pluricanonical formulation and the monotone conjecture. Follow-up. Continuing, with the Cukierman–Fong lead above.
  • Limit linear series along collisions. Developed in the reduction entry and the confluence entry. Follow-up. Developed.

Next step

On the highest-risk item, the middle range of open statement 3 in dimension 4, start one step past the boundary, at \(m=N+1\) with \(h=d+1\). The solution module there has rank 2. By Cramer's rule its elements come from the maximal minors of \(N\times(N+1)\) submatrices of the \(N\times(N+2)\) constraint matrix. So \(\ell_0(d+1,N+1)\) is the initial degree of an ideal generated by explicit minors divided by their gcds. The collision and confluence machinery computes the exponents of those minors. The recorded value \(\ell_0(3,13)=12\) at \(d=2\), against 15 at the boundary, is the first test.

26 September 2026 — Past the boundary the threshold ideals have height two: no collision or other divisor divides them once the boundary gcd is collision-only

Working proof in characteristic 0: for m > N_{2,n}(h−1), every height-one prime containing I^{(h)}_m divides g^nc_{n,h−1}; so all these ideals have height ≥ 2 for n = 3, and for n = 4 with 3 ≤ h ≤ 10. Residue duality holds in every dimension. Cycle bmd-r110. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. Route review 16 moved the line to the middle range of dimension 4, the thresholds \(\ell_0(h,m)\) with \(m\) between the boundary \(N=N_{2,n}(h-1)\) and order zero. The recorded row for \(h=3\) is \(15,12,11,6,5,2,2,0\) at \(m=12,\ldots,19\). The first step is \(m=N+1\), where the solution module has rank 2.

  • What does the threshold ideal look like there?
  • Is its least-degree generator a product of collision forms and a known invariant, such as \(\prod\ell_D\cdot Q\) of degree \(10+2=12\)?
  • Or is it something else?

The test ends with a structure theorem for these ideals, or with a generator that contradicts it. This cycle develops the Buchsbaum–Eisenbud lead of route review 14 (lead 2), on the structure of the non-free middle-range modules.

Setting. As in the threshold-ideal lemma: \(R=F[y_1,\ldots,y_n]\), \(d=h-1\), \(N=N_{2,n}(d)\), and \(A_m\) is the \(N\times(m+1)\) constraint matrix (coefficients of \(T^0,\ldots,T^m\) in the basis of \(V_d\)). \(I^{(h)}_m=\{W_m:A_mW=0,\ W\in R^{m+1}\}\). Also \(g_{n,d}=c\prod_D\ell_D^{E_n(d)}g^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}\) (collision-exponent theorem).

The height of the middle-range threshold ideals

Proposition (prop:cube-middle-threshold-height). Let \(F\) have characteristic 0, \(n\ge2\), \(h\ge2\), \(d=h-1\) and \(m>N\). Every height-one prime of \(R\) containing \(I^{(h)}_m\) is a prime factor of \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}\). So:

  • when \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}=1\), \(I^{(h)}_m\) is either \(R\) or an ideal of height \(\ge2\);
  • this holds for \(n=3\) and every \(h\), by the boundary theorem;
  • it holds for \(n=4\) and \(3\le h\le10\), by the dimension-4 corollary (\(2\le d\le9\)).

Proof. Split \(A_m=[A'\mid a]\), where \(A'\) has the columns \(0,\ldots,m-1\) and \(a\) is the column of \(T^m\).

  • A colon ideal. \(W\) is a solution exactly when \(A'(W_0,\ldots,W_{m-1})=-W_ma\). So \(I^{(h)}_m=(\operatorname{Im}A':_Ra)\), the annihilator of the class of \(a\) in \(\operatorname{coker}A'\). Colon ideals commute with localization and completion, which are flat. Completion is faithfully flat over the local ring, so the colon ideal is the unit ideal in \(R_{(y_1)}\) exactly when it is in its completion.
  • Other primes. Let \(\pi\) be a height-one prime not dividing \(g_{m-1}\), the gcd of the maximal minors of \(A'\). Then some maximal minor of \(A'\) is a unit in \(R_\pi\), so \(A'\) maps onto \(R_\pi^N\) and \(I_\pi=R_\pi\). The minors of \(A_N\) are among those of \(A'\), since \(m-1\ge N\), so \(g_{m-1}\mid g_N=g_{n,d}\). Also \(g_{m-1}\ne0\), since \(\pm\Delta_{n,d}\ne0\) is one of these minors (characteristic 0). This excludes \(I=0\).
  • The collision divisor \(y_1=0\). Work over \(O=F'[[\varepsilon]]\), \(y_1=\varepsilon\), as in the collision limit lemma. By its part 2, the rows of \(A_m\) (the basis of \(V\)) are \(S\,D\) times the rows of the saturated lattice \(\Lambda\). Here \(S\in GL_N(O)\), and \(D=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,\varepsilon^{d-e(P)},\ldots)\). So \(A'=SDA'_\Lambda\) and \(a=SDa_\Lambda\), with \(A'_\Lambda\) and \(a_\Lambda\) over \(O\). Modulo \(\varepsilon\), \(A'_\Lambda\) is the truncation of a basis of the limit space \(U_d\) to \(T^0,\ldots,T^{m-1}\). \(U_d\) is normal by the generic normality lemma, and \(m-1\ge N-1\), so this truncation has rank \(N\). By Nakayama, \(\operatorname{Im}A'_\Lambda=O^N\). Hence \(a=SDa_\Lambda\in SD\,O^N=\operatorname{Im}A'\), and \(I\) is the unit ideal locally at \(y_1=0\).
  • Other collision divisors. The symmetry theorem states, for every \(n\), \(d\) and \(m\) over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\), that \(I^{(d+1)}_m\) is stable under \(S_{n+1}\). That group permutes the collision divisors transitively.

So a height-one prime containing \(I\) is not a collision form, and divides \(g_{n,d}\), hence \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}\). \(\square\)

The boundary \(m=N\) is different. There \(A'\) is square with determinant \(\pm\Delta_{n,d}\), and \(I=(\Delta_{n,d}/g_{n,d})\) is principal, generated by the non-collision part. When \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n,d}=1\), one step past the boundary that divisor disappears. What remains is an ideal of height \(\ge2\): in \(\mathbb P^{n-1}\), a locus of codimension \(\ge2\), possibly empty (for \(n=2\) it is empty). A factor of \(\Delta/g\) that also divides \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}\) could persist. So middle-range thresholds are initial degrees of codimension-2 schemes, not degrees of divisors.

The first step in dimension 4

Finite check (check:cube-dimension-four-first-step-generator). On \(\{0,1\}^4\) over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), at \(h=3\), \(m=13=N+1\): research/tools/bmd_cube_thresholds_m2.m2 in incremental mode finds no syzygy at all in excess \(\le11\). In excess 12 it finds exactly one syzygy, a minimal generator, whose top coordinate is a form \(F_{12}\) of degree 12, irreducible over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\) (157 s, research/results/bmd-r110-middle-range/m13-top.txt). research/tools/bmd_cube_top_symmetry.py checks that \(F_{12}\) is invariant up to sign under the transpositions of \(y_1,\ldots,y_4\) and under \(\psi\), so it is \(S_5\)-semi-invariant (m13-top-symmetry.txt). The recorded global run at \(m=13\) (dimension-4 entry) found five generators of the rank-2 module, of excesses 12, 13, 14, 14, 15.

So over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\) the guess \(\prod_D\ell_D\cdot Q\) is refuted: the degree-12 generator is irreducible. This is consistent with the proposition, which is proved in characteristic 0: a threshold ideal of height \(\ge2\) contains elements outside the collision primes. The irreducibility of \(F_{12}\) is a fact modulo 32003, not established in characteristic 0.

Residue duality in every dimension

To identify the codimension-2 loci, the residue duality lemma of dimension 3 extends to every \(n\). For \(n\ge3\), the fibre curve \(C\) (\(w_i^2=1+4y_iT\), \(y\) with distinct nonzero entries) has genus \(g=1+2^{n-2}(n-3)\). Its canonical class is \(K\sim(n-3)H_\infty\): the map by \(1,w_1,\ldots,w_n\) is a complete intersection of \(n-1\) quadrics in \(\mathbb P^n\), so \(K=\mathcal O(-n-1+2(n-1))=\mathcal O(n-3)\).

Lemma (lem:cube-residue-duality-all-n). Let \(F\) be algebraically closed of characteristic \(\ne2\), \(n\ge3\), \(d>n-3\), and \(y\) with distinct nonzero entries. Suppose \(A_m(y)\) has rank \(N\), for some \(m\ge N-1\). Then:

  • \(\eta\mapsto(\operatorname{Res}_{p_0}(T^c\eta))_{c\le m}\) is an isomorphism from the differentials with \(\operatorname{div}\eta\ge dH_\infty-(m+1)p_0\) onto \(\ker A_m(y)\);
  • equivalently, the solutions are the Laurent tails of \(\varphi\omega_0\), \(\varphi\in L((n-3-d)H_\infty+(m+1)p_0)\), where \(\omega_0\) has divisor \((n-3)H_\infty\);
  • \(W_0=0\) always, and \(W_m\ne0\) exactly when \(\varphi\) has pole order \(m+1\).

Proof. As in dimension 3, with three changes.

  • \(V_d=L(dH_\infty)\). The inclusion holds by pole orders. Both sides have dimension \(2^{n-1}d+1-g\): \(N_{2,n}(d)\) by the collision limit lemma's count, and \(h^0(dH_\infty)\) by Riemann–Roch, since \(\deg dH_\infty>2g-2\) when \(d>n-3\).
  • Injectivity: if all residues vanish, \(\eta\) is regular at \(p_0\), so \(\eta/\omega_0\in L((n-3-d)H_\infty)=0\).
  • Dimensions: \(D=(n-3-d)H_\infty+(m+1)p_0\) has degree \(m+1-N-1+g\). By Riemann–Roch, \(h^0(D)=m+1-N+h^0(dH_\infty-(m+1)p_0)\), and the last term is 0 because \(A_m(y)\) has rank \(N\).

So both sides have dimension \(m+1-N\), and the residue theorem gives the inclusion. The claim about \(W_0\) is the residue theorem for \(\eta\), which has its only pole at \(p_0\). \(\square\)

At the boundary this is Riemann–Roch's form of the Weierstrass condition. \(\Delta_{n,d}\) vanishes where \((n-3-d)H_\infty+Np_0\), of degree \(g-1\), is effective, that is, on the pullback of the theta divisor \(W_{g-1}\). Off the collision divisors this is the zero set of \(\Delta/g\) when \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}=1\). One step past the boundary, the proof gives one inclusion: off the collision divisors, \(V(I^{(d+1)}_{N+1})\) lies inside \(\{\operatorname{rank}A_N(y)<N\}=\{h^0(dH_\infty-(N+1)p_0)\ge1\}\). That is a condition on a class of degree \(g-2\), of expected codimension 2 (\(W_{g-2}\) inside \(\operatorname{Pic}^{g-2}\)), in line with the proposition.

General statement. prop:cube-middle-threshold-height, for every \(n\ge2\), \(h\ge2\) and \(m>N_{2,n}(h-1)\) in characteristic 0. lem:cube-residue-duality-all-n, for every \(n\ge3\) and \(d>n-3\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the threshold-ideal lemma, the collision limit lemma, the generic normality lemma, the collision-exponent theorem, the dimension-3 residue duality lemma, and the symmetry theorem's statement. A claim search (height, colon, middle range, residue duality) found only the dimension-3 duality, which the lemma extends. A fresh-context referee checked:

  • the colon ideal and both localizations;
  • the genus, the canonical class via smooth diagonal quadrics, and the count \(N_{2,n}(d)=2^{n-1}d+1-g\) (exactly for \(d\ge n-2\));
  • the Riemann–Roch count, injectivity and \(W_0\);
  • the M2 output, and a rerun of the symmetry script.

It found nothing that breaks a stated result. Its corrections are made:

  • faithful flatness of completion;
  • \(g_{m-1}\ne0\);
  • the exact form of the symmetry theorem used;
  • the range \(3\le h\le10\) for \(n=4\);
  • the boundary remark qualified by \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}=1\), with codimension \(\ge2\), possibly empty;
  • the theta remark stated for \(\Delta\), and only one inclusion claimed one step past the boundary;
  • the stronger "no syzygy at all" in excess \(\le11\), and irreducibility over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\) only;
  • the symmetry output saved, with the script's handling of a negative constant factor fixed.

Assessment. The middle range has a first structural result. Once the boundary gcd consists of collision forms alone, every threshold ideal past the boundary has height at least 2. So thresholds there are initial degrees of codimension-2 loci, and the dimension-3 product mechanism has no divisorial counterpart in dimension 4. The first generator, of degree 12 at \(m=13\), is an irreducible \(S_5\)-semi-invariant, not a product. Residue duality now holds in every dimension. It identifies the relevant loci as Brill–Noether-type conditions on the fibre curve: the effectivity of \(dH_\infty-(m+1)p_0\) and its refinements. The next step is to compute the degree-12 locus and see whether it is cut out by such a condition, with the saturated ideal of the codimension-2 locus as the candidate for the whole threshold ideal.

26 September 2026 — One step past the boundary the threshold ideal is saturated, and in dimension 4 it cuts out the rank-drop curve: a degree-120 curve on a unique surface of degree 12

Working proof for n ≥ 3: I^{(d+1)}_{N+1} is a saturated ideal. Finite check over F₃₂₀₀₃: on {0,1}⁴ at d = 2 its plane section is the 120 points where the boundary matrix drops rank; conjectured for all d. Cycle bmd-r111. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. Past the boundary the threshold ideals have height \(\ge2\) when \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}=1\) (height proposition). By residue duality, off the collision hyperplanes, the zero set of \(I^{(d+1)}_{N+1}\) lies in the rank-drop locus \(Z_d=\{\operatorname{rank}A_N(y)<N\}=\{h^0(dH_\infty-(N+1)p_0)\ge1\}\). The threshold \(\ell_0(d+1,N+1)\) would be computable from geometry if two things held:

  • the threshold ideal is the whole ideal of its zero scheme;
  • that zero scheme is the closure \(\bar Z_d\) of \(Z_d\) off the collisions.

Then \(\ell_0\) would be the least degree of a hypersurface through \(\bar Z_d\). In dimension 4 at \(d=2\), is the degree-12 generator \(F_{12}\) of the previous entry the unique surface of least degree through that curve? The test ends with an equality of ideals on a plane section, or with a component of the zero scheme inside the collision hyperplanes, as in dimension 3.

The first step is saturated

Proposition (prop:cube-first-step-saturated). Let \(n\ge3\), \(d\ge1\), \(N=N_{2,n}(d)\), over a field where \(\Delta_{n,d}\ne0\). By the determinant criterion this is \(\mathrm{Ord}_n(d)=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}\), the hypothesis of Part 2 of the threshold-ideal lemma; it holds in characteristic 0 and for \(p>2^{n-1}d\) (characteristic-0 theorem, large-characteristic theorem). Then \(I=I^{(d+1)}_{N+1}\) is a saturated homogeneous ideal (possibly \(R\)): \(R/I\) has depth \(\ge1\), and \(I\) is the ideal of all forms vanishing on the subscheme \(V(I)\subseteq\mathbb P^{n-1}\).

Proof. Let \(\mathfrak m\) be the irrelevant ideal of \(R=F[y_1,\ldots,y_n]\), and let \(\mathrm{Sol}\subseteq R^{N+2}\) be the kernel of \(A_{N+1}\), graded as in the threshold-ideal lemma.

  • The sequence. The top-coordinate map \(t:\mathrm{Sol}\to R\) has image \(I\). Its kernel is the set of solutions with \(W_{N+1}=0\), which is the boundary solution module at \(m=N\). By Part 2 of the threshold-ideal lemma, which applies since \(\Delta_{n,d}\ne0\), that module is free of rank 1, generated by the primitive vector \(G=M/g\). Its top coordinate at \(m=N\) has degree \(\deg\Delta_{n,d}-\deg g\), so as a solution at \(m=N+1\) it has excess \(e=\deg\Delta_{n,d}-\deg g-1\). This gives an exact sequence of graded modules \(0\to R(-e)\to\mathrm{Sol}\to I\to0\).
  • Depth of \(\mathrm{Sol}\). \(\mathrm{Sol}\) is the kernel of a map between free modules. The exact sequence \(0\to\mathrm{Sol}\to R^{N+2}\to\operatorname{Im}A_{N+1}\to0\), with \(\operatorname{Im}A_{N+1}\subseteq R^N\) torsion-free (depth \(\ge1\)), gives \(\operatorname{depth}_{\mathfrak m}\mathrm{Sol}\ge2\) by the depth lemma. So \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(\mathrm{Sol})=H^1_{\mathfrak m}(\mathrm{Sol})=0\).
  • Local cohomology. \(H^1_{\mathfrak m}(R)=0\) for \(n\ge2\), and \(H^2_{\mathfrak m}(R)=0\) needs \(n\ge3\). The long exact sequence gives \(H^1_{\mathfrak m}(\mathrm{Sol})\to H^1_{\mathfrak m}(I)\to H^2_{\mathfrak m}(R(-e))\), so \(H^1_{\mathfrak m}(I)=0\). From \(0\to I\to R\to R/I\to0\) and \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(R)=0\), \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(R/I)\) embeds in \(H^1_{\mathfrak m}(I)=0\). So \(R/I\) has no \(\mathfrak m\)-torsion, which is saturation. \(\square\)

The argument needs a free kernel. So it applies at \(m=N+1\), where the boundary module is free of rank 1, and not directly at larger \(m\), where the kernel is the non-free module of the previous step. For \(n=3\) the proposition holds, but the rank-drop description does not. There \(dH_\infty-(N+1)p_0\) has degree \(g-2=-1\), so \(Z_d\) is empty off the collisions. For \(d\ge3\), \(\ell_0(d+1,4d+1)=B(d,2)>0\), so \(I\) is proper, and a proper saturated ideal has a nonempty zero scheme. By residue duality that zero scheme lies inside the collision hyperplanes. For \(d\le2\), \(B(d,2)=0\) and \(I=R\).

Dimension 4, one step past the boundary

Finite check (check:cube-first-step-rank-drop). On \(\{0,1\}^4\) over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), at \(d=2\) (\(N=12\), \(m=13\)), on one random plane \(y_4=\sum_{i<4}c_iy_i\) (seed 111):

  • The rank-drop locus (research/tools/bmd_cube_rankdrop_section.m2, rankdrop-section-d2.txt). The maximal minors of \(A_{12}\), saturated by the ten collision forms, define 120 points of the plane. Their ideal is radical, with one minimal generator in each of degrees 12, 13, 14, 15. \(F_{12}\) lies in it.
  • The threshold ideal (research/tools/bmd_cube_threshold_zero_scheme.m2, zero-scheme-d2-limit15.txt; 593 s wall time by the launcher, 765 s CPU by Macaulay2). The syzygies of \(A_{13}\) up to excess 15 give a threshold ideal \(I\) with one minimal generator in each of degrees 12, 13, 14, 15. The recorded global run found the module's generators in excesses \(\{12,13,14,14,15\}\), one of which is the boundary generator. On the plane, \(V(I)\) is 0-dimensional of degree 120, both before and after saturating by the collision forms. Its collision-saturated ideal equals that of the rank-drop points.

With generators up to excess 13 only, \(V(F_{12},F_{13})\) on the plane has degree \(156=12\cdot13\) (zero-scheme-d2-limit13.txt): a complete intersection, which the generators of degrees 14 and 15 cut down to the 120 points.

So at \(d=2\) the zero scheme of the threshold ideal has no curve component inside the collision hyperplanes, as far as this one random plane can show: every curve meets a general plane. Surface components are excluded by the 0-dimensional section, and in characteristic 0 by the height proposition. Embedded or isolated points would not be seen by a plane section. On the plane it is the reduced set of 120 rank-drop points. With the proposition, this is evidence that \(I^{(3)}_{13}\) is the saturated ideal of \(\bar Z_2\), a curve of degree 120 in \(\mathbb P^3\). If so, \(\ell_0(3,13)=12\) is the least degree \(\alpha(\bar Z_2)\) of a surface containing that curve, and \(F_{12}=0\) is the unique such surface.

Conjecture (conj:cube-first-step-rank-drop). On \(\{0,1\}^4\) in characteristic 0, for every \(d\ge2\), \(I^{(d+1)}_{8d-3}\) is the saturated ideal of the curve \(\bar Z_d\subset\mathbb P^3\). This is the closure of the set of \(y\), off the collision hyperplanes, where \(dH_\infty-(8d-3)p_0\) is effective on the Humbert curve, a class of degree \(g-2=3\). Hence \(\ell_0(d+1,8d-3)\) is the least degree of a surface containing \(\bar Z_d\). Evidence: the finite check at \(d=2\), modulo 32003 only, where \(\deg\bar Z_2=120\) and the least degree is 12.

The class \(dH_\infty-(8d-3)p_0\) has degree 3. Its effectivity is the condition \(dK-(8d-3)p_0\in W_3\) in \(\operatorname{Pic}^3\) of the genus-5 curve, of expected codimension 2 in the 3-dimensional family. So \(\bar Z_d\) is the pullback of the Brill–Noether locus \(W_3\), and its degree should follow from a Porteous-type class computation, once the excess along the collision hyperplanes is removed. The least degree \(\alpha(\bar Z_d)\) is subtler. The plane section of 120 points lies on a curve of degree 12, while 120 general points of a plane lie on no curve of degree below 15, since \(\binom{16}2=120\). So the section is far from general. This concerns the plane section, not space curves of degree 120 in general.

General statement. prop:cube-first-step-saturated, for every \(n\ge3\) and \(d\ge1\) where \(\Delta_{n,d}\ne0\). conj:cube-first-step-rank-drop, for every \(d\ge2\) on \(\{0,1\}^4\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the threshold-ideal lemma (Part 2), the height proposition and residue duality in every dimension, and the dimension-3 values \(B(d,2)\). A claim search (saturated, first step, rank drop, Brill–Noether, curve) found no earlier version. A fresh-context referee checked the proof (the exact sequence, the depth of \(\mathrm{Sol}\), where \(n\ge3\) enters), both scripts against the definitions, and every number against the outputs, including the meaning of the printed degree lists. It found nothing that breaks a stated result. Its corrections are made: the hypothesis stated as \(\Delta_{n,d}\ne0\) with citations for the characteristics; the degree \(e\) of \(G\); \(H^1_{\mathfrak m}(R)=0\) already for \(n\ge2\); the dimension-3 remark derived from the degree \(-1\) and properness; the timing measures; the generator count; the scope of the plane section; the modulus of the evidence; and the plane-section scope of the general-position count.

Assessment. The first step of the middle range now has a geometric description: a saturated ideal whose zero scheme, in the one case computed, is exactly the Brill–Noether-type rank-drop curve of the boundary matrix. The threshold 12 at \(d=2\) is the least degree of a surface through a degree-120 curve. The next steps are the degree of \(\bar Z_d\) for every \(d\), by a class computation, and an explanation of its least-degree surface. The \(S_5\) semi-invariance of \(F_{12}\) suggests a symmetric description, perhaps the pullback of a theta-type divisor containing \(W_3\).
