26 September 2026 — The zero set of the first-step threshold ideal lies between two rank loci, and in dimension 4 it is the Brill–Noether locus off a smaller one

Working proof: over any field, {rank A_N < N, rank A_{N+1} = N} ⊆ V(I^{(d+1)}_{N+1}) ⊆ {rank A_N < N}; off the collisions (n ≥ 3, d > n−3) this is h⁰(dH∞−(N+1)p₀) ≥ 1 where h⁰(dH∞−(N+2)p₀) = 0. Cycle bmd-r112. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The first-step conjecture says that on \(\{0,1\}^4\) the threshold ideal \(I^{(d+1)}_{N+1}\) is the saturated ideal of the rank-drop curve \(\bar Z_d\). Saturation is proved (proposition), and the plane section at \(d=2\) supports the rest. The finisher requires a general statement this cycle, not another case. Which part of the conjecture can be proved for every \(d\) and \(n\)? The test ends with a proof of the set-theoretic part, or with the obstruction to it.

Setting. As before: \(A_m\) is the \(N\times(m+1)\) constraint matrix, \(N=N_{2,n}(d)\), and \(I=I^{(d+1)}_{N+1}\subseteq R=F[y_1,\ldots,y_n]\) is the ideal of top coordinates of solutions of \(A_{N+1}W=0\). For a point \(y^*\) of affine space over \(\bar F\), \(A_m(y^*)\) is the specialized matrix. \(V(I)\) is the zero set in \(\bar F^n\).

The sandwich

Lemma (lem:cube-first-step-sandwich). Over any field, for every \(n\ge1\), \(d\ge1\) and every point \(y^*\):

  1. if \(\operatorname{rank}A_N(y^*)=N\), then some element of \(I\) is nonzero at \(y^*\);
  2. if \(\operatorname{rank}A_N(y^*)<N\) and \(\operatorname{rank}A_{N+1}(y^*)=N\), then every element of \(I\) vanishes at \(y^*\).

So \(\{\operatorname{rank}A_N<N,\ \operatorname{rank}A_{N+1}=N\}\subseteq V(I)\subseteq\{\operatorname{rank}A_N<N\}\).

Proof. Write \(A_{N+1}=[A_N\mid a]\), with \(a\) the column of \(T^{N+1}\). As in the height proposition, \(I=(\operatorname{Im}A_N:_Ra)\).

  • Part 1. Let \(\mathfrak p\) be the maximal ideal of \(y^*\) (over \(\bar F\); the colon ideal commutes with the flat extension to \(\bar F[y]\) and with localization). If \(A_N(y^*)\) has rank \(N\), some maximal minor of \(A_N\) is a unit in the local ring at \(y^*\). So \(A_N\) maps onto the free module of rank \(N\) there, \(a\in\operatorname{Im}A_N\) locally, and \(I\) is the unit ideal at \(y^*\). So some element of \(I\) does not vanish at \(y^*\).
  • Part 2. Let \(W\in R^{N+2}\) be a solution. Its value \(W(y^*)\) lies in \(\ker A_{N+1}(y^*)\), which has dimension \(N+2-N=2\). The vectors \((u,0)\) with \(u\in\ker A_N(y^*)\) lie in \(\ker A_{N+1}(y^*)\), and they form a space of dimension \(N+1-\operatorname{rank}A_N(y^*)\ge2\). So these are all of \(\ker A_{N+1}(y^*)\), and every kernel vector has last coordinate 0. In particular \(W_{N+1}(y^*)=0\). \(\square\)

The lemma is linear algebra. It needs neither characteristic 0 nor the collision theory, and it holds on the collision hyperplanes too. There \(\operatorname{rank}A_N<N\) everywhere, since each collision form divides \(g_{n,d}\) with exponent \(E_n(d)\ge1\) (collision-exponent theorem). In characteristic 0 the collision step of the height proposition gives \(I\not\subseteq(\ell_D)\) without any hypothesis on \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}\). So by part 2, \(\operatorname{rank}A_{N+1}<N\) at a general point of each collision hyperplane.

The Brill–Noether form

Corollary (cor:cube-first-step-brill-noether). Let \(F\) be algebraically closed of characteristic \(\ne2\), \(n\ge3\), \(d>n-3\), and let \(y^*\) have distinct nonzero entries. On the fibre curve \(C\), with \(D_k=dH_\infty-kp_0\), we have \(\operatorname{rank}A_m(y^*)=N-h^0(D_{m+1})\). Hence:

  • if \(h^0(D_{N+1})=0\), then \(y^*\notin V(I)\);
  • if \(h^0(D_{N+1})\ge1\) and \(h^0(D_{N+2})=0\), then \(y^*\in V(I)\).

So off the collision hyperplanes, \(V(I)\) agrees with the Brill–Noether locus \(\{h^0(D_{N+1})\ge1\}\) outside the smaller locus \(\{h^0(D_{N+2})\ge1\}\). The class \(D_{N+1}\) has degree \(g-2\) and \(D_{N+2}\) has degree \(g-3\). For \(n=4\) these are 3 and 2, with expected codimensions 2 and 3 in the 3-dimensional family of \((y\bmod\text{scaling})\).

Proof. For \(d>n-3\), \(V_d=L(dH_\infty)\) has dimension \(N\) (residue duality lemma, first step). The rows of \(A_m(y^*)\) are the truncations modulo \(T^{m+1}\) of a basis of \(V_d\). So the kernel of the truncation is \(L(dH_\infty-(m+1)p_0)\), since \(T\) is a local parameter at \(p_0\), and \(\operatorname{rank}A_m(y^*)=N-h^0(D_{m+1})\). The lemma gives the two statements. The degrees are \(2^{n-1}d-(N+1)=g-2\) and \(g-3\), using \(N=2^{n-1}d+1-g\). \(\square\)

What this proves of the conjecture. For \(n=4\) in characteristic 0, the following hold:

  • \(I\) is saturated (every \(d\));
  • \(V(I)\) contains no collision hyperplane (every \(d\)), and it has height \(\ge2\) overall for \(2\le d\le9\);
  • off the collision hyperplanes, \(V(I)\) agrees with the Brill–Noether locus \(\{h^0(D_{8d-3})\ge1\}\) outside \(\{h^0(D_{8d-2})\ge1\}\), whose expected dimension is 0, while its actual dimension is not proved.

The conjecture adds three more claims:

  • no component of \(\{h^0(D_{8d-3})\ge1\}\) lies inside \(\{h^0(D_{8d-2})\ge1\}\);
  • \(V(I)\) has no component (curve or isolated point) inside the collision hyperplanes;
  • \(I\) is radical.

At \(d=2\), modulo 32003 and on one random plane, all three hold on the section computed in the finite check. A plane section cannot see isolated or embedded points, and it shows radicality only generically along the curve. In dimension 3 the corollary's locus is empty, because \(D_{N+1}\) has degree \(-1\). This agrees with the zero scheme lying in the collision hyperplanes there.

General statement. lem:cube-first-step-sandwich, for every \(n\ge1\), \(d\ge1\) over any field. cor:cube-first-step-brill-noether, for every \(n\ge3\), \(d>n-3\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the height proposition, residue duality in every dimension, the saturation proposition and the first-step conjecture. A claim search (rank drop, zero set, first step) found only the conjecture this entry addresses. A fresh-context referee checked:

  • both parts of the lemma over any field, including points on the collision hyperplanes;
  • the rank formula, since \(T\) is a local parameter at the unramified point \(p_0\);
  • the degrees \(g-2\), \(g-3\) and the codimensions of \(W_3\), \(W_2\).

It found nothing that breaks a stated result. Its corrections are made:

  • the collision remark needs only \(E_n(d)\ge1\) and the collision step of the height proposition, not \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}=1\);
  • the ranges of what is proved;
  • isolated points in the remaining claims;
  • the limits of the plane-section evidence;
  • the unproved dimension of \(\{h^0(D_{N+2})\ge1\}\);
  • the curve claim restricted to where it is justified.

Assessment. The set-theoretic part of the first-step conjecture is now proved up to the locus \(\{h^0(D_{N+2})\ge1\}\). That locus has expected dimension 0, but its actual dimension is not proved, and its components could be curves. The first middle-range threshold in dimension 4 is the least degree of a surface through the scheme cut out by \(I\). Its reduced support off the collisions is the Brill–Noether locus \(\{h^0(dK-(8d-3)p_0)\ge1\}\) of the Humbert family, up to that smaller locus. For \(2\le d\le9\) it has codimension exactly 2 where nonempty: the Eagon–Northcott bound gives codimension \(\le2\), and \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}=1\) excludes divisors. It is a curve at \(d=2\); for larger \(d\) it could a priori be empty. What remains is scheme-theoretic, together with the least degree of a surface through that curve, which is 12 at \(d=2\). The next computation-free target is the degree of the curve, from the class of \(W_3\) pulled back along \(y\mapsto dK-(8d-3)p_0\).

26 September 2026 — Where the threshold ideals vanish: Brill–Noether loci up to m = 2^{n−1}d, collision hyperplanes beyond it

Working proof: for m > N the zero set of I^{(d+1)}_m lies between two rank loci; off the collisions these are Brill–Noether loci of dH∞−mp₀, so for m > 2^{n−1}d every threshold ideal vanishes only on collision hyperplanes. Cycle bmd-r113. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The sandwich lemma locates the zero set of the threshold ideal one step past the boundary. The recorded savings-3 row of dimension 4, \(\ell_0(3,m)=15,12,11,6,5,2,2,0\) for \(m=12,\ldots,19\), has two regimes: large values up to \(m=16\), small ones from \(m=17\). Does the same argument locate the zero set at every \(m\) past the boundary, and does it explain where the regimes change? The test ends with a statement for every \(m\), or with a step where the argument breaks.

Setting. As before: \(A_m\) is the \(N\times(m+1)\) constraint matrix, \(N=N_{2,n}(d)\), \(I_m=I^{(d+1)}_m\), and \(D_k=dH_\infty-kp_0\) on the fibre curve.

The sandwich at every step

Lemma (lem:cube-threshold-sandwich). Over any field, for every \(n,d\ge1\), every \(m>N\) and every point \(y^*\):

  1. if \(\operatorname{rank}A_{m-1}(y^*)=N\), then some element of \(I_m\) is nonzero at \(y^*\);
  2. if \(\operatorname{rank}A_{m-1}(y^*)<N\) and \(\operatorname{rank}A_m(y^*)=N\), then every element of \(I_m\) vanishes at \(y^*\).

So \(\{\operatorname{rank}A_{m-1}<N,\ \operatorname{rank}A_m=N\}\subseteq V(I_m)\subseteq\{\operatorname{rank}A_{m-1}<N\}\). At \(m=N+1\) this is exactly the lemma of the previous entry, which it extends to every \(m\).

Proof. Write \(A_m=[A_{m-1}\mid a]\). Then \(I_m=(\operatorname{Im}A_{m-1}:_Ra)\).

  • Part 1. If some maximal minor of \(A_{m-1}\) is a unit at \(y^*\), then \(A_{m-1}\) maps onto the free module of rank \(N\) locally, so \(a\) is in its image and \(I_m\) is the unit ideal at \(y^*\).
  • Part 2. The value of a solution lies in \(\ker A_m(y^*)\), of dimension \(m+1-N\). The padded vectors \((u,0)\), with \(u\in\ker A_{m-1}(y^*)\), form a subspace of dimension \(m-\operatorname{rank}A_{m-1}(y^*)\ge m+1-N\). So they are the whole kernel, and every solution has top coordinate 0 at \(y^*\). \(\square\)

Beyond \(2^{n-1}d\) the zero sets lie on the collision hyperplanes

Theorem (thm:cube-threshold-collision-support). Let \(F\) have characteristic \(\ne2\), \(n\ge3\), \(d>n-3\), and \(m>N\). At \(y^*\in\bar F^n\) with distinct nonzero entries:

  • if \(h^0(D_m)=0\), then \(y^*\notin V(I_m)\);
  • if \(h^0(D_m)\ge1\) and \(h^0(D_{m+1})=0\), then \(y^*\in V(I_m)\).

The class \(D_m\) has degree \(2^{n-1}d-m=g-1-(m-N)\). Hence, for every \(m>2^{n-1}d\), \(V(I_m)\) is contained in the union of the collision hyperplanes.

Proof. For \(d>n-3\), \(V_d=L(dH_\infty)\) has dimension \(N\) (residue duality lemma). The rows of \(A_k(y^*)\) are the truncations modulo \(T^{k+1}\) of a basis of \(V_d\), and \(T\) is a local parameter at \(p_0\). So \(\operatorname{rank}A_k(y^*)=N-h^0(D_{k+1})\). With \(k=m-1\) and \(k=m\), the lemma gives the two statements. The degree is \(2^{n-1}d-m\), and \(N=2^{n-1}d+1-g\). If \(m>2^{n-1}d\), then \(D_m\) has negative degree, so \(h^0(D_m)=0\) at every \(y^*\) with distinct nonzero entries, and no such point lies in \(V(I_m)\). \(\square\)

The two regimes. Past the boundary, the middle range splits at \(m=2^{n-1}d\).

  • Brill–Noether regime, \(N<m\le2^{n-1}d\). Off the collisions, the zero set agrees with the locus \(\{h^0(dH_\infty-mp_0)\ge1\}\), for a class of degree \(g-1-j\) with \(j=m-N\), outside the smaller locus \(\{h^0(dH_\infty-(m+1)p_0)\ge1\}\), where the inclusion is left undetermined. Its expected dimension in \(\mathbb P^{n-1}\) is \((n-1)-(j+1)\), since \(W_{g-1-j}\) has codimension \(j+1\) in \(\operatorname{Pic}\).
  • Collision regime, \(m>2^{n-1}d\). The zero set lies in the collision hyperplanes, as in dimension 3, where the double points on the collision lines produce the thresholds \(B(d,\rho)\).

For \(n=3\), \(2^{n-1}d=4d=N\), so the whole middle range is collision regime. This is consistent with the dimension-3 theorem: every threshold past the boundary there comes from the collision structure (theorem).

For \(n=4\) and \(d=2\) (\(N=12\), \(2^{n-1}d=16\), \(g=5\)), the recorded row \(\ell_0(3,m)\) divides as follows. The values come from the dimension-4 entry (\(m=12,13\)), route review 14 (\(m=14,\ldots,18\); global-m14.txt, global-m15-18.txt) and the order-zero check (\(m=19\)).

  • Brill–Noether regime, \(m=13,14,15,16\), degrees of \(D_m\) equal to \(3,2,1,0\): thresholds \(12,11,6,5\). At \(m=13\), off the collisions, the zero set agrees with the Brill–Noether curve of the first-step entry outside \(\{h^0(D_{14})\ge1\}\). That it is the curve itself rests on a plane-section check modulo 32003. For \(m\ge14\) the expected dimension is \(\le0\), so the zero set off the collisions is expected to be finite or empty. Any positive-dimensional part of \(V(I_m)\) must then lie in the collision hyperplanes, or in a family with excess Brill–Noether behaviour.
  • Collision regime, \(m=17,18,19\): thresholds \(2,2,0\). The zero sets lie in the collision hyperplanes. At \(m=17\) the degree-2 part is the quadric \(Q\). At \(m=18\) the recorded run found two minimal syzygies with nonzero top in excess 2, so the degree-2 part is spanned by at most two quadrics, one of them \(Q\). Together with the other generators they cut the zero set down to a locus inside the collision hyperplanes.

So the change from values \(\ge5\) to values \(\le2\) in the row happens exactly where the theorem says the Brill–Noether conditions become impossible. The theorem predicts no threshold values, and a drop is not implied by it. The row is consistent with the picture, and the drop was recorded before this explanation.

What it changes. The dimension-3 machinery (collision lifts, double points, peeling) applies directly to the collision regime of every dimension. There the relevant loci are curves in the collision hyperplanes, and the restriction to a collision hyperplane is a problem in one dimension less (collision limit lemma). The Brill–Noether regime is special to \(n\ge4\). It has \(2^{n-1}d-N=g-1\) steps for every \(d>n-3\): four for \(n=4\) and \(d\ge2\).

General statement. lem:cube-threshold-sandwich, for every \(n,d\ge1\), \(m>N\) over any field. thm:cube-threshold-collision-support, for every \(n\ge3\), \(d>n-3\), \(m>N\) in characteristic \(\ne2\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the first-step sandwich lemma and corollary, residue duality in every dimension, the colon-ideal description, and the recorded row data. A claim search (sandwich, collision support, Brill–Noether) found only the previous entry's lemma, which this one extends. A fresh-context referee checked:

  • both parts of the lemma for every \(m>N\);
  • the rank formula, the degree \(2^{n-1}d-m=g-1-(m-N)\) and the conclusion beyond \(2^{n-1}d\);
  • the codimension \(j+1\) of \(W_{g-1-j}\);
  • the dimension-3 consistency.

It found nothing that breaks a stated result. Its corrections are made:

  • "extends" in place of "refines";
  • "agrees with, outside the smaller locus" in the regime description;
  • the status of the \(m=13\) curve;
  • the degree-2 part at \(m=18\), where two syzygies have nonzero top;
  • sources for the values 11 and 0;
  • "consistent" rather than "a check";
  • the range \(d>n-3\);
  • \(dH_\infty\) in general.

Assessment. The middle range now has a map. After the boundary come \(g-1\) Brill–Noether steps, in which the zero sets are governed by effectivity of \(dH_\infty-mp_0\) on the fibre curve (\(dK-mp_0\) for \(n=4\)). After them the zero sets lie in the collision hyperplanes, the regime that dimension 3 already solved. The recorded dimension-4 row breaks exactly at this transition. The next step is the collision regime in dimension 4: restrict the threshold ideal at \(m>8d\) to a collision hyperplane. There, compare its zero set with the double-point loci of the limit problem, which lives on the genus-1 curve. The quadric \(Q\), restricted to a collision hyperplane, is the first test.

26 September 2026 — In the collision regime of dimension 4 the threshold ideals retreat to torsion curves, then to the lines where collision planes meet

Working proof in characteristic ≠ 2: on {0,1}⁴, V(I^{(d+1)}_{8d}) meets each open collision plane only where 2d·[H∞−4p₀] = 0 on the genus-1 limit curve, and for m ≥ 8d+1 not at all: those zero sets lie in the 25 lines. Cycle bmd-r114. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. Past \(m=2^{n-1}d\) the threshold ideals vanish only on the collision hyperplanes (collision-support theorem). On \(\{0,1\}^4\) at \(d=2\) the recorded thresholds there are \(2,2,0\) at \(m=17,18,19\). Where on the collision hyperplanes do these ideals vanish? The collision limit of the collision limit lemma lives on a genus-1 curve, as the whole dimension-3 problem does. The test ends with a description of the zero sets on the open collision hyperplanes, or with a point where the limit argument fails.

Setting. \(n=4\) and \(d\ge2\), so \(N=8d-4\) and \(2^{n-1}d=8d\). \(D=\{y_1=0\}\), and \(D^\circ\subseteq D\) is the open set where \(y_2,y_3,y_4\) are distinct and nonzero. For \(y'=(y_2,y_3,y_4)\) with distinct nonzero entries, \(E_{y'}\) is the genus-1 curve \(w_i^2=1+4y_iT\) (\(i=2,3,4\)). It carries the point \(p_0\) and the divisor \(H_\infty\) of degree 4 at infinity, and \(x_{y'}=[H_\infty-4p_0]\) is a point of its Jacobian. In the notation of the dimension-3 law, \(x_{y'}\) is the point \(2c_1\), which is never 0. \(U_d=U^{(3)}_d\) is the collision limit space.

The theorem

Theorem (thm:cube-collision-regime-torsion). In characteristic \(\ne2\), on \(\{0,1\}^4\) with \(d\ge2\) and \(y^*=(0,y')\in D^\circ\):

  1. if no nonzero element of \(U_d(y')\) has order \(\ge m\) at \(p_0\), then \(y^*\notin V(I^{(d+1)}_m)\);
  2. every nonzero element of \(U_d(y')\) has order \(\le8d\), and order \(8d\) occurs only if \(2d\cdot x_{y'}=0\).

Hence \(V(I_m)\cap D^\circ=\emptyset\) for \(m\ge8d+1\), and \(V(I_{8d})\cap D^\circ\) lies in the torsion locus \(\{2d\cdot x_{y'}=0\}\). The same holds on every collision hyperplane, with the torsion locus read in the transformed coordinates. With the collision-support theorem it follows that, for \(m\ge8d+1\), \(V(I_m)\) lies in the union of the 25 lines of \(\mathbb P^3\) where two collision hyperplanes meet: 10 triple lines \(L_{abc}\), each in 3 hyperplanes, and 15 double-double lines \(L_{ab|cd}\), each in 2. These account for all \(\binom{10}2=45\) pairs.

Proof. Part 1. As in the height proposition, the basis of \(V_{4,d}\) is unitriangular over \(F[y]\) to the basis of \(V_{3,d}\) together with the lifts \(L_P\). The lifts are \(y_1^{d-e(P)}\) times rows \(\lambda_P=y_1^{-(d-e(P))}L_P\) with polynomial entries (reduction theorem, part 1). So \(A_k=S\,\Delta_1\,A^\Lambda_k\) for every \(k\). Here:

  • \(S\) is unitriangular over \(F[y]\);
  • \(\Delta_1=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,y_1^{d-e(P)},\ldots)\);
  • \(A^\Lambda_k\) is the matrix of truncations modulo \(T^{k+1}\) of the rows \(b_i\) (the basis of \(V_{3,d}\)) and \(\lambda_P\), with polynomial entries.

Write \(A^\Lambda_m=[A^\Lambda_{m-1}\mid a^\Lambda]\). If \(W^\Lambda\) solves \(A^\Lambda_mW^\Lambda=0\), then \(A_mW^\Lambda=0\). So \(I_m\supseteq I^\Lambda_m:=(\operatorname{Im}A^\Lambda_{m-1}:a^\Lambda)\). At \(y_1=0\) the rows of \(A^\Lambda\) are, up to nonzero constants, the basis \(\{T^Qz^r:Q+|r|\le d\}\) of \(U_d(y')\) (collision limit lemma, part 1). If no nonzero element of \(U_d(y')\) has order \(\ge m\), the truncation of \(U_d(y')\) modulo \(T^m\) is injective. So \(A^\Lambda_{m-1}(y^*)\) has rank \(N\), some maximal minor of \(A^\Lambda_{m-1}\) is a unit at \(y^*\), and \(I^\Lambda_m\), hence \(I_m\), is the unit ideal at \(y^*\).

Part 2. \(U_d(y')=\bigoplus_{r\in\{0,1\}^3}w^rF[T]_{\le d-|r|}\) (reduction theorem, setting). On \(E_{y'}\) each of the four points at infinity is a ramification point of \(T\), where \(T\) has a pole of order 2 and each \(w_i\) a simple pole (dimension-3 law, the elliptic curve). So \(T^jw^r\) has pole order \(2j+|r|\le2(d-|r|)+|r|\le2d\) there, and \(U_d(y')\subseteq L(2dH_\infty)\), of degree \(8d\). A nonzero \(f\in L(2dH_\infty)\) has \(\deg\operatorname{div}f=0\), so \(\operatorname{ord}_{p_0}f\le8d\). Equality forces \(\operatorname{div}f=8d\,p_0-2dH_\infty\), that is \(2dH_\infty\sim8d\,p_0\), which is \(2d\cdot x_{y'}=0\).

The consequences. For \(m\ge8d+1\), part 2 gives no element of order \(\ge m\), and part 1 gives \(y^*\notin V(I_m)\). For \(m=8d\), wherever \(2d\cdot x_{y'}\ne0\) no element has order \(\ge8d\), so \(y^*\notin V(I_{8d})\). By the symmetry theorem, each ideal \(I_m\) is stable under the \(S_5\) permuting the points \(r_0,\ldots,r_4\), which acts on \(y\) linearly and transitively on the collision hyperplanes. So for \(\sigma(D_{01})=D\), \(V(I_m)\cap D=\sigma(V(I_m)\cap D_{01})\), and the statements transfer. For \(m>8d\) the collision-support theorem excludes points off the hyperplanes. \(\square\)

At \(d=2\). For \(m=17,18,19\), \(V(I_m)\) lies in the 25 lines \(L_{abc}=\{r_a=r_b=r_c\}\) and \(L_{ab|cd}=\{r_a=r_b,\ r_c=r_d\}\). The quadric \(Q=-\frac12\sum_{a<b}(r_a-r_b)^2\) restricts to each line as a binary quadratic form with two zeros. On \(L_{abc}\), with values \((u,u,u,v,w)\), it is \(-\frac12(3(u-v)^2+3(u-w)^2+(v-w)^2)\). Threshold ideals past the first step need not be saturated. So a positive threshold, such as 2 at \(m=17,18\), is compatible with a zero set of points on these lines, or with an empty one. At \(m=16=8d\), the last Brill–Noether step, \(V(I_{16})\cap D^\circ\) lies in the 4-torsion curve of \(x\) (\(4x=0\), \(x\ne0\)). In the dimension-3 notation these are the loci where \(2c_1\) has order 2 or 4. There \(\Delta_{3,4}\) vanishes, and \(\Delta_{3,2}\) vanishes on the order-2 part (dimension-3 law, factors). Since \(Q\in I_{17}\), and \(Q\) has two distinct zeros on each of the 25 lines (both restricted discriminants are nonzero), \(V(I_{17})\) consists of at most 50 projective points.

General statement. thm:cube-collision-regime-torsion, for every \(d\ge2\) on \(\{0,1\}^4\) in characteristic \(\ne2\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the collision-support theorem, the reduction theorem's polynomial lifts, the collision limit lemma, and the dimension-3 law's elliptic curve and point \(2c_1\). A claim search (collision regime, torsion, limit curve) found no earlier version. A fresh-context referee checked:

  • the factorization and the colon-ideal inclusion;
  • the evaluation at \(y_1=0\), with Kummer independence at specialized \(y'\);
  • the pole orders, the bound \(8d\) and the torsion condition;
  • \(x=2c_1\ne0\), and the count of 25 lines.

It found nothing that breaks a stated result. Its corrections are made:

  • the transfer to all hyperplanes through the \(S_5\)-stability of the ideals themselves;
  • characteristic \(\ne2\) in place of 0, since 0 is not used;
  • the lines as subspaces of \(\mathbb P^3\);
  • the vanishing of \(\Delta_{3,2}\) only on the order-2 part;
  • the bound of 50 points for \(V(I_{17})\);
  • the expected dimensions at \(m=8d-2,8d-1\);
  • the genus-0 claim marked as expected.

Assessment. The map of the middle range sharpens. On \(\{0,1\}^4\), the zero sets of the threshold ideals move:

  • from a Brill–Noether curve (\(m=8d-3\)),
  • through points (\(m=8d-2\), expected) and an expected empty locus off the collisions (\(m=8d-1\)),
  • to torsion curves inside the collision planes, together with a possible torsion-type locus off them (\(m=8d\), where \(dK\sim8d\,p_0\)),
  • and then into the 25 lines where collision planes meet (\(m\ge8d+1\)).

At each stage the relevant curve is one dimension of branch points lower: the genus-5 Humbert curve, then the genus-1 limit curve, then genus 0 on the lines. So we expect the thresholds from \(m=8d+1\) on, the last ones before order zero, to be governed by a genus-0 problem on the 25 lines. No limit along these codimension-2 loci is established yet. The next step is that genus-0 problem: the limit spaces along the lines \(L_{abc}\) and \(L_{ab|cd}\), their maximal orders, and the torsion analogue that decides when the zero sets leave the lines too.

26 September 2026 — The collision regime of dimension 4: no zeros at d = 2, and point windows that grow like 10d

Working proof: arc limits put points into threshold zero sets, for every n. Finite checks on {0,1}⁴ in characteristics 32003 and 1000003: V(I₁₇) = V(I₁₈) = ∅ at d = 2, and windows growing by about 10 per step in d. Conjecture. Cycle bmd-r115. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. For \(m\ge8d+1\) the zero sets \(V(I^{(d+1)}_m)\) on \(\{0,1\}^4\) lie in the 25 lines where collision hyperplanes meet (collision-regime theorem). The last entry expected a genus-0 problem on those lines to govern the thresholds from \(8d+1\) up to order zero. That expectation predicts zeros on the lines. Are there any, which lines or points carry them, and for which \(m\)? The test ends with the zero sets at \(d=2\), and with the orders that arc limits reach at the collision points for larger \(d\).

Setting. \(n=4\), \(N=8d-4\), \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_4)\). The branch points are \((r_0,\ldots,r_4)=(0,y_1,\ldots,y_4)\) up to affine maps, and \(S_5\) permutes them (symmetry theorem). The collision points of \(\mathbb P^3\) fall into these classes:

  • the 10 triple lines \(r_a=r_b=r_c\);
  • the 15 double-double lines \(r_a=r_b,\ r_c=r_d\);
  • the 10 triple-double points, such as \((1{:}1{:}0{:}0)\) (\(r_0=r_3=r_4\), \(r_1=r_2\));
  • the 5 quadruple points, such as \((1{:}1{:}1{:}1)\).

An arc is \(\gamma=y(\varepsilon)\in O^4\), \(O=F[[\varepsilon]]\), \(K=F((\varepsilon))\), with nonzero, pairwise distinct coordinates in \(K\). \(V\) and the limit space \(S_\gamma\) are as in the flat-limit order bound. For a point \(P\) and a set of arcs through \(P\), \(\Sigma_P\) is the span of their limit spaces.

Arc limits put points into the zero sets

Lemma (lem:cube-point-window-membership). On \(\{0,1\}^n\) over a field \(F\), let \(d\ge0\), \(m\ge0\), \(P\in F^n\setminus\{0\}\), and let \(\gamma\in O^n\) be any arc with \(\gamma(0)=P\). Let \(g\in V\otimes K\) have truncation \(\tau_m(g)\in O^{m+1}\), with reduction \(\overline{\tau_m(g)}\in F^{m+1}\) modulo \(\varepsilon\). Then \(W(P)\) kills \(\overline{\tau_m(g)}\) for every solution \(W\in F[y]^{m+1}\) of the \((d+1)\)-system at \(m\). Consequently:

  • if the span of these reductions, over any set of arcs through \(P\), contains \(T^m\), then the projective point \([P]\) lies in \(V(I^{(d+1)}_m)\);
  • in particular this holds when \(\Sigma_P\), over arcs with nonzero, pairwise distinct coordinates, has an element of \(T\)-order exactly \(m\).

Proof. Write \(g=\sum_ia_if_i\) with \(a_i\in K\) and \(f_i\) in the basis of \(V\). A solution satisfies \(\sum_cW_c(y)[T^c]f=0\) for every basis element \(f\), identically in \(y\). Substituting the arc, \(W(\gamma)\in O^{m+1}\) kills \(\tau_m(f_i(\gamma))\) for each \(i\), so by \(K\)-linearity it kills \(\tau_m(g)\). Both vectors lie in \(O^{m+1}\), and reducing modulo \(\varepsilon\) gives that \(W(P)\) kills \(\overline{\tau_m(g)}\). If \(T^m\), that is \((0,\ldots,0,1)\), is a combination of such reductions, then \(W_m(P)=0\). By the threshold-ideal lemma, \(I_m\) consists of the top coordinates \(W_m\) of solutions, so every element of \(I_m\) vanishes at \(P\). An element \(\bar g\in S_\gamma\) is the reduction of some \(g\in\Lambda_\gamma\), whose whole expansion lies in \(O[[T]]\). An element of \(\Sigma_P\) is a combination \(\sum_jc_j\bar g_j\) with \(\bar g_j\in S_{\gamma_j}\) the reductions of \(g_j\in\Lambda_{\gamma_j}\), and its truncation is \(\sum_jc_j\overline{\tau_m(g_j)}\). If the element has order exactly \(m\), this truncation is \(cT^m\) with \(c\ne0\), a combination of reductions as in the first bullet. \(\square\)

The proof uses neither the characteristic nor the shape of the arc: a solution is an identity in \(y\), so any arc through \(P\) may be substituted. Characteristic \(\ne2\) and distinct nonzero coordinates enter only through the definition of \(\Lambda_\gamma\) and \(S_\gamma\) in the second bullet.

This extends the point-window bound from order-zero solutions to every solution. In dimension 3 at the double points, for every solution, it is the argument of the window lemma (lem:cube-double-point-windows). The lemma only puts points into zero sets; it never excludes them. The compiled kernel saturates the truncations \(\tau_M(V)\), \(M>m\), modulo \(\varepsilon^{\mathrm{prec}}\). Each saturation step divides a combination by \(\varepsilon\) and shifts it by one digit, and the kernel discards an arc whose steps reach \(\mathrm{prec}-2\) (the failed arcs). For the arcs it keeps, the digit \(\varepsilon^0\) of every output row comes from exact digits, so each output row is the reduction of some \(\tau_M(g)\) as in the lemma.

At d = 2 the collision-regime ideals have no zeros

Computation. research/tools/bmd_cube_collision_zero_sets.m2 is new. For given \(m\) it computes the generators of \(\operatorname{Sol}_m=\ker A_m\) of excess at most a limit (Macaulay2 syz with a degree limit, over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\)). The ideal \(J\) of their top coordinates satisfies \(J\subseteq I_m\), so \(V(I_m)\subseteq V(J)\). The script decomposes \(V(J)\), and for each component reports which collision forms vanish on it and whether the quadric \(Q\) lies in it. It also tests the pentagon point.

Finite check (check:cube-collision-regime-empty-d2). Over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), \(n=4\), \(d=2\), excess limit 4, in research/results/bmd-r115-collision-windows/zero-sets-d2-m17.txt and zero-sets-d2-m18-m16.txt:

  • At \(m=17\), 6 generators; the top coordinates have degrees 2, 3, 4. At \(m=18\), 13 generators, with top coordinates of the same degrees.
  • In both cases \(J\) is saturated and \(V(J)\) is zero-dimensional of degree 24: six prime components of degree 4, on none of which a collision form vanishes.
  • \(V(J)\) contains the pentagon point \(y_i=\zeta^i-1\), where \(\zeta\) is a primitive fifth root of unity, so \(r_i=\zeta^i\) up to translation (tested at \(m=17\)). The part of excess \(\le4\) is \(S_5\)-stable by the symmetry theorem, since \(W_m\mapsto\pm W_m\circ\psi\) preserves the excess. So \(V(J)\) contains the \(S_5\)-orbit of the pentagon point. The orbit has \(120/5=24\) points, because the stabilizer, affine maps modulo scaling, is the cyclic group of order 5. So the orbit is the whole of \(V(J)\).
  • The six prime components printed at \(m=18\) are identical to those at \(m=17\), so \(V(J_{18})=V(J_{17})\).

With the collision-support theorem this gives \(V(I_{17})=V(I_{18})=\emptyset\) in characteristic 32003, over its algebraic closure. Emptiness modulo one prime does not pass to characteristic 0 without lifting the syzygies, which was not done. By that theorem, both zero sets lie in the collision hyperplanes for \(m>8d=16\), and \(V(J)\) meets none of them. So the two ideals are primary to the irrelevant ideal, yet their initial degree is 2. Their degree-2 parts are spanned by \(Q\) (recorded generators in research/results/bmd-r100-dimension-four-generators/factored-generators.txt). At \(m=16\) there is no generator of excess \(\le4\), as \(\ell_0=5\) predicts.

Point windows at the collision points

Computation. The kernel research/tools/bmd_cube_point_windows.cpp (point-window entry) now takes a series of \(d\) in one run, with \(M\) and the precision given as multiples of \(d\). It was revalidated by reproducing the recorded \(d=2\) orders (the \(d=2\) block of point-windows-d2-d3.txt, against research/results/bmd-r65-point-windows/n4-d2-points.txt). It uses 150 arcs per point, with the arc families of that entry, over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\), and truncation \(M=16d\).

Finite check (check:cube-collision-windows). Every computed \(\Sigma_P\) has orders exactly \(0,\ldots,\mu\). The largest \(\mu\) found (point-windows-d2-d3.txt, point-windows-d3-d5.txt):

point class (representatives)d = 2345
triple-double \((1,1,0,0)\), \((1,1,1,0)\)13243444
double-double line \((1,1,5,5)\)12223242
quadruple \((1,1,1,1)\), \((1,0,0,0)\)12202836
triple line \((0,0,3,7)\), \((1,1,1,5)\)–192735
random point, and \(8d\)11; 1619; 24–; 32–; 40

The two triple-double representatives lie in one \(S_5\)-orbit, but at \(d=3,4\) they give 24 and 23, then 34 and 33. At the triple-double and quadruple points up to 47 of the 150 arcs failed for precision. So each entry is a lower bound for the full span of arc limits. The lemma needs only that.

Consequences (in characteristic 1000003, over its algebraic closure, by the lemma and the \(S_5\)-stability of \(I_m\), which is transitive on the 10 triple-double points):

  • at \(d=4\), the 10 triple-double points lie in \(V(I_{33})\) and \(V(I_{34})\);
  • at \(d=5\), they lie in \(V(I_m)\) for \(41\le m\le44\), and the \(S_5\)-orbit of \((1{:}1{:}5{:}5)\) lies in \(V(I_{41})\) and \(V(I_{42})\).

So, in characteristic 1000003, the collision-regime zero sets are not empty in general. At \(d\le3\) no computed window passes \(8d\). The windows are nearly linear in \(d\): 10 per step at the double-double points, 10 or 11 at the triple-double points, and \(\mu=N-1\) at the generic points of the triple lines, which is no gain at all. The order-zero thresholds \(M(d)=19,39\) at \(d=2,3\), and \(M(4)>50\) (first point at d = 4), lie far beyond these windows. The collision-regime ideals computed so far (\(d=2\), \(m=17,18\)) have no zeros.

The conjecture

Conjecture (conj:cube-collision-regime-windows). On \(\{0,1\}^4\) in characteristic 0, let \(d\ge3\) and \(m\ge8d+1\). Then \(V(I^{(d+1)}_m)\) is the union of:

  • the 15 double-double lines, if \(m\le10d-8\);
  • the 10 triple-double points, if \(m\le10d-6\).

It is empty for \(m\ge10d-5\). Behind this is a criterion, stated only for \(m\ge8d+1\) and points of the 25 lines: such a point lies in \(V(I_m)\) exactly when the span of all arc limits there has an element of order \(m\). The maximal orders of these spans would be \(10d-8\) on the double-double lines, \(10d-6\) at the triple-double points, \(N\) at the quadruple points and \(N-1\) elsewhere on the triple lines. On the open collision planes the collision-regime theorem already excludes every point for \(m\ge8d+1\); the conjecture concerns only the lines. At \(d=3\) the prediction is \(V(I_m)=\emptyset\) for every \(m\ge25\).

Status. Conjecture. All evidence comes from characteristics 32003 and 1000003. The inclusions "\(\supseteq\)" at the computed points are the finite check above. Each class was sampled at one or two points; on the double-double lines only \((1{:}1{:}5{:}5)\) was tested, while the conjecture claims all 15 lines. The converse direction, that a point whose windows stop below \(m\) is not in \(V(I_m)\), is checked only at \(d=2\) (\(m=17,18\)). The maximal orders are fitted to \(d\le5\). The formula needs \(d\ge3\): at \(d=2\) the triple-double value is 13, not 14.

General statement. lem:cube-point-window-membership, for every \(n\), \(d\), \(m\), point and arc over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\). conj:cube-collision-regime-windows is the all-\(d\) statement for the collision regime of \(\{0,1\}^4\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the threshold-ideal lemma, the collision-support theorem, the point-window bound, the flat-limit order bound and the symmetry theorem. Claim searches (point window, arc limit, membership, threshold zero set) found the order-zero point-window bound and the dimension-3 window lemma, which this lemma extends; the dual form is cited, not restated. The table was read from the saved outputs by a script. A fresh-context referee checked every table value, failure count and zero-set output against the files. It found nothing that breaks a stated result. Its corrections are made:

  • the linearity step for spans over several arcs;
  • the unused hypotheses (characteristic, arc shape) are dropped from the first part, and \(P\ne0\) is required;
  • the kernel's precision handling is stated;
  • the pentagon orbit is derived from the \(S_5\)-stability of \(J\), and \(m=18\) from identical components;
  • the characteristic scope is stated for both checks, in the status line, the consequences and the conjecture's status;
  • the criterion is restricted to \(m\ge8d+1\) and the lines, and related to the collision-regime theorem;
  • the sampling of each class is stated;
  • the overclaims in the assessment are removed.

Assessment. The expectation of the last entry fails at \(d=2\) and needs correcting for larger \(d\). In characteristic 1000003 the lines where collision hyperplanes meet carry zeros from \(d=4\) on, through windows that grow by about 10 per step in \(d\): first the triple-double points, then the double-double lines. At \(d=3\) there is no evidence of zeros, and the generic points of the triple lines show no window beyond the generic one; neither absence is proved. The last thresholds before order zero look like a different phenomenon. At \(d=2\), in characteristic 32003, the ideals \(I_{17}\) and \(I_{18}\) have no zeros at all, yet contain no linear form. Their degree-2 parts are spanned by the quadric \(Q\), which vanishes on the pentagon orbit. Whether these thresholds are governed by the geometry of special branch configurations, such as that orbit, or by the degree structure of ideals primary to the irrelevant ideal, is open. The natural next object is the order-zero threshold \(M(d)\) itself. In the dual polynomial form it asks for the least \(m\) with a polynomial \(\Phi(u_1,\ldots,u_4)\), \(\Phi(0)=1\), \(\deg\Phi\le m\), such that each \(\Phi z^a\) has vanishing homogeneous components in the prescribed top degrees: a multivariate Padé problem, with no zero set to localize it. The route review now due should weigh that formulation against the recorded values \(19,39\).

26 September 2026 — Route review of the cube: the middle range is mapped by zero sets, and near order zero the threshold ideals are ideals of S₅-invariants

Route review: the collision-window conjecture survives four more line points; near order zero at d = 2 the threshold ideals begin with S₅-invariants cutting out Springer eigen-orbits. Next: invariant solutions near order zero. Cycle bmd-r116. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

The line's general claim. The per-order function on \(\{0,1\}^n\) in characteristic \(\ne2\) is determined by the thresholds \(\ell_0(h,m)\), the initial degrees of the threshold ideals (threshold-ideal lemma). Dimension 3 is solved over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\). For \(n\ge4\) the claim to establish is a law for the thresholds.

What the goal needs. Open statement 3 for \(n\ge4\): the thresholds at the boundary, in the middle range and at order zero; and open statement 2, small primes. Since route review 16, six cycles worked on the middle range of dimension 4:

  • past the boundary the threshold ideals have height two (entry);
  • one step past it, the ideal is saturated and cuts out a curve, conjecturally of degree 120 at \(d=2\) (entry);
  • the zero sets lie between two rank loci (sandwich);
  • they are Brill–Noether loci for \(m\le2^{n-1}d\) and lie in the collision hyperplanes beyond (theorem);
  • in dimension 4 they then retreat to torsion curves and to the 25 lines (theorem);
  • at \(d=2\) the collision-regime ideals have no zeros, and for larger \(d\) arc-limit windows of about \(10d\) carry points and lines (entry).

Falsification attempt

conj:cube-collision-regime-windows claims the whole double-double lines for \(m\le10d-8\), but only the point \((1{:}1{:}5{:}5)\) had been tested. Along the line \(\{r_1=r_2,\ r_3=r_4\}\) the ratio \(t\) of the two pair positions to the free point is a genuine parameter: only affine maps are symmetries, so points of the line need not be equivalent. The kernel bmd_cube_point_windows ran at \(t=2,3,-1,7\) for \(d=4,5\), with 150 arcs each, over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\) (research/results/bmd-r116-route-review/line-windows-d4-d5.txt). The point \(t=-1\), where the free branch point is the midpoint of the pairs, has an extra symmetry and was the likeliest to differ. All eight spans have orders exactly \(0,\ldots,10d-8\): 32 at \(d=4\) and 42 at \(d=5\), with at most 3 failed arcs. The prediction could have failed at any of them; it passed.

Assessment of this line

The middle range is now mapped by its zero sets, from the boundary to the collision regime. The map does not give the thresholds. The zero sets bound the ideals from below (\(\ell_0\ge\alpha\) of the saturation), but the ideals are not saturated past the first step. Near order zero they have no zeros at all, so the zero sets say nothing there. Only the first step has a conjectured value (the least degree of a surface through a degree-120 curve), and it is unexplained. The geometric program has found structure in every cycle but has not moved the missing implication, a law for \(\ell_0\).

The tests of this review point to a different mechanism near order zero: invariant theory of \(S_5\), not branch-point geometry. With branch points \((0,y_1,\ldots,y_4)\) and centred power sums \(p_k=\sum_i(r_i-\bar r)^k\), the invariant ring is \(F[p_2,p_3,p_4,p_5]\) (characteristic 0 or \(>5\)). At \(d=2\) the lowest parts of the threshold ideals are:

  • \(m=17\) and \(18\) (last before order zero): \((p_2,p_3,p_4)\) exactly, in degrees \(\le4\);
  • \(m=16\): the degree-5 invariants \(p_5\) and \(p_2p_3\);
  • \(m=15\): one invariant sextic in \((p_2,p_3,p_4)^2\).

So the recorded thresholds 6, 5, 2, 2 are degrees of invariants. If this persists, the thresholds near order zero become a problem on the weighted projective space \(\mathbb P(2,3,4,5)=\mathbb P^3/S_5\), the moduli of the branch configurations. The invariant ring changes in characteristics 3 and 5, which ties this to open statement 2. The prospects of the middle range are fair only through this new mechanism. The geometric route should stop at the map it has, and not descend further into special loci.

Outside leads

  • Springer's theorem on regular elements (T. A. Springer, Regular elements of finite reflection groups, Invent. Math. 25, 1974). For a reflection group with basic invariants of degrees \(d_i\), the union of the \(\zeta\)-eigenlines of elements, \(\zeta\) a primitive \(k\)-th root of unity, is the common zero set of the basic invariants of degrees not divisible by \(k\). For \(S_5\) with \(k=5\) this gives \(V(p_2,p_3,p_4)\), the 24 pentagon configurations (degree \(2\cdot3\cdot4\)). With \(k=4\) it gives \(V(p_2,p_3,p_5)\), the 30 square configurations \(r=(0,1,i,-1,-i)\). With \(k=3\) it gives \(V(p_2,p_4,p_5)\), 40 points. It targets open statement 3 near order zero. It would break if the ideals were not generated by invariants. Test. Passed. research/tools/bmd_cube_invariant_ideals.m2 (new) computes the kernel generators of excess \(\le L\), over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\) (invariant-ideals-m15-17.txt, invariant-ideals-m15-16-orbits.txt). At \(m=17\), \(J=(p_2,p_3,p_4)\) exactly. At \(m=16\) both quintics lie in \((p_2,p_3,p_5)\cap(p_2,p_4,p_5)\); they vanish simply at the square point and not at the pentagon point. At \(m=15\) the sextic lies in \((p_2,p_3,p_4)^2\cap(p_2,p_3,p_5)\), not in \((p_2,p_4,p_5)\), and vanishes to order 2 at the pentagon point. At \(m=18\) the saturated excess-\(\le4\) ideal has the same 24 reduced points (check), so it is also \((p_2,p_3,p_4)\).
  • Chevalley's theorem and the isotypic decomposition (C. Chevalley, Amer. J. Math. 77, 1955; the invariant ring of \(S_5\) on the reflection representation is polynomial in \(p_2,\ldots,p_5\) when the characteristic is 0 or \(>5\)). Each graded piece of the \(S_5\)-stable ideal \(I_m\) (symmetry theorem) is a representation. A one-dimensional piece in degree \(<10\) is invariant, since a sign-type form is divisible by the Vandermonde, of degree 10. A two-dimensional piece is a sum of two such, since \(S_5\) has no two-dimensional irreducible representation. So \(\ell_0\) is the least degree of an invariant in \(I_m\) whenever the lowest piece has dimension \(\le2\) and degree \(<10\). It targets open statement 3: the thresholds near order zero would be computed on invariant solutions, a much smaller system. It breaks where the lowest piece is a 4-, 5- or 6-dimensional irreducible. Test. Passed at \(d=2\): the lowest pieces at \(m=15,16,17\) have dimensions 1, 2, 1. The first is the one sextic. The second is the whole two-dimensional degree-5 invariant space, spanned by \(p_5\) and \(p_2p_3\). The third is \(p_2\). So they are invariant by the argument above.
  • Fröberg's conjecture on Hilbert functions of generic Artinian ideals (R. Fröberg, Math. Scand. 56, 1985). Near order zero \(I_m\) is primary to the irrelevant ideal. If it were generic among ideals with given generator degrees, its Hilbert function, and so its behaviour in \(m\), would be predicted. It targets the order-zero threshold \(M(d)\). It breaks if \(I_m\) is special among such ideals, as an \(S_5\)-stable ideal may be. Test. Not run: the low part \((p_2,p_3,p_4)\) is a complete intersection, so it has the generic Hilbert function of three forms of degrees 2, 3, 4, which tests nothing. A real test needs the generators of \(I_{17}\) beyond excess 4, a long Macaulay2 computation (at \(m=13\) excess 15 took 650 s).

Absurd bridges

  • De Bruijn's pentagrid and cut-and-project quasicrystals (N. G. de Bruijn, Algebraic theory of Penrose's non-periodic tilings, Indag. Math. 43, 1981). Penrose tilings arise by projecting \(\mathbb Z^5\), or the root lattice \(A_4\), along the eigenplanes of the Coxeter element of \(S_5\); the octagonal (Ammann–Beenker) tilings use four-fold eigenplanes. Translation: the configuration space \(\mathbb P^3\) is \(\mathbb P(A_4\otimes\mathbb C)\). The last thresholds before order zero select the five-fold eigenlines, the "physical planes" of the Penrose tiling. Then the four-fold eigenlines should appear one step earlier. Test. Passed: the \(m=17\) ideal cuts out the five-fold lines, and the \(m=16\) quintics vanish on the four-fold lines, not the five-fold ones (invariant-ideals-m15-16-orbits.txt). A tiling theorem would add nothing yet; the working content is Springer's theorem above.
  • BCH syndrome decoding (Peterson 1960; Gorenstein–Zierler, J. SIAM 9, 1961). Translation: the centred power sums \(p_1=0,p_2,p_3,\ldots\) of the branch points are the syndromes of an error pattern whose locators are the \(r_i\). \(V(p_2,p_3,p_4)\) is the set of patterns with syndromes \(S_1,\ldots,S_4\) all zero, whose error-locator polynomial is \(x^5-c\). The decoder's rule, "\(t\) vanishing syndromes force the locator's shape", would then read: the \(j\)-th threshold before order zero kills \(j\) further syndromes. Test. Falsified as a monotone rule: from \(m=15\) to \(16\) the vanishing pattern changes type, from \((p_2,p_3,p_4)^2\) to the square and three-fold orbits, instead of adding one syndrome.

Bridge follow-up

  • Chip-firing on a cycle. Not worked. Follow-up. Continuing: it belongs to the boundary conjecture, which is parked while the middle range is worked.
  • Odd–even staggering. The row it described, \(\ell_0(3,m)=15,12,11,6,5,2,2,0\), now has a reading near its end: 6, 5, 2 are the degrees of invariants (a sextic, the quintics, \(p_2\)). The pairing picture is an effect of the invariant degrees 2, 3, 4, 5. Follow-up. Continuing: the first values 15, 12, 11 lie in the Brill–Noether regime, which the invariant reading does not reach.
  • The non-crossing rule. Not worked; its content is the monotone squarefreeness conjecture. Follow-up. Continuing.

Lead follow-up

  • Buchsbaum–Eisenbud acyclicity. Developed in the height and first-step entries (height two, saturation one step past the boundary). Past the first step the ideals are not saturated, and the complexes give no initial degrees. Follow-up. Closed: it has given height and saturation, and cannot give \(\ell_0\) for unsaturated ideals.
  • General Weierstrass points are simple. Not worked. Follow-up. Continuing, with the boundary conjecture.
  • Limit linear series along collisions. Developed in the collision-regime entry, whose limit rows on the genus-1 curve give the torsion curves and the 25 lines. Follow-up. Closed: the collision regime's zero sets are mapped, and near order zero the ideals have no zeros for limits to see.
  • Higher Weierstrass points on the universal curve. Not worked. Follow-up. Continuing, with the boundary conjecture.

Next step

On the highest-risk item, open statement 3 in dimension 4, work near order zero with invariant solutions. The symmetry theorem makes \(\psi\) act on solutions with a sign. Averaging over \(S_5\) (invertible in characteristic 0 or \(>5\)) projects the solutions whose top coordinate is invariant onto the invariant part of \(I_m\). A kernel restricted to them, like bmd_cube_symmetric_solutions for \(S_4\), is far smaller. The first question is whether \(\ell_0\) is attained by an invariant at \(d=3\) for \(25\le m\le38\), where \(M(3)=39\). If it is, state the order-zero system in invariant coordinates and look for the mechanism of \(M(d)\) there. If the lowest pieces become 4-, 5- or 6-dimensional irreducibles, the invariant reading fails, and that is the answer.

Process. Three kernel runs (two Macaulay2 runs of the new invariant test, one run of the window kernel).

26 September 2026 — Thresholds are attained by invariants: exact in dimension 3, and the tail before order zero in dimension 4

Working proof: invariant solutions of Young subgroups detect every piece of a threshold ideal below a fake degree; a finite check and a conjecture on invariant thresholds. Cycle bmd-r117. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. Route review 17 found the lowest parts of the dimension-4 threshold ideals near order zero, at \(d=2\), to be invariants of \(S_5\). Is \(\ell_0\) always attained by an invariant? If so, the thresholds are computed on invariant solutions, a system about \(n!\) times smaller. The symmetric reduction of an earlier entry already computes the \(S_n\)-invariant part, so the review's lead partly restates it. The symmetry-theorem entry already used the full \(S_{n+1}\) for linear forms (cor:cube-quadric-threshold-d3, including \(\ell_0(4,38)=2\)), and identified the dimension-3 cubic \(L_2\) as an invariant. What is new here is the general form, which pieces of \(I_m\) the invariant part sees in every degree, and whether the invariant threshold equals \(\ell_0\) where \(\ell_0\) is known. The test ends with that comparison on the proved dimension-3 law and the recorded dimension-4 row.

Setting. \(\{0,1\}^n\) over a field \(F\) of characteristic 0 or \(p>n+1\), so that \(F[S_{n+1}]\) is semisimple. \(I_m=I^{(h)}_m\) is stable under \(S_{n+1}\), acting linearly on \(F[y]\) through the reflection representation on the branch points \((0,y_1,\ldots,y_n)\) (symmetry theorem). \(S_n\subseteq S_{n+1}\) fixes the branch point 0 and permutes the \(y_i\). For a partition \(\lambda\vdash n+1\), \(U_\lambda\) is the irreducible representation (Specht module), and \(n(\lambda)=\sum_i(i-1)\lambda_i\). For a partition \(\nu\vdash n\), \(S_\nu\subseteq S_n\) is the Young subgroup; inside \(S_{n+1}\) it is the Young subgroup of \(\mu=\nu\cup(1)\), sorted. The invariant threshold \(\ell_0^{S_\nu}(h,m)\) is the least excess of an \(S_\nu\)-invariant solution with nonzero top coordinate.

What invariant solutions see

Lemma (lem:cube-isotypic-detection). In this setting let \(\nu\vdash n\), \(\mu=\nu\cup(1)\), and \(e\ge0\). Suppose every \(\lambda\vdash n+1\) with \(n(\lambda)\le e\) dominates \(\mu\). Then the degree-\(e\) part \(I_{m,e}\) is nonzero if and only if some \(S_\nu\)-invariant solution of excess \(e\) has a nonzero top coordinate. In particular:

  • with \(\nu=(n)\), for \(e\le1\): \(\ell_0\le1\) is decided by \(S_n\)-invariant solutions, for every \(n\);
  • for \(n=4\): \(S_3\)-invariant solutions (\(\nu=(3,1)\)) decide every \(e\le3\), \(S_2\times S_2\)-invariant ones every \(e\le5\), and \(S_2\)-invariant ones every \(e\le9\).

Proof. \(I_{m,e}\) is an \(F[S_{n+1}]\)-submodule of \(F[y]_e\), hence a direct sum of irreducibles \(U_\lambda\) occurring in \(F[y]_e\).

  1. Occurrence needs degree \(n(\lambda)\). Since \(|S_{n+1}|\) is invertible, \(F[y]\cong F[y]^{S_{n+1}}\otimes H\) as graded representations, with \(H\) the coinvariant algebra (Chevalley). In \(H\) the representation \(U_\lambda\) first occurs in degree \(n(\lambda)\), the lowest exponent of its fake-degree polynomial \(q^{n(\lambda)}[n+1]_q!/\prod_{x}[h(x)]_q\) (Steinberg; Lusztig; see Stanley, Bull. AMS 1, 1979, Prop. 4.11). So \(U_\lambda\) occurs in \(F[y]_e\) only if \(e\ge n(\lambda)\). In characteristic \(p>n+1\) the same multiplicities hold: \(F[y]_e\) is the reduction of \(\mathbb Z[y]_e\), and the Specht modules reduce to distinct absolutely irreducible modules.
  2. Young's rule. \(\dim U_\lambda^{S_\mu}\) is the Kostka number \(K_{\lambda\mu}\), which is positive if and only if \(\lambda\trianglerighteq\mu\).
  3. If \(I_{m,e}\ne0\), it contains some \(U_\lambda\) with \(n(\lambda)\le e\). By hypothesis \(\lambda\trianglerighteq\mu\), so \(U_\lambda\) has a nonzero \(S_\mu\)-fixed vector, and so does \(I_{m,e}\). As in the symmetric reduction, \(S_\nu\) acts on solutions by permuting the variables. Averaging a solution whose top coordinate is an \(S_\nu\)-invariant \(f\) gives an \(S_\nu\)-invariant solution with top coordinate \(f\) (\(|S_\nu|\) is invertible). The converse is immediate.

For the special cases: the \(\lambda\) with \(n(\lambda)\le1\) are \((n+1)\) and \((n,1)\), both \(\trianglerighteq(n,1)\). For \(n=4\) the values are \(n(5)=0\), \(n(4,1)=1\), \(n(3,2)=2\), \(n(3,1,1)=3\), \(n(2,2,1)=4\), \(n(2,1,1,1)=6\), \(n(1^5)=10\). The first four dominate \((3,1,1)\); all but the last two dominate \((2,2,1)\); all but \((1^5)\) dominate \((2,1,1,1)\). \(\square\)

The case \(e\le1\) generalizes the argument of cor:cube-quadric-threshold-d3: \(I_1\) is 0 or the whole reflection representation. The lemma also says what the \(S_n\)-invariants miss. For \(n=4\) and \(e=2\), the component \(U_{(3,2)}\) of the quadrics has no \(S_4\)-fixed vector. So the invariant test of the symmetric-kernel entry at \(m=38\) could not decide the whole degree-2 part.

Invariant thresholds against known values

Computation. research/tools/bmd_cube_symmetric_solutions.cpp (FLINT, \(\mathbb F_{32003}\)) now scans the excess upward and stops at the first invariant top. research/tools/bmd_cube_torsion_partition.py (new) tabulates \(B(d,\rho)\) and writes the jobs. Two runs are saved in research/results/bmd-r117-invariant-thresholds/.

Finite check (check:cube-invariant-thresholds). Over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\):

  • Dimension 3, \(2\le d\le6\), all \(1\le\rho\le d\) (20 cases, from the boundary \(\rho=1\) to order zero). \(\ell_0^{S_3}(d+1,4d+\rho-1)=B(d,\rho)\) in every case: for example 35, 16, 9, 6, 3, 0 at \(d=6\). By the dimension-3 law this is \(\ell_0\) itself.
  • Dimension 4, \(d=2\), \(13\le m\le18\). \(\ell_0^{S_4}=12,11,6,5,2,2\), the \(\ell_0\) row recorded over the same field \(\mathbb F_{32003}\) by Gröbner computations (route review 14, research/results/bmd-r99-route-review/).
  • Dimension 4, \(d=3\), \(35\le m\le38\). \(\ell_0^{S_4}=4,3,2,2\). No invariant solution of excess 0 or 1 has a nonzero top. By the lemma with \(\nu=(4)\), \(I_{m,0}=I_{m,1}=0\). So \(\ell_0(4,37)=\ell_0(4,38)=2\), \(2\le\ell_0(4,36)\le3\) and \(2\le\ell_0(4,35)\le4\).

The value \(\ell_0(4,38)=2\) reproduces cor:cube-quadric-threshold-d3. The values at \(m=35,36,37\) are new.

The tail before order zero is not the same for all \(d\). At \(d=2\) it is \(6,5,2,2,0\) (\(m=15,\ldots,19\)). At \(d=3\) it is at most \(4,3\), then \(2,2,0\) (\(m=35,\ldots,39\)); the values 4 and 3 are invariant upper bounds. The order-zero values \(M(2)=19\) and \(M(3)=39\) are recorded in the order-zero check. Since \(6>4\) and \(5>3\), the tails differ. Only the last two steps agree, with the quadric of the quadric conjecture.

The conjecture

Conjecture (conj:cube-invariant-attainment). On \(\{0,1\}^n\) in characteristic 0 or \(p>n+1\), for every \(h\ge1\) and \(m\ge0\), the initial degree of \(I^{(h)}_m\) is attained by an \(S_n\)-invariant element: \(\ell_0(h,m)=\ell_0^{S_n}(h,m)\).

Status. Conjecture. The checks test it over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\) only, where it holds in the 20 dimension-3 cases and the 6 dimension-4 cases above; one prime gives no statement in characteristic 0. Where \(\ell_0\le1\) it holds for every \(n\) by the lemma. It would make \(\ell_0\) computable on the invariant system at every \(m\). In dimension 3 it is consistent with the proved law, but no proof uses invariance there. A proof would need the lowest piece of \(I_m\) to contain the trivial or reflection representation of \(S_{n+1}\).

General statement. lem:cube-isotypic-detection, for every \(n\), \(h\), \(m\) and \(\nu\vdash n\) in characteristic 0 or \(p>n+1\). conj:cube-invariant-attainment is the all-parameter statement tested here.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the symmetric reduction, the symmetry theorem and its corollary, and the dimension-3 law. Claim searches (invariant, symmetric, isotypic, threshold) found lem:cube-symmetric-reduction and cor:cube-quadric-threshold-d3, which the lemma generalizes, and which already recorded \(\ell_0(4,38)=2\). The dimension-3 values were compared with \(B(d,\rho)\) by a script. A fresh-context referee found the proof correct: the sign in the symmetry theorem is harmless for a linear space, and the fake degrees, Young's rule, the Young-subgroup embedding and every value \(n(\lambda)\) and dominance claim check out. It confirmed every number against the outputs. Its corrections are made:

  • the rediscovery of \(\ell_0(4,38)=2\) is attributed;
  • the refinement of the earlier argument is linked;
  • the conjecture is stated in the lemma's setting, with the evidence over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\) only;
  • the field of the recorded row is stated;
  • the \(d=3\) tail values 4 and 3 are called upper bounds;
  • the order-zero values are linked;
  • the lower bound 2 is made conditional;
  • the status line is shortened, and the characteristic-\(p\) step of the proof is tightened.

Assessment. The invariant reading passed its first real test. In dimension 3, where \(\ell_0\) is proved, the invariant thresholds reproduce the law exactly in all 20 cases, including the boundary. In dimension 4 they reproduce the whole recorded \(d=2\) row past the boundary. The lemma turns the invariant computations into exact values where \(\ell_0\le1\). It gives the lower bound 2 wherever the invariant scan finds no invariant top at excess 0 or 1 (over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\)). At \(d=3\) near order zero this gives \(\ell_0=2\) at \(m=37,38\). The tail before order zero depends on \(d\) (\(6,5\) against at most \(4,3\)), so there is no universal tail. For open statement 3 the gain is computational and structural. If the conjecture holds, the dimension-4 row at \(d=3\), and the order-zero thresholds, can be computed on invariant systems, and a law can be sought there. The next step is to prove the conjecture in dimension 3, where the answer is known: is the lowest piece of each \(I_m\) there an invariant? Or else to find the representation-theoretic reason. The order-zero kernel is already symmetric, which is the case \(\ell_0=0\) of the conjecture.

26 September 2026 — In dimension 3 every threshold is attained by an S₄-invariant: the boundary generators are invariant

Working proof in characteristic ≠ 2: on {0,1}³ the boundary generators are S₄-invariant, and every threshold ideal's initial degree is attained by a product of them; so the invariant-attainment conjecture holds for n = 3 (characteristic ≠ 2, 3). Cycle bmd-r118. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The invariant-attainment conjecture says that \(\ell_0(h,m)\) is always attained by an \(S_n\)-invariant element. It held in all 20 dimension-3 cases computed. In dimension 3, \(\ell_0\) is known (dimension-3 law), and its upper bound comes from explicit products (product bound). Are those products invariant? That would prove the conjecture for \(n=3\). The test ends with a proof, or with a threshold whose minimal elements carry the sign character.

Setting. \(\{0,1\}^3\) over a field \(F\) of characteristic \(\ne2\). For \(d\ge1\), \(N=4d\), and \(D_d=W_N=\Delta_{3,d}/g_{3,d}\) is the top coordinate of the primitive boundary solution, of degree \(d^2-1\) (boundary theorem). \(S_4\) permutes the branch points \((0,y_1,y_2,y_3)\) and acts linearly on \(F[y]\). Every threshold ideal is \(S_4\)-stable (symmetry theorem). The mirrors of the transpositions are the six collision lines \(y_i=0\), \(y_i=y_j\).

The boundary generators are invariant

Lemma (lem:cube-boundary-generator-invariant). For every \(d\ge1\), \(D_d\) is \(S_4\)-invariant and does not vanish identically on any collision line.

Proof.

  1. \(D_d\) is a semi-invariant. \(A_N\) has rank \(N\) over \(F(y)\), since \(\Delta_{3,d}\ne0\) (boundary theorem), so the solution module at \(m=N\) has rank \(N+1-N=1\). It is the kernel of a map of free modules, hence reflexive of rank 1 over the factorial ring \(F[y]\), hence free. So \(I_N=(D_d)\) is principal. \(S_4\) preserves \(I_N\) and degrees, so \(\sigma D_d=\chi(\sigma)D_d\) for a character \(\chi\colon S_4\to F^\times\). The abelianization of \(S_4\) has order 2, so \(\chi\) is trivial or the sign.
  2. The sign is excluded by one mirror. If \(\chi\) is the sign, then for the transposition \(s\) with mirror \(H\), \(D_d|_H=(sD_d)|_H=-D_d|_H\), since \(s\) fixes \(H\) pointwise. So \(D_d\) vanishes on \(H\) (characteristic \(\ne2\)). It is enough to find a point of the mirror \(y_3=0\), the collision of \(r_3\) with \(r_0\), where \(D_d\ne0\). (The transposition \(r_0\leftrightarrow r_3\) acts by \((y_1,y_2,y_3)\mapsto(y_1-y_3,y_2-y_3,-y_3)\), a reflection fixing \(y_3=0\) pointwise.)
  3. Lifting to the collision limit. Let \(P=(c_1,c_2,0)\) with \(c_1,c_2\) nonzero and distinct. The collision lifts (lem:cube-collision-lifts, as in the local-limits lemma, Part 3) are stated at \(y_1=0\); permuting the coordinates, which preserves the system, carries them to \(y_3=0\). The rows of \(A\) are \(F[y]\)-combinations, with invertible unitriangular transition, of powers of \(y_3\) times rows \(\lambda\) with polynomial entries. At \(y_3=0\) those rows are, up to nonzero constants (characteristic \(\ne2\)), the basis \(T^Qz^r\) (\(Q+|r|\le d\), \(r\in\{0,1\}^2\)) of the collision limit space \(U=U_d(c_1,c_2)\), of dimension \((d+1)+2d+(d-1)=4d\). Since \(z_i=(1-w_i)/2\) is affine in \(w_i\), \(U=\bigoplus_{r}w^rF[T]_{\le d-|r|}\). Since \(A=S\Delta A^\Lambda\) with \(S\Delta\) invertible over \(F(y)\), the \(F[y]\)-kernels of \(A_N\) and \(A^\Lambda_N\) are equal, so \(I_N\) is also the ideal of top coordinates for \(A^\Lambda\). As in the proof of the collision-regime theorem, Part 1, \(I_N\) is the unit ideal at \(P\) as soon as the square matrix \(A^\Lambda_{N-1}(P)\) has rank \(N\): its determinant lies in \(I_N\). That holds when no nonzero element of \(U\) has order \(\ge N=4d\) at \(p_0\).
  4. The genus-0 limit has no element of order \(4d\). On the curve \(C\colon w_1^2=1+a_1T\), \(w_2^2=1+a_2T\) (\(a_i=4c_i\)), which has genus 0, the place \(T=\infty\) splits into two points \(P_1,P_2\), each ramified of index 2. There \(T\) has poles of order 2 and each \(w_i\) of order 1. Let \(H_\infty=P_1+P_2\). Then \(U\subseteq L(2dH_\infty)=\bigoplus_rw^r\{T^j:2j+|r|\le2d\}\), which has dimension \(4d+1\) and degree \(4d\). \(U\) is the hyperplane where the coefficient \(\lambda\) of \(w_1w_2T^{d-1}\) vanishes. On a curve of genus 0 the orders at \(p_0\) of \(L(2dH_\infty)\) are \(0,\ldots,4d\), and the functions of order \(4d\) are the multiples of \(\varphi=\psi^{2d}\). Here \(\psi=(a_1-a_2)+a_2w_1-a_1w_2\) has a double zero at \(p_0\) and divisor \(2p_0-H_\infty\). Write the odd-odd part of \(\varphi\) as \(w_1w_2D(T)\), with \(\deg D\le d-1\); it is \(\tfrac14\sum_{\varepsilon}\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2\,\psi(\varepsilon_1w_1,\varepsilon_2w_2)^{2d}\). As \(T\to\infty\), \(w_i\sim\sqrt{a_iT}\), so the leading coefficient is \[ \lambda(\varphi)=[T^{d-1}]D=-(a_1a_2)^d\sum_{k\text{ odd}}\binom{2d}k\,a_1^{(k-1)/2}a_2^{\,d-(k+1)/2}. \] This polynomial is nonzero in every characteristic \(\ne2\). Write \(2d=p^as\) with \(p\nmid s\) when \(p=\operatorname{char}F>0\); then \(k=p^a\) is odd and \(\binom{2d}{p^a}\equiv s\not\equiv0\) by Lucas. In characteristic 0 take \(k=1\). So for general \(c_1,c_2\), \(\varphi\notin U\). Then every nonzero element of \(U\) has order \(\le4d-1\), and with \(\dim U=4d\) the orders are exactly \(0,\ldots,4d-1\).
  5. Hence \(I_N\) is the unit ideal at a general point of \(y_3=0\), so \(D_d\) does not vanish there, \(\chi\) is trivial, and \(D_d\) is invariant. An invariant nonvanishing on one mirror is nonvanishing on all of them, since \(S_4\) permutes them transitively. \(\square\)

The formula for \(\lambda(\varphi)\) was checked by exact expansion of \(\psi^{2d}\) for \(d\le7\) (research/tools/bmd_cube_genus0_limit_check.py, research/results/bmd-r118-invariant-dimension-three/genus0-limit-check.txt). For \(d=1\) it is \(-2a_1a_2\).

Every threshold of the 3-cube is attained by an invariant

Theorem (thm:cube-invariant-attainment-dimension-three). On \(\{0,1\}^3\) over a field of characteristic \(\ne2\), let \(h=d+1\) and suppose \(I^{(h)}_m\ne0\). Then its initial degree \(\ell_0(h,m)\) is attained by an \(S_4\)-invariant form, namely a nonzero multiple of \(\prod_iD_{p_i}\), with \(p_1,\ldots,p_q\) the balanced partition of the dimension-3 law. The form is invariant under the full branch-point group \(S_4\), which is more than the \(S_3\)-invariance the conjecture asks for. If moreover the characteristic is not 3, then \(\ell_0(h,m)=\ell_0^{S_3}(h,m)\). This is conj:cube-invariant-attainment for \(n=3\); the conjecture's scope, characteristic 0 or \(p>4\), is covered.

Proof. For \(m<4d\), \(I_m=0\): the savings at \(m\) are at most the root-curve order \(\kappa_3(m)=\lfloor m/4\rfloor+1\le d\) (stable law). For \(m\ge5d-1\), \(\ell_0=0\) and constants are invariant: the \(\delta_F\) formula of the dimension-3 law gives savings \(\ge\lfloor(m+1)/5\rfloor+1\ge d+1\) at \(\ell=0\). For \(m=4d+\rho-1\) with \(1\le\rho\le d-1\), \(\ell_0=B(d,\rho)\) by the same law, which holds over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\) and supplies the lower bound \(\ell_0\ge B\). The product bound multiplies boundary witnesses for \(p_1,\ldots,p_q\) with an order-zero witness. By its lowest-part statement, the element of \(I_m\) of degree \(B\) it produces is, up to sign, the product of the lowest parts of the factors. The lowest part of a boundary witness for \(p\) is a nonzero element of degree \(p^2-1\) in \(I_{4p}=(D_p)\), so it is \(c_pD_p\) with \(c_p\ne0\) (the sign and the substitution \(-y\) only change constants, as \(D_p\) is homogeneous). The order-zero factor contributes a nonzero constant. So \(c\prod_iD_{p_i}\in I_m\) with \(c\ne0\) has degree \(B=\ell_0\), and it is invariant by the lemma. If \(|S_3|=6\) is invertible, lem:cube-symmetric-reduction (symmetric reduction) gives an \(S_3\)-invariant solution with this top coordinate. So \(\ell_0^{S_3}\le\ell_0\), and the reverse inequality is trivial. \(\square\)

This explains the 20 agreements of the invariant-threshold check. The earlier observation that the degree-3 generator at \((3,13)\) is the invariant cubic \(L_2=D_2\), up to a constant (symmetry-theorem entry), is the case \(p=2\) of the lemma.

General statement. lem:cube-boundary-generator-invariant and thm:cube-invariant-attainment-dimension-three, for every \(d\ge1\) and every \(m\) in characteristic \(\ne2\) (\(\ne2,3\) for the equality with the \(S_3\)-invariant threshold). The all-\(n\) statement remains conj:cube-invariant-attainment.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the boundary theorem, the product bound with its lowest-part statement, the collision-regime theorem's Part 1, the local-limits lemma's Part 3, and the exact statement of the dimension-3 law. That law gives \(\ell_0(d+1,4d+\rho-1)=B(d,\rho)\) for all \(1\le\rho\le d\) over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\), with the \(\delta_F\) formula for all \(k,\ell\); it carries the lower bound. Claim searches (invariant, semi-invariant, boundary generator, mirror) found only this thread's symmetric-reduction, isotypic-detection and symmetry results. The formula for \(\lambda(\varphi)\) was checked by exact expansion for \(d\le7\).

A fresh-context referee verified each step independently:

  • the rank-1 freeness;
  • the reflection fixing \(y_3=0\);
  • the equality of kernels;
  • the genus, the pole orders, the hyperplane and the divisor of \(\psi\);
  • the coefficient formula, which it derived in the equivalent form \(k\mapsto2d-k\);
  • Lucas for every odd \(p\), including 3;
  • the use of the lowest parts.

It found nothing that breaks a stated result. Its corrections are made:

  • the scope of the dimension-3 law is quoted, and the case \(m>5d-1\) sourced;
  • the mirror is transferred from \(y_1=0\), with the constants of the limit rows;
  • the \(z\) and \(w\) bases are identified;
  • the rank of \(A_N\) is stated;
  • the constant replaces the sign in the theorem;
  • \(S_4\) against \(S_3\) and the characteristic scope are stated, and the averaging is cited;
  • two overclaims in the assessment are removed.

Assessment. The invariant reading is now a theorem in dimension 3, by a short mechanism. Each threshold ideal at a boundary is principal, so its generator is a semi-invariant. A semi-invariant of sign type must vanish on every mirror. The collision limit on one mirror is a genus-0 space without the extremal function, so the generator does not vanish there. The same argument reduces the invariance of any principal threshold generator, in any dimension, to its nonvanishing on one mirror. That nonvanishing is the hard step. For \(n=4\), the boundary ideal \(I_{8d-4}\) is principal. Its generator is invariant as soon as it does not vanish on the mirror \(y_1=0\), which needs the genus-1 collision limit \(U_d(y')\) to have no element of order \(\ge8d-4\). Past the boundary the ideals are no longer principal, and the lowest pieces can be larger representations. There the conjecture needs a new argument, and the dimension-3 route suggests one: in dimension 3 some minimal element of every threshold ideal is a product of boundary generators. The next step is the dimension-4 boundary generator, then whether dimension-4 minimal elements past the boundary factor through boundary generators, as the recorded factorizations at \(d=2\) may already show.

26 September 2026 — In every dimension the boundary generator is an S_{n+1}-invariant

Working proof in characteristic 0, for every n ≥ 2 and d ≥ 1: the boundary threshold ideal is principal, with an S_{n+1}-invariant generator that vanishes on no collision hyperplane. Cycle bmd-r119. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. In dimension 3 the invariance of the thresholds came from the boundary generators. Each generates a principal ideal, so it is a semi-invariant. It is not of sign type, because it does not vanish on a mirror (dimension-3 lemma). Does the same hold in every dimension? The invariant-attainment conjecture would then hold at every boundary \(m=N_{2,n}(d)\). The test ends with a proof, or with a boundary generator that vanishes on a collision hyperplane.

Setting. \(\{0,1\}^n\) with \(n\ge2\), over a field of characteristic 0. \(N=N_{2,n}(d)\), \(\Delta_{n,d}\) is the boundary determinant, and \(g_{n,d}\) is the gcd of the maximal minors of the \(N\times(N+1)\) matrix \(A_N\). \(W_N=\Delta_{n,d}/g_{n,d}\) is the top coordinate of the primitive boundary solution. The collision forms are \(\ell_D\) for the \(\binom{n+1}2\) hyperplanes \(y_i=0\), \(y_i=y_j\), the mirrors of the transpositions of \(S_{n+1}\).

The theorem

Theorem (thm:cube-boundary-generator-invariant-all-n). In characteristic 0, for every \(n\ge2\) and \(d\ge1\):

  1. \(I^{(d+1)}_N=(W_N)\) is principal;
  2. \(W_N\) is \(S_{n+1}\)-invariant and vanishes identically on no collision hyperplane;
  3. so \(\ell_0(d+1,N)=\deg W_N\) is attained by an \(S_{n+1}\)-invariant form, and conj:cube-invariant-attainment holds at every boundary.

Proof.

  1. Principal. \(\Delta_{n,d}\ne0\) by the generic normality lemma, so \(A_N\) has rank \(N\) over \(F(y)\). Its kernel has rank 1, and it is reflexive over the factorial ring \(F[y]\), hence free. Its primitive generator is the Cramer vector divided by \(g_{n,d}\), whose top entry is \(\pm\Delta_{n,d}/g_{n,d}\). So \(I_N=(W_N)\).
  2. Semi-invariant. \(I_N\) is \(S_{n+1}\)-stable and homogeneous (symmetry theorem), and the units of \(F[y]\) are constants. So \(\sigma W_N=\chi(\sigma)W_N\) for a homomorphism \(\chi\colon S_{n+1}\to F^\times\). It factors through the abelianization \(\mathbb Z/2\), so it is trivial or the sign. If it were the sign, \(W_N\) would vanish on every mirror: a transposition fixes its mirror \(H\) pointwise, so \(W_N|_H=-W_N|_H\).
  3. No collision factor. By the collision-exponent theorem, \(v_D(\Delta_{n,d})=v_D(g_{n,d})=E_n(d)\) for every collision hyperplane \(D\). So \(v_D(W_N)=0\): \(W_N\) vanishes on no collision hyperplane.
  4. So \(\chi\) is trivial and \(W_N\) is invariant. Part 3 follows. \(I_N\) is principal, so every element of degree \(\ell_0\) is a constant multiple of \(W_N\). By the symmetric reduction, averaging a solution with top coordinate \(W_N\) over \(S_n\) gives an \(S_n\)-invariant solution with the same top coordinate. \(\square\)

For \(n=3\) this reproves the dimension-3 lemma in characteristic 0. That lemma holds in every characteristic \(\ne2\), by its genus-0 computation.

Write \(g_{n,d}=c\prod_D\ell_D^{\,E_n(d)}g^{\mathrm{nc}}\) and \(\Delta_{n,d}=c'\prod_D\ell_D^{\,E_n(d)}\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\), so that \(W_N=c''\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}/g^{\mathrm{nc}}\). The determinant \(\Delta_{n,d}\) is transported up to a constant by the permutations of the branch points (Möbius transport and coordinate permutations), so \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\) is a semi-invariant with no collision factor, hence an invariant by the same argument. Then \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}=c\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}/W_N\) is invariant too. So the non-collision part of the gcd, whose absence the boundary conjecture asserts, defines an \(S_{n+1}\)-invariant hypersurface if it is nonconstant. Its irreducible factors are only permuted.

Check. For \(n=4\), \(d=2\), \(m=N=12\), over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), the bmd_cube_symmetric_solutions kernel finds a one-dimensional space of \(S_4\)-invariant solutions with nonzero top coordinate at excess 15, the recorded threshold, and none at excess 14 (research/results/bmd-r119-boundary-invariant/n4-d2-boundary-invariant.txt). The kernel imposes only \(S_4=S_n\), not the transposition \(r_0\leftrightarrow r_1\). So it confirms that \(\chi\) is trivial on \(S_4\) and that \(\deg W_N=15\), in one characteristic. The absence at excess 14 is just the recorded threshold. This is a consistency check, not a new finite result.

General statement. thm:cube-boundary-generator-invariant-all-n, for every \(n\ge2\) and \(d\ge1\) in characteristic 0. The conjecture remains open strictly between the boundary and order zero, where \(\ell_0\ge2\) and the ideals are not principal.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the collision-exponent theorem, the reduction theorem, the generic normality lemma, the symmetry theorem and the symmetric reduction. A claim search (boundary generator, invariant, semi-invariant) found the dimension-3 lemma, which this theorem extends. A fresh-context referee checked the principality, the character argument and the exponents, and recomputed the degrees 0, 15 and 55. It found nothing that breaks a stated result. Its corrections are made:

  • the direct valuation argument replaces a detour through the reduction theorem, which widens the scope to \(n\ge2\);
  • the remark on \(\Delta^{\mathrm{nc}}\) and \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}\) is sourced correctly, and speaks of the hypersurface, not its factors;
  • the check is described as what it tests;
  • the dimension and the conditional degrees in the assessment are stated.

Assessment. The invariance of the thresholds now holds at both ends of every row, in every dimension. At the boundary it holds by this theorem. At order zero and wherever \(\ell_0\le1\), it holds by the isotypic detection lemma. In dimension 3 it holds everywhere. The open part is the middle range for \(n\ge4\). There the ideals are not principal, and the dimension-3 route through products of boundary generators is closed. Products lose savings in dimension 4: the savings of a product are \(h_1+h_2-n+2=h_1+h_2-2\) (product bound, its product rule). The recorded dimension-4 minimal elements at \(d=2\), of degrees 12, 11, 6, 5 and 2, are not products of boundary generators by degree alone. Those generators have degrees 0, 15, 55 at \(d=1,2,3\); the general value \(10d^2-10d-5\) needs \(\deg g^{\mathrm{nc}}=0\), certified for \(d\le9\). The next step is the lowest pieces of the middle-range ideals as \(S_5\)-representations, and whether a middle-range analogue of the semi-invariance argument exists. Candidates are principal ideals attached to the Brill–Noether loci, or the saturations.
