26 September 2026 — The savings-4 row on {0,1}⁴ near order zero, and monotone thresholds

Finite check: invariant thresholds of the savings-4 row on {0,1}⁴ for 28 ≤ m ≤ 38. Conjecture: thresholds never increase with m, proved for n ≤ 3 and false in characteristic 2. Cycle bmd-r120. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. Open statement 3 needs a law for the dimension-4 thresholds, and only one row was known, \(d=2\): \(\ell_0(3,m)=15,12,11,6,5,2,2,0\) for \(m=12,\ldots,19\). One row cannot suggest a law. What is the row \(d=3\) (savings 4, boundary \(m=20\), order zero at \(m=39\))? The Gröbner computations did not reach it. The invariant thresholds \(\ell_0^{S_4}\) are always upper bounds for \(\ell_0\), and equal to it under the invariant-attainment conjecture, which holds at every boundary (theorem) and in dimension 3. The test ends with the row as far down from order zero as a dense computation reaches.

The row

Computation. research/tools/bmd_cube_symmetric_solutions.cpp has a new rank mode. The top coordinates of the invariant solutions of excess \(e\) span a space of dimension \(\#\mathrm{top}-(\operatorname{rank}A-\operatorname{rank}A_{\mathrm{nontop}})\). Here \(A_{\mathrm{nontop}}\) omits the columns of the top block. The two ranks come from fflas-ffpack (FFPACK::Rank over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\) in double storage), about five times faster than the FLINT nullspace. Validation: it reproduces the \(d=2\) row \(12,11,6,5,2,2\) for \(m=13,\ldots,18\) and the recorded \(d=3\) values at \(m=35,36,38\) (research/results/bmd-r120-row-d3/rank-mode-validation.txt). Each scan starts at excess 0 and stops at the first invariant top. The largest system had 13720 rows and 9301 columns (25 s).

Finite check (check:cube-dimension-four-row-d3). Over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), on \(\{0,1\}^4\) at savings 4 (row-d3-m28-34.txt, and the previous check for \(35\le m\le38\)):

\(m\)282930313233343536373839
\(\ell_0^{S_4}(4,m)\)1513111087543220

The value 0 at \(m=39\) is the recorded order-zero threshold (order-zero check). At every \(m\) of the table no invariant solution of excess 0 or 1 has a nonzero top coordinate. So, in characteristic 32003, \(2\le\ell_0(4,m)\le\ell_0^{S_4}(4,m)\), with equality under the conjecture. The lower bound is the isotypic detection lemma with \(\nu=(4)\): it holds for every \(m\) and every \(e\le1\), in characteristic 0 or \(p>5\). A rank modulo one prime can drop relative to characteristic 0, so neither bound transfers to characteristic 0 without a lift. Rows for \(m<28\) need excesses whose dense systems exceed the memory budget in this form, and they are not computed.

In terms of the per-order function: \(I^{(h)}_m\) decreases in \(h\) (threshold-ideal lemma), so the savings at \((k,\ell)\) are \(\ge4\) exactly when \(\ell_0(4,k-\ell-1)\le\ell\). For each order \(\ell\), the least such \(k\) is \(\ell+1\) plus the least \(m\) with \(\ell_0(4,m)\le\ell\). Reading the table as the values of \(\ell_0\), and assuming no \(m<28\) has \(\ell_0(4,m)\le\ell\), this least \(k\) is \(40,40,40,40,41,41,41,42,42,42,43,43,44\) for \(\ell=2,\ldots,14\). The assumption needs the monotonicity conjecture below. Without both conjectures the list only bounds the least \(k\) from above. For \(\ell=0,1\) the least \(k\) is 40 and 41 (order zero at \(m=39\), and \(\ell_0\ge2\) below it), so it is not monotone in \(\ell\) there. From \(\ell=2\) on, raising the order at the origin by 3 costs about one unit of multiplicity.

Monotone thresholds

Every computed row is nonincreasing in \(m\). This is equivalent to monotonicity of the savings in \(k\) at fixed origin order. Indeed, by the threshold-ideal lemma, \(h(k,\ell)\ge h\) exactly when \(\ell_0(h,k-\ell-1)\le\ell\), for each \(h\); here the lemma's nesting \(I^{(h+1)}_m\subseteq I^{(h)}_m\) is used. So \(\ell_0(h,m+1)\le\ell_0(h,m)\) for all \(h,m\) is the same as \(h(k+1,\ell)\ge h(k,\ell)\) for all \(k,\ell\). With \(h=n+2k-2-\delta\), that is \(\delta(n,k+1,\ell)\le\delta(n,k,\ell)+2\).

Conjecture (conj:cube-threshold-monotone). On \(\{0,1\}^n\) over a field of characteristic \(\ne2\), \(\ell_0(h,m+1)\le\ell_0(h,m)\) for all \(h\) and \(m\), with \(\ell_0=\infty\) when \(I^{(h)}_m=0\). Equivalently, \(\delta_F(n,k+1,\ell)\le\delta_F(n,k,\ell)+2\).

Proposition (prop:cube-threshold-monotone-low-dimension). The conjecture holds for \(n\le3\), over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\).

Proof. For \(n=1\) the least degree is \(k+\ell\), attained by \(x^\ell(x-1)^k\) and forced by the root count, so the savings \(n+2k-2-\delta\) are \(m\). For \(n=2\) the square theorem gives \(\delta=2k-\lceil(k-\ell-1)/2\rceil\), so the savings are \(\lceil m/2\rceil\). Both are nondecreasing in \(m\). For \(n=3\), by the dimension-3 law and the stable law, \(\ell_0(d+1,m)\) is \(\infty\) for \(m<4d\), \(B(d,m-4d+1)\) for \(4d\le m\le5d-1\), and 0 beyond. So it suffices that \(B(d,\rho+1)\le B(d,\rho)\) for \(1\le\rho<d\). With \(j=d-\rho\):

  • If \(\rho\ge j\), then \(B(d,\rho)=3j\) (all parts equal to 2), and it decreases with \(\rho\).
  • If \(\rho+1<d-\rho-1\), both values are \(S_\rho(d)=\min\sum(p_i^2-1)\) over partitions of \(d\) into \(\rho\) parts, respectively \(\rho+1\) parts. Splitting a part \(p\ge2\) (one exists, as \(d>\rho\)) into \(p-1\) and \(1\) changes \(\sum(p_i^2-1)\) by \(-(2p-1)<0\). So \(S_{\rho+1}(d)<S_\rho(d)\).
  • At the transition, \(\rho<d-\rho\) and \(\rho+1\ge d-\rho-1\), so \(d\in\{2\rho+1,2\rho+2\}\) and \(B(d,\rho+1)=3(d-\rho-1)=3\rho\) or \(3\rho+3\). For \(d=2\rho+1\), \(B(d,\rho)=3(\rho-1)+8=3\rho+5\). For \(d=2\rho+2\), \(B(d,\rho)=3(\rho-2)+16=3\rho+10\) (\(\rho\ge2\)), or \(15\) (\(\rho=1\)). Both exceed \(B(d,\rho+1)\).

\(\square\) A check of \(B(d,\rho+1)\le B(d,\rho)\) for all \(d\le400\) agrees (dimension-three-monotone.txt).

Over \(\mathbb F_2\) it fails. Over \(\mathbb F_2\) the per-order value is \(\delta=n+2\ell+\sum_{j<n}\lfloor m/2^j\rfloor\) (per-order theorem), so the savings are \(h=m-\sum_{1\le j<n}\lfloor m/2^j\rfloor\). They drop from \(m\) to \(m+1\) whenever \(4\mid m+1\) and \(n\ge3\) (for \(n=4\): \(h=2\) at \(m=3\), \(h=1\) at \(m=4\)). So the savings form of the conjecture is false over \(\mathbb F_2\). The threshold-ideal translation is set up in characteristic \(\ne2\), so this speaks only to the savings form; it shows that the hypothesis on the characteristic cannot simply be dropped from that form.

Evidence for \(n=4\). The \(d=2\) row, exact in characteristic 32003 (Gröbner), is nonincreasing. The \(d=3\) invariant row above is nonincreasing; these are upper bounds for \(\ell_0\) in characteristic 32003. All the evidence for \(n=4\) is in that one characteristic, while the conjecture claims every characteristic \(\ne2\).

General statement. conj:cube-threshold-monotone, for every \(n\), \(h\), \(m\) in characteristic \(\ne2\); prop:cube-threshold-monotone-low-dimension proves it for \(n\le3\). The row check tests it, and supplies the second row that a law for open statement 3 needs.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read:

  • the threshold-ideal lemma, including its nesting in \(h\);
  • the isotypic detection lemma;
  • the dimension-3 law, the square theorem and the per-order theorem;
  • the collision-window conjecture.

A claim search (monotone threshold, nonincreasing) found no earlier version. A fresh-context referee checked:

  • the rank formula, as the dimension of the projection of the kernel;
  • every table value against the outputs, and that every scan starts at excess 0;
  • the least-\(k\) list;
  • the proof for \(n\le3\), including the regime values against the recorded dimension-3 scans;
  • the \(\mathbb F_2\) example.

It found nothing that breaks a stated result. Its corrections are made:

  • the nesting in \(h\) is cited, and \(\delta\) is related to the savings;
  • the least-\(k\) list is cut at \(\ell=14\), called conditional on both conjectures, and noted as non-monotone at \(\ell=0,1\);
  • the \(\mathbb F_2\) paragraph is scoped;
  • the characteristic of every bound and of the evidence is stated;
  • the regime ranges are sourced;
  • the proved case is registered as its own proposition.

Assessment. The second row gives a first comparison. Near order zero, the savings-3 row descends \(2,2,5,6,11,12\) from \(m=18\) down to \(m=13\), and the savings-4 row descends \(2,2,3,4,5,7,8,10,11,13,15\) from \(m=38\) down to \(m=28\). The second is much flatter. By the collision-support theorem the collision regime is \(m>8d\): from \(m=25\) to 38 at \(d=3\), against 17 to 18 at \(d=2\). There the ideals conjecturally have no zeros (collision-window conjecture). Over \(28\le m\le38\) the thresholds grow by about 1.3 per step. A law would have to explain these slopes. A quadratic order-zero threshold, which remains open, means that the flat stretch lengthens with \(d\). The monotonicity conjecture is a structural statement the rows suggest. Its natural proof would map solutions at \(m\) to solutions at \(m+1\) with the same top coordinate, and no such map is known in dimension 4.

26 September 2026 — Order zero on {0,1}⁴ is at most 20d − 21, by products; the quadratic conjecture is false

Working proof in characteristic 0: the least m with savings d + 1 at origin order 0 on {0,1}⁴ is at most 20d − 21. This refutes the recorded quadratic conjecture (65 predicted at d = 4). Conjecture: equality. Cycle bmd-r121. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. Open statement 3 includes the order-zero thresholds \(M(d)\) of \(\{0,1\}^4\): the least \(m=k-1\) with savings \(\ge d+1\) at origin order \(\ell=0\). The recorded values are 5, 19, 39 (order-zero check). They were fitted by \(3d^2+5d-3\) (quadratic conjecture) and equally by \(20d-21\). The second row (savings-4 row) near order zero agrees at \(m=35,37,38,39\) with sums of values of the first row. Is the second row, at least at order zero, built from the first by products? The test ends with a proof of the product bound at order zero, or with a product that fails.

The product bound at order zero

Products. Let \(P_1,P_2\in F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) have Hasse multiplicity \(\ge k_i\) at every nonzero point of \(\{0,1\}^n\), and \(P_i(0)\ne0\). Then \(P_1P_2\) has multiplicity \(\ge k_1+k_2\) at those points, because lowest forms multiply, and \((P_1P_2)(0)\ne0\). Its degree is \(\delta_1+\delta_2\). With savings \(h=n+2k-2-\delta\), the product has savings \(h_1+h_2-n+2\) at \(k=k_1+k_2\), that is at \(m=m_1+m_2+1\). This is the product rule of the product bound, at origin order 0. For \(n=4\) the savings are \(h_1+h_2-2\). With \(h_i=d_i+1\) this gives, over every field,

\[ M(d_1+d_2-1)\le M(d_1)+M(d_2)+1\qquad(d_1,d_2\ge1). \]

For \(d_1=1\) the inequality is empty. The first useful factor is \(d_1=2\): \(M(d)\le M(d-1)+M(2)+1\).

Theorem (thm:cube-order-zero-dimension-four-linear-bound). On \(\{0,1\}^4\) in characteristic 0, and in every odd characteristic other than 5, 179, 281 and 2959174039205819, \(M(d)\le20d-21\) for every \(d\ge2\): there is a polynomial of degree at most \(2k+1-d\) with multiplicity \(\ge k=20d-20\) at the nonzero points of \(\{0,1\}^4\) and nonzero value at the origin.

Proof. \(M(2)\le19\) in these characteristics, by the certificate below. By induction with the product inequality, \(M(d)\le M(d-1)+20\le19+20(d-2)=20d-21\). Concretely, the product of \(d-1\) copies of a \(d=2\) witness (multiplicity 20, degree \(\le39\), savings \(\ge3\)) has multiplicity \(20(d-1)\), degree \(\le39(d-1)\) and savings \(\ge3(d-1)-2(d-2)=d+1\). \(\square\) Existence at larger \(k\) with the same savings would follow from the monotonicity conjecture; it is not claimed.

The certificate at \(d=2\). research/tools/bmd_cube_order_zero_exact.cpp (new) solves the symmetric order-zero system of the dual form exactly over \(\mathbb Q\), with FLINT's fmpz_mat_can_solve. It verifies \(Ax=b\) in exact arithmetic. Averaging over \(S_n\) reduces a solution to a symmetric one in characteristic 0, so the symmetric system decides existence there. Validation: in dimension 3 it gives unsolvable at \(m=8,13\) and solvable at \(m=9,14\) (\(d=2,3\)), the proved \(M_3(d)=5d-1\) (exact-n3-validation.txt). In dimension 4 (exact-n4-d1-d2.txt, research/results/bmd-r121-order-zero-linear/):

  • \(d=1\): unsolvable at \(m=4\), solvable at \(m=5\);
  • \(d=2\): unsolvable at \(m=18\) (815 rows, zero rows included, 514 unknowns); solvable at \(m=19\) (932 rows, 608 unknowns). The solution is verified exactly. The primes dividing its denominators are 5, 179, 281 and 2959174039205819.

A further run finds the system unsolvable over \(\mathbb Q\) at every smaller \(m\): \(m\le3\) for \(d=1\) and \(m\le17\) for \(d=2\) (exact-n4-below-thresholds.txt). So \(M(1)=5\) and \(M(2)=19\) in characteristic 0. The rational solution reduces modulo every other odd prime to a solution there. At the four listed primes this certificate says nothing; another solution may exist.

The quadratic conjecture is false

Refutation (ex:cube-order-zero-quadratic-false). conj:cube-order-zero-dimension-four-quadratic predicts \(M(d)=3d^2+5d-3\) in characteristic 0, which is 65 at \(d=4\). The theorem gives \(M(4)\le59\). The quadratic exceeds \(20d-21\) for every \(d\ge4\), since \(3d^2-15d+18=3(d-2)(d-3)>0\) there. So the conjecture fails for every \(d\ge4\), in characteristic 0 and in every odd characteristic outside the four primes of the certificate, so both parts of its statement (characteristic 0 and large odd characteristic) are refuted. It agrees with the linear formula exactly at \(d=2,3\), which is why the two fits could not be separated. The recorded negative check at \(d=4\), \(m=50\), is consistent with both.

The linear conjecture

Conjecture (conj:cube-order-zero-dimension-four-linear). On \(\{0,1\}^4\) in characteristic 0, \(M(d)=20d-21\) for every \(d\ge2\): products of the \(d=2\) order-zero witness with itself are optimal.

Status. Conjecture. Upper bound: the theorem. The lower bound is exact over \(\mathbb Q\) for \(d\le2\). At \(d=3\) it is known only modulo 1000003 (order-zero check, a scan of all \(m\)), with \(m=38\) also excluded modulo 32003 (symmetric kernel). At \(d=4\) it is known only up to \(m=50\), modulo 1000003 and 2039 (check). Unsolvability modulo \(p\) does not imply unsolvability over \(\mathbb Q\): when \(p\) divides the denominators of every rational solution, the rank of \(A\) drops modulo \(p\) while that of \([A\mid b]\) does not. The analogy supports it: in dimension 3 the order-zero thresholds \(5d-1\) are exactly additive under the product rule, \(M_3(d_1+d_2)=M_3(d_1)+M_3(d_2)+1\).

The rows near order zero. The same product rule gives \(\ell_0(h_1+h_2-2,m_1+m_2+1)\le\ell_0(h_1,m_1)+\ell_0(h_2,m_2)\). From the \(d=2\) row it predicts, at savings 4, the bounds 0, 2, 2, 4, 4 at \(m=39,38,37,36,35\), and 7 at \(m=34\). The computed invariant values are 0, 2, 2, 3, 4 and 5. So products of two savings-3 factors attain the row at \(m=35,37,38,39\), but not at \(m=34,36\). There the ideals contain elements that are not such products. Other splittings (savings 2 times savings 4, or factors of higher savings) were not examined. Both rows are taken over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), where the inequality applies.

General statement. thm:cube-order-zero-dimension-four-linear-bound for every \(d\ge2\), and conj:cube-order-zero-dimension-four-linear for its equality.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the dual form, the product rule of the product bound, the order-zero checks at \(d=3,4\) and the quadratic conjecture's exact statement. A claim search (order zero, dimension four, product) found the conjecture refuted here and the product rule. The exact kernel was validated on the proved dimension-3 thresholds.

A fresh-context referee checked:

  • the product rule and the induction;
  • the refutation arithmetic;
  • that the exact system matches the modular kernel and the dual form;
  • the use of fmpz_mat_can_solve and the exact verification;
  • the bad primes;
  • that symmetric solvability decides characteristic 0;
  • the product predictions for the row.

It found nothing that breaks a stated result. Its corrections are made:

  • the reason why modular unsolvability does not transfer;
  • the row claim restricted to two-factor products, in one characteristic;
  • degree bounds rather than exact degrees;
  • the refutation's scope in odd characteristic;
  • the evidence scopes at \(d\le2\), 3 and 4;
  • rows counted as rows;
  • the history sourced;
  • the process lesson moved into the framework.

Assessment. A conjecture of this route is refuted, by a two-line argument that was available when it was made. The product rule was recorded before the conjecture, in the dimension-3 order-zero upper bound and the product bound, and applying it to the order-zero witnesses at \(d=2\) gives the linear bound. At the time the quadratic was preferred on the grounds that point windows gave no linear mechanism. The mechanism is not a window but products. For open statement 3 the order-zero end is now: at most \(20d-21\) in characteristic 0, conjecturally equal. It needs a lower-bound mechanism, the analogue of the dimension-3 window lemma, which in dimension 4 must be of higher order (point windows stop at \(m\le13\) at \(d=2\)). The process lesson, to apply the known composition rules to computed witnesses before fitting a formula, is added to the framework's computation rules.

26 September 2026 — The order-zero savings grow at a rate: 1, 2, 5 in dimensions 1 to 3, and between 8 and 20 in dimension 4

Working proof: in every dimension the order-zero thresholds are subadditive after a shift, so a savings rate c_n exists, with 2^{n−1} ≤ c_n; c₁, c₂, c₃ = 1, 2, 5 and 8 ≤ c₄ ≤ 20 in characteristic 0. Cycle bmd-r122. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The linear bound came from the product rule at origin order 0. What does that rule say in every dimension? At origin order 0 the per-order value is \(\delta_F(n,k,0)=n+2k-2-h\). Its growth is set by how fast the savings \(h\) grow with \(k\). The test ends with a statement for all \(n\), or with a dimension where the product rule gives nothing.

Setting. Over a field \(F\), for \(e\ge1\) let \(b_n(e)\) be the least multiplicity \(k\) with savings \(\ge e+n-2\) at \((k,0)\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), or \(\infty\) if there is none. It is nondecreasing in \(e\), since savings \(\ge e+1+n-2\) imply savings \(\ge e+n-2\). In terms of the order-zero thresholds \(M_n(d)\) (the least \(m=k-1\) with savings \(\ge d+1\) at origin order 0), \(b_n(e)=M_n(e+n-3)+1\).

The rate

Theorem (thm:cube-order-zero-rate). Over every field \(F\) and for every \(n\ge1\):

  1. \(b_n(e_1+e_2)\le b_n(e_1)+b_n(e_2)\) for \(e_1,e_2\ge1\);
  2. \(b_n(e)\ge2^{n-1}e\) for every \(e\ge1\);
  3. if some \(b_n(e_0)\) is finite, then all are, and the limit \(c_n(F)=\lim_{e\to\infty}b_n(e)/e=\inf_eb_n(e)/e\) exists, with \(c_n\ge2^{n-1}\).

So, under the hypothesis of part 3, the savings at origin order 0 and every multiplicity \(k\) are at most \(n-2+k/c_n\), and at least \(k/c_n-o(k)\). For the lower bound, take \(e\) maximal with \(b_n(e)\le k\). Then \(r=k-b_n(e)<b_n(1)\), since \(b_n(e+1)\le b_n(e)+b_n(1)\). Multiply the witness by \(\prod_i(1-x_i)^r\), which has multiplicity \(\ge r\) at every nonzero point, value 1 at the origin and degree \(nr\). By the product rule the savings at \(k\) are \(\ge e+n-2-(n-2)r\), and \(r\) is bounded. Without the hypothesis of part 3 the savings are \(\le n-2\) at every \(k\).

Proof.

  1. Subadditivity. Products of witnesses with \(P_i(0)\ne0\) have multiplicities adding, degrees adding, and savings \(h_1+h_2-n+2\) (product rule). With \(h_i=e_i+n-2\), the product has savings \(e_1+e_2+n-2\) at multiplicity \(k_1+k_2\), which is part 1.
  2. Lower bound. The multiplicity Schwartz–Zippel bound on \(\{0,1\}^n\) (binary multiplicity note, valid over every field) gives \(\delta\ge2k-\lfloor k/2^{n-1}\rfloor\) for a polynomial with multiplicity \(\ge k\) at the nonzero points. So the savings satisfy \(h=n+2k-2-\delta\le n-2+\lfloor k/2^{n-1}\rfloor\). Savings \(e+n-2\) therefore need \(k\ge2^{n-1}e\).
  3. The limit. \(b_n\) is nondecreasing, since \(M_n\) is. If \(b_n(e_0)<\infty\), part 1 gives \(b_n(je_0)<\infty\) for every \(j\), and monotonicity gives finiteness of every \(b_n(e)\le b_n(\lceil e/e_0\rceil e_0)\). Fekete's lemma for the finite subadditive sequence \(b_n\) gives the limit and its equality with the infimum. Part 2 bounds it below. \(\square\)

Values.

  • \(n=1\): the savings are \(m\), so \(M_1(d)=d+1\), \(b_1(e)=e\) and \(c_1=1\). Schwartz–Zippel is tight here.
  • \(n=2\): the savings are \(\lceil m/2\rceil\) (square theorem), so \(M_2(d)=2d+1\), \(b_2(e)=2e\) and \(c_2=2\). Tight.
  • \(n=3\), characteristic \(\ne2\): \(M_3(d)=5d-1\) (order-zero theorem), so \(b_3(e)=5e\) and \(c_3=5\), above the Schwartz–Zippel value 4.
  • \(n=4\): \(b_4(1)=M_4(2)+1\le20\) in characteristic 0 and in every odd characteristic except 5, 179, 281 and 2959174039205819, with equality in characteristic 0 (linear bound). So \(8\le c_4\le20\) in those characteristics. The linear conjecture is \(b_4(e)=20e\), that is \(c_4=20\).
  • Over \(\mathbb F_2\) the per-order value (per-order theorem) gives savings \(m-\sum_{1\le j<n}\lfloor m/2^j\rfloor=m/2^{n-1}+O(n)\) at order 0. So \(c_n(\mathbb F_2)=2^{n-1}\). An \(\mathbb F_2\)-witness stays a witness over every field containing \(\mathbb F_2\), which gives the upper bound, and Schwartz–Zippel holds over every field. So \(c_n(F)=2^{n-1}\) for every field of characteristic 2: there Schwartz–Zippel is asymptotically tight at order zero, in every dimension.

In characteristic 0 the sequence begins \(1,2,5\), with \(c_4\in[8,20]\) (and the same in odd characteristic, outside the four primes for \(c_4\)). The ratios \(c_n/2^{n-1}\) are \(1,1,5/4\), and at most \(5/2\) for \(n=4\). For \(n\ge5\) the theorem is conditional on one finite \(b_n(e_0)\), which is not computed.

General statement. thm:cube-order-zero-rate, for every \(n\ge1\) over every field; the value of \(c_4\), and whether \(c_n/2^{n-1}\) grows, are open.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the product rule, the Schwartz–Zippel bound of the binary multiplicity note, the order-zero theorem in dimension 3, the square theorem, the per-order theorem over \(\mathbb F_2\), and the linear bound with its characteristic scope. A claim search (order zero, rate, subadditive) found no earlier version.

A fresh-context referee checked every part and every listed value. It found nothing that breaks a stated result. Its corrections are made:

  • the lower bound at every \(k\) is now unconditional, by padding with \(\prod(1-x_i)^r\);
  • the characteristic scope of \(c_4\le20\) is stated;
  • characteristic 2 in general is derived from \(\mathbb F_2\);
  • \(b_n\) is defined directly;
  • the hypothesis of part 3 is stated where it is used.

Assessment. This turns the order-zero question of open statement 3 into one number per dimension. It fixes the shape: order-zero thresholds are asymptotically linear in \(d\) in every dimension where one witness beyond savings \(n-2\) exists. The quadratic reading, now refuted, was impossible for that reason too. What remains at order zero is the value of \(c_4\), with 20 conjectured. A lower bound above Schwartz–Zippel in dimension 4 needs the dimension-4 analogue of the dimension-3 window mechanism, which gave \(c_3=5>4\). In dimension 3 the windows came from double points, where two collision lines cross. In dimension 4 the corresponding loci are the triple-double points and double-double lines of the collision-window entry, whose point windows are too short. So the lower-bound mechanism must use jets of higher order. The next research is route review 18.

26 September 2026 — Route review of the cube: invariant thresholds, products at order zero, and a rate per dimension

Route review: the linear order-zero conjecture survives its sharpest test (no solution at d = 4, m = 58 modulo 2039). Structure is proved; no law yet for dimension 4. Next: a lower bound on c₄ above Schwartz–Zippel. Cycle bmd-r123. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

The line's general claim. The per-order function on \(\{0,1\}^n\) in characteristic \(\ne2\) is determined by the thresholds \(\ell_0(h,m)\), the initial degrees of the threshold ideals. Dimension 3 is solved. For \(n\ge4\) the claim to establish is a law for the thresholds.

What the goal needs. Open statement 3 for \(n\ge4\): thresholds at the boundary, in the middle range and at order zero; and open statement 2, small primes. Since route review 17, six cycles:

  • thresholds are attained by invariants: detection lemma, dimension 3 in full, every boundary in every dimension (entry, entry, entry);
  • the savings-4 row near order zero, and the monotonicity conjecture, proved for \(n\le3\) (entry);
  • order zero on \(\{0,1\}^4\) is at most \(20d-21\) by products, refuting the quadratic conjecture (entry);
  • order-zero savings grow at a rate \(k/c_n\) in every dimension, with \(2^{n-1}\le c_n\), \(c_3=5\) and \(8\le c_4\le20\) (entry).

Falsification attempt

conj:cube-order-zero-dimension-four-linear predicts \(M(4)=59\): the product of three \(d=2\) witnesses is optimal. So there should be no order-zero solution at \(m=58\), one step below the product bound. A solution there would refute it, and \(m=58\) is where a better irreducible witness would first show. The sparse kernel bmd_cube_order_zero_sparse ran in compress mode over \(\mathbb F_{2039}\) (research/results/bmd-r123-route-review/):

  • \(m=54\) as a sizing run: 17604 unknowns, not solvable (322 s);
  • \(m=58\): 23159 unknowns, 34736 equations, rank 23159, not solvable (939 s).

The compress mode is probabilistic, with failure probability below \(1/((p-1)p^3)\). At \(m=59\) the product theorem gives a solution in this characteristic, since 2039 is not among its four excluded primes. So modulo 2039 the order-zero threshold at \(d=4\) lies in \((58,59]\) at the tested points (50, 54, 58 unsolvable). The prediction could have failed; it passed. Unsolvability modulo one prime does not transfer to characteristic 0.

Assessment of this line

The line is strong in structure and weak on its target. It now has a proved frame for the thresholds of every dimension:

  • they are attained by invariants at both ends of each row and wherever \(\ell_0\le1\);
  • the order-zero end is asymptotically linear, with a rate \(c_n\) between the Schwartz–Zippel value and the best product;
  • in dimension 4 the product of the \(d=2\) witness gives \(c_4\le20\).

What it lacks is any lower-bound mechanism beyond Schwartz–Zippel in dimension 4. There \(c_4\) could be anything in \([8,20]\), and the middle range has two computed rows and no law. Every lower bound so far in dimension 4 is computational and modular. The dimension-3 lower bounds came from windows at double points, but in dimension 4 the point windows are too short (point windows). The review's first outside lead shows why no field-free argument can help. The prospects of the line rest on one missing mechanism: a lower bound that uses the characteristic, through the square roots \(w_i\), and jets of higher order.

Outside leads

  • The punctured Combinatorial Nullstellensatz with multiplicities (Ball–Serra, Punctured combinatorial Nullstellensatz, Combinatorica 29, 2009; Kós–Mészáros–Rónyai, Some extensions of Alon's Nullstellensatz, 2011). These bound the degree of a polynomial that vanishes with multiplicity on a grid except at a punctured set, which is exactly the order-zero setting. It targets a lower bound on \(c_4\). It breaks if the bound is valid over every field. Test. Falsified as a route to \(c_4>8\): any lower bound valid over every field is at most the value over \(\mathbb F_2\), and \(c_n(\mathbb F_2)=2^{n-1}\) (rate theorem). So such bounds cannot exceed Schwartz–Zippel asymptotically, and a bound above 8 must use characteristic \(\ne2\).
  • Chudnovsky's bound for the Waldschmidt constant (G. V. Chudnovsky, 1981; the bound \(\hat\alpha(Z)\ge(\alpha(Z)+N-1)/N\) for points in \(\mathbb P^N\), proved by Esnault–Viehweg in characteristic 0). At order zero, \(\lim\delta(n,k,0)/k=2-1/c_n\) is a Waldschmidt-type constant of the 15 nonzero vertices, with the extra condition at the origin. It targets \(c_4\). It breaks if the bound is weaker than Schwartz–Zippel. Test. Falsified. The least degree of a polynomial vanishing at the 15 nonzero vertices of \(\{0,1\}^4\) and not at the origin is \(\alpha=4\) (Alon–Füredi). With \(N=4\) the bound gives \(\hat\alpha\ge7/4\). Schwartz–Zippel already gives \(2-1/8=15/8>7/4\).
  • Springer's regular elements and Chevalley's invariant theory (followed from route review 17). The invariant ring \(F[p_2,p_3,p_4,p_5]\) and its weighted projective space \(\mathbb P(2,3,4,5)\) carry the thresholds wherever invariance holds. The \(d=2\) order-zero witness is, after averaging, an invariant \(\Phi\) in \(u\). A lower bound on \(c_4\) could come from bounding the degrees of invariant solutions of the order-zero system in the invariant coordinates, where the unknowns are about \(120\) times fewer. It targets \(c_4\). It breaks if invariant solutions are no easier to bound than general ones. Test. Passed as a consistency check: the \(S_4\)-symmetric order-zero system, with 24 times fewer unknowns, already decides \(M(2)=19\) exactly over \(\mathbb Q\) (certificate). A bound needs a structural argument, not yet found.

Absurd bridges

  • The renewal-reward theorem (queueing theory; Ross, Stochastic Processes, Ch. 3). Translation: an order-zero witness is a renewal cycle whose cost is its multiplicity and whose reward is its savings above \(n-2\). Products concatenate cycles, and \(c_n\) is the long-run cost per unit reward. The theorem says the rate is attained by repeating a single optimal cycle when cycles combine additively. Here that means \(c_4=20\) unless some irreducible witness at larger \(e\) has a better ratio. Test. Passed: \(b_4(2)=M_4(3)+1=40=2\,b_4(1)\) (modulo 1000003), so the second cycle length gives no better ratio, and in dimension 3, \(b_3(e)=5e\) exactly.
  • Natural monopoly and subadditive cost functions (economics: Baumol, On the proper cost tests for natural monopoly, Amer. Econ. Rev. 67, 1977). Translation: \(b_n(e)\) is the cost of producing \(e\) units of savings. Subadditivity is the natural-monopoly condition. Baumol's test for economies of scale is the ray average cost \(b_n(e)/e\), which declines exactly when larger single firms (irreducible witnesses) are cheaper per unit. A declining ray average cost would predict \(c_4<20\). Test. Passed as a null: the ray average cost is constant where computed (\(20,20\) for \(n=4\); \(5\) for all \(e\) in \(n=3\); 1 and 2 for \(n=1,2\)). There are no economies of scale in any computed dimension, consistent with \(c_4=20\).

Bridge follow-up

  • Chip-firing on a cycle. Not worked. Follow-up. Continuing, with the boundary conjecture.
  • Odd–even staggering. The second row tests it. For the savings-4 row \(2,2,3,4,5,7,8,10,11,13,15\) (from order zero down), the second differences \(\Delta(j)=\ell_0(j)-\tfrac12(\ell_0(j-1)+\ell_0(j+1))\) are \(-\tfrac12,0,0,-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,-\tfrac12,0\). They alternate only in the middle and vanish elsewhere. Follow-up. Closed: pairing is not a law of the rows. The \(d=2\) pairs are explained by invariant degrees and products.
  • The non-crossing rule. Not worked. Follow-up. Continuing, with the boundary conjecture.
  • De Bruijn's pentagrid. Its content, the Coxeter eigenlines, is Springer's theorem, and was developed as the invariant reading. Follow-up. Closed: the tiling picture adds nothing beyond the eigen-orbits.

Lead follow-up

  • General Weierstrass points are simple. Not worked. Follow-up. Continuing, with the boundary conjecture.
  • Higher Weierstrass points on the universal curve. Not worked. Follow-up. Continuing, with the boundary conjecture.
  • Springer's theorem on regular elements. Developed into invariant attainment: the boundary theorem and the dimension-3 theorem. Follow-up. Continuing, as the third outside lead above.
  • Chevalley's theorem and the isotypic decomposition. Developed into the isotypic detection lemma. Follow-up. Closed: its content is now a working lemma used in every invariant computation.

Next step

On the highest-risk item, open statement 3 in dimension 4, look for a lower bound on \(c_4\) above 8 that uses the characteristic. The dimension-3 mechanism is the template. There, two collision lines through a double point each impose a window of \(4d\) powers of \(w\), and the Möbius transport shifts one window against the other. In dimension 4 the analogous objects are the double-double lines, where two collision hyperplanes meet. The windows must be taken with derivatives of \(W\) along the line, which is what point windows miss. The first test is whether first-order jets along a double-double line at \(d=2\) exclude any \(m\) between 14 and 18.

Process. Two runs of the sparse kernel (a sizing run and the test).

26 September 2026 — Windows at the triple-double points: order zero on {0,1}⁴ is at least 11d − 11, so 11 ≤ c₄ ≤ 20

Working proof in characteristic ≠ 2: on {0,1}⁴ every solution vanishes at the triple-double points for m ≤ 11d − 12, so the order-zero threshold is at least 11d − 11 and 11 ≤ c₄ ≤ 20. Cycle bmd-r124. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. Route review 18 asked for a lower bound on the order-zero rate \(c_4\) above the Schwartz–Zippel value 8. Such a bound must use the characteristic. The dimension-3 mechanism is the template: two windows of powers of \(w\) at a double point, one from each collision divisor, shifted against each other by the Möbius transport (window lemma). Computed arc limits in dimension 4 show windows of about \(10d\) at the triple-double points (check). Can the dimension-3 argument be run there, by hand and for every \(d\)? The test ends with a window lemma for every \(d\), or with the step where the transport fails.

Setting. \(\{0,1\}^4\) over a field of characteristic \(\ne2\), \(d\ge2\), \(m\ge0\), and \(W\) any solution of the \((d+1)\)-system at \(m\). Branch points are \((0,y_1,\ldots,y_4)\). The point \(P=(0,0,c,c)\) with \(c\ne0\) is a triple-double point: \(r_0=r_1=r_2\) and \(r_3=r_4\). Put \(a=4c\) and \(w=(1+aT)^{1/2}\), so \(T=(w^2-1)/a\). "\(W(P)\) kills \(g\)" means \(\sum_cW_c(P)[T^c]g=0\).

The window lemma

Lemma (lem:cube-triple-double-windows). \(W(P)\) kills \(w^i\) for every integer \(i\) with \(-(4d-5)\le i\le7d-7\), and also for \(i=4d\). For \(d\ge3\) this is an interval of \(11d-11\) exponents; for \(d=2\) it is \([-3,8]\), of 12.

Proof. Four steps give the first window; the Möbius transport gives the second.

  1. Restriction to \(y_1=0\). As in Part 1 of the collision-regime theorem, \(A=S\Delta_1A^\Lambda\) with \(S\Delta_1\) invertible over \(F(y)\). So every solution satisfies \(A^\Lambda W=0\), and \(W|_{y_1=0}\) kills the collision limit space \(U=\bigoplus_{r\subseteq\{2,3,4\}}w^rF[T]_{\le d-|r|}\), identically in \(y_2,y_3,y_4\).
  2. Merging \(w_2\) into 1. Since \(w_2-1=4y_2T/(w_2+1)\), the series \((w_2-1)^k\) is divisible by \(y_2^k\), with quotient \((4T)^k(w_2+1)^{-k}\), whose coefficients are polynomial in \(y_2\). Expanding \(w_2^i=(1+4y_2T)^{\lfloor i/2\rfloor}w_2^{i\bmod2}\) writes \((w_2-1)^k=A_k(T)+w_2B_k(T)\), with \(\deg A_k\le\lfloor k/2\rfloor\) and \(\deg B_k\le\lfloor(k-1)/2\rfloor\), polynomial in \(y_2\). For \(r\subseteq\{3,4\}\) and \(k\le2(d-|r|)\), \((w_2-1)^kw^r\) is therefore an \(F[y_2]\)-combination of elements of \(U\). Dividing the identity by \(y_2^k\) (in the domain \(F[y_2,y_3,y_4]\)) and setting \(y_2=0\): \(W|_{y_1=y_2=0}\) kills \(2^kT^kw^r\). So it kills \(U_2=\bigoplus_{s\subseteq\{3,4\}}w^sF[T]_{\le2d-2|s|}\), identically in \(y_3,y_4\).
  3. The arc \(y_3=c(1+\varepsilon)\), \(y_4=c\). Then \(w_4=w\) and \(w_3^2=w^2+\varepsilon(w^2-1)\). As polynomials in \(w\):
    • the part of \(U_2\) without \(w_3\) contains all polynomials of degree \(\le4d-3\), and \(w^{4d-2}\), \(w^{4d}\): even degrees \(\le4d\) from \(F[T]_{\le2d}\), odd degrees \(\le4d-3\) from \(wF[T]_{\le2d-2}\);
    • the \(w_3\)-part contains \(w_3\cdot\{\text{polynomials of degree}\le4d-6\}\): even degrees \(\le4d-4\) from \(F[T]_{\le2d-2}\), odd degrees \(\le4d-7\) from \(wF[T]_{\le2d-4}\).
    As in the dimension-3 window lemma, \((w_3-w)^k=A_k(w)+w_3B_k(w)\) with \(\deg A_k\le k\), \(\deg B_k\le k-1\), over \(F[\varepsilon]\). So \(G_{k,e}=w^e(w_3-w)^k\) lies in the \(F[\varepsilon]\)-span of \(U_2\) when \(k=0\) and \(e\le4d-3\), or \(e=4d-2,4d\); or when \(k\ge1\), \(e\ge0\) and \(e+k\le4d-5\). Also \(w_3-w=\varepsilon(w^2-1)/(w_3+w)\), and \(w_3+w\) is a unit with constant term 2. So \(H_{k,e}=\varepsilon^{-k}G_{k,e}\) has coefficients in \(F[[\varepsilon]]\), with value \(\bar H_{k,e}=2^{-k}w^{e-k}(w^2-1)^k\) at \(\varepsilon=0\). Since \(W(y(\varepsilon))\) kills every \(G_{k,e}\), \(W(P)\) kills every \(\bar H_{k,e}\).
  4. The first window. \(\bar H_{k,e}\) has lowest exponent \(e-k\) and highest \(e+k\le4d-5\). The lowest exponents reach every \(i\in[-(4d-5),-1]\) (take \(e=0\), \(k=-i\)). The case \(k=0\) gives \(w^e\) for \(0\le e\le4d-2\) and \(e=4d\). By induction from the top, \(W(P)\) kills \(w^i\) for \(i\in[-(4d-5),4d-2]\cup\{4d\}\).
  5. The second window, by transport. The Möbius transport of the boundary theorem holds in every dimension. It substitutes \(T=\tilde T/(1-a_3\tilde T)\), multiplies by \(\tilde w_3^{\,d}\), and changes \(a\) to \(\tilde a=(a_1-a_3,a_2-a_3,-a_3,a_4-a_3)\). It sends a solution \(W\) to a solution \(\tilde W\), with the same top coordinate, and \(W(P)\) kills \(w_3^{\,d}\sigma(g)\) whenever \(\tilde W(\tilde P)\) kills \(g\). Here \(\tilde P=(-c,-c,-c,0)\): the triple is finite, at root \(\tilde w=(1-a\tilde T)^{1/2}\), and the pair contains \(\tilde r_0\). At \(P\), \(w_3=w\) and \(\sigma(\tilde w_i)=w_i/w_3=w^{-1}\) for \(i\le3\), so \(W(P)\) kills \(w^{d-j}\) whenever \(\tilde W(\tilde P)\) kills \(\tilde w^{\,j}\).
    At \(\tilde P\), \(\tilde W\) is a solution for \(\tilde V_d(\tilde a)\). Step 1, applied to it at \(\tilde y_4=0\) after permuting coordinates, gives \(U\) in \(\tilde w_1,\tilde w_2,\tilde w_3\) with \(\nu_r=d-|r|\). Then take the arc \(\tilde y_1=\tilde y_2(1+\varepsilon)\), with \(\tilde y_2,\tilde y_3\) free. For each \(r_3\), with \(e=d-r_3\), the block is \(\mathrm{Poly}_{\le2e}(v)+\tilde w_1\mathrm{Poly}_{\le2e-2}(v)\) in \(v=\tilde w_2\). The dimension-3 window lemma, whose lifts are polynomial in \(\tilde y_2\) and free of \(\tilde y_3\), gives: \(\tilde W\) kills \(\tilde w_3^{\,r_3}v^i\) for \(i\in[-(2e-1),2e]\), identically in \(\tilde y_2,\tilde y_3\).
    These identities specialize to the arc \(\tilde y_3=\tilde y_2(1+\varepsilon)\), which we take next. Let \(L_0=\mathrm{span}\{v^i:-(2d-1)\le i\le2d\}\) and \(L_1=\mathrm{span}\{v^i:-(2d-3)\le i\le2d-2\}\). The lift \(v^e(\tilde w_3-v)^k=v^eA_k(v)+\tilde w_3v^eB_k(v)\) lies in \(L_0+\tilde w_3L_1\) when the exponents \([e,e+k]\) of \(v^eA_k\) lie in \([-(2d-1),2d]\) and those \([e,e+k-1]\) of \(v^eB_k\) lie in \([-(2d-3),2d-2]\). The binding conditions are \(e\ge-(2d-3)\) and \(e+k\le2d-1\). Their limits have lowest exponents \(e-k\ge-(6d-7)\) and highest \(\le2d-1\). With the \(v^i\), \(i\in[-(2d-1),2d]\), this gives: \(\tilde W(\tilde P)\) kills \(\tilde w^{\,j}\) for \(j\in[-(6d-7),2d]\). Transported, \(W(P)\) kills \(w^{d-j}\), that is \(w^i\) for \(i\in[-d,7d-7]\).

The two windows, \([-(4d-5),4d-2]\cup\{4d\}\) and \([-d,7d-7]\), have union \([-(4d-5),7d-7]\) for \(d\ge3\), and \([-3,8]\) for \(d=2\). \(\square\)

Order zero from below

Theorem (thm:cube-order-zero-dimension-four-lower-bound). On \(\{0,1\}^4\) over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\), for \(d\ge3\) and \(m\le11d-12\) (\(m\le11\) for \(d=2\)), every solution of the \((d+1)\)-system at \(m\) vanishes at the ten triple-double points. So \(\ell_0(d+1,m)\ge1\), the order-zero threshold satisfies \(M(d)\ge11d-11\), and \(c_4\ge11\). With the linear bound, \(11\le c_4\le20\) in characteristic 0.

Proof. As in Part 1 of the dimension-3 order-zero theorem. Let \(\mathrm{lo}=-(4d-5)\). For \(0\le c'\le m\), the Laurent polynomial \(E_{c'}=(2c)^{-c'}w^{\mathrm{lo}}(w-1)^{c'}\) has exponents in \([\mathrm{lo},\mathrm{lo}+c']\). That lies inside the window when \(c'\le11d-12\) (\(c'\le11\) for \(d=2\), window \([-3,8]\)). As a series, \(E_{c'}=T^{c'}+O(T^{c'+1})\). So \(W(P)\) kills a unitriangular family spanning \(F^{m+1}\), and \(W(P)=0\). The other nine points follow from the \(S_5\) symmetry, which acts on solution vectors: permutations of the \(y_i\) act by substitution, and the elements moving \(r_0\) act through the invertible transport \(\Lambda\) (symmetry theorem). So \(W(P)=0\) transfers. A nonzero constant does not vanish at \(P\), so \(\ell_0\ge1\). Order zero at \(m\) needs \(\ell_0=0\), so \(M(d)\ge11d-11\). In the notation of the rate theorem, \(b_4(e)=M(e+1)+1\ge11e+1\), so \(c_4\ge11\). \(\square\)

The lemma is the dimension-4 form of the dimension-3 window lemma (lem:cube-double-point-windows). There the two windows had \(4d\) exponents each and union \(5d-1\), which is exactly \(M_3(d)\). In dimension 4 the union, \(11d-11\), stays below the proved upper bound \(M(d)\le20d-21\), which is conjectured to be equality. For \(d\ge3\) the gap is \(9d-10\), and \(19-12=7\) at \(d=2\).

Consistency. The computed arc-limit spans at the triple-double points have orders \(0,\ldots,\mu\) with \(\mu\ge13,24,34,44\) for \(d=2,\ldots,5\) (check). The lemma gives \(11,21,32,43\), so it never exceeds the computed spans. They are lower bounds of the same kind, from different arc families.

The fitted window slope fails

Refutation (ex:cube-collision-windows-slope). conj:cube-collision-regime-windows asserted, in characteristic 0 for \(d\ge3\), that the triple-double points lie in \(V(I_m)\) exactly for \(m\le10d-6\), and that \(V(I_m)=\emptyset\) for \(m\ge10d-5\). By the theorem they lie in \(V(I_m)\) for every \(m\le11d-12\), which exceeds \(10d-6\) for \(d\ge7\). So both statements fail for every \(d\ge7\). The slope 10 was fitted to \(d\le5\). For \(d\le6\), \(11d-12\le10d-6\), so the theorem does not conflict there: at \(d=3,4,5\) it gives 21, 32, 43 against the computed 24, 34, 44. From \(d=7\) on it does. The conjecture's other parts, the double-double lines and the triple lines, are not affected.

General statement. lem:cube-triple-double-windows and thm:cube-order-zero-dimension-four-lower-bound, for every \(d\ge2\) over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the dimension-3 window lemma and order-zero theorem (the template, including the transport step), the collision-regime theorem's Part 1, and the boundary theorem's transport with its every-dimension remark. A claim search (window lemma, triple-double, dimension four) found the dimension-3 lemma, which this adapts, and the computed windows, which it bounds from below. A fresh-context referee checked every step by hand, including \(d=2\) separately:

  • the degree bounds and divisibility in Step 2;
  • the polynomial contents in Step 3;
  • the frame change and the transported window in Step 5, and that the lifts there are polynomial in \(\tilde y_2\);
  • the union and its size;
  • the vanishing range, \(c_4\ge11\), the refutation threshold \(d\ge7\) and the consistency numbers.

No step fails. Its corrections are made:

  • the gap at \(d=2\) is 7, not 8;
  • 20d − 21 is the proved upper bound, conjectured sharp;
  • the intervals \(L_0\), \(L_1\) are written out, and the lift conditions derived;
  • the restriction for \(\tilde W\) is justified;
  • the \(d=2\) case of the theorem is stated;
  • the symmetry is applied to solution vectors;
  • the refutation's range is stated precisely;
  • the status line is shortened.

Assessment. This is the first lower bound in dimension 4 beyond Schwartz–Zippel, and it holds in every characteristic \(\ne2\). The order-zero rate is now pinned to \([11,20]\) in characteristic 0. The mechanism is the dimension-3 one, and it uses the characteristic through \(w\) and the transport. A window lemma cannot close the gap to 20. By the collision-window entry, at \(d=2\) the collision-regime ideals have no projective zeros for \(m=17,18\), so no point of \(\mathbb P^3\) carries an obstruction there. The rest of the gap between \(11d\) and \(20d\) is carried, at least in part, by ideals primary to the irrelevant ideal, which no local argument sees. Closing it needs either better windows, from more frames or from jets at the points, or a global degree argument at the origin of the cone.

26 September 2026 — Order zero restricted to lines and planes: generic planes come within one of the threshold on {0,1}⁴

Working proof: restricting the order-zero system to any linear subspace gives a lower bound for the threshold. Finite check over F₁₀₀₀₀₀₃ (random lines and planes): on {0,1}³ lines give 5d − 1 for d = 2, 3, 4; on {0,1}⁴ lines give 17, 30, 42 and planes 19, 38 (global 19, 39). Cycle bmd-r125. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. On \(\{0,1\}^4\) the order-zero threshold \(M(d)\) lies between \(11d-11\), from windows at the triple-double points (theorem), and \(20d-21\), from products (theorem). Point windows cannot close the gap. At \(d=2\) the ideals just below order zero have no zeros, so the obstruction there is not carried by any point. What sees it? Restricting the system to a line or a plane of \(\mathbb P^3\) gives smaller systems that keep part of the global structure. The test ends with how close each restriction comes to \(M(d)\).

Restriction

Lemma (lem:cube-order-zero-restriction). On \(\{0,1\}^n\) over any field, let \(L\subseteq F^n\) be a linear subspace. Write \(F[L]=\mathrm{Sym}(L^*)\) for the polynomial ring of \(L\), the image of \(F[y_1,\ldots,y_n]\) under restriction. Call an order-zero solution on \(L\) at \(m\) a family \(W_c\in F[L]\), homogeneous of degree \(m-c\) (possibly 0), with \(W_m=1\) and \(\sum_cW_c\,([T^c]f)|_L=0\) in \(F[L]\) for all basis elements \(f\) of \(V_{n,d}\). The identities are polynomial identities, not pointwise ones, which matters over a finite field. Let \(M_L(d)\) be the least \(m\) with such a solution. Then:

  • \(M_L(d)\le M_{L'}(d)\) for \(L\subseteq L'\);
  • in particular \(M_L(d)\le M(d)=M_{F^n}(d)\).

More precisely, a solution on \(L'\) at \(m\) restricts to a solution on \(L\) at the same \(m\).

Proof. Restriction \(F[L']\to F[L]\) is a homomorphism of graded rings. It maps a form of degree \(m-c\) to a form of degree \(m-c\) or to 0, fixes \(W_m=1\), and maps each identity to the restricted identity. \(\square\)

The choice of the cube \(\{0,1\}^n\) plays no role in the proof; it only fixes the space \(V_{n,d}\).

So a restricted system that is unsolvable at \(m\) shows that the global system is unsolvable at that \(m\). It does not by itself give \(M(d)>m\), since solvability is not known to be monotone in \(m\) (monotonicity conjecture, proved only for \(n\le3\)). The lemma gives \(M(d)\ge M_L(d)\), and \(M(d)>m\) once some restrictions cover every \(m'\le m\). The systems are much smaller. On a plane of \(\mathbb P^3\) (a 3-dimensional \(L\)), there are about \(m^3/6\) unknowns rather than \(m^4/24\); on a line, about \(m^2/2\). The same principle, restriction of solutions to a line, underlies the line-restriction bound (lem:cube-line-restriction-bound), which bounds \(\ell_0\) in dimension 3 from the restricted system on a line through a point of known vanishing order. For lines in dimension 3 the lemma here is essentially the order-zero case of that bound. It extends the principle to subspaces of every dimension and every \(n\), with no point hypothesis. That bound transfers to characteristic 0 by semicontinuity because its hypothesis is a zero kernel of a homogeneous system. The consistency test here, with the inhomogeneous condition \(W_m=1\), has no such transfer. Restriction at order zero is also recorded for one special subspace. The obstructions entry restricts to the coordinate hyperplane \(y_1=0\), where the system becomes the two-variable \(U_d\), with value \(4d+1\) for \(d\ge2\) in dimension 3 (check:cube-dual-order-zero-thresholds). That falls short of \(5d-1\); the generic line below does not.

The thresholds of restrictions

Computation. Two new kernels solve the restricted systems over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\), with results in research/results/bmd-r125-restrictions/.

  • research/tools/bmd_cube_line_order_zero.cpp (lines \(y=sv_1+v_2\), FLINT ranks).
  • research/tools/bmd_cube_plane_order_zero.cpp (planes \(y=sv_1+tv_2+v_3\), fflas-ffpack ranks).

Chart encoding: for independent \(v_1,v_2\) (or \(v_1,v_2,v_3\)), forms of degree \(m-c\) on \(L\) correspond one to one with chart polynomials of degree \(\le m-c\). Each identity is homogeneous of degree \(m-Q\), so it vanishes exactly when its dehomogenization does. The plane scans start at \(m=17\) (\(d=2\)) and \(m=30\) (\(d=3\)). The random lines are not inside the random planes, so the plane values are the least solvable \(m\) from that start. The lower bound on \(M(d)\) is argued per \(m\): the first random line is unsolvable at every \(m\le16\), respectively \(m\le29\) (the line kernel scans from \(m=1\)), and the plane at every \(m\) from the start to one below its value.

Validation: the plane kernel on the whole space in dimension 3 gives \(M_3(3)=14\) (plane-n3-validation.txt), and the line kernel on the whole space in dimension 2 gives \(5,7,9=2d+1\) for \(d=2,3,4\) (line-n2-validation.txt).

Finite check (check:cube-order-zero-restrictions). Over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\), the least \(m\) with a restricted order-zero solution. "Generic" means random over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\), one or two samples. Solvability at fixed \(m\) is a constructible condition, so a random line or plane is generic with high probability, not certainly:

restrictiond = 2d = 3d = 4
\(\{0,1\}^3\), a random line91419
\(\{0,1\}^3\), collision lines \(y_1=y_2\) or \(y_2=y_3\)579
\(\{0,1\}^4\), two random lines173042
\(\{0,1\}^4\), three lines through the triple-double point \((0,0,1,1)\)15–1627–2838–40
\(\{0,1\}^4\), a generic line in the collision hyperplane \(y_1=y_2\)91419
\(\{0,1\}^4\), collision lines (double-double, triple)579

Readings:

  • Codimension 1 in dimension 3 is exact. A random line of \(\mathbb P^2\) gives \(5d-1=M_3(d)\) for \(d=2,3,4\). A general line misses the double points where the window lemma places the obstruction, so the obstruction appears to be carried by the restricted problem on a line without any special point; the sampled line was not checked against the double points.
  • Codimension 2 in dimension 4 is not. Random lines of \(\mathbb P^3\) give 17, 30, 42, differences 13 and 12, against 20. They exceed the point windows (\(11d-11\)).
  • Codimension 1 in dimension 4 is nearly exact. Two planes give 19 at \(d=2\), the threshold, and two give 38 at \(d=3\), one below. So the guess that a general hyperplane section decides order zero fails at \(d=3\) modulo this prime, by one, on the two sampled planes.
  • Special lines are weaker than generic ones. In dimension 3 the coordinate line \(y_1=0\) gives \(4d+1\) (recorded above). In a collision hyperplane the dimension-4 system restricts to the dimension-3 one and gives \(5d-1\). On collision lines it gives \(2d+1\), the dimension-2 value.

These are lower bounds for \(M(d)\) over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\) only. A solution modulo \(p\) of a restricted system does not certify anything in characteristic 0. An unsolvable one does not transfer to characteristic 0 either (the reason given in the linear conjecture's status).

General statement. lem:cube-order-zero-restriction, for every \(n\), \(d\) and subspace \(L\) over every field. The finite check measures how much of \(M(d)\) each restriction captures.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the order-zero system and the \(d\le3\) values of the dimension-4 order-zero check, the line-restriction bound (the same principle for \(\ell_0\)), and the coordinate restriction \(U_d\) of the obstructions entry, which the claim search found. A fresh-context referee checked the lemma, the chart encoding, the kernels (row counts, the right-hand side from \(W_m=1\), the rank test) and every table number against the output files. It found the lemma and kernels correct. Its corrections are made:

  • the identities are stated in the polynomial ring of \(L\), not pointwise;
  • unsolvability at one \(m\) no longer claims \(M(d)>m\), since monotonicity is unproved;
  • the plane scans' starting points are justified per \(m\), not by containment, and the kernel comment says so;
  • the third line through \((0,0,1,1)\) is in the table;
  • "generic" is stated as random sampling;
  • the line kernel is validated in dimension 2;
  • a second plane at \(d=3\) was run (also 38);
  • the unchecked claim about the double points is weakened;
  • the relation to the line-restriction bound and the characteristic caveat are stated.

Assessment. Modulo \(1000003\), the dimension-4 order-zero obstruction is captured mostly on planes: points give slope 11 (proved), random lines 17, 30, 42, and random planes 19 and 38, against \(M(2)=19\) and \(M(3)=39\). The global value 39 is itself known only over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\) (check); only \(M(2)=19\) is exact in characteristic 0. The plane values have difference 19 from two points, so a plane bound \(19(d-1)\) would give \(c_4\ge19\), but two values do not suggest a formula. In dimension 3 a random line is exact. A structural proof of the generic-line value \(5d-1\) there, not passing through the double points, would be the template for a plane argument in dimension 4. A general line of \(\mathbb P^2\) meets each of the six special lines (three coordinate lines, three collision lines) once. The coordinate-line restriction gives \(4d+1\) and the collision lines \(2d+1\), so any such proof must use how the line meets them. That is the next step.

26 September 2026 — Restriction is exact where the solution module has depth 3: why a general line sees the whole threshold on {0,1}³

Working proof: restriction of a graded kernel to a general hyperplane is exact exactly when the kernel has depth at least 3. On {0,1}³ general lines therefore carry every threshold ℓ₀(d+1, m) with m ≤ 5d − 1. Cycle bmd-r126. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The restrictions entry found that a random line of \(\mathbb P^2\) gives the full order-zero threshold \(5d-1\) on \(\{0,1\}^3\), although it meets none of the double points that carry the proof of the order-zero theorem. On \(\{0,1\}^4\) random planes fell one short at \(d=3\). The missing implication for open statement 3 is a lower-bound mechanism for \(M(d)\) in dimension 4. This cycle asks when a restriction loses nothing, as a template for when a plane computation or argument decides \(M(d)\). The test ends with a proof of the observed exactness, or with a reason it is accidental.

Setting

Fix \(n\ge3\), a field \(F\) of characteristic \(\ne2\), \(d\ge1\) and \(m\ge0\), and let \(R=F[y_1,\ldots,y_n]\) with irrelevant ideal \(\mathfrak m\). The (d+1)-system at \(m\) is the degree-0 map of graded free modules

\[A:\;S=\bigoplus_{c=0}^mR(c-m)\longrightarrow T=\bigoplus_{(Q,r)}R(Q-m),\qquad W\mapsto\Big(\sum_cW_c\,[T^c]\big(T^Qw^r\big)\Big)_{(Q,r)},\]

over the basis \(T^Qw^r\) (\(2Q+|r|\le d\)) of \(V_{n,d}\). An element of \(S\) of degree \(\ell\) is a vector with \(W_c\) a form of degree \(\ell+m-c\). The solution module is \(K=\ker A\), and \(C=\operatorname{coker}A\). The \(W_m\)-coordinates of the elements of \(K\) form the threshold ideal \(I_m=I^{(d+1)}_m\), with \(\ell_0(d+1,m)=\operatorname{indeg}I_m\) (threshold-ideal lemma). For a nonzero linear form \(\lambda\) put \(R_L=R/\lambda\), the polynomial ring of \(L=V(\lambda)\). Put \(A_L=A\otimes R_L\) and \(K_L=\ker A_L\), the restricted solution module, whose degree-0 part is the space of restricted order-zero solutions of the restriction lemma once \(W_m=1\) is imposed.

The exactness lemma

Lemma (lem:cube-restriction-exactness, the restriction exactness lemma). Let \(A:S\to T\) be any degree-0 map of finitely generated graded free modules over \(R=F[y_1,\ldots,y_n]\), \(n\ge2\), over any field. Let \(K=\ker A\), \(C=\operatorname{coker}A\), and let \(\lambda\) be a nonzero linear form. Nothing specific to the cube, the characteristic, \(d\) or \(m\) is used; the setting above is the case applied here. Then:

  1. \(K/\lambda K\to K_L\) is injective, with cokernel \(\operatorname{Tor}^R_1(C,R_L)\cong(0:_C\lambda)(-1)\).
  2. Suppose \(\lambda\) lies in no associated prime of \(C\) other than \(\mathfrak m\), and \(\operatorname{depth}K\ge3\). Examples: \(K\) free, or \(K=0\). Then \(K_L=K/\lambda K\), and the restricted threshold ideal \(I^L_m\) (the \(W_m\)-coordinates of \(K_L\)) is the image of \(I_m\) in \(R_L\). Consequently:
    • \(\operatorname{indeg}I^L_m\ge\ell_0(d+1,m)\), with equality when \(\lambda\) does not divide every element of \(I_m\) of degree \(\ell_0\);
    • the restricted order-zero system is solvable at \(m\) exactly when the global one is.
  3. In general, \(K_L=K/\lambda K\) if and only if \(\lambda\) is a nonzerodivisor on \(C\). If \(\lambda\) lies in no associated prime of \(C\) other than \(\mathfrak m\), this holds if and only if \(\mathfrak m\notin\operatorname{Ass}C\). For \(n\ge3\) that is equivalent to \(\operatorname{depth}K\ge3\) (including \(K=0\)). If \(\operatorname{depth}K=2\), then \(K_L\ne K/\lambda K\) for every nonzero \(\lambda\).

Over an infinite field every \(\lambda\) outside a finite union of proper subspaces of \(R_1\) satisfies the associated-prime condition. Each associated prime \(P\ne\mathfrak m\) is homogeneous and does not contain all linear forms, so \(P\cap R_1\) is proper.

Proof. Let \(I=\operatorname{im}A\), so that \(0\to K\to S\to I\to0\) and \(0\to I\to T\to C\to0\).

Part 1. Since \(I\subseteq T\) is torsion-free, \(\operatorname{Tor}_1(I,R_L)=(0:_I\lambda)=0\). So \(0\to K/\lambda K\to S/\lambda S\to I/\lambda I\to0\) is exact. From the second sequence, \(0\to\operatorname{Tor}_1(C,R_L)\to I/\lambda I\to T/\lambda T\), because \(\operatorname{Tor}_1(T,R_L)=0\). The map \(A_L\) factors as \(S/\lambda S\twoheadrightarrow I/\lambda I\to T/\lambda T\). So \(K_L\) is the preimage of \(\operatorname{Tor}_1(C,R_L)\), and \(K_L/(K/\lambda K)\cong\operatorname{Tor}_1(C,R_L)\). Finally, \(\operatorname{Tor}_1(C,R_L)\) is the kernel of multiplication by \(\lambda\) on \(C(-1)\), from \(0\to R(-1)\xrightarrow{\lambda}R\to R_L\to0\).

Part 2. Let \(x\in C\) with \(\lambda x=0\). Every associated prime of \(Rx\subseteq C\) is an associated prime of \(C\) containing \(\operatorname{ann}(x)\ni\lambda\), so by hypothesis it is \(\mathfrak m\). Hence \(x\in H^0_{\mathfrak m}(C)\), which has finite length. So \(Q:=K_L/(K/\lambda K)\) has finite length.

Since \(K\subseteq S\) is torsion-free, \(\lambda\) is regular on \(K\), so \(\operatorname{depth}_{R_L}K/\lambda K=\operatorname{depth}K-1\ge2\). \(K_L\) is the kernel of a map of free \(R_L\)-modules, so \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(K_L)=0\). The local cohomology sequence of \(0\to K/\lambda K\to K_L\to Q\to0\) gives \(0=H^0_{\mathfrak m}(K_L)\to H^0_{\mathfrak m}(Q)=Q\to H^1_{\mathfrak m}(K/\lambda K)=0\). So \(Q=0\).

The \(W_m\)-coordinate commutes with restriction, so \(I^L_m\) is the image of \(I_m\). A nonzero element of \(I^L_m\) of degree \(\ell\) lifts to an element of \(I_m\) of degree \(\ell\), which gives the inequality. The image of an element of degree \(\ell_0\) is zero only if \(\lambda\) divides it, which gives the equality clause. For order zero, a degree-0 element of \(I^L_m\) is a nonzero constant and lifts to the same constant.

Part 3. The first equivalence is Part 1. Under the associated-prime hypothesis, the zero-divisors on \(C\) that \(\lambda\) can be are those coming from \(\mathfrak m\), as in Part 2. So \(\lambda\) is a nonzerodivisor iff \((0:_C\lambda)\cap H^0_{\mathfrak m}(C)=0\). This holds iff \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(C)=0\): a nonzero finite-length module has a nonzero socle element, which every linear form kills. That is, iff \(\mathfrak m\notin\operatorname{Ass}C\).

For the depth: \(K\) is a second syzygy, so \(K=0\) or \(\operatorname{depth}K\ge2\). By Auslander–Buchsbaum, \(\mathfrak m\in\operatorname{Ass}C\) iff \(\operatorname{pd}C=n\). When \(\operatorname{pd}C\ge2\), the sequences give \(\operatorname{pd}K=\operatorname{pd}C-2\); when \(\operatorname{pd}C\le1\), \(K\) is free or zero. So for \(n\ge3\), \(\operatorname{pd}C=n\) iff \(\operatorname{pd}K=n-2\), iff \(\operatorname{depth}K=2\). In that case \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(C)\ne0\), and its socle is killed by every \(\lambda\), so exactness fails for every \(\lambda\). \(\square\)

The lemma is the standard behaviour of kernels under a general hyperplane section: the defect is the part of \(\operatorname{Tor}_1\) supported at \(\mathfrak m\), and depth 3 removes it.

General lines on the 3-cube

Corollary (cor:cube-general-line-exact). On \(\{0,1\}^3\) over a field of characteristic \(\ne2\), let \(d\ge1\) and let \(L=V(\lambda)\) be a line of \(\mathbb P^2\) such that, for every \(m\le5d-1\), \(\lambda\) lies in no associated prime of \(C_m\) other than \(\mathfrak m\). Over an infinite field this holds for all lines outside a proper closed set. Then:

  • \(K_{m,L}=K_m/\lambda K_m\) for every \(m\le5d-1\);
  • the restricted order-zero threshold is \(M_L(d)=5d-1\);
  • \(\operatorname{indeg}I^L_m=\ell_0(d+1,m)\) for \(4d\le m\le5d-1\), when moreover \(\lambda\) does not divide every element of \(I_m\) of degree \(\ell_0\). For \(m\le4d-1\) both sides are infinite.

In particular, on such a line the generator degrees of the free module \(K_{m,L}\) over \(F[s,t]\) are those of \(K_m\).

Proof. For \(m\le4d-1\): the orders of \(V_{3,d}\otimes F(y)\) are \(\{0,\ldots,4d-1\}\) (dimension-three law). So its truncations modulo \(T^{m+1}\) span \(F(y)^{m+1}\), and \(K_m\otimes F(y)=0\). Since \(K_m\subseteq S\) is torsion-free, \(K_m=0\).

For \(4d\le m\le5d-1\), that is \(m=4d+\rho-1\) with \(1\le\rho\le d\): \(K_m\) is free (every-field theorem).

In both cases Part 2 of the lemma applies. At \(m\le5d-2\) the global system has no order-zero solution (order-zero theorem), so neither has the restricted one. At \(m=5d-1\) it has one, whose restriction is one on \(L\). The rest is Part 2. \(\square\)

This explains the \(\{0,1\}^3\) row of the restrictions check, whose random line over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\) behaved as a general line; being general is not proved for it. Special lines fall short when \(\lambda\) is a zero-divisor on \(C_m\), that is, when it lies in some associated prime. Examples are the coordinate and collision lines, which give \(4d+1\) and \(2d+1\).

Interpretation, conditional. Lines through a double point \(P\) have restricted modules \(E_L\) (the same module as \(K_L\)). Their least generator degree is conjectured to be \(\beta(d,\rho)=B(d,\rho)-\mu(d,\rho)\) (conj:cube-line-splitting-sharp, sharp-order entry), computed in 22 cases on specific lines over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\). Where the \(W_m\)-image of \(E_L\) also starts below \(B=\ell_0\), Part 2 fails for such lines. If that holds for all general lines through \(P\), then \(\lambda\) lies in an associated prime \(\ne\mathfrak m\) for each of them. A prime \(\ne\mathfrak m\) containing all linear forms through \(P\) is the ideal of \(P\), so \(P\) would be an associated point of \(C_m\). The order squeeze and the line-restriction bound work at the same points.

What it says about dimension 4

By Part 3, the two random planes of the restrictions check at \(d=3\), \(m=38\) show the following over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\), if they avoid the associated primes of \(C_{38}\) other than \(\mathfrak m\), as general planes do: \(\mathfrak m\in\operatorname{Ass}C_{38}\), and the solution module \(K_{38}\) of \(\{0,1\}^4\) has depth 2. It is not free, unlike every dimension-3 module with \(m\le5d-1\). At \(d=2\) the planes were exact, which is consistent with, but does not prove, depth \(\ge3\) at \(m\le18\). So restriction to planes decides order zero in dimension 4 wherever the solution modules have depth \(\ge3\). The one-short value 38 is a depth-2 phenomenon: the extra restricted solution comes from \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(C_{38})\) in degree \(-1\), a finite-length piece supported only at the irrelevant ideal, so invisible after localizing at any point of \(\mathbb P^3\). This matches the Artinian range at \(d=2\) (collision-windows entry): there too the obstruction to order zero has no zeros. These statements about \(d=3\) are interpretations of a finite check, not proved facts.

General statement. lem:cube-restriction-exactness, for every degree-0 map of graded free modules over a polynomial ring in \(n\ge2\) variables over any field (the depth equivalence for \(n\ge3\)), in particular for every (d+1)-system on \(\{0,1\}^n\). cor:cube-general-line-exact applies it on \(\{0,1\}^3\) for all \(d\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the every-field theorem (freeness for \(1\le\rho\le d\)), the dimension-three law (orders \(\{0,\ldots,4d-1\}\)), the threshold-ideal lemma (the system and \(I_m\)), the order-zero theorem, and the line-restriction bound with its splitting records. Claim searches (restriction, hyperplane, exact, depth, general line, solution module) found no exactness lemma. The nearest records are the trivial inclusion in the line-restriction bound and the order squeeze at double points. A fresh-context referee checked:

  • the Tor identification, the finite length and the local cohomology step, including \(K=0\);
  • the Auslander–Buchsbaum chain and the shift;
  • the corollary's ranges against the dependencies.

It found the lemma and corollary correct. Its corrections are made:

  • the converse (depth 2 forces inexactness for every \(\lambda\)) is proved, so "exactly when" is justified;
  • the lemma is stated for any graded map, with the inert hypotheses named;
  • the corollary's divisibility clause is stated precisely;
  • the double-point remark is conditional and compares \(W_m\)-images;
  • support is replaced by zero-divisors;
  • the dimension-4 and assessment remarks are marked as interpretation;
  • the lower-bound logic is corrected: a plane gives a lower bound unconditionally.

Assessment. This cycle turns an observation into a theorem and identifies what a hyperplane section loses: exactly the \(\mathfrak m\)-torsion of the cokernel, one degree down. In dimension 3 the modules with \(m\le5d-1\) are zero or free. So on a general line (over an infinite field, or on a line checked against the associated primes) every threshold \(\ell_0(d+1,m)\) with \(m\le5d-1\) can be computed. In dimension 4 the inclusion \(K/\lambda K\subseteq K_L\) always gives \(M(d)\ge M_L(d)\), so a lower bound needs only the plane value. The defect \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(C_m)_{-1}\) measures the gap \(M-M_L\), which is 1 at \(d=3\) modulo \(p\). Our interpretation is that no window or zero-set argument sees this defect, since it is supported at the irrelevant ideal. For the goal, the dimension-4 lower bound therefore splits in two:

  • the plane value \(M_L\), a 3-variable problem with five points in general position in place of four, which gives lower bounds unconditionally;
  • the depth-2 defect, needed only to close the gap to \(M\).

The next step is to compute the defect at \(d=2\) and \(d=3\) in dimension 4, from the dimensions of \(K_0\), \(K_{-1}\) and \(K_{L,0}\), and to see whether it is small and \(S_5\)-invariant.

26 September 2026 — The zero-free criterion: order zero fails without zeros only through a cohomology class, so dimension 4 needs depth 2

Working proof: if the threshold ideal has no zeros and the previous solution module has depth at least 3, order zero is solvable; otherwise a local cohomology class obstructs it. Cycle bmd-r127. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. On \(\{0,1\}^3\) every order-zero lower bound came from zeros of the threshold ideal, at the double points (order-zero theorem). On \(\{0,1\}^4\) at \(d=2\) the ideals \(I_{17}\), \(I_{18}\) have no zeros (check:cube-collision-regime-empty-d2), yet order zero first holds at \(m=19\). The missing implication for open statement 3 is a lower-bound mechanism for \(M(d)\) in dimension 4. Can zeros be the only obstruction in some dimensions, and what replaces them when they are not? The test ends with a criterion that separates the two cases.

Setting and notation are those of the restriction exactness entry, now for every \(n\ge2\): \(R=F[y_1,\ldots,y_n]\), \(\mathbb P=\mathbb P^{n-1}\), \(K_m\) the solution module of the (d+1)-system at \(m\), graded so that in degree \(\ell\) the coordinates \(W_c\) have degree \(\ell+m-c\), and \(I_m\) its ideal of top coordinates \(W_m\). The order-zero system is solvable at \(m\) iff \(1\in I_m\). Zero sets \(V(I_m)\) are taken over the algebraic closure \(\bar F\), so \(V(I_m)=\emptyset\) means \(\tilde I_m=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P}\).

The criterion

Lemma (lem:cube-zero-free-criterion, the zero-free criterion). Let \(n\ge2\), \(d\ge1\), \(m\ge1\), over any field. The characteristic and the cube enter only through the setting. The proof uses only that the equations at \(m-1\) are those at \(m\) with \(W_m=0\).

  1. The top-coordinate map gives an exact sequence of graded modules \(0\to K_{m-1}(1)\to K_m\to I_m\to0\).
  2. Suppose \(V(I_m)=\emptyset\) in \(\mathbb P\). Then the order-zero system is solvable at \(m\) if and only if a connecting class \(\delta_m\in H^1(\mathbb P,\tilde K_{m-1}(1))=H^2_{\mathfrak m}(K_{m-1})_1\) vanishes. In particular it is solvable when \(\operatorname{depth}K_{m-1}\ge3\), or \(K_{m-1}=0\).
  3. Consequently, if \(V(I_m)=\emptyset\) and the system is not solvable at \(m\), then \(H^2_{\mathfrak m}(K_{m-1})\ne0\), so \(\operatorname{depth}K_{m-1}=2\). For \(n\ge3\), restriction of \(K_{m-1}\) to every hyperplane is then inexact (exactness lemma, Part 3).

Proof. Part 1. An element of \(K_m\) of degree \(\ell\) with \(W_m=0\) is a vector \((W_0,\ldots,W_{m-1})\) with \(W_c\) of degree \((\ell+1)+(m-1)-c\). The identities for \(m-1\) are the same as those for \(m\) with \(W_m=0\), because the equations are \(\sum_{c}W_c[T^c]f=0\) over the same basis. So the kernel of \(W\mapsto W_m\) is \(K_{m-1}\) shifted by one, and the image is \(I_m\) by definition.

Part 2. Sheafification is exact, so \(0\to\tilde K_{m-1}(1)\to\tilde K_m\to\tilde I_m\to0\) is exact on \(\mathbb P\), and \(\tilde I_m=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P}\) because \(I_m\) has no zeros. Take cohomology in degree 0:

\[H^0(\tilde K_m)\to H^0(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P})=F\xrightarrow{\ \partial\ }H^1(\tilde K_{m-1}(1)).\]

Put \(\delta_m=\partial(1)\). Each \(K_j\) is the kernel of a map of free modules, a second syzygy, so \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(K_j)=H^1_{\mathfrak m}(K_j)=0\) and \((K_j)_\ell=H^0(\tilde K_j(\ell))\). Also \(H^1(\tilde K_{m-1}(1))=H^2_{\mathfrak m}(K_{m-1})_1\).

If \(\delta_m=0\), then \(1\) lifts to a section of \(\tilde K_m\), that is, to \(W\in(K_m)_0\). Its top coordinate is a degree-0 element of \(I_m\) whose sheaf image is \(1\), so \(W_m=1\). Conversely, a solution \(W\in(K_m)_0\) with \(W_m=1\) lifts \(1\), so \(\delta_m=0\). Depth \(\ge3\) gives \(H^2_{\mathfrak m}(K_{m-1})=0\).

Part 3 is the contrapositive of Part 2, since a nonzero second syzygy has depth \(\ge2\). \(\square\)

The new content is Part 2: once the zeros are gone, the only obstruction left is one class in a local cohomology module.

Dimension 3: why zeros were the whole story

On \(\{0,1\}^3\) the order-zero theorem already shows directly that, for \(m\le5d-1\), order zero holds at \(m\) iff \(V(I_m)=\emptyset\), and it gives \(M_3(d)=5d-1\). The criterion explains why a pointwise proof could succeed there. For \(m\le5d-1\) the modules \(K_{m-1}\) are zero or free, by the dimension-three law and the every-field theorem, so \(H^2_{\mathfrak m}(K_{m-1})=0\). No cohomological obstruction can occur, and only zeros can block order zero. This is an explanation, not a new result.

Dimension 4: an obstruction without zeros

Computation. The solutions invariant under \(S_4\), permuting \(y_1,\ldots,y_4\), with excess 0 decide order zero. Averaging over \(S_4\) is possible since \(24\) is invertible, and it preserves \(W_m=1\). The kernel bmd_cube_symmetric_solutions in rank mode over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\) gives, in research/results/bmd-r127-route-review/:

  • at \(d=2\): not solvable at \(m=16,17,18\), solvable at \(m=19\) (order-zero-d2-p32003.txt);
  • at \(d=3\): not solvable at \(m=37,38\), solvable at \(m=39\) (order-zero-d3-p32003.txt). This reproduces the recorded row check:cube-dimension-four-row-d3, which has invariant thresholds 2, 2, 0 at \(m=37,38,39\) over the same field; it is not new evidence.

Only the \(d=2\) facts at \(m=17,18\) are used below. Monotonicity in \(m\) is proved only for \(n\le3\), so the runs show nothing about smaller \(m\).

Consequence over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\). The recorded check check:cube-collision-regime-empty-d2 gives \(V(I_{17})=V(I_{18})=\emptyset\) at \(d=2\) over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\). Its zero-set half rests on the collision-support theorem. Order zero is not solvable at \(17\) or \(18\) there. The zero sets there are geometric: the 24 points involve fifth roots of unity, which are not in \(\mathbb F_{32003}\). By Part 3, \(\operatorname{depth}K_{16}=\operatorname{depth}K_{17}=2\) over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), with \(\delta_{17},\delta_{18}\ne0\). So these two modules are not free, unlike every dimension-3 module with \(m\le5d-1\). The obstruction to order zero at \(m=17,18\) is a class in \(H^1(\mathbb P^3,\tilde K_{m-1}(1))\), which no point window can see. This is a finite-check consequence over one prime, not a proof in characteristic 0.

General statement. lem:cube-zero-free-criterion, for every \(n\ge2\), \(d\ge1\), \(m\ge1\) and every field.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read:

  • the setting of the exactness entry;
  • the collision-support theorem (its hypotheses \(n\ge3\), \(d>n-3\), \(m>N\) and characteristic \(\ne2\) hold at \(d=2\), \(m=17,18\));
  • the \(d=2\) zero-free check over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\);
  • the freeness results and the order-zero theorem in dimension 3.

Claim searches (local cohomology, depth, zero set, connecting class; order zero, monotone, dimension 4) found no earlier criterion; the nearest is the exactness lemma. They found the recorded \(d=3\) row, which the new \(d=3\) run reproduces. A fresh-context referee found the lemma correct and new, and the averaging argument and output numbers right. Its corrections are made:

  • the unused characteristic hypothesis is dropped;
  • zero sets are taken over \(\bar F\);
  • the dimension-3 corollary, which restates the order-zero theorem, is recast as an explanation and not registered;
  • the \(d=3\) run is credited to the recorded row;
  • no claim about \(m<16\) is drawn;
  • the depth conclusion is limited to \(K_{16}\) and \(K_{17}\);
  • the duality remark is corrected;
  • an unsupported link to the excess-sum lemma is removed.

Assessment. The criterion splits the lower-bound problem for \(M(d)\) into two parts:

  • zeros of \(I_m\), which point windows detect and which carry all of dimension 3;
  • the class \(\delta_m\in H^2_{\mathfrak m}(K_{m-1})_1\), which lives only where the solution modules have depth 2.

In dimension 4 the windows reach only \(11d-11\), and at \(d=2\) the zeros are gone two steps before order zero. So a proof of \(M(d)\ge20d-21\) must show that \(\delta_m\ne0\) through most of the range. The natural tools are Serre duality on \(\mathbb P^3\) and the resolution of \(C_m\). Duality turns \(H^1(\tilde K(1))\) into \(\operatorname{Ext}^2(\tilde K(1),\omega)^*\); since \(\tilde K\) need not be locally free, this is not simply \(H^2(\tilde K^\vee(-5))\). The resolution computes these local cohomology modules. The next step is to compute \(H^2_{\mathfrak m}(K_{m-1})\) at \(d=2\), \(m=17,18\) in Macaulay2, and to see what generates it, before the route review due next.
