26 September 2026 — Route review of the cube: in dimension 4 order zero is blocked by cohomology, not by points

Route review: the depth-2 prediction of the zero-free criterion passes a direct test at d = 2 on {0,1}⁴. The line has structure but no lower-bound mechanism above 11d. Cycle bmd-r128. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

The line's general claim. The per-order function on \(\{0,1\}^n\) in characteristic \(\ne2\) is determined by the thresholds \(\ell_0(h,m)\), the initial degrees of the threshold ideals. Dimension 3 is solved. For \(n\ge4\) the claim to establish is a law for the thresholds. The current target is its order-zero row, \(M(d)=20d-21\) on \(\{0,1\}^4\) (linear conjecture).

What the goal needs. Open statement 3 for \(n\ge4\): thresholds at the boundary, in the middle range and at order zero; and open statement 2, small primes. Since route review 18, four research cycles:

  • windows at the triple-double points give \(M(d)\ge11d-11\), so \(11\le c_4\le20\) (entry);
  • restrictions to lines and planes give lower bounds; random planes give 19 and 38 against 19 and 39 (entry);
  • restriction to a general hyperplane is exact iff the solution module has depth \(\ge3\) (entry);
  • without zeros, order zero fails only through a class in \(H^2_{\mathfrak m}(K_{m-1})_1\) (zero-free criterion).

Falsification attempt

The zero-free criterion, applied to the recorded zero-free ideals at \(d=2\), \(m=17,18\), where order zero fails, predicts \(\operatorname{depth}K_{16}=\operatorname{depth}K_{17}=2\) over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\). That prediction chains three results: the zero-free check, the collision-support theorem under it, and the criterion. A direct computation of the depth could refute it.

By the exactness lemma, for a hyperplane \(L\) avoiding the associated primes of \(C\) other than \(\mathfrak m\),

\[\operatorname{defect}(\ell)=\dim(K_L)_\ell-\dim K_\ell+\dim K_{\ell-1}=\dim(0:_C\lambda)_{\ell-1},\]

and the depth is at least 3 iff every defect vanishes.

The new compiled kernel research/tools/bmd_cube_graded_defect.cpp computes these dimensions by fflas-ffpack ranks. It replaces a Macaulay2 script (research/tools/bmd_cube_solution_depth.m2, same statement), which was too slow beyond \(\ell=3\). The two agree on the control. Results over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), one random hyperplane, in research/results/bmd-r128-route-review/:

  • control, \(\{0,1\}^3\), \(d=2\), \(m=9\) (a free module, generators of degrees 0 and 2): \(\dim K_\ell=0,0,1,3,7,13\) for \(\ell=-2,\ldots,3\), every defect 0;
  • \(\{0,1\}^4\), \(d=2\), \(m=16\): \(\dim K_\ell=0\) for \(\ell\le4\), then \(3,16\) at \(\ell=5,6\); defects \(0,0,17,37\) at \(\ell=3,\ldots,6\);
  • \(\{0,1\}^4\), \(d=2\), \(m=17\): \(\dim K_\ell=0,1,5,18,50\) at \(\ell=1,\ldots,5\); defects \(0,0,1,22,39\).

Positive defects show that \(\lambda\) is a zero-divisor on \(C_{16}\) and \(C_{17}\). For a hyperplane avoiding the other associated primes, as a random one does with high probability, this means \(\operatorname{depth}K_{16}=\operatorname{depth}K_{17}=2\). The prediction could have failed; it passed. The result also shows how much a plane misses in these degrees: about half of \((K_L)_\ell\) does not come from \(K\).

Assessment of this line

The line is strong in structure and still has no lower-bound mechanism in dimension 4 above \(11d-11\). This review period explained why:

  • In dimension 3 the solution modules are free. So every obstruction to order zero is a zero of the threshold ideal, and point windows prove the whole value \(5d-1\).
  • In dimension 4 the modules below order zero have depth 2 (at \(d=2\), computed). The obstruction becomes a local cohomology class once the zeros are gone, two steps before order zero at \(d=2\).
  • Point windows, and every argument by zeros, cannot reach this class. The restriction to a plane gives only a lower bound, since the plane misses the class and adds solutions of its own.

So the prospects rest on computing or bounding \(\delta_m\in H^2_{\mathfrak m}(K_{m-1})_1\) in general. That is a question about the cokernel of an explicit matrix of power-series coefficients, and no recorded result bounds it. The evidence for \(M(d)=20d-21\) is unchanged:

  • exact at \(d=2\) over \(\mathbb Q\);
  • at \(d=3\) modulo two primes;
  • at \(d=4\), no solution at \(m=58\) modulo 2039.

Outside leads

  • The Grauert–Mülich theorem (Okonek–Schneider–Spindler, Vector bundles on complex projective spaces, Ch. II.2). For a semistable bundle on \(\mathbb P^N\), the splitting type on a general line has gaps at most 1. With the exactness lemma, the generator degrees of a free solution module are its splitting type on a general line. Gaps at most 1 would let the excess-sum lemma's total determine the least excess, hence the thresholds. It targets open statement 3. It breaks if the recorded splittings have larger gaps. Test. Falsified as a law. At \((d,\rho)=(e,e)\) the recorded generator excesses are \(0,2,3,\ldots,e\), with one gap of 2 (near-diagonal theorem). The \((d,d-1)\) excesses \(3,\ldots,d+1\) have gaps 1. Split bundles with distinct degrees are not semistable anyway.
  • Normality of Hermite–Padé systems (Nikishin–Sorokin, Rational approximations and orthogonality, 1991, Ch. 4, perfect systems). At a fixed \(y\), the order-zero system asks for \(\Phi\) with \(\Phi(0)=1\) and \(\Phi\,w^r\) having prescribed vanishing homogeneous parts: a type-II Hermite–Padé problem for the \(2^n\) functions \(w^r(yT)\). Normality of all indices predicts the pointwise solvability counts, and in dimension 1 it predicts \(M_1(d)=d+1\): \(\Phi\) has \(m-\lfloor d/2\rfloor-1\) free coefficients against \(\lceil d/2\rceil\) conditions. It targets open statement 2, where normality at small primes is the question. It breaks where the polynomial dependence on \(y\) matters, from \(n=2\) on. Test. Passed: over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), order zero fails at \(m=d\) and holds at \(m=d+1\) for \(d=1,\ldots,5\) and \(d=8\) (order-zero-n1.txt).
  • Horrocks' splitting criterion (G. Horrocks, Vector bundles on the punctured spectrum of a local ring, Proc. LMS 1964). A vector bundle on \(\mathbb P^N\) splits iff its intermediate cohomology vanishes. The zero-free criterion's class lies in \(H^1(\tilde K_{m-1}(1))\), which is intermediate cohomology. So order zero can fail without zeros only where \(\tilde K_{m-1}\) is not split. It targets open statement 3, locating the dimension-4 obstruction. It breaks if \(\tilde K\) is not locally free, where Horrocks does not apply as stated. Test. Passed in the direction available: the depth-2 modules \(K_{16}\), \(K_{17}\) (falsification attempt above) are not free, as the criterion requires. Local freeness of \(\tilde K\) is not checked.

Absurd bridges

  • Algebraic-geometry codes and the Feng–Rao order bound (coding theory; Høholdt–van Lint–Pellikaan, Algebraic geometry codes, Handbook of Coding Theory, 1998). Translation: at a point \(y\) the functions \(w^r\) live on the \((\mathbb Z/2)^n\) cover \(w_i^2=1+4y_iT\) of the \(T\)-line, and \(V_{n,d}\) is the Riemann–Roch space \(L(dD)\) of the divisor \(D\) over \(T=\infty\). The order-zero condition says a principal part at one point \(P_0\) over \(T=0\) annihilates \(L(dD)\). That is membership in a one-point residue code, whose dimensions the Feng–Rao bound computes from the Weierstrass semigroup at \(P_0\). A theorem there would give the pointwise solvability counts in every dimension from the genus. Test. Passed. By Riemann–Hurwitz the cover for \(n=4\) has \(2g-2=16\cdot(-2)+5\cdot8=8\), so \(g=5\). With \(\deg D=8\), \(\dim L(dD)=8d-4\) for \(d\ge2\). This equals \(\dim V_{4,d}=12,20,28\) for \(d=2,3,4\), and for \(n=3\) (\(g=1\), \(\deg D=4\)) it gives \(4d\). This picture is the one behind the collision-support theorem. What is new is only the coding-theory dictionary.
  • Vector equilibrium problems of electrostatics (Gonchar–Rakhmanov, Equilibrium distributions and degree of rational approximation of analytic functions, Math. USSR Sb. 1989; Stahl's theorem on Padé convergence). Translation: the zeros of Hermite–Padé polynomials for algebraic functions with branch cuts distribute like charges in equilibrium on the cuts. For \(w_i=(1+4y_iT)^{1/2}\) the cuts end at \(T=-1/(4y_i)\). The rate \(c_n=\lim M(d)/d\) would be the degree ratio at which the vector equilibrium problem for \(2^n\) functions with \(n\) cuts becomes solvable with the required multiplicities, a potential-theoretic number. A theorem there would compute \(c_n\) in characteristic 0 as an energy ratio. Test. Not run: no cheap test; computing vector equilibrium measures with \(n=4\) interacting cuts needs a numerical solver that is not set up.

Bridge follow-up

  • Chip-firing on a cycle. Not worked this period. Follow-up. Continuing, with the boundary conjecture.
  • The non-crossing rule. Not worked this period. Follow-up. Continuing, with the boundary conjecture.
  • The renewal-reward theorem. Modulo 32003, \(M(2)=19\) and \(M(3)=39\) again, so \(b_4(1)=20\) and \(b_4(2)=40\): no better second cycle. A lower bound needs superadditivity of \(b_4\), and the zero-free criterion shows the obstruction is cohomological, with no cycle decomposition in sight. Follow-up. Continuing.
  • Natural monopoly and subadditive costs. Its ray-average test is the renewal bridge's ratio \(b_4(e)/e\), with no separate content or test. Follow-up. Closed: merged into the renewal-reward bridge.

Lead follow-up

  • General Weierstrass points are simple. Not worked this period. Follow-up. Continuing, with the boundary conjecture.
  • Higher Weierstrass points on the universal curve. Not worked this period. Follow-up. Continuing, with the boundary conjecture.
  • Springer's theorem on regular elements. Its remaining content is the invariant-solution lead of route review 18. Follow-up. Closed: merged into that lead.
  • Invariant solutions of the order-zero system. The \(S_4\)-invariant kernel decided order zero at \(d=2\) and \(d=3\) modulo 32003 in seconds (entry). It gives values, not bounds. Follow-up. Continuing: a bound would need the invariant part of \(H^2_{\mathfrak m}(K_{m-1})\).

Next step

On the highest-risk item, open statement 3 in dimension 4, the next research cycle identifies the obstruction module. Compute \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(C_m)\) at \(d=2\), \(m=16,17\): its dimensions by degree from the defects of several independent hyperplanes, and its \(S_5\)-structure from the invariant kernel. Then ask whether it comes from an explicit source, such as the collision arrangement or the Springer orbits. A general source is what a lower bound \(M(d)\ge20d-21\) needs: a proof that \(\delta_m\ne0\) for \(m\le20d-22\).

26 September 2026 — The threshold ideal is the annihilator of one cokernel class; point-supported certificates decide nothing

Working proof, a reformulation of the zero-free criterion: the threshold ideal is the annihilator of the order-zero column's class in the previous cokernel. Point-supported certificates cannot detect it. Cycle bmd-r129. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The route review located the dimension-4 obstruction to order zero in \(H^2_{\mathfrak m}(K_{m-1})\), with depth 2 confirmed at \(d=2\), \(m=16,17\). Its next step was to identify that module. The missing implication for open statement 3 is still a lower-bound mechanism for \(M(d)\) on \(\{0,1\}^4\). Two questions:

  • What is the obstruction class concretely?
  • Can it be certified by functionals supported on a finite set, such as the 24-point Springer orbit?

The first ends with a formula; the second with a test calibrated against random points.

Setting and notation: those of the zero-free criterion. \(A_m\) is the (d+1)-system at \(m\), \(K_m=\ker A_m\), \(C_m=\operatorname{coker}A_m\), and \(I_m\) is the ideal of top coordinates. Write \(a_m\) for the column of \(W_m\) in \(A_m\): row \((Q,r)\) is \([T^{m-Q}]\prod_{i\in r}w_i\), a form of degree \(m-Q\). It is a degree-0 element of the target of \(A_{m-1}\) twisted by 1, so its class \([a_m]\) lies in \(C_{m-1}(1)\).

The annihilator form

Corollary (cor:cube-threshold-annihilator, the annihilator form of the zero-free criterion). Over any field, for \(n\ge1\), \(d\ge1\), \(m\ge1\). The row set does not depend on \(m\), so \(T_{m-1}(1)=T_m\) and \(a_m\) lies in degree 0.

  1. \(I_m=\operatorname{ann}_R([a_m])\), so \(R/I_m\cong R\cdot[a_m]\subseteq C_{m-1}(1)\). The order-zero system is solvable at \(m\) iff \([a_m]=0\).
  2. \(V(I_m)=\emptyset\) iff \([a_m]\in H^0_{\mathfrak m}(C_{m-1})(1)\). Then \(R/I_m\) is an Artinian cyclic submodule of \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(C_{m-1})(1)\).
  3. For \(n\ge3\), \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(C_{m-1})\cong H^2_{\mathfrak m}(K_{m-1})\). If \(V(I_m)=\emptyset\), the zero-free criterion's class \(\delta_m\in H^2_{\mathfrak m}(K_{m-1})_1\) corresponds to \([a_m]\in H^0_{\mathfrak m}(C_{m-1})_1\), up to sign.

Proof. Part 1. A form \(f\) lies in \(I_m\) iff some \(W\in K_m\) has \(W_m=f\). That means \(\sum_{c<m}A_{\cdot,c}W_c=-f\,a_m\), that is, \(f\,a_m\in\operatorname{im}A_{m-1}\) after the twist, as in Part 1 of the zero-free criterion. So \(I_m=\operatorname{ann}([a_m])\), and \(R\to R\cdot[a_m]\), \(1\mapsto[a_m]\), has kernel \(I_m\). Solvability at order zero is \(1\in I_m\), that is, \([a_m]=0\).

Part 2. \(V(I_m)=\emptyset\) iff \(I_m\) is \(\mathfrak m\)-primary or the unit ideal, iff \(R/I_m\cong R[a_m]\) has finite length, iff \([a_m]\) is killed by a power of \(\mathfrak m\).

Part 3. Write \(G=\operatorname{im}A_{m-1}\), so that \(0\to K\to S\to G\to0\) and \(0\to G\to T\to C\to0\), with \(S,T\) free of depth \(n\ge3\). Then \(H^1_{\mathfrak m}(S)=H^2_{\mathfrak m}(S)=0\) gives \(H^2_{\mathfrak m}(K)\cong H^1_{\mathfrak m}(G)\), and \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(T)=H^1_{\mathfrak m}(T)=0\) gives \(H^1_{\mathfrak m}(G)\cong H^0_{\mathfrak m}(C)\).

For the class: on each basic open set \(D(f)\) with \(f\in I_m\), a solution \(W^{(f)}\) with top coordinate \(f\) gives \(W^{(f)}/f\), which lifts \(1\). Its lower part \(w_f\) satisfies \(A_{m-1}w_f=-a_m\). So \(a_m\) is a global section of \(\tilde G\), that is, it lies in the saturation of \(G\). The differences \(w_f-w_g\) form a Čech cocycle in \(\tilde K_{m-1}(1)\). It represents \(\delta_m\) by definition of the connecting map, and it represents the image of \([a_m]\) under \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(C)\to H^1_{\mathfrak m}(G)\cong H^2_{\mathfrak m}(K)\), up to sign. \(\square\)

Parts 1 and 2 restate the definition of \(I_m\). Part 3 identifies the zero-free criterion's class with an explicit vector. In the zero-free range, \(R/I_m\) is a graded Artinian algebra. Its Hilbert function is computable from the graded kernel dimensions, since \(\dim(I_m)_\ell=\dim(K_m)_\ell-\dim(K_{m-1})_{\ell+1}\) by the zero-free criterion's sequence.

The Artinian algebra at d = 2, m = 17

Finite check over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), not part of the working proof. It is computed by script from the saved graded dimensions of the route review (research/results/bmd-r128-route-review/defect-n4-d2-m16.txt, …-m17.txt). The inputs are:

  • \(\dim(K_{17})_\ell=0,1,5,18,50\) for \(\ell=1,\ldots,5\);
  • \(\dim(K_{16})_{\ell+1}=0,0,0,3,16\);
  • \((K_{16})_2=0\), since \((K_{16})_2\hookrightarrow(K_{17})_1=0\);
  • \(H(0)=1\), by the recorded unsolvability at \(m=17\).

With these, \(R/I_{17}\) on \(\{0,1\}^4\) at \(d=2\) has Hilbert function

\[1,\;4,\;9,\;15,\;20,\;22\qquad(\ell=0,\ldots,5).\]

Here \(\dim(I_{17})_\ell=0,1,5,15,34\) for \(\ell=1,\ldots,5\), and the single quadric is the recorded element of degree 2 (check:cube-collision-regime-empty-d2). The algebra has finite length, since \(V(I_{17})=\emptyset\), and \(H(5)=22>0\). So its top degree is at least 5; the computed range does not show where it ends.

Point-supported certificates: an uninformative test

By Part 1, the order-zero system at \(m\) is unsolvable iff a linear functional kills \(\operatorname{im}A_{m-1}\) in degree 1 and not \(a_m\). In dimension 3 the recorded proofs use functionals built from jets at the three double points. The idea was to look for certificates supported on the Springer orbit at \(d=2\), \(m=17\), as a collective, Cayley–Bacharach-type obstruction.

The kernel research/tools/bmd_cube_orbit_certificate.cpp (fflas-ffpack ranks) tests whether jets of order \(\le k\) at a point set \(Z\) contain such a functional. The calibration came first, on \(\{0,1\}^3\), \(d=2\), \(m=8=5d-2\), where order zero fails, over \(\mathbb F_{1000081}\) (research/results/bmd-r129-annihilator/):

  • at the three double points a certificate first exists at \(k=4\);
  • at three random points it already exists at \(k=1\).

So point-supported certificates exist at random points of low order. The jets of forms of degree \(\le m\) at a few points are dependent once there are more functionals than the rank of \(EA\), and a random \(Ea\) then leaves the column space. The test measures dimension counting, not the location of the obstruction. It cannot decide the question, and the Springer-orbit runs were not made.

This is so by design. The test uses affine jets of forms of fixed degree against only the degree-0 image of \(A_{m-1}\). It is not the module-local condition \(a_m\notin\operatorname{im}A_{m-1}+\mathfrak m_p^{k+1}T\). Jets of order \(\ge m\) at one generic point already span the whole dual, so every unsolvable system has a one-point certificate of this kind; the random run reaches full rank 164 at \(k=5\). In the module sense no finite point set can carry a certificate. When \(V(I_m)=\emptyset\), \([a_m]\) vanishes locally at every prime other than \(\mathfrak m\) (Part 2), so no local conditions at finitely many points can detect it. A collective Cayley–Bacharach obstruction is excluded by Part 2 itself.

General statement. cor:cube-threshold-annihilator, for every \(n\ge1\), \(d\ge1\), \(m\ge1\) over every field (Part 3 for \(n\ge3\)). With lem:cube-zero-free-criterion it is the all-parameter statement this entry refines.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the zero-free criterion (its sequence, grading and connecting class) and the saved graded dimensions. One claim search found no earlier annihilator statement. A fresh-context referee checked:

  • the grading of \([a_m]\) and Parts 1–3, including the Čech chase for Part 3, which it verified;
  • the Hilbert-function arithmetic against the files;
  • the certificate test's logic.

Its corrections are made:

  • Part 3 assumes \(V(I_m)=\emptyset\), holds up to sign in degree 1, and has its proof written out;
  • the result is registered as a corollary (a reformulation) of the zero-free criterion;
  • a wrong socle-degree claim is removed;
  • the data inputs are listed and labelled a finite check;
  • the reason the certificate test cannot decide is given.

Assessment. The obstruction to order zero is now one explicit vector: the column \(a_m\) of power-series coefficients, modulo the image of the previous system. In the zero-free range it lies in the \(\mathfrak m\)-torsion of the cokernel and vanishes locally everywhere. So no argument by points, windows, jets or finite point sets can see it. That closes the pointwise family of methods for dimension 4 beyond the last zeros.

A lower bound must bound \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(C_{m-1})\) and place \([a_m]\) in it by global means: a graded duality (local duality turns \(H^0_{\mathfrak m}(C)\) into \(\operatorname{Ext}^n(C,R(-n))\), the last module of the dual resolution), or an explicit construction. Exploring the Artinian algebra \(R/I_{17}\) (its Hilbert function and inverse system) is a possible next step, but no link to a general bound is in view.

The route item's other open statements (the boundary for every \(d\), small primes) have concrete reductions. The next step is to weigh them against this one.

26 September 2026 — On the conic the Weierstrass points are simple: the monotone squarefreeness conjecture for n = 2 and ν = d − |r|

Working proof: for n = 2 and ν_r = d − |r| the non-collision part of Δ_ν is squarefree for every d in characteristic 0. Cycle bmd-r130. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The dimension-4 boundary law \(\ell_0(d+1,8d-4)=10d^2-10d-5\) is proved for \(d\le9\). For every \(d\) it reduces to squarefreeness of non-collision parts of Hermite–Padé determinants \(\Delta_\nu\) (reduction theorem, triple-multiplicity corollary). The monotone squarefreeness conjecture states this for monotone degree vectors, with a planned induction on the number of branch points. This cycle turns from the dimension-4 order-zero line, which the last three entries closed to pointwise methods, to that other half of open statement 3. It asks whether the base case \(n=2\) can be proved, for the cube's vector \(\nu_r=d-|r|\), by the lead that general Weierstrass points are simple (route review 15, lead 1).

Setting: \(V_\nu=\bigoplus_rw^rF[T]_{\le\nu_r}\) with \(w_i=(1+a_iT)^{1/2}\), \(r\in\{0,1\}^2\), and \(\Delta_\nu(a_1,a_2)\) the determinant of the truncated expansions at \(T=0\), as in the generic normality lemma. The collision forms are \(a_1,a_2,a_1-a_2\). Take \(\nu=(\nu_{00},\nu_{10},\nu_{01},\nu_{11})=(d,d-1,d-1,d-2)\) for \(d\ge1\) (entry \(-1\) meaning an empty summand). This is the dimension-3 cube's collision limit space \(U\) (limit-space lemma) in the coordinates \(a_i=4y_i\).

The data

The exact factorizations over \(\mathbb Q\) (research/tools/bmd_cube_nu_noncollision.py, sympy; research/results/bmd-r130-conic/noncollision-n2.txt), with \(a_1=1\), \(a_2=x\), give these non-collision parts of \(\Delta_{(d,d-1,d-1,d-2)}\):

  • \(d=2\): \(x+1\);
  • \(d=3\): \((x+3)(3x+1)\);
  • \(d=4\): \((x+1)(x^2+6x+1)\);
  • \(d=5\): \((x^2+10x+5)(5x^2+10x+1)\).

These are the odd and even parts of \((1+\sqrt x)^d\). Their product is \(\bigl((1+\sqrt x)^{2d}-(1-\sqrt x)^{2d}\bigr)/(4\sqrt x)\), with the \(d-1\) simple roots \(x=-\cot^2(\pi j/2d)\), \(j=1,\ldots,d-1\). The collision multiplicities are \(2d^2\) at \(x=0\) and \(d(2d-1)\) at \(x=1\). The monotone vectors \((4,2,2,0)\), \((6,4,4,2)\), \((3,2,1,0)\), \((4,3,2,1)\), \((4,2,1,0)\) and \((5,3,2,1)\) are also squarefree, with non-collision parts of degrees 3, 9, 4, 7, 5 and 9 that have no closed form of the \((1+\sqrt x)^d\) type.

The theorem

Theorem (thm:cube-conic-squarefree, the conic squarefreeness theorem). In characteristic 0, for every \(d\ge1\), the part of \(\Delta_{(d,d-1,d-1,d-2)}(a_1,a_2)\) prime to \(a_1,a_2,a_1-a_2\) is squarefree. Up to a constant it equals

\[Q_d=\frac{(\alpha-\beta)^d-(\alpha+\beta)^d}{2\beta},\qquad\alpha=\tfrac12(a_1+a_2),\ \beta^2=a_1a_2,\]

a binary form of degree \(d-1\) whose zeros are the configurations with \(\zeta^{2d}=1\), \(\zeta\ne\pm1\), where \(\zeta=(\sqrt{a_1}-\sqrt{a_2})/(\sqrt{a_1}+\sqrt{a_2})\).

Proof. Work over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\). Fix \(a\) with \(a_1,a_2\) nonzero and distinct, and let \(\Gamma\) be the conic of \(w_1,w_2\), with \(p_0\) over \(T=0\) and the two points \(\infty_1,\infty_2\) over \(T=\infty\). As recorded in the proof of the collision-free lemma, step 3:

  • \(\Gamma\cong\mathbb P^1\);
  • \(T\) has a double pole and \(w_i\) a simple pole at each \(\infty_j\);
  • \(V=V_\nu\) is the hyperplane of \(L=L(2d(\infty_1+\infty_2))\), of dimension \(4d+1\), cut out by the functional \(\phi\) = coefficient of \(w_1w_2T^{d-1}\) in the unique decomposition \(f=A+Bw_1+Cw_2+Dw_1w_2\).

Step 1: \(\phi\) is a combination of the two top Laurent coefficients, with both weights nonzero. For \(f\in L\) let \(\mathrm{lc}_j(f)\) be the coefficient of order \(-2d\) at \(\infty_j\) in a fixed local parameter. Only \(T^d\) and \(w_1w_2T^{d-1}\) among the basis elements \(T^Qw^r\) of \(L\) reach pole order \(2d\). So \(\mathrm{lc}_j(f)=A_d\,\tau_j+D_{d-1}\,\mu_j\), with \(\tau_j=\mathrm{lc}_j(T^d)\ne0\) and \(\mu_j=\mathrm{lc}_j(w_1w_2T^{d-1})\ne0\).

At \(\infty_j\), \(w_1w_2/T=(w_1/w_2)(w_2^2/T)\to\pm\sqrt{a_1a_2}\), with the sign of \(w_1/w_2\) there, which is opposite at the two points. So \(\mu_1/\tau_1=-\mu_2/\tau_2\), and the matrix \(\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\tau_1&\mu_1\\\tau_2&\mu_2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\) has nonzero determinant \(\det=\tau_1\mu_2-\tau_2\mu_1\). Solving, \(\phi(f)=D_{d-1}=\gamma_1\,\mathrm{lc}_1(f)+\gamma_2\,\mathrm{lc}_2(f)\) with \(\gamma_1=-\tau_2/\det\ne0\) and \(\gamma_2=\tau_1/\det\ne0\).

Step 2: every point of \(\Gamma\) other than \(\infty_1,\infty_2\) has weight at most 1 for \(V\). On \(\mathbb P^1\) the complete series \(L\), of degree \(4d\), has orders exactly \(0,\ldots,4d\) at every point \(p\). So \(V=\ker\phi\) has these orders with one value \(j^*\) removed, and weight \(4d-j^*\). Weight \(\ge2\) means \(j^*\le4d-2\), that is, \(\phi\) vanishes on the 2-dimensional space \(L(2d(\infty_1+\infty_2)-(4d-1)p)\).

That space contains \(f_1\ne0\) in \(L(2d\infty_1+(2d-1)\infty_2-(4d-1)p)\), which has degree 0 and dimension 1. Then \(\mathrm{lc}_2(f_1)=0\). Also \(\mathrm{lc}_1(f_1)\ne0\), since otherwise \(f_1\) would lie in a space of degree \(-1\). So \(\phi(f_1)=\gamma_1\mathrm{lc}_1(f_1)\ne0\), and the weight of \(p\) is at most 1.

Step 3: multiplicities equal weights. \(\Delta_\nu\) is homogeneous in \(a\), by the substitution \(T\mapsto\lambda T\), so its non-collision part is a binary form. The Wronskian identity of the doubled-factor proposition holds for \(V_\nu\) by the generic normality lemma, which gives it for every degree vector. It rests on two facts:

  • \(w_i(T+t)=(1+a_it)^{1/2}(1+\varphi_t(a)_iT)^{1/2}\), with \(\varphi_t(a)_i=a_i/(1+a_it)\);
  • \(\operatorname{span}\{(T+t)^Q:Q\le\nu_r\}=\operatorname{span}\{T^Q:Q\le\nu_r\}\).

So translation maps \(V_\nu(a)\) to \(V_\nu(\varphi_t(a))\) by a triangular change of basis with the constants \(\prod_i(1+a_it)^{r_i/2}\).

So a prime factor \(\pi\) of \(\Delta_\nu\), other than a collision form, with multiplicity \(\mu\), satisfies \(\mu=\) the weight of \(p_0\) at a general point \(a^*\) of \(V(\pi)\): one with \(a^*_1,a^*_2\) nonzero and distinct, \(R(a^*)\ne0\) and \((X\pi)(a^*)\ne0\), where \(X=a_1^2\partial_1+a_2^2\partial_2\).

For \(n=2\), \(\pi=\lambda_1a_1+\lambda_2a_2\) is linear, and \(V(\pi)\) is one line through 0. There \(R(a^*)\ne0\): \(R\) is homogeneous, so vanishing at one nonzero point of the line would force \(\pi\mid R\). And \((X\pi)(a^*)=\lambda_1a_1^2+\lambda_2a_2^2=\lambda_1a_1^2(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)/\lambda_2\) at \(a_2=-\lambda_1a_1/\lambda_2\). This is nonzero unless \(\lambda_1=0\), \(\lambda_2=0\) or \(\lambda_1+\lambda_2=0\), that is, unless \(\pi\) is one of the collision forms \(a_2\), \(a_1\), \(a_1-a_2\). By step 2, \(\mu\le1\), so the non-collision part is squarefree.

Step 4: the zeros. For \(a_1,a_2\) nonzero and distinct, \(\dim V_\nu=N=4d\) (Kummer theory), so \(\Delta_\nu(a)=0\) iff \(V_\nu\) has a nonzero element of order \(\ge N\) at \(p_0\), that is, iff \(p_0\) has positive weight. And \(p_0\) has positive weight iff \(\phi\) vanishes on \(L(2d(\infty_1+\infty_2)-4dp_0)\). That space is spanned by the \(2d\)-th power of the tangent line at \(p_0\), whose \(w_1w_2T^{d-1}\) coefficient the collision-free lemma computes, up to a nonzero factor, as \(Q_d\) in the present coordinates. Its zeros are exactly \(\zeta^{2d}=1\), \(\zeta\ne\pm1\) (\(\zeta=\pm1\) are collisions). These give \(d-1\) distinct ratios \(a_2/a_1\), since \(\zeta\) and \(\zeta^{-1}\) give the same configuration. So \(Q_d\), of degree \(d-1\), is squarefree. It is prime to the collision forms: at \(\beta=0\) it equals \(-d\alpha^{d-1}\ne0\), and at \(a_1=a_2\) it equals \(-(2a_1)^d/(2\beta)\ne0\). Both it and the non-collision part of \(\Delta_\nu\) are squarefree forms with the same zeros, so they agree up to a constant. \(\square\)

Cross-check by degrees. By homogeneity \(\deg\Delta_\nu=\sum_{k<4d}k-\sum Q=2d(4d-1)-(2d^2-2d+1)=6d^2-1\). The collision exponents \(2d^2\) at \(a_1\) and at \(a_2\) (confluence lemma) and \(d(2d-1)\) at \(a_1-a_2\) (data, \(d\le5\)) leave exactly \(d-1\).

Check. With \(a_1=1\), \(a_2=x\), \(\zeta=(1-\sqrt x)/(1+\sqrt x)\), and \(\zeta^{2d}=1\) is \((1+\sqrt x)^{2d}=(1-\sqrt x)^{2d}\). This is the product of the odd and even parts found in the data, for \(d=2,\ldots,5\).

Scope. The theorem covers the vector \(\nu_r=d-|r|\), the case where \(V_\nu\) is a hyperplane of a complete series on the conic. Steps 1–3 use only that \(V\) has codimension 1 in \(L(D)\), \(D=c(\infty_1+\infty_2)\), and that \(\phi\) weighs both top coefficients; for \(n=2\) the transversality of Step 3 holds for every non-collision linear factor. So they give squarefreeness for every such vector, for example \((d-1,d-1,d-1,d-1)\), which is cut out by the \(T^d\) coefficient. Monotonicity is never used. Monotone vectors of larger codimension, such as \((4,2,2,0)\), are squarefree in the data, but the argument needs more than one functional.

General statement. thm:cube-conic-squarefree, for every \(d\ge1\) in characteristic 0. It proves conj:cube-monotone-squarefree for \(n=2\) and \(\nu_r=d-|r|\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read:

  • the collision-free lemma (the conic, the hyperplane, the coefficient);
  • the doubled-factor proposition (Wronskian identity, weights, flow);
  • the generic normality lemma;
  • the monotone-squarefree entry.

Claim searches (conic, squarefree, Weierstrass weight, monotone, Hermite–Padé) found the conjecture, its finite check and the collision-free lemma's order-\(4d\) computation, but no proof of the \(n=2\) case. A fresh-context referee checked every step and every data claim, and found the proof correct. Its corrections are made:

  • two sign slips (the \(\gamma_j\) and \(X\pi\)), neither affecting nonvanishing;
  • the opposite signs derived from the limit;
  • homogeneity stated where used;
  • the translation facts written out;
  • the link \(\Delta_\nu=0\Leftrightarrow\) positive weight;
  • \(Q_d\) prime to the collision forms;
  • the degree cross-check;
  • the scope widened to all hyperplane vectors;
  • the status line shortened.

Characteristic 0 enters only through Step 3 (Wronskian order equals weight). Step 2 holds in every characteristic, and monotonicity is not used.

Assessment. The base case of the planned induction is proved for the cube's own vector, by the simple-Weierstrass-point lead. The mechanism is that \(V\) has small codimension in a complete series on a curve with no Weierstrass points of its own, and the missing functionals weigh the top coefficients at every point over \(T=\infty\).

The dimension-4 boundary needs the next case: \(n=3\), \(\nu=d-|r|\), which is \(U_d\) on the genus-1 curve of \(w_2,w_3,w_4\). There \(V\) has codimension 4 in \(L(2dH_\infty)\), \(\deg H_\infty=4\) (reduction theorem). The four missing functionals are:

  • the three coefficients of \(w_iw_jT^{d-1}\), top coefficients at the four points at infinity;
  • one coefficient of \(w_2w_3w_4T^{d-2}\), at the next order.

An elliptic curve's complete series have simple Weierstrass points (at torsion translates). The next step is the same weight analysis there: show that \(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_4\) are independent on \(L(2dH_\infty-(8d-5)p)\) for every non-collision \(p\), which gives weight \(\le1\) and, by step 3, the limit conjecture and the dimension-4 boundary law for every \(d\).

26 September 2026 — The limit space on the genus-1 curve: four character functionals, and when a Weierstrass point can be double

Working proof: U_d is cut out of L(2dH) on the genus-1 curve by three character components of the top coefficients and one of the next order; weight ≥ 2 needs one of two explicit rank drops. Cycle bmd-r131. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The conic theorem proved the base case \(n=2\) of the squarefreeness behind the dimension-4 boundary law. Its mechanism was that the series is a hyperplane of a complete series, and every Weierstrass point then has weight 1. The case the boundary needs is \(n=3\), \(\nu_r=d-|r|\): the limit space \(U_d\) on the genus-1 curve (the limit conjecture of the reduction entry, whose first half the triple-multiplicity corollary proves). This cycle asks two things:

  • Does the non-collision part of \(\Delta_U\) have a closed form, as \(Q_d\) was on the conic?
  • If not, what exactly must a weight argument control?

No closed form at d = 2

The exact determinant over \(\mathbb Q\) (research/tools/bmd_cube_nu_noncollision3.py, sympy Bareiss in two variables with \(a_3=1\); research/results/bmd-r131-elliptic/noncollision-n3-d2.txt, 86 s) gives \(\deg\Delta_U=60\):

  • collision multiplicities 10 at \(a_1,a_2\), and 10 at \(a_3\) by homogeneity (\(60\) minus the degree 50 of the dehomogenized determinant) or by symmetry; 7 at each \(a_i-a_j\);
  • a single irreducible non-collision factor of degree 9, symmetric in \(x=a_1\), \(y=a_2\).

These values match the reduction entry's line data (10, 7, and degree \(4d^2+2d-11=9\)). Unlike the conic there is no product of simple pieces, so squarefreeness for every \(d\) has to come from a weight argument.

Setting

Take characteristic \(\ne2\) and \(a=(a_1,a_2,a_3)\) with distinct nonzero entries. Let \(E\) be the curve \(w_i^2=1+a_iT\) (\(i=1,2,3\)), a \(G=(\mathbb Z/2)^3\)-cover of the \(T\)-line branched at \(T=-1/a_i\) and \(T=\infty\). It has genus 1. For \(r\in\{0,1\}^3\) write \(w^r=\prod_{r_i=1}w_i\), and \(\chi_r\) for the character by which \(G\) acts on \(w^r\).

At \(T=\infty\) every \(w_i\) changes sign around the branch point, so the inertia group there is \(\langle g_0\rangle\), \(g_0=(1,1,1)\). The fibre consists of four points \(\infty_1,\ldots,\infty_4\), each ramified of index 2, permuted simply transitively by \(G/\langle g_0\rangle\). Put \(H=\sum_k\infty_k\). Then \(T\) has a double pole and each \(w_i\) a simple pole at every \(\infty_k\), and \(L=L(2dH)\) has dimension \(8d\). The recorded limit space is \(U_d=V_\nu\), \(\nu_r=d-|r|\), of dimension \(8d-4\) (reduction theorem).

The four functionals

Fix a local parameter \(s\) at \(\infty_1\) with \(g_0^*s=-s\), and transport it to \(s_k=s\circ g_k^{-1}\) at \(\infty_k=g_k\infty_1\). For \(f\in L\) let \(\mathrm{lc}(f)\in F^4\) be the vector of coefficients of \(s_k^{-2d}\), and \(\mathrm{sc}(f)\) that of \(s_k^{-(2d-1)}\).

Lemma (lem:cube-limit-four-functionals).

  1. \(L=\bigoplus_rw^rF[T]_{\le j_r}\) with \(j_r=d\), \(d-1\), \(d-1\), \(d-2\) for \(|r|=0,1,2,3\). \(U_d\) omits exactly \(w_iw_jT^{d-1}\) (three elements, pole order \(2d\)) and \(w_1w_2w_3T^{d-2}\) (pole order \(2d-1\)).
  2. \(\mathrm{lc}(f)=A_d\,\tau+\sum_{i<j}D^{ij}_{d-1}\,\mu^{ij}\), where \(A_d\) and \(D^{ij}_{d-1}\) are the coefficients of \(T^d\) and \(w_iw_jT^{d-1}\) in \(f\), and \(\tau,\mu^{ij}\) are the \(\mathrm{lc}\) vectors of those basis elements. These four vectors are \(c_{\cdot}(\chi_r(g_k))_k\) for the four even characters, with a nonzero constant \(c_0\) or \(c_{ij}\) for each basis element, so they form a basis of \(F^4\). The constants depend on the chosen representatives \(g_k\): replacing \(g_k\) by \(g_kg_0\) flips the sign of \(s_k\), which changes the signs of the \(\mathrm{sc}\) vectors.
  3. Likewise, \(\mathrm{sc}(f)=\sum_iB^i_{d-1}\nu^i+E_{d-2}\,\nu^{123}\) over the four odd characters, again a basis. Here \(B^i_{d-1}\) and \(E_{d-2}\) are the coefficients of \(w_iT^{d-1}\) and \(w_1w_2w_3T^{d-2}\).
  4. Hence \(U_d=\{f\in L:\mathrm{lc}(f)\in F\tau,\ [\mathrm{sc}(f)]_{123}=0\}\), where \([\cdot]_{123}\) is the \(\nu^{123}\)-coordinate. That is four functionals \(\Phi=(\phi_{12},\phi_{13},\phi_{23},\psi)\) with \(U_d=\ker\Phi\).
  5. (Weight criterion.) A point \(p\) of \(E\) other than the \(\infty_k\) has positive weight for \(U_d\) iff \(\Phi\) is singular on \(L(2dH-(8d-4)p)\). It has weight \(\ge2\) iff \(\Phi\) has rank \(\le3\) on \(L(2dH-(8d-5)p)\) or a kernel on \(L(2dH-(8d-3)p)\).

Proof. Part 1. An element of \(L\) of type \(\chi_r\) is \(w^rg\) with \(g\) a \(G\)-invariant function, that is, a rational function of \(T\). Near \(T=-1/a_i\), \(w_i\) has a simple zero at each point over it, where \(T+1/a_i\) has a double zero. So a pole of \(g\) there would give a pole of \(w^rg\), and \(g\) is a polynomial. The element \(w^rT^j\) has pole order \(2j+|r|\le2d\) at every \(\infty_k\), which gives \(j_r\). The dimension is \((d+1)+3d+3d+(d-1)=8d\). Comparing with \(\nu_r=d-|r|\) gives the omitted elements, 4 in all.

Parts 2 and 3. An element of type \(\chi_r\) satisfies \(f\circ g^{-1}=\chi_r(g)^{-1}f\). So its expansions at the \(\infty_k\) are one series times \(\chi_r(g_k)^{\pm1}\), and at \(\infty_1\) it contains only powers \(s^e\) with \((-1)^e=\chi_r(g_0)=(-1)^{|r|}\). Only \(T^d\) and \(w_iw_jT^{d-1}\) reach pole order \(2d\), and only \(w_iT^{d-1}\) and \(w_1w_2w_3T^{d-2}\) reach odd order \(2d-1\); every other basis element has a smaller pole. Each of these has a nonzero leading coefficient \(c_r\) at \(\infty_1\).

The even characters are trivial on \(g_0\), so they are the four characters of \(G/\langle g_0\rangle\), and their value table on the coset representatives \(g_k\) is invertible. The odd characters are \(\chi_{123}\) times the even ones, so their table is invertible as well.

Part 4 follows from Part 1 and the unique decomposition of \(f\). Part 5 is proved in the next section. \(\square\)

When a point can have weight 2

For a point \(p\) of \(E\) other than the \(\infty_k\) write \(L_k=L(2dH-kp)\). On genus 1, \(\dim L_k=8d-k\) for \(k\le8d-2\). The orders \(\varepsilon_0<\cdots<\varepsilon_{8d-5}\) of \(U_d\) at \(p\) satisfy \(\#\{i:\varepsilon_i\ge k\}=\dim(U_d\cap L_k)=\dim\ker(\Phi|_{L_k})\). So:

  • \(p\) has positive weight iff \(\Phi|_{L_{8d-4}}\) (four functionals on a 4-dimensional space) is singular;
  • \(p\) has weight \(\ge2\) iff (A) \(\operatorname{rank}\Phi|_{L_{8d-5}}\le3\), so that two orders are \(\ge8d-5\), or (B) \(\Phi|_{L_{8d-3}}\) has a kernel, so that the top order is \(\ge8d-3\).

The lemma makes both conditions concrete.

(A) \(\mathrm{lc}\) maps \(L_{8d-5}\) onto \(F^4\): its kernel \(L((2d-1)H-(8d-5)p)\) has degree 1, so dimension 1, spanned by some \(g_p\). So the three \(\phi_{ij}\) have rank 3 there, and (A) says that \(\psi\) vanishes on the plane \(\{f\in L_{8d-5}:\mathrm{lc}(f)\in F\tau\}\). That plane is spanned by \(g_p\) and any \(f_\tau\) with \(\mathrm{lc}(f_\tau)=\tau\).

(B) \(\mathrm{lc}\) is injective on \(L_{8d-3}\), since the kernel has degree \(-1\). So (B) says there is \(f\in L_{8d-3}\) with \(\mathrm{lc}(f)=\tau\) and \([\mathrm{sc}(f)]_{123}=0\). By the residue theorem, applied to \(f\eta\) for the one differential \(\eta\) (up to scalars) with divisor \(\ge(2d-1)H-(8d-3)p\), the image \(\mathrm{lc}(L_{8d-3})\) is the hyperplane \(\{v:\sum_kv_k\eta_k=0\}\). Here \(\eta_k\) is the leading coefficient of \(\eta\) at \(\infty_k\). So (B) needs \(\sum_k\tau_k\eta_k=0\), and \(\sum_k\tau_k\eta_k=-\operatorname{Res}_p(T^d\eta)\) since \(T^d\eta\) has simple poles at the \(\infty_k\) and no other pole except \(p\). It also needs one more condition on the next order.

So a Weierstrass point of weight \(\ge2\) is a point of positive weight satisfying one further explicit condition. Squarefreeness of \(\Delta_U\) needs only that this does not happen at \(p=p_0\) (over \(T=0\)) at a general point of any component of the Weierstrass divisor. Multiplicity equals weight there by the flow step of the doubled-factor proposition, applied to \(U_d\), which is transported by the same translations, as the reduction entry states. So the open statement is now: on no component of the non-collision part of \(V(\Delta_U)\) in \(a\)-space does (A) or (B) hold at \(p_0\) at a general point.

General statement. lem:cube-limit-four-functionals, including the weight criterion, for every \(d\ge2\) and every configuration with distinct nonzero \(a_i\), in characteristic \(\ne2\). The open part remains conj:cube-limit-determinant-squarefree.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the reduction theorem and triple-multiplicity corollary (the limit space and its data), the collision limit-space lemma, and the doubled-factor proposition's flow step. A claim search (limit space, genus 1, character functionals) found nothing implying the lemma. A fresh-context referee checked:

  • the inertia, the ramification and the genus;
  • the pole orders and the isotypic basis;
  • the parity at \(\infty_1\) and the character tables;
  • the order counting, the dimensions on genus 1 and the residue step;
  • the \(d=2\) data.

It found no error. Its corrections are made:

  • the \(a_3\) multiplicity comes from homogeneity;
  • the flow step is cited for \(U_d\), at \(p_0\);
  • the characteristic is \(\ne2\), since characteristic 0 enters only through multiplicity = weight;
  • the weight criterion is part 5 of the lemma;
  • the open statement is made precise;
  • the constants are indexed per element, and depend on the representatives;
  • the residue sign is written out.

Assessment. The genus-1 case has the same shape as the conic, with four functionals in place of one. They are the three non-trivial even Fourier components of the top coefficients at the four points at infinity, and the \(\chi_{123}\) component one order down. There is no closed form to exploit, so the proof must show that the weight-2 conditions are independent of the Weierstrass condition.

Two routes are visible:

  • the residue description, which turns (A) and (B) into conditions on differentials with a pole at \(p\), where addition on \(E\) may make them explicit, as the root of unity did on the conic;
  • the quadrangle route of the reduction entry, which needs squarefreeness on the triple sides, for the conic vector \((2d,2d-2,2d-2,2d-4)\) of codimension 5, and on the double-double sides.

For the conic vectors, apolarity makes the weight of \(V_\nu\) at \(p\) equal to that of the dual series spanned by the missing functionals. That dual series lies in \((\lambda-\kappa)^{m-i}\mathrm{Poly}_i\oplus(\lambda+\kappa)^{m-i}\mathrm{Poly}_i\), a two-point space whose Wronskians are of hypergeometric type. The next step is that computation for \((2d,2d-2,2d-2,2d-4)\).

26 September 2026 — The triple sides of the limit determinant: a diagonal factor and one irreducible palindromic factor, squarefree through d = 5

Finite check, exact over Q: on the triple sides the non-collision part of the conic determinant (2d, 2d−2, 2d−2, 2d−4) is (a₁ + a₂) times one irreducible palindromic factor, squarefree for d ≤ 5. Cycle bmd-r132. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The dimension-4 boundary law needs the limit conjecture: the non-collision part of \(\Delta_U\) is squarefree (reduction entry). The four-functionals lemma showed that \(\Delta_U\) itself has no closed form at \(d=2\). The recorded alternative is the quadrangle lemma, which needs the restriction of \(\Delta_U\) to each of the six collision lines of the \(a\)-plane to be squarefree apart from collision forms.

On a triple side \(a_j=0\) that restriction is, up to powers of the collision forms of the side, the conic determinant \(\Delta_{\nu'}\) with \(\nu'_d=(2d,2d-2,2d-2,2d-4)\) (triple-multiplicity corollary). This cycle asks what that determinant looks like, and whether it has a closed form that the conic theorem's method, or classical polynomials, could handle.

Data

The PARI/GP tool research/tools/bmd_cube_nu_factor_n2.gp computes \(\Delta_\nu(1,x)\) exactly and factors it over \(\mathbb Q\). It replaces the sympy tool for larger vectors and reproduces its factorization of \((3,2,2,1)\). Output is in research/results/bmd-r132-triple-sides/.

Finite check (check:cube-triple-side-squarefree). For \(\nu'_d\), \(d=2,\ldots,5\), exactly over \(\mathbb Q\):

  • the multiplicity at \(x=0\) is \(18,50,98,162=2(2d-1)^2\);
  • the multiplicity at \(x=1\) is \(11,37,79,137=8d^2-14d+7\);
  • the rest is \((x+1)\cdot P_d\), with \(x+1\) simple and \(P_d\) one irreducible factor of degree \(2,8,14,20=6d-10\);
  • \(P_d\) is palindromic, reflecting the symmetry \(a_1\leftrightarrow a_2\).

So the non-collision part is squarefree for \(d\le5\).

No closed form appears. \(P_d(x)=x^{3d-5}R_d(u)\) with \(u=(1+x)^2/x\):

  • \(R_2=7u-12\);
  • \(R_3=165u^4+1056u^2+2560u-3840\), whose \(u^3\) coefficient vanishes, so \(R_d\) is not a hypergeometric polynomial in \(u\).

The factor \(x+1\), that is \(a_1+a_2\) on the side \(a_3=0\), is not a collision form. It is simple in every case.

What this settles and what remains

For the quadrangle route, the triple sides need the non-collision part of \(\Delta_{\nu'_d}\) to be squarefree for every \(d\). That is an instance of the monotone squarefreeness conjecture for \(n=2\), a codimension-5 case of the conic setting (\(V_{\nu'}\subset L(4d(\infty_1+\infty_2))\), missing \(w_iT^{2d-1}\) and \(w_1w_2T^{2d-3},w_1w_2T^{2d-2},w_1w_2T^{2d-1}\)). The data give it only for \(d\le5\), which adds no instance to the recorded certification of the whole limit conjecture for \(d\le9\). So, by the rule on stopping runs, no larger \(d\) is computed.

The double-double sides \(a_i=a_j\) need the transported space, computed here from the boundary theorem's transport. Substitute \(T=\tilde T/(1-a_3\tilde T)\), put \(\tilde a=(a_1-a_3,a_2-a_3,-a_3)\) and \(\tilde w_3=(1-a_3\tilde T)^{1/2}\), and multiply by \(\tilde w_3^{\,2d}\). Then \(w_i=\tilde w_i/\tilde w_3\) for \(i=1,2\), and \(w_3=1/\tilde w_3\). An element \(T^Qw^r\) of \(U_d\) goes to

\[\tilde T^Q\,\tilde w_1^{r_1}\tilde w_2^{r_2}\,\tilde w_3^{\,2(d-Q)-|r|},\]

with exponent \(\ge|r|\ge0\), since \(Q\le d-|r|\). Writing \(\tilde w_3^{\,2e}=(1-a_3\tilde T)^e\), the part of character \((r_1,r_2,|r|\bmod2)\) is spanned by \(\tilde T^Q(1-a_3\tilde T)^{\lfloor(2(d-Q)-|r|)/2\rfloor}\), of the fixed degree \(d-\lceil|r|/2\rceil\) in \(\tilde T\), each divisible by \((1-a_3\tilde T)^{\lfloor|r|/2\rfloor}\). So the transported space is, character by character, \(\tilde w^{\tilde r}\) times polynomials of one fixed degree divisible by a fixed power of \(1-a_3\tilde T\). That is a space with a prescribed vanishing order at a branch point, not a degree vector. The collision \(a_1=a_3\) becomes the triple-type confluence \(\tilde a_1=0\) of this larger class. This is the class the monotone-squarefree entry expected an induction to need.

General statement. conj:cube-monotone-squarefree, for every monotone degree vector; this check tests the family \(\nu'_d\) its triple sides need.

Verification gate. A finite check and a transport computation; no new proof is claimed. Dependencies re-read: the triple-multiplicity corollary (the restriction to triple sides, up to powers of the side's collision forms), the quadrangle lemma's hypothesis, and the boundary theorem's transport. The PARI tool reproduces the sympy factorization of \((3,2,2,1)\). Every number above is read from the saved output.

Assessment. The route to the boundary law for every \(d\) is now a pair of conic statements:

  • squarefreeness for \(\nu'_d\), which has codimension 5;
  • the same for the transported space on the double-double sides.

The quadrangle lemma then closes the argument. Neither has a closed form. The conic theorem's method needs extending from one missing functional to several: the weight at \(p\) is the rank drop of the missing functionals on \(L(D-kp)\), and all of them read Laurent coefficients at the two points \(\infty_\pm\). In the coordinate \(\rho=(\lambda-\kappa)/(\lambda+\kappa)\) this makes the Weierstrass condition a polynomial in \(\rho\) supported on few exponents. The next step is to write that polynomial for \(\nu'_d\) and prove its zeros simple.

26 September 2026 — On the conic every determinant is a Wronskian of binomials: the n = 2 squarefreeness problem becomes explicit

Working proof: for every n = 2 degree vector the non-collision part of Δ_ν is the image of the Wronskian of an explicit binomial series on a fixed curve, with multiplicities. Checked exactly on nine vectors, including a failure. Cycle bmd-r133. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The quadrangle route to the dimension-4 boundary law needs squarefreeness of conic determinants \(\Delta_\nu\) (\(n=2\)) for two families, which have no closed form (triple-sides entry). The conic theorem handled one missing functional by hand. Is there a uniform description of \(\Delta_\nu\) for every \(n=2\) vector, from which squarefreeness becomes a concrete statement? The test ends with such a description, validated exactly, or with a vector where it fails.

The rigid curve

Let \(n=2\), in characteristic 0. The conic \(\Gamma\) of \(w_1,w_2\) is \(\mathbb P^1\), with the Klein group \(G=\langle\sigma_1,\sigma_2\rangle\) acting, where \(\sigma_i\) flips \(w_i\), and with the two points over \(T=\infty\). The element \(\sigma_1\sigma_2\) is the inertia there, since both \(w_i\) change sign around \(T=\infty\). So it fixes both points, and \(\sigma_1\) swaps them.

Choose a coordinate \(\mu\) with the two points at \(0,\infty\). Then \(\sigma_1\sigma_2\), an involution fixing \(0,\infty\), is \(\mu\mapsto-\mu\). Its commuting involution \(\sigma_1\), which swaps them, is \(\mu\mapsto b/\mu\), and scaling \(\mu\) makes \(b=1\). So \(\sigma_1:\mu\mapsto1/\mu\) and \(\sigma_2:\mu\mapsto-1/\mu\), independently of \(a\).

The ramification over \(T=\infty\) has index 2, so \(w_i\) has a simple pole and \(T\) a double pole at \(0\) and \(\infty\), and no other poles. A function with these pole orders is determined up to scalars by its parities under \(\mu\mapsto-\mu\) and \(\sigma_1\):

  • \(w_1=\mu-\mu^{-1}\) (odd under \(\mu\mapsto-\mu\) and under \(\sigma_1\));
  • \(w_2=\mu+\mu^{-1}\);
  • \(T\in\mathrm{span}\{\mu^2+\mu^{-2},1\}\).

The point \(p_0\) over \(T=0\) is some \(\mu_0\). Normalizing \(w_i(p_0)=1\) gives \(w_i^2-1=a_iT\) with \(T=\Theta-\Theta(\mu_0)\), \(\Theta=\mu^2+\mu^{-2}\), and \(a_1^{-1}=(\mu_0-\mu_0^{-1})^2\), \(a_2^{-1}=(\mu_0+\mu_0^{-1})^2\). So

\[x:=a_2/a_1=\Bigl(\frac{\mu_0^2-1}{\mu_0^2+1}\Bigr)^2,\]

a \(G\)-invariant function of degree 4. The collisions \(x\in\{0,1,\infty\}\) correspond to \(\mu_0\in\{\pm1\}\), \(\{0,\infty\}\), \(\{\pm i\}\).

Since \(F[T]_{\le j}=F[\Theta]_{\le j}\), the space \(V_\nu=\bigoplus_rw^rF[T]_{\le\nu_r}\) is, up to the scalars of the \(w_i\), the fixed space of Laurent polynomials

\[V_\nu=\mathrm{span}\{\mu^m+\mu^{-m}:m\in M_{00}\cup M_{01}\}\oplus\mathrm{span}\{\mu^m-\mu^{-m}:m\in M_{10}\cup M_{11}\},\]

with the frequency ranges:

  • \(M_{00}=\{0,2,\ldots,2\nu_{00}\}\);
  • \(M_{10}\) and \(M_{01}\): the odd \(m\le2\nu_{10}+1\), respectively \(\le2\nu_{01}+1\);
  • \(M_{11}=\{2,4,\ldots,2\nu_{11}+2\}\).

Each \(w^rF[\Theta]\) is triangular to these: for example \((\mu-\mu^{-1})(\mu^{2k}+\mu^{-2k})=s_{2k+1}-s_{2k-1}\) with \(s_m=\mu^m-\mu^{-m}\). It does not depend on \(a\). Only the marked point \(\mu_0\) moves.

The theorem

Let \(c\) be the largest frequency present. Then \(\mu^cV_\nu\subseteq\mathrm{Poly}_{2c}\). Define the dual series \(S_\nu\subseteq\mathrm{Poly}_{2c}\), spanned, for each \(0\le m\le c\), by:

  • \(\mu^{c-m}-\mu^{c+m}\) if \(V\) contains \(\mu^m+\mu^{-m}\) but not \(\mu^m-\mu^{-m}\);
  • \(\mu^{c-m}+\mu^{c+m}\) in the opposite case;
  • both \(\mu^{c-m}\) and \(\mu^{c+m}\) if it contains neither;
  • \(\mu^c\) if \(m=0\) and the constant is missing.

Theorem (thm:cube-conic-duality, the conic duality theorem). In characteristic 0, for every degree vector \(\nu\in\{-1,0,1,\ldots\}^4\) with \(N_\nu=\sum_r(\nu_r+1)\ge1\), the part of \(\Delta_\nu(a_1,a_2)\) prime to \(a_1,a_2,a_1-a_2\) equals, up to a constant,

\[\prod_{G\mu\subset Z}\bigl(a_2-x(\mu)\,a_1\bigr)^{\operatorname{ord}_\mu W(S_\nu)},\]

the product over the \(G\)-orbits of zeros \(\mu\notin\{0,\infty,\pm1,\pm i\}\) of the Wronskian \(W(S_\nu)\). In particular it is squarefree iff \(W(S_\nu)\) has only simple zeros off \(\{0,\infty,\pm1,\pm i\}\). By multilinearity and \(W(\mu^{e_1},\ldots,\mu^{e_s})=\prod_{i<j}(e_j-e_i)\,\mu^{\sum e_i-\binom s2}\), \(W(S_\nu)\) is an explicit sum of at most \(2^s\) Vandermonde-weighted monomials.

Proof.

1. For \(a\) with distinct nonzero entries, \(\dim V_\nu=N\) by Kummer theory. So \(\Delta_\nu(a)=0\) iff \(V_\nu\) has a nonzero element of order \(\ge N\) at \(p_0\), that is, iff \(\mu_0\) has positive weight for \(V_\nu\). Over \(\overline F\), as in the conic theorem's step 3, every non-collision prime factor of the binary form \(\Delta_\nu\) is linear, \(\pi=a_2-x_0a_1\) with \(x_0\notin\{0,1,\infty\}\). Its multiplicity is the weight of \(p_0\) at a point of \(V(\pi)\), by the Wronskian identity of the generic normality lemma and the transversality computed there, which uses only that \(\pi\) is not a collision form.

2. The series \(V_\nu\) is fixed and \(G\)-stable, so its weights are \(G\)-invariant. The non-identity elements of \(G\) fix only \(\{0,\infty\}\), \(\{\pm1\}\) and \(\{\pm i\}\), so a non-special fibre of \(x\) is a single free \(G\)-orbit of 4 points, all of the same weight. Hence the multiplicity of \(a_2-x_0a_1\) is the weight of \(V_\nu\) at any \(\mu\) with \(x(\mu)=x_0\).

3. Apolarity. Pair \(\mathrm{Poly}_{2c}\) with itself by the \(SL_2\)-invariant form \(\langle\mu^i,\mu^j\rangle=\delta_{i+j,2c}(-1)^i\binom{2c}i^{-1}\). Let \(F_k(p)\subseteq\mathrm{Poly}_{2c}\) be the polynomials vanishing to order \(\ge k\) at \(p\). At \(p=0\) the annihilator of \(F_k(0)\) is \(F_{2c+1-k}(0)\), and \(SL_2\)-invariance carries this to every \(p\): the polynomials vanishing to order \(\ge k\) at \(p\) have annihilator the polynomials vanishing to order \(\ge2c+1-k\) at \(p\). So for \(S=V^\perp\), of dimension \(s\), \(\dim(S\cap F_{2c+1-k}(p))=k-(2c+1)+s+\dim(V\cap F_k(p))\) for every \(k\). The two jump sequences therefore determine each other, and the weights of \(V\) and \(S\) at \(p\) are equal.

4. \(V_\nu\) is cut out by the conditions \(a_{c+m}=\pm a_{c-m}\), or \(a_{c\pm m}=0\), on the coefficients of its elements. The functional "coefficient \(a_j\)" is paired with \(\binom{2c}j(-1)^j\mu^{2c-j}\), and the weights at \(j=c\pm m\) are equal because \(2c\) is even. So \(V_\nu^\perp=S_\nu\) as listed.

5. At \(p\ne0,\infty\) the orders of \(\mu^cV\) in \(\mathrm{Poly}_{2c}\) are the orders of \(V\) on \(\Gamma\), which is all the proof uses. The weight of \(S\) at \(\mu\ne0,\infty\) is \(\operatorname{ord}_\mu W(S)\), in characteristic 0. Combining 1–5 gives the formula. \(\square\)

Checks and consequences

The PARI/GP tool research/tools/bmd_cube_conic_dual.gp builds \(S_\nu\), factors \(W(S_\nu)\) and maps it to \(x\) by a resultant. One run of it, research/results/bmd-r133-conic-dual/dual-vs-delta.txt, compares nine vectors with the exact factorization of \(\Delta_\nu\). They agree, multiplicities included, each root appearing 4 times in the resultant. The vectors are:

  • \((2,1,1,0)\), \((3,2,2,1)\), \((4,3,2,1)\), \((4,2,1,0)\);
  • the triple-side vectors \((4,2,2,0)\), \((6,4,4,2)\), \((8,6,6,4)\);
  • the non-monotone \((3,0,1,1)\) and \((3,3,4,1)\).

For \((3,0,1,1)\), \(W(S)=(\mu^2-\mu+1)^3(\mu^2+\mu+1)^3\) times special factors, which gives \((x+3)^3\). That is the recorded failure \((3a_1+a_2)^3\), now a triple zero at the primitive sixth roots of unity.

The conic theorem in one line. For \(\nu=(d,d-1,d-1,d-2)\), only \(\mu^{2d}-\mu^{-2d}\) is missing, so \(S=\mathrm{span}\{1-\mu^{4d}\}\). Its zeros \(\mu^{4d}=1\) are simple, and the non-special ones give \(x=-\cot^2(\pi j/2d)\).

The triple sides. For \(\nu'_d\), \(S=\mathrm{span}\{1-\mu^{8d},\ \mu^2-\mu^{8d-2},\ \mu^4-\mu^{8d-4},\ \mu,\ \mu^{8d-1}\}\). The lowest power of \(\mu\) in \(W(S)\) is \(\mu^{8d-4}\), and \(W(S)/\mu^{8d-4}\) is a palindromic 8-nomial in \(t=\mu^4\), with exponents \(0,2d-2,2d-1,2d,4d-3,4d-2,4d-1,6d-3\) and Vandermonde coefficients. After removing \((t-1)^6(t+1)\), its squarefreeness for every \(d\) is exactly what the triple sides need. The quotient \(Q_d\), of degree \(6d-10\), has nonzero discriminant and does not vanish at \(t=-1\) for every \(d\le10\) (same run). So the triple sides are squarefree through \(d=10\), by the theorem. Only two roots of each \(Q_d\) are real, so real-rootedness is not the mechanism.

General statement. thm:cube-conic-duality, for every \(n=2\) degree vector in characteristic 0. It turns conj:cube-monotone-squarefree for \(n=2\) into the statement that \(W(S_\nu)\) has simple zeros off \(\{0,\infty,\pm1,\pm i\}\) for monotone \(\nu\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the conic theorem (the multiplicity step), the generic normality lemma, and the monotone-squarefree data. A claim search (conic, Wronskian, binomial, dual series, apolar) found no earlier duality result; the nearest is the binomial order criterion (Stöhr–Voloch), which concerns orders, not this duality. A fresh-context referee checked:

  • the rigidity and the formulas for \(w_i\), \(T\), \(a_i\) and \(x\);
  • the collision correspondence and the frequency ranges, including entries \(-1\);
  • the apolarity annihilator and the equality of weights, and the dual signs;
  • the tool against the outputs, including the \(x\) convention, on the asymmetric vectors.

It found the proof correct, and confirmed extra vectors \((2,-1,0,-1)\) and \((1,-1,-1,1)\). Its corrections are made:

  • the lowest power \(\mu^{8d-4}\), not \(\mu^6\);
  • the evidence regenerated by one run of the committed tool;
  • the pole orders stated in the rigidity argument;
  • \(N_\nu\ge1\);
  • \(F_k(p)\) defined;
  • the linear factors taken over \(\overline F\);
  • the free-orbit clause;
  • the orders compared only off \(0,\infty\);
  • the assessment's proof idea rephrased.

Assessment. For two branch points the whole problem is now explicit. The curve with its group action is rigid, and every \(V_\nu\) is a fixed space of trigonometric polynomials. Its non-collision Weierstrass points are the zeros of the Wronskian of a binomial space, a fewnomial with Vandermonde coefficients. This explains the conic theorem and the recorded failures, and it reduces both conic statements of the quadrangle route to simple zeros of explicit fewnomials in \(t=\mu^4\). The next step is that statement for the triple-side 8-nomial, which has integer exponents linear in \(d\) and coefficients polynomial in \(d\). Since the exponents are linear in \(d\), a proof may use asymptotics in \(d\): the terms fall into four clusters, which locate the roots near circles by Rouché's theorem. A finite range of small \(d\) would then be checked directly.

26 September 2026 — The triple-side determinant in closed form: a palindromic 8-nomial, and where its roots lie

Working proof: on the triple sides, the non-collision part of the limit determinant is given by an explicit palindromic 8-nomial in t = μ⁴. Cycle bmd-r134. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The conic duality theorem reduced the triple sides of the dimension-4 boundary route to simple zeros of the Wronskian of \(S=\mathrm{span}\{1-\mu^{8d},\mu^2-\mu^{8d-2},\mu^4-\mu^{8d-4},\mu,\mu^{8d-1}\}\). What is that Wronskian exactly, for every \(d\)? Does its shape suggest a proof of simple zeros?

The closed form

Lemma (lem:cube-triple-side-closed-form). For \(d\ge2\), put \(n=2d-1\), \(D=8d\) and \(t=\mu^4\). Then

\[\frac{W(S)}{\mu^{8d-4}}=48(D-1)(D-2)(D-3)(D-5)\,F_n(t),\] \[F_n(t)=1+t^{3n}-t^{n-1}q(t)-t^{2n-1}q^*(t),\] \[q(t)=n(2n-1)-(4n^2-1)\,t+n(2n+1)\,t^2,\qquad q^*(t)=t^2q(1/t),\]

with sign \(+\) for the basis order shown. Moreover \(q(1)=1\), so \(F_n(1)=0\). \(F_n\) is palindromic of odd degree \(3n\), so \(F_n(-1)=-F_n(-1)=0\) as well.

Proof. By multilinearity of the Wronskian,

\[W(S)=\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^3}(-1)^{|\varepsilon|}\,W(\mu^{e_1},\mu^{e_2},\mu^{e_3},\mu,\mu^{D-1}),\]

with \(e_1\in\{0,D\}\), \(e_2\in\{2,D-2\}\) and \(e_3\in\{4,D-4\}\) chosen by \(\varepsilon\). Each term is the Vandermonde product \(\prod_{i<j}(e_j-e_i)\) times \(\mu^{\sum e-10}\).

The eight products, divided by \((D-1)(D-2)(D-3)(D-5)\), are:

  • \(48\) for \(\varepsilon=000\) and \(111\);
  • \(-6(D-4)(D-6)\) for \(001\) and \(110\);
  • \(12(D-2)(D-6)\) for \(010\) and \(101\);
  • \(-6(D-2)(D-4)\) for \(100\) and \(011\).

The \(t\)-exponents are \(0,2d-2,2d-1,4d-3,2d,4d-2,4d-1,6d-3\), in the same order of \(\varepsilon\) (research/results/bmd-r134-triple-closed/vandermonde-coefficients.txt, symbolic in \(D\)). With \(D=4(n+1)\), \(D-4=4n\), \(D-6=2(2n-1)\) and \(D-2=2(2n+1)\), dividing by 48 gives the coefficients \(n(2n-1)\), \(4n^2-1\), \(n(2n+1)\) with the signs shown. The value is \(q(1)=n(2n-1)-(4n^2-1)+n(2n+1)=1\). \(\square\)

Check. The tool research/tools/bmd_cube_triple_side_closed.gp compares \(F_n\) with the Wronskian computed from the dual series by bmd_cube_conic_dual.gp. For every \(d=2,\ldots,12\) the ratio is exactly \(-48(D-1)(D-2)(D-3)(D-5)\), the sign coming from the tool's basis order (closed-form-roots.txt). A fresh-context referee recomputed the Wronskian independently with sympy for \(d=2,3,4\), in the order shown, and found sign \(+\). At \(d=2\), \(F_3=1-15t^2+35t^3-21t^4-21t^5+35t^6-15t^7+t^9\).

Where the roots lie

Exact facts, checked for every \(d\le12\) by the same tool:

  • \(F_n\) has order exactly 6 at \(t=1\), and \(Q_d:=F_n/((t-1)^6(t+1))\), of degree \(6d-10\), satisfies \(Q_d(\pm1)\ne0\);
  • writing the palindromic \(Q_d\) as \(t^{3d-5}R_d(t+1/t)\), a Sturm count shows that \(R_d\) has exactly \(d-2\) distinct roots in \((-2,2)\), so \(Q_d\) has exactly \(2d-4\) distinct zeros on the unit circle.

The order 6 at \(t=1\) for every \(d\) is a polynomial identity in \(n\): the first six moments \(\sum_\varepsilon c_\varepsilon a_\varepsilon^k\), \(k\le5\), vanish. It is checked here only for \(d\le12\).

A heuristic: writing \(z=t^n\), the equation \(F_n(t)=0\) reads as the cubic

\[z^3-\frac{q^*(t)}{t}\,z^2-\frac{q(t)}{t}\,z+1=0.\]

This is self-inversive on \(|t|=1\), since \(q^*(t)/t=\overline{q(t)/t}\) there, though \(z\) depends on \(t\). On \(|t|=1\), \(q(t)/t=4n^2\cos\theta-(4n^2-1)+2in\sin\theta\) is large away from \(\theta=0\) but has size 1 at \(\theta=0\), where the sixfold root sits. The floating-point roots (60 digits, modulus threshold \(10^{-9}\)) of \(Q_d\) for \(d\le12\) fall into three families:

  • \(2d-3\) inside the unit circle, near the curve \(|t|^{n-1}|q(t)|=1\);
  • \(2d-4\) on it, the exact count above;
  • \(2d-3\) outside, the images of the inner ones under \(t\mapsto1/t\).

The minimal distance between roots is \(4.58,0.446,0.388,\ldots,0.191\) for \(d=2,3,4,\ldots,12\), decreasing slowly. The exact discriminant check of the duality entry already gives squarefreeness for \(d\le10\); the floating-point separation is only evidence.

A proof for every \(d\) can follow this picture, using lower bounds on the number of distinct zeros in three disjoint sets:

  • Unit circle: \(e^{-3in\theta/2}F_n(e^{i\theta})\) is real for \(\theta\in(0,\pi)\). So \(d-2\) sign changes on the open upper arc, with conjugation, give \(2d-4\) distinct zeros away from \(\pm1\).
  • Inside: \(1-t^{n-1}q(t)\) has \(2d-1\) zeros in the open unit disc. At \(d=5\) their moduli, computed by the referee, are \(0.481\), \(0.488\) (twice), \(0.511\) (twice), \(0.562\) (twice) and \(0.787\) (twice, near argument \(\pm0.136\)). The first \(2d-3\) match the inner roots of \(Q_d\) to about \(10^{-3}\), while the pair near \(t=1\) is absorbed into \((t-1)^6\). So Rouché's theorem has to be applied on \(2d-3\) disjoint small discs, one zero each, which also gives simplicity.
  • Near \(t=1\): a separate argument must show that \(F_n\) has no zeros in a neighbourhood of \(t=1\) other than the sixfold root. This is where \(q(t)/t\) is small and the three families meet, and it is the real difficulty.
  • Outside: the outer zeros follow by palindromy.

The count \(2(2d-3)+(2d-4)=6d-10=\deg Q_d\) and the disjointness of the three sets then force all zeros to be simple. The constants must be made explicit, since \(q\) grows like \(n^2\) away from \(t=1\).

General statement. lem:cube-triple-side-closed-form, for every \(d\ge2\). Squarefreeness of \(Q_d\) for every \(d\) is the open step, which the three-family argument above targets.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the conic duality theorem and its dual series. A fresh-context referee recomputed the Wronskian with sympy for \(d=2,3,4\) and confirmed the formula with sign \(+\), the Vandermonde coefficients, the exponents, \(q(1)=1\) and palindromy. Its corrections are made:

  • \(F_n(-1)=0\) and the order 6 at \(t=1\) are justified, the latter only for \(d\le12\);
  • the tool now asserts the constant, and certifies the unit-circle count exactly;
  • the floating-point claims are labelled;
  • the size of \(q\) near \(t=1\) is corrected;
  • the cubic remark is labelled heuristic;
  • the Rouché plan is corrected: \(1-t^{n-1}q\) has \(2d-1\) inner zeros, two of which belong to the neighbourhood of \(t=1\), so the argument needs disjoint discs and a separate treatment of that neighbourhood.

Assessment. The triple sides are now one explicit family, \(F_n(t)=1+t^{3n}-t^{n-1}q(t)-t^{2n-1}q^*(t)\) with an explicit quadratic \(q\). Its roots fall into three families, with \(2d-4\) simple zeros on the unit circle exactly and \(2d-3\) on each side in floating point, for \(d\le12\). A sign-change and Rouché argument can settle simplicity once the error terms are explicit, except near \(t=1\), where the sixfold root sits and a separate local analysis is needed. A route review is due next, and it should weigh this against the other items of open statement 3.

26 September 2026 — Route review of the cube: the dimension-4 boundary reduced to explicit polynomial families; order zero blocked by cohomology

Route review: the monotone squarefreeness conjecture for n = 2 survives 808 monotone vectors, and fails for 18 non-monotone ones. The boundary line is now concrete; order zero has no mechanism. Cycle bmd-r135. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

The line's general claim. The per-order function on \(\{0,1\}^n\) in characteristic \(\ne2\) is determined by the thresholds \(\ell_0(h,m)\). Dimension 3 is solved. For \(n\ge4\) the claims to establish are laws for the thresholds, at the boundary, in the middle range and at order zero (open statement 3), and at small primes (open statement 2).

What the goal needs. Since route review 19, six research cycles:

  • the threshold ideal is the annihilator of one cokernel class, which vanishes locally in the zero-free range, so no pointwise method reaches order zero in dimension 4 (entry);
  • the base case of the boundary route: on the conic every Weierstrass point of the cube's hyperplane series has weight 1 (conic theorem);
  • on the genus-1 curve the limit space is cut out by four character functionals (entry);
  • the triple sides of the limit determinant, exact through \(d=5\) (entry);
  • for \(n=2\), every conic determinant is the Wronskian of an explicit binomial series (duality theorem);
  • the triple-side Wronskian in closed form, a palindromic 8-nomial with three root families (entry).

Falsification attempt

The duality theorem makes the \(n=2\) case of the monotone squarefreeness conjecture cheap to test: each vector needs one sparse Wronskian. The recorded test covered entries \(\le4\). The new tool research/tools/bmd_cube_conic_sweep.gp (PARI/GP) takes every \(\nu\in\{-1,\ldots,7\}^4\) with \(N\ge2\) and a nonempty dual series. It computes \(W(S_\nu)\), removes the special factors \(\mu,\mu\pm1,\mu^2+1\), and tests the rest for squarefreeness (research/results/bmd-r135-route-review/conic-sweep-e7.txt).

  • All 808 monotone vectors pass.
  • 18 of 5733 non-monotone vectors fail, in pairs exchanged by \(a_1\leftrightarrow a_2\). The failures include the four recorded ones, \((3,0,1,1)\), \((3,3,4,1)\) and their images, and new ones such as \((5,1,2,3)\), \((6,0,1,4)\) and \((7,2,3,5)\).

The sizing run for entries \(\le4\) reproduces the recorded tally exactly: 4 non-monotone failures. Its 185 monotone vectors are the recorded 194 minus 9 whose series is complete. The conjecture could have failed on a larger monotone vector; it did not.

Assessment of this line

The two halves of open statement 3 in dimension 4 have diverged.

  • Order zero and the middle range: stuck. Point windows reach only \(11d-11\), and the remaining obstruction is a local cohomology class of a depth-2 module, which vanishes at every point (zero-free criterion, annihilator form). No method recorded here bounds such a class. The evidence for \(M(d)=20d-21\) is unchanged.
  • The boundary for every \(d\): concrete and progressing. The law \(\ell_0(d+1,8d-4)=10d^2-10d-5\) is proved for \(d\le9\). For every \(d\) it needs squarefreeness of the limit determinant \(\Delta_U\), and by the quadrangle route that comes down to two conic families. The triple sides are the explicit 8-nomial \(F_{2d-1}\), squarefree through \(d=10\) exactly. Its roots lie in three families, and a sign-change and Rouché argument is outlined, the neighbourhood of \(t=1\) being the hard part. The double-double sides are a transported space with vanishing at a branch point. In the rigid picture that is again a fixed space on the conic, so the duality theorem should extend to it with evaluation functionals at \(\pm1\) or \(\pm i\).

The quadrangle lemma's exact hypothesis must also be matched: restrictions equal to a power of the diagonal form times a squarefree part. That is not yet checked for the double-double sides. The line's prospects on the boundary are good; on order zero they are poor without a new idea.

Outside leads

  • Tropical root estimates for polynomials (Hadamard–Ostrowski–Pólya; the Newton polygon of \(\log|c_k|\) predicts the moduli of the roots and how many share each modulus). Target: the triple-side squarefreeness, by locating the three root families of \(F_n\) before Rouché's theorem. It breaks where two tropical slopes nearly coincide. Test. Passed. The upper hull of the points \((k,\log|c_k|)\) of \(F_n=1+t^{3n}-t^{n-1}q-t^{2n-1}q^*\) has vertices \((0,0)\), \((n,\log B)\), \((2n,\log B)\) and \((3n,0)\), since \(B=4n^2-1\) exceeds \(A=n(2n-1)\) and \(C=n(2n+1)\) for \(n\ge2\). This predicts \(n\) roots of modulus about \(B^{-1/n}\), \(n\) near the unit circle and \(n\) outside. The actual counts match: \(2d-3=n-2\) inner roots of \(Q_d\) plus two absorbed into \((t-1)^6\); \(2d-4\) on the circle plus \(t=-1\), plus \(6-4\) at \(t=1\), giving \(n\); and \(n\) outer.
  • Sturm sequences and the Hermite criterion for self-reciprocal polynomials (the substitution \(u=t+1/t\), as in the theory of Salem polynomials). Target: the \(2d-4\) unit-circle zeros for every \(d\). The count of real roots of \(R_d(u)\) on \((-2,2)\) is a sign-variation count that a closed form of \(R_d\) could make uniform in \(d\). It breaks if \(R_d\) has no tractable closed form. Test. Passed for \(d\le12\): the exact Sturm count gives \(d-2\) roots of \(R_d\) in \((-2,2)\) (closed-form entry). A uniform proof is not attempted.
  • Bethe ansatz for spaces of polynomials with prescribed Wronskian (Mukhin–Tarasov–Varchenko, Annals 2009; Scherbak). A space of polynomials whose Wronskian has simple zeros corresponds to solutions of Bethe equations, which are non-degenerate under genericity conditions. Target: simple zeros of \(W(S_\nu)\) for monotone \(\nu\), by recognizing the binomial dual series as a family covered by that non-degeneracy. It breaks where the dual series fails their genericity, which is exactly where squarefreeness fails, so it would give only a restatement unless their conditions are checkable. Test. Not run: matching the dual series to their weight data needs the \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) weights of the spaces, which are not set up.

Absurd bridges

  • Lee–Yang circle theorem (statistical mechanics; Lee and Yang, Phys. Rev. 87, 1952). Translation: \(F_n(t)\) is a palindromic "partition function" in the fugacity \(t\). A ferromagnetic structure would force every zero onto the unit circle, which would prove simplicity through a sign-change count alone. Test. Falsified: \(F_n\) has \(2(2d-3)\) zeros off the unit circle (exact count by degree minus the Sturm count), so no Lee–Yang property holds for it. Only its unit-circle factor behaves that way.
  • Hückel theory of cyclic polyenes (quantum chemistry; the spectrum \(2\cos(2\pi k/N)\) of the cycle graph). Translation: the conic theorem's roots \(x=-\cot^2(\pi j/2d)\) come from \(\mu^{4d}=1\), a circulant spectrum, the Hückel spectrum of a cycle of length \(4d\). The triple sides might be the spectrum of a cycle with a few decorated sites, making \(R_d(u)\) the characteristic polynomial of a structured matrix, whose eigenvalues are simple for connected graphs of that kind. Test. Not run: it needs a candidate graph for \(R_d\), and no cheap test separates candidates.

Bridge follow-up

  • Chip-firing on a cycle. Not worked this period. Follow-up. Continuing, with the boundary conjecture.
  • The non-crossing rule. Not worked this period. Follow-up. Continuing, with the boundary conjecture.
  • The renewal-reward theorem. Not worked this period; order zero has no new data. Follow-up. Continuing.
  • Algebraic-geometry codes. On rereading, this repeats route review 16's bridge on Weierstrass semigroups of AG codes, which was closed. The curve and divisor identification it tested is recorded there. Follow-up. Closed: a repetition of a closed bridge.

Lead follow-up

  • General Weierstrass points are simple. Developed this period: weight 1 on the conic for the cube's vector, the duality theorem for every \(n=2\) vector, and the four-functional structure in genus 1. Follow-up. Continuing: genus 1 and the double-double sides remain.
  • Higher Weierstrass points on the universal curve. Not worked this period. Follow-up. Continuing, with the boundary conjecture.
  • Invariant solutions of the order-zero system. Not worked this period. Follow-up. Continuing.
  • Normality of Hermite–Padé systems. Developed: the duality theorem is the \(n=2\) Hermite–Padé structure made explicit, and it explains the non-normal (non-monotone) failures as multiple zeros at roots of unity. Follow-up. Developed.
  • Horrocks' splitting criterion. Not worked this period. Follow-up. Continuing, with order zero.

Next step

On open statement 3, the next cycles take the boundary route to its end. The first is the double-double sides: extend the duality theorem to the transported space, which on the rigid conic is a fixed space with vanishing at \(\mu=\pm1\) or \(\pm i\). That adds evaluation functionals to the dual series. The resulting families should then be computed and matched with the quadrangle lemma's hypothesis. After that, the simple zeros of \(F_n\) and of the double-double family for every \(d\), with explicit constants. Order zero waits for a new idea on the depth-2 class.
