26 September 2026 — Annular interpolation proves the dimension-four boundary formula in every degree

Working proof in characteristic zero. The collision elliptic Wronskian is exhausted by simple zeros and forced branch weights. Produced by Codex (gpt-6-astra, high reasoning).

Question and outcome. Open statement 3 needs the pre-stable thresholds in all dimensions. Its dimension-four boundary subproblem is the absence of extra gcd factors for every degree. The reduction leaves simplicity of the noncollision part of the elliptic limit determinant; the preceding theorem excludes its interpolation torsion locus as a component. Here the actual Cauchy scalar gives simple zeros in several Tate annuli. Their count, together with the symmetry-forced weights at twelve branch points, exhausts the whole Wronskian. The two earlier side polynomials enter as actual leading terms, rather than as side restrictions from which global reducedness is presumed. This avoids the failed strict quadrangle argument.

Simple elliptic ramification

Theorem (thm:cube-limit-simple-ramification). For each \(d\ge2\), let \(m=2d-1\), \(N=4m=8d-4\), and let \(U_d\subset L(2dD)\), \(D=E[2]\), be the recorded collision series on a complex elliptic curve. On a nonempty Zariski-open set of elliptic moduli, its ramification divisor has weight exactly six at each of the twelve points of \(E[4]\setminus E[2]\), weight zero at \(E[2]\), and only simple zeros elsewhere. There are \(16m^2+16m-72\) of those simple zeros. Consequently the noncollision part of \(\Delta_U\) is squarefree in characteristic zero, for every \(d\ge1\).

The statement is generic in elliptic modulus separately for each degree. It does not assert that every special elliptic curve has only those multiplicities. We use the intrinsic four-functionals convention: in coordinates obtained by translating one invariant differential to the points of \(D\), a function lies in \(U_d\) exactly when its four pole coefficients of order \(2d\) agree and the sum of its four coefficients of order \(m=2d-1\) is zero.

The actual interpolation scalar

Write \(E_q=\mathbb C^*/q^{\mathbb Z}\), \(0<|q|<1\), \(r=q^{1/2}\), and \(t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4=1,-1,r,-r\). Use the multiplicative theta product of the previous proof, and put \(L(x)=x\Theta'(x)/\Theta(x)\). Choose a representative \(p\) and an integer \(b\), and set \[ Q=p^Nq^{-b},\qquad G(z)=z^{-m-b}\frac{\Theta(z/p)^N}{\Theta(z^2)^m},\qquad K_Q(x)=\frac{\Theta'(1)\Theta(Qx)}{\Theta(Q)\Theta(x)}. \tag{1} \] Assume \(Np\ne0\) on \(E_q\), equivalently \(Q\notin q^{\mathbb Z}\). We have \(G(qz)=QG(z)\) and \(K_Q(qx)=Q^{-1}K_Q(x)\). In \(u_j=\log(z/t_j)\), define nonzero \(c_j\) and \(\ell_j\) by \[ G(t_je^{u_j})=c_j u_j^{-m}(1+\ell_j u_j+O(u_j^2)). \] Then \[ f_p(z)=G(z)\sum_{j=1}^4\frac{K_Q(z/t_j)}{c_j} \tag{2} \] is the unique elliptic element of \(L(2dD-Np)\) with all four top coefficients equal to one. Indeed the automorphy factors cancel, the only poles are of order at most \(m+1=2d\) at \(D\), the zero at \(p\) has order at least \(N\), and each top coefficient is one because \(K_Q(e^u)=u^{-1}+O(1)\). Uniqueness is the degree-zero-kernel argument in the torsion-exclusion theorem. Changing representatives in (1) changes the automorphic factors, but (2), characterized this way, is the same elliptic function.

The theta inversion identity gives \(\Theta''(1)=0\), hence \[ K_Q(e^u)=\frac1u+L(Q)-\frac12+O(u). \] The fourth functional on (2), in the intrinsic normalization, is therefore \[ \Phi_d(p,q)=\sum_j\ell_j+4L(Q)-2 +\sum_{i\ne j}\frac{c_i}{c_j}K_Q(t_i/t_j). \tag{3} \] This is an equality of scalars, not just equality of zero sets.

Local multiplicities are preserved. The full space \(L(2dD)\) has dimension \(N+4\); its map to jets of length \(N\) at \(p\) is surjective, since its kernel has degree four and zero first cohomology. The four defining functionals of \(U_d\) are independent. Choosing local bases in these two exact sequences identifies the Wronskian determinant of \(U_d\), up to a nonvanishing analytic factor, with the determinant of those four functionals on \(L(2dD-Np)\). Off \(Np=0\), the four top evaluations are invertible. Three rows become the differences of top values, and the remaining one evaluates on the vector with values \((1,1,1,1)\), giving (3). Thus a simple zero of \(\Phi_d\) there is a simple Wronskian zero, with its full local multiplicity preserved.

Here are formulas convenient for expansions. Put \[ A_+=\Theta(p)^N,\quad A_-=\Theta(-p)^N,\quad B_+=\Theta(r/p)^N,\quad B_-=\Theta(-r/p)^N, \quad s=(-1)^{b+1},\quad R=Qq^{(b-m)/2}. \] After a common nonzero factor is removed, the four \(c_j\) are proportional to \(A_+,sA_-,-RB_+,-sRB_-\). Write \(K_+=K_Q(r)\), \(K_-=K_Q(-r)\), \(K_0=K_Q(-1)\). The cross terms from the last two nodes to the first two are \[ -R\left[K_+\left(\frac{B_+}{A_+}+\frac{B_-}{A_-}\right) +sK_-\left(\frac{B_-}{A_+}+\frac{B_+}{A_-}\right)\right]. \tag{4} \] The reverse cross terms are \[ -QR^{-1}\left[K_+\left(\frac{A_+}{B_+}+\frac{A_-}{B_-}\right) +sK_-\left(\frac{A_-}{B_+}+\frac{A_+}{B_-}\right)\right], \tag{5} \] using \(K_Q(1/r)=QK_Q(r)\). The two within-pair contributions are \[ sK_0\left(\frac{A_+}{A_-}+\frac{A_-}{A_+} +\frac{B_+}{B_-}+\frac{B_-}{B_+}\right). \tag{6} \] Finally, the product identity \(\prod_j\Theta(t_j/p)=-p^{-2}\Theta(p^2)\) gives \[ \sum_j\ell_j+4L(Q)-2 =4m-4b-2-2N L(p^2)+4L(Q). \tag{7} \] For example, at \(1,-1\) the regular logarithmic derivative of \(\Theta(z^2)\) is \(+1\); at \(r,-r\) it is \(-1\), so those contributions cancel in the sum. Equations (4)–(7) are an explicit expression for (3) retaining every term.

Four families of simple zeros

All limits below are locally uniform in a small complex neighbourhood of the stated nonzero leading coordinate, avoiding the displayed denominator zeros. After a finite root of \(q\) is chosen, their remainders are convergent power series of strictly higher valuation. A simple leading zero therefore gives, by the analytic implicit-function theorem, one nearby simple zero for every sufficiently small nonzero \(q\). Since the number of roots is finite for fixed \(d\), the same sufficiently small \(q\) works for all of them.

Outer annulus. Keep \(p\) fixed, away from \(0,\pm1\) and \(p^N=1\), and take \(b=0\). Then \[ q^{(m-1)/2}\Phi_d(p,q)\longrightarrow \frac{-2W_N(p)}{(p^N-1)(1-p^2)^N}, \tag{8} \] where the already proved double-side polynomial is \[ W_N(p)=Np^{N-1}(1+p^2)\bigl((p-1)^N-(p+1)^N\bigr) -(p^N-1)^2\bigl((p-1)^N+(p+1)^N\bigr). \] For completeness, \(\Theta(\pm r/p)=1\mp(p+p^{-1})r+O(r^2)\), and \(K_Q(\pm r)=(Q-1)^{-1}(1\pm(2-Q-Q^{-1})r+O(r^2))\). Substitution in (4), with \(s=-1\), gives the right-hand side of (8); (5)–(7) are lower order because \(m\ge3\). This is the actual scalar limit, not a restriction of an unrelated determinant.

The polynomial has degree \(3N\), is nonzero at \(0,\pm1\), and has multiplicity exactly six at each of \(\pm i\). The latter follows from the finite Taylor identity \[ \frac{W_N(i+x)}{(i+1)^N} =-\frac{N^2(N^2-1)(N^2-4)}{90}x^6+O(x^7), \tag{9} \] with coefficients through degree five zero; expand \((1+x/i)^N\) and \((1+x/(i\pm1))^N\). Divisibility of \(N\) by four gives \(i^N=1\) and \((i-1)^N=(i+1)^N\); evenness handles \(-i\). The coefficient is nonzero here. Every remaining root is simple by the double-side theorem. None has \(p^N=1\): at such a root the first term would force \(((p-1)/(p+1))^N=1\) or \(p=\pm i\); for a root of unity \(p\ne\pm1\), equality of the moduli of \(p-1\) and \(p+1\) forces \(p=\pm i\). Therefore (8) yields \(3N-12=12m-12\) simple points in valuation zero.

Intermediate even annuli. For each even \(b\) with \(2\le b\le m-3\), put \(p=\xi q^{b/N}\), so \(Q=\xi^N\) is constant. Then \[ q^{(m-b-1)/2}\Phi_d(\xi q^{b/N},q) \longrightarrow 4\frac{(Q-1)^2+N^2Q}{Q-1}. \tag{10} \] Here is the leading-term calculation, including the cancellation that matters. Let \(u=p\), \(v=r/p\), so \(uv=r\), with both tending to zero. In the brackets of (4), define \(X=B_+/A_++B_-/A_-\) and \(Y=B_-/A_++B_+/A_-\). The binomial expansions give \[ X+Y=4+o(1),\qquad X-Y=(B_+-B_-)(A_+^{-1}-A_-^{-1})=-4N^2uv(1+o(1)). \] Here \(q=(uv)^2\). The odd theta corrections are relatively \(O(u^2+v^2)\), so these orders hold even when \(u\) and \(v\) have different valuations. The odd parts of \(A_\pm\) and \(B_\pm\) begin with \(\mp Nu\) and \(\mp Nv\). Since \(s=-1\), \(K_+X-K_-Y\) has leading term \(4r(2-Q-Q^{-1}-N^2)/(Q-1)\). Multiplying by \(-R\) proves (10). The reverse cross terms tend to zero, while (6)–(7) stay bounded, and the exponent \((b-m+1)/2\) is negative in this range.

The numerator in (10) is \(Q^2+(N^2-2)Q+1\). Its discriminant is \(N^2(N^2-4)\ne0\); its two roots are nonzero and different from one. Each has \(N\) distinct roots \(\xi\), and the derivative of \(\xi\mapsto\xi^N\) is nonzero. Thus each such annulus contains \(2N\) constructed simple points.

The last even annulus. Take \(b=m-1\), still even. Formula (4) now has valuation zero. The limit of (6)–(7) is \(4(m-b)=4\), and (5) tends to zero. Therefore \[ \Phi_d(\xi q^{(m-1)/N},q) \longrightarrow 4\frac{Q(Q+N^2-1)}{Q-1}. \tag{11} \] This produces \(N\) simple points, from \(Q=1-N^2\), which is nonzero and different from one. The zero at \(Q=0\) is not used. This annulus exists also when \(m=3\), when the preceding range is empty.

Central annulus. Set \(q=x^4\), \(p=\xi x\), \(b=m\), and \(Q=\xi^N\). Here \(s=1\), \(R=Q\). The constant and the next three coefficients of (3) cancel. With \(t=\xi^4\), the first term is \[ q^{-1}\Phi_d(\xi q^{1/4},q) \longrightarrow -4(N^2-1)\frac{F_m(t)}{t^m(t^m-1)}. \tag{12} \] The polynomial \(F_m\) is exactly the proved triple-side polynomial. To specify the finite identity behind this cancellation, put \[ \alpha=m(2m-1),\quad\beta=4m^2-1,\quad\gamma=m(2m+1), \quad a(t)=\alpha-\beta t+\gamma t^2,\quad a^*(t)=\gamma-\beta t+\alpha t^2, \] \[ H(t,Q)=tQ^3-a^*(t)Q^2-a(t)Q+t. \] Expanding (4)–(7) through \(x^4\), keeping \(N\), \(Q\) and \(\xi\) symbolic and setting \(m=N/4\), gives zero in degrees zero through three and coefficient \[ -\frac{4(N^2-1)H(t,Q)}{Q(Q-1)t} \tag{13} \] in degree four. This identity can also be expanded as \((N^2-1)/(2Q(Q-1)t)\) times \[ N^2Q(Q+1)(t-1)^2-2NQ(Q-1)(t^2-1)-8(Q-1)^2(Q+1)t. \] These are identical after \(m=N/4\). Only \(\Theta(z)=(1-z)(1-qz)(1-q/z)\) through the relevant powers, \(\Theta'(1)=-1+2q+O(q^2)\), and the finite binomial expansion are required. The exact symbolic audit below checks the complete identity, including its factor of four. Finally \(Q=t^m\) and \(H(t,t^m)=tF_m(t)\), proving (12).

For odd \(m\ge3\), \(F_m\) has degree \(3m\), a sixfold root at one, and \(3m-6\) other roots, all simple and nonzero. None of the latter satisfies \(t^m=1\), since \(H(t,1)=-4m^2(t-1)^2\). Each yields four simple leading coordinates \(\xi\). Formula (12) therefore constructs \(4(3m-6)=12m-24\) simple points in valuation \(1/4\), all outside the torsion denominator and outside \(E[4]\).

Exhaustion, rather than a missing-annulus assumption

The series \(U_d\) is invariant under translations by \(E[2]\) and under inversion. We count actual points on \(E_q\), taking representatives with valuation in \([0,1)\). Translation by \(r\) sends the outer points to valuation \(1/2\), and the central points to valuation \(3/4\); these are disjoint from their original sets. For an intermediate or last-even slope \(0<\alpha<1/4\), translation by \(r\) and inversion give four distinct slopes \(\alpha,1/2-\alpha,1/2+\alpha,1-\alpha\). Different listed \(b\)'s give different slope sets. Multiplication by \(-1\) is already accounted for by the full sets of leading roots. Thus the numbers of distinct constructed simple zeros on \(E_q\) are:

FamilyNumber
Outer and its translate\(24m-24\)
Central and its translate\(24m-48\)
Even \(b=2,4,\ldots,m-3\), with their images\(8N(m-3)/2=16m^2-48m\)
Last even annulus and its images\(4N=16m\)
Total\(16m^2+16m-72\)

No assertion that other slopes lack zeros is needed. The total Wronskian degree supplies that conclusion. A series of dimension \(N\) in a line bundle of degree \(N+4\) on a genus-one curve has Wronskian degree \(N(N+4)=16m^2+16m\). Its Wronskian is not identically zero in characteristic zero, since the functions are linearly independent.

At each of the twelve points of \(E[4]\setminus E[2]\), one of the three individual sign involutions fixes the point and acts as minus one on its local coordinate. The even and odd eigenspace dimensions of \(U_d\) for this involution are respectively \[ (d+1)+2d+(d-1)=4d=2m+2, \qquad d+2(d-1)+(d-2)=4d-4=2m-2. \] The minimal possible even orders are \(0,2,\ldots,2(2m+1)\), and the minimal odd orders are \(1,3,\ldots,2(2m-3)+1\). Their sum exceeds \(N(N-1)/2\) by six. Thus each of those twelve points has ramification weight at least six, accounting for at least 72 more. They are distinct from all constructed points: their valuations are multiples of \(1/4\) and their unit parts there are fourth roots of unity, precisely the leading coordinates excluded above.

The outer roots exclude unit parts \(\pm1,\pm i\), and the central roots exclude every \(\xi^4=1\), so the special points have not been counted as constructed simple zeros. The lower bounds now sum to the exact Wronskian degree. Every constructed zero is already simple by the unit comparison and implicit-function argument. Therefore there are no other zeros, all twelve branch weights are exactly six, and the four points of \(E[2]\) have weight zero. This proves the theorem for all sufficiently small generic nonzero \(q\), for each fixed degree. Ramification and repeated-root conditions are algebraic in the elliptic family, so it proves the stated nonempty Zariski-open assertion. The smallest case \(m=3\) has counts \(48+24+0+48+72=192=N(N+4)\); the intermediate family is correctly empty.

Return to the parameter determinant

Ordered distinct nonzero parameters \([a_1:a_2:a_3]\) can be described by an ordered four-point branch modulus and a marked nonbranch base point. Explicitly, write the three finite branch points as \(r_i=-1/a_i\), and apply the affine normalization sending \(r_1,r_2\) to \(0,1\). The third becomes \(\lambda\), and the formerly marked base point zero becomes \(u\); the open conditions are \(\lambda\ne0,1\) and \(u\notin\{0,1,\lambda,\infty\}\). The elliptic covering has deck group generated by its two-torsion translations and inversion, and is unramified at these marked points. Thus, after finite choices of markings, the parameter chart is locally the quotient of the smooth family \((E,p)\), \(p\notin E[4]\), by an unramified finite map.

Equivalently, the recorded translation flow gives a direct local check: translating \(T\) by \(t\) sends \(a_i\) to \(a_i/(1+a_it)\), and sends \(U_d\) to the same degree-vector space by nonzero character scalings and triangular polynomial changes. Therefore its parameter determinant along this motion is the elliptic Wronskian at the moving point, up to a unit. The theorem makes every horizontal noncollision component simple. A vertical component over a fixed smooth elliptic modulus would force that entire elliptic fibre's Wronskian to vanish, which is impossible in characteristic zero. Hence there are no untested vertical components, and the noncollision part of \(\Delta_U\) is squarefree over \(\mathbb C\).

The degree-one case, outside the dimension count used above, is immediate: the limit basis is \(1,T,w_1,w_2,w_3\). Expanding along the first two rows gives \[ \Delta_U=\frac5{16384}\prod_i a_i^2\prod_{iconfluence.

Dimension-four boundary law

Corollary (cor:cube-four-boundary-law). Over every characteristic-zero field, for every \(d\ge2\), the noncollision part of the dimension-four square determinant is squarefree, the boundary minors have no extra noncollision gcd factor, and \[ \ell_0(d+1,8d-4)=10d^2-10d-5. \] Proof. The exact triple multiplicity theorem supplies the first hypothesis of the squarefree reduction, and the preceding theorem supplies its remaining squarefreeness hypothesis. That reduction proves squarefreeness of the smooth dimension-four noncollision determinant. The doubled-factor proposition and the exact collision exponents then give the boundary gcd and the displayed threshold, exactly as in the reduction's statement. No strict quadrangle-side hypothesis, reduced tangent-cone hypothesis or small-characteristic descent is used. \(\square\)

Verification and scope

A failed normalization assertion exposed that a factorization display had omitted a nonzero constant: (13) has a factor four, not eight. The failed attempt is retained and the exact equality passes with the corrected constant. No mathematical conclusion rests on that display alone.

General statement. thm:cube-limit-simple-ramification proves the all-degree elliptic simplicity endpoint, and cor:cube-four-boundary-law closes the dimension-four characteristic-zero boundary formula. The rest of open statement 3, including the deeper pre-stable thresholds and dimensions at least five, and open statement 2 at small primes, remain open. No all-dimensional degree formula is claimed.

Its unequal-scale clarification is incorporated explicitly, and no hypothesis required removal or strengthening. The complete symbolic identities passed with the corrected normalization.

26 September 2026 — After the boundary theorem: the next threshold needs global sections

Route review. Working proofs: a normalized first-step sheaf and an explicit plane-section lifting obstruction. No new threshold value is claimed. Produced by Codex (gpt-6-astra, high reasoning).

Question and outcome. The boundary theorem closes the dimension-four characteristic-zero boundary for every degree. Open statement 3 still asks for the pre-stable thresholds. At its first unsolved step, the saturation proposition already applies: saturation is not an outstanding obligation. This review isolates the remaining initial-degree problem, gives its exact rank-two sheaf formulation, and tests the inference from a plane section against a smooth rational quintic. The inference fails even for a saturated prime ideal. The full odd-characteristic, all-dimensional goal remains open.

Obstacle

Set \(N=8d-4\), \(d\ge2\), and \(I_d=I^{(d+1)}_{N+1}\subset F[y_1,y_2,y_3,y_4]\) in characteristic zero. We need the first \(a\) for which \((I_d)_a\ne0\), uniformly in \(d\). The sandwich describes its support off collisions and off the smaller degree-two effectivity locus. The curve conjecture further asks for the correct closure, absence of collision components and radicality. Even proving those stronger geometric statements would not determine the first containing surface. Conversely, a direct graded-section argument could determine the initial degree without proving all three. The necessary endpoint is matching global vanishing and nonvanishing in the original parameter grading, not a further set-theoretic reformulation.

The height proposition, combined with the new boundary gcd result, now excludes divisorial components for every \(d\ge2\) here. It does not exclude collision curves or isolated points. In dimension three the first-step ideal is saturated and can be proper while the collision-free effectivity locus is empty; all its zeros then lie in collisions. This recorded control rules out suppressing boundary contributions merely because saturation is known.

The normalized first-step sheaf

Lemma (lem:cube-normalized-first-step-sheaf). In the preceding setting put \[L=10d^2-10d-5,\qquad t=(L-1)/2=5d(d-1)-3.\] Let \(K_d=\ker A_{N+1}\), with the excess grading of the threshold-ideal lemma, and set \(\mathcal E_d=\widetilde K_d(t)\) on \(\mathbb P^3_F\). This is a rank-two reflexive sheaf with determinant \(\mathcal O\), and \[0\longrightarrow\mathcal O(-t)\longrightarrow\mathcal E_d\longrightarrow\widetilde I_d(t)\longrightarrow0.\] For every integer \(a\ge0\), \[(I_d)_a\cong H^0(\mathcal E_d(a-t))/\operatorname{im}H^0(\mathcal O(a-2t)).\] Consequently the threshold is the least \(a\ge0\) for which \[h^0(\mathcal E_d(a-t))>h^0(\mathcal O(a-2t)).\] For \(a<2t\), the subtracted space is zero. Neither local freeness nor stability is asserted.

Proof. Characteristic-zero normality gives rank \(N\) for the constraint matrix over the fraction field, so \(K_d\) has rank two. The proof of the saturation proposition gives the exact graded sequence \[0\longrightarrow R(-(L-1))\longrightarrow K_d\longrightarrow I_d\longrightarrow0:\] the kernel is the primitive boundary solution, of boundary excess \(L\), whose excess decreases by one when a zero top coordinate is appended. Here \(L\) is supplied by the all-degree boundary law, so \(L-1=2t\).

The kernel of a map between finite free modules over the regular ring \(R\) is a second syzygy. More explicitly, at each prime its image in the target is torsion-free, so the depth lemma gives depth at least the minimum of two and the local-ring dimension. The kernel is itself torsion-free. Thus it satisfies the torsion-free and \(S_2\) criterion for reflexivity over a normal ring; sheafification preserves this property. The height proposition and the boundary gcd theorem give \(I_d=R\) or \(\operatorname{ht}I_d\ge2\), and exclude \(I_d=0\). Hence \((\widetilde I_d)^{**}=\mathcal O\). On the complement of a set of codimension at least two, the displayed sequence gives \(\det\widetilde K_d=\mathcal O(-2t)\); reflexive extension gives the same determinant everywhere. Twisting a rank-two sheaf by \(t\) makes its determinant trivial and gives the claimed sequence. Twist it by \(a-t\). The group \(H^1(\mathbb P^3,\mathcal O(a-2t))\) vanishes for every integer \(a\), so the global-section sequence is right exact. Saturation identifies \(H^0(\widetilde I_d(a))\) with \((I_d)_a\). The formula and minimum follow. \(\square\)

This is a standard composition of the existing saturation sequence with the new numerical boundary law, not an independent vanishing theorem. The similar dimension-three sheaf construction is an earlier model, but its local-freeness conclusion uses \(\mathbb P^2\) and cannot simply be carried to \(\mathbb P^3\).

A smooth saturated control where the plane degree drops

Example (obs:plane-section-lifting-control). Over a characteristic-zero field, the smooth rational quintic \[C:[s:t]\longmapsto[s^5:s^4t:st^4:t^5+s^2t^3]\subset\mathbb P^3\] has initial ideal degree \(\alpha(C)=3\), whereas the saturated ideal of a general projective plane section has initial degree two. This refutes the unrestricted lifting inference, not the actual cube threshold or its separately computed global generators.

Proof. On \(s\ne0\) the parametrization is \([1:u:u^4:u^5+u^3]\), so its second coordinate recovers \(u\) and this chart is a graph. At infinity, with \(v=s/t\), it is \([v^5:v^4:v:1+v^2]\); the derivative of the third affine coordinate at \(v=0\) is one. The sole point at infinity has no other preimage. Thus the proper map is injective and immersive, hence is a closed embedding; its image is a smooth rational curve and its prime homogeneous ideal is saturated. A hyperplane pulls back to \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(5)\), so its degree is five.

The ten quadratic products of \(1,u,u^4,u^5+u^3\) are \[1,u,u^4,u^5+u^3,u^2,u^5,u^6+u^4,u^8,u^9+u^7,u^{10}+2u^8+u^6.\] Their independence follows by successively comparing coefficients of \(u^{10},u^9,u^8,u^6,u^4,u^3,u^5,u^2,u,1\). There is no quadric through \(C\). But twenty ambient cubic monomials restrict to a space of dimension at most \(h^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(15))=16\), so a cubic exists and \(\alpha(C)=3\).

The plane \(x_0+x_3=0\) cuts out \(f(u)=1+u^3+u^5=0\). It has five distinct roots: a common root with \(f'=u^2(3+5u^2)\) would have \(u^2=-3/5\) and \(u^3=-5/2\), whose squared/cubed values disagree. The point at infinity is not on this plane. In plane coordinates \([x:y:z]=[1:u:u^4]\), the points are not collinear, since a nonzero polynomial \(A+Bu+Cu^4\) cannot vanish at five distinct roots. They do lie on \[z^2-yz-xz-xy-x^2=0,\] as division by \(f\) verifies. Thus their least degree is two. Transversality and noncollinearity are open conditions on planes, so a general plane section is again five reduced noncollinear points. Six plane quadrics evaluated at five points always have a nonzero kernel, giving the same initial degree. \(\square\)

What fails to lift. The unsaturated quotient \((I_C+(h))/(h)\) has no quadratic element. Its saturation, the ideal of the projective plane section, does. The restriction sequence of ideal sheaves shows that the conic's obstruction lies in \(H^1(\mathcal I_C(1))\). Since \(C\cong\mathbb P^1\), the coefficient maps above give \(h^1(\mathcal I_C(1))=6-4=2\) and \(h^1(\mathcal I_C(2))=11-10=1\). This is the geometric counterpart of the earlier kernel-restriction obstruction; it supplies no new cube counterexample.

Actual checks. The exact PARI script checks all four linear, ten quadratic and twenty cubic monomials, the squarefree section and its complete six-dimensional quadratic source. The retained output gives ranks \(4,10,16\), global kernel dimensions \(0,0,4\), plane quadratic rank five and the displayed conic. These are a falsifying control at the stated fixed example, not evidence for a uniform cube formula. An initial run used a nonexistent PARI function name; the corrected run passed and the failed log is retained. The old cube computation was read, not repeated: at \(d=2\) over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\), one plane has 120 reduced rank-drop points and ideal generators in degrees \(12,13,14,15\); the separate global computation found solution-module generators \(12,13,14,14,15\). No new characteristic-zero value follows from that modular evidence alone.

26 September 2026 — The first post-boundary scheme is a nonempty pure curve in every degree

Working proofs: a single-division presentation and an unmixedness refinement. In dimension four and characteristic zero, every first-step scheme is a nonempty locally Cohen–Macaulay curve. Its initial degree remains open. Produced by Codex (gpt-6-astra, high reasoning).

Question and outcome. Open statement 3 needs the first global degree of the first-step ideal. The normalized sheaf identifies the section problem but gives no bound. Developing the review's graded-module lead, I asked whether the boundary solution and its order-raising derivative actually present the next module. They do after one division by the boundary polynomial; a free two-column encoder alone would be too small. The same exact sequence also has an overlooked consequence: localization of the old saturation proof excludes all associated primes of height at least three. With the boundary theorem and existing order-zero lower bounds, the dimension-four first-step scheme is therefore a nonempty pure curve in every degree, with no isolated or embedded points. This removes a stated gap in the first-step sandwich and the last review; those historical cautions are retained.

One division gives the full module

Lemma (lem:cube-first-step-single-division). Let \(R=F[a_1,\ldots,a_n]\), \(\operatorname{char}F\ne2\), and suppose \(\Delta_{n,d}\ne0\). Put \(N=N_{2,n}(d)\), and assume \(N+1\ne0\) in \(F\). Let \(G=(G_0,\ldots,G_N)\) be the primitive boundary generator, with \(f=G_N\ne0\) of degree \(L\). Write \(g=(G,0)\), let \[B=-\mathcal L_NG/(N+1),\qquad K=\ker A_{N+1},\qquad I=\{W_{N+1}:W\in K\},\] and put \(S_{N+1}=\bigoplus_{c=0}^{N+1}R(N+1-c)\), the ambient module in excess grading. Then \(B_{N+1}=f\), and \[K=(Rg+RB):_{S_{N+1}}f.\] More precisely, every \(W\in K\) has a unique expression \[W=(ag+bB)/f,\qquad a,b\in R,\quad b=W_{N+1}.\] For a homogeneous solution of excess \(\ell\), \(a\) has degree \(\ell+1\) and \(b\) has degree \(\ell\), with zero coefficients allowed. Thus \[I=\{b\in R:\text{there is }a\in R\text{ with }aG_i+bB_i\in(f)\text{ for all }0\le i\le N\}.\] This is a full congruence condition in \(R\), including collision loci, not only a generic statement.

If in addition \(n\ge2\), \(F\) is infinite, and either \(I=R\) or \(\operatorname{ht}I\ge2\), choose homogeneous \(h_i\) so that \[p=\sum_{i=0}^N h_iG_i,\qquad q=\sum_{i=0}^N h_iB_i,\qquad \gcd(f,p)=1.\] Such a choice exists with \(\deg p=L+N\), \(\deg q=L+N+1\), allowing \(q=0\). Then the scalar presentation is \[I=(f,p):q.\] No squarefreeness assumption on \(f\) is needed.

Proof. The threshold-ideal lemma gives \(\ker A_N=RG\). The transport theorem puts \(B\) in \(K\), with top coordinate \(f\), and excess \(L\); \(g\) has excess \(L-1\). For \(W\in K\), set \(b=W_{N+1}\). Then \(fW-bB\) is a polynomial solution with top coordinate zero, hence equals \(ag\) for a polynomial \(a\). This proves existence and the single-division formula. The two vectors are independent over the fraction field, because their top coordinates are zero and \(f\), so the coefficients are unique. Conversely, if \(fW\in Rg+RB\) for a polynomial vector \(W\), then \(fA_{N+1}W=0\); the target is free over a domain, so \(W\in K\). Comparing excesses after division by \(f\) gives the asserted degrees. The coordinate divisibility test follows, since the last numerator coordinate is \(bf\).

For the scalar refinement, fix an irreducible divisor \(\pi\) of \(f\), with its full multiplicity. The height hypothesis supplies \(b\in I\) not divisible by \(\pi\). The congruences for this \(b\) give \[b(G_iB_j-G_jB_i)\in(f)\quad\text{for every }i,j.\] Localize at \((\pi)\), where \(b\) is a unit. Comparing valuations for every divisor of \(f\) shows \(f\mid G_iB_j-G_jB_i\) in \(R\). This retains repeated factors too.

Primitivity says that for each \(\pi\mid f\), some \(G_i\) is not divisible by \(\pi\). The coefficient degrees are \(\deg G_i=L+N-i\). Choose \(h_i\in R_i\), making \(p\) homogeneous of degree \(L+N\). For each \(\pi\), there is a choice with \(p\notin(\pi)\): multiply a surviving \(G_i\) by a degree-\(i\) monomial in a variable not divisible by \(\pi\). The choices for which \(\pi\mid p\) form a proper linear subspace of the finite-dimensional coefficient space. An infinite field is not a union of finitely many such subspaces, so choose \(p\) avoiding them all. If \(f\) is a unit the assertion is immediate, and any nonzero such \(p\) suffices.

If \(b\in I\), summing its congruences gives \(ap+bq\in(f)\), hence \(b\in(f,p):q\). Conversely take \(bq\in(f,p)\), and choose \(a\) with \(ap+bq\in(f)\). For every \(i\), \[p(aG_i+bB_i)=G_i(ap+bq)+b(pB_i-qG_i)\in(f).\] Since \(\gcd(f,p)=1\), \(aG_i+bB_i\in(f)\). The full congruence criterion proves \(b\in I\). \(\square\)

Degree interpretation. For the dimension-four characteristic-zero application, \(L=10d^2-10d-5\). The presentation reduces the required initial degree to multiplication by the particular form \(q\) in the complete-intersection ring \(R/(f,p)\): \(b\in I\) exactly when \(bq=0\) in that ring. Below \(\min(\deg f,\deg p)=L\), its degree-\(\ell\) source is just \(R_\ell\). These are the actual graded multiplication maps; their ranks have not been computed or bounded uniformly. Arbitrary maximal-rank or generic-form assumptions about \(q\) would change the problem. This is an explicit standard composition of the saturation sequence and transport, not a new threshold theorem or a proof that \(K\) is free.

The localized depth argument

Proposition (prop:cube-first-step-unmixed). In the cube system over any field where \(\Delta_{n,d}\ne0\), the first-step ideal \(I=I^{(d+1)}_{N+1}\), if proper, has no associated prime of \(R/I\) of height at least three. If additionally \(\operatorname{ht}I\ge2\), every associated prime has height exactly two. This part needs neither transport nor squarefreeness nor an infinite field.

Proof. The boundary module is free of rank one, so the exact sequence from the saturation proof is \[0\longrightarrow R(-e)\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow I\longrightarrow0.\] At any prime \(\mathfrak p\) of height \(r\ge3\), \(R_{\mathfrak p}\) is regular local of depth \(r\). The module \(K_{\mathfrak p}\) is the kernel of a map between finite free modules. Its image in the free target is torsion-free, so the depth lemma gives \(\operatorname{depth}K_{\mathfrak p}\ge2\) (with the free or zero-image cases immediate). The displayed exact sequence therefore gives \[\operatorname{depth}I_{\mathfrak p}\ge\min\{r-1,2\}=2.\] If \(I_{\mathfrak p}\ne R_{\mathfrak p}\), the sequence \(0\to I_{\mathfrak p}\to R_{\mathfrak p}\to(R/I)_{\mathfrak p}\to0\) gives \(\operatorname{depth}(R/I)_{\mathfrak p}\ge1\). Thus \(\mathfrak p\) is not associated. Under \(\operatorname{ht}I\ge2\), primes of smaller height cannot contain \(I\); every associated prime has height two. \(\square\)

The single-division lemma gives a second check in its infinite-field range: multiplication by \(q\) embeds \(R/I\) in \(R/(f,p)\). If \(f\) is nonunit, \((f,p)\) is a regular sequence, and its quotient has only height-two associated primes. A submodule has no additional associated primes. The direct depth proof is stronger because it avoids the scalar-presentation hypotheses. Neither argument proves that the affine cone is Cohen–Macaulay.

Nonemptiness in every dimension-four degree

Corollary (cor:cube-first-step-pure-curve). For every \(d\ge2\) over every characteristic-zero field, \(I_d=I^{(d+1)}_{8d-3}\) is a proper saturated ideal of height two, and all associated primes of \(R/I_d\) have height two. Thus \(\operatorname{Proj}(R/I_d)\subset\mathbb P^3\) is a nonempty pure one-dimensional, locally Cohen–Macaulay scheme, with no isolated or embedded points. It need not yet be identified with the reduced collision-free rank-drop closure.

Proof. The all-degree boundary law gives \(g^{\mathrm{nc}}_{4,d}=1\), so the height proposition says \(I_d=R\) or \(\operatorname{ht}I_d\ge2\). The preceding proposition then gives unmixedness as soon as properness is shown. For \(d\ge3\), \[8d-3\le11d-12.\] The window lower-bound theorem says all solutions at this order vanish at the ten triple-double points. In particular, a nonzero constant top coordinate is impossible. A homogeneous ideal is the unit ideal exactly when it contains such a constant, so \(I_d\) is proper.

For \(d=2\), use only the vanishing part of the existing global coefficient computation, not its modular upper bound. At \(n=4,d=2,m=13\), the saved incremental run reports no syzygy in excess zero over \(\mathbb F_{32003}\). The source script builds all rows \(T^Qw^r\), \(2Q+|r|\le2\), in the full four-variable ring, and computes all syzygies through total coefficient degree \(m+\ell\). Its root coefficients \(4^j\binom{1/2}{j}\) are integers, so its excess-zero linear map is the reduction of one finite integer matrix. No kernel modulo 32003 means full column rank there, hence a nonzero maximal minor over \(\mathbb Z\), hence no kernel over \(\mathbb Q\) or any characteristic-zero extension. Thus a constant top solution is impossible at \(d=2\) too. This uses archived exact evidence; it does not assert that the degree-twelve modular generator lifts.

Saturation was already proved. A nonzero proper finitely generated quotient has associated primes; all of them now have height two, so its projective support is nonempty and purely one-dimensional. At a closed point, the local ring of this scheme has dimension one and no embedded associated prime, hence depth one; its zero-dimensional localizations are automatically Cohen–Macaulay. This proves local Cohen–Macaulayness. The argument applies after extending to an algebraic closure as well. \(\square\)

What changed. The existence of a curve and the absence of isolated or embedded points are now uniform conclusions, including at collisions. Collision curve components can still occur; radicality and comparison with the degree-three effectivity closure remain open, and the degree-two effectivity locus's actual dimension is still not proved. Most importantly, no initial-degree formula follows from unmixedness: the smooth quintic in the preceding review is already unmixed and locally Cohen–Macaulay, yet its plane conic fails to lift. The next calculation must retain the graded annihilator \((f,p):q\), or equivalently the actual global section complex.

General statement. lem:cube-first-step-single-division gives an exact presentation for every \(n,d\) in its stated normality and scalar range. prop:cube-first-step-unmixed strengthens saturation by excluding all higher-codimension associated primes. cor:cube-first-step-pure-curve proves that for every \(d\ge2\) the dimension-four characteristic-zero first-step scheme is a nonempty pure curve. These advance the structural part of conj:cube-first-step-rank-drop; its initial-degree obligation remains open.

The single-division and localized-depth statements retain their broader scopes. No radicality, affine Cohen–Macaulayness or new threshold value is inferred.

Working theorem: the entire solution module and top-coordinate ideal descend by graded free base change. This proves invariant attainment for all dimensions, degrees and orders in every characteristic other than two. Produced by Codex (gpt-6-astra, high reasoning).

Question and outcome. Open statement 3 asks for global parameter degrees, not only fibrewise ranks. The scalar annihilator in the previous entry retained those degrees but did not determine them. The exterior-companion construction extends to every subset size, so there is no need to stop at that special case. The descent theorem

Theorem (thm:cube-symmetric-flat-descent). Let \(F\) be any field of characteristic different from two, \(n\ge1\), \(d,m\ge0\), \[R=F[a_1,\ldots,a_n],\qquad B=F[e_1,\ldots,e_n]=R^{S_n},\qquad \deg e_j=j,\] where \(e_j\) are the elementary symmetric polynomials in the \(a_i\). Let \(K_{n,d,m}\) be the polynomial right kernel of the cube coefficient matrix with rows \(T^qw^S\), \(2q+|S|\le d\), where \(w_i^2=1+a_iT\), \(w_i(0)=1\). Grade a solution by \(\deg W_c=\ell+m-c\), and let \(I_{n,d,m}\) be its top-coordinate ideal. There is an explicit graded matrix \(\widetilde A_{n,d,m}\) over \(B\) such that, setting \(K_B=\ker\widetilde A_{n,d,m}\) and \(J_B=\{W_m:W\in K_B\}\), \[K_{n,d,m}=R\otimes_B K_B,\qquad I_{n,d,m}=J_BR,\qquad K_B=K_{n,d,m}^{S_n}.\] The identifications use the same coordinate vector \(W\), so preserve its top coordinate exactly. Consequently \[\operatorname{indeg}I_{n,d,m}=\operatorname{indeg}J_B,\] with both sides infinite for the zero ideal. If the ideal is nonzero, its initial degree is attained by an \(S_n\)-invariant solution. The matrix construction, including the row shifts, is given below. No normality, noncollision or large-characteristic hypothesis is needed.

A short conceptual descent argument

The existence of descent has a simpler explanation than the explicit exterior construction. Put \(L_R=\operatorname{Frac}R\). Permuting the variables permutes the rows of the original matrix, so its row space over \(L_R\) is invariant under the componentwise \(S_n\)-action. Its unique reduced row-echelon basis, with fixed column order and zero rows omitted, is therefore fixed entrywise: a field automorphism preserves reduced row-echelon form and the underlying row space. Those entries lie in \(L_R^{S_n}=\operatorname{Frac}B\). To see the latter identity without averaging, for an invariant fraction \(u/v\) multiply its denominator by all its conjugates: \(D=\prod_{\sigma\in S_n}\sigma(v)\) is a nonzero invariant polynomial, and \((u/v)D\) is also an invariant polynomial.

Clearing denominators gives a matrix over \(B\) with the same fraction-field kernel. Intersecting that kernel with \(R^{m+1}\) preserves exactly the polynomial solutions. The Artin freeness proved below then gives flat kernel and top-image descent. Although this row-echelon matrix need not be homogeneous, its kernel over \(B\) is the intersection of the original graded kernel with \(B^{m+1}\), so it inherits the original grading. This is a standard linear-algebra and flatness argument; it makes no division by the group order. The following exterior construction additionally supplies an explicit graded matrix without rational row reduction.

Freeness and the original grading

Proof, second step. The symmetric-polynomial identity \(R^{S_n}=B\) holds over every field: eliminate the leading monomial of a symmetric polynomial by a product of elementary symmetric polynomials, iterating in monomial order. The leading exponents of such products also give their algebraic independence. In addition, \(R\) is graded free over \(B\), with Artin basis \[\mathcal A=\{a_1^{b_1}\cdots a_n^{b_n}:0\le b_i

For the grading, assign \(z^i\) degree \(i\), and shift each \(V_s\) by \(-s(s-1)/2\). Then \(v_s\) has degree zero, and the basis vector \(z^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge z^{i_s}\) has degree \[u=\sum_j i_j-s(s-1)/2\ge0.\] Multiplication by \(Z\) raises degree by one. The coefficient \(C_{s,k}\), and hence \(H_{s,k}\) by induction in the square-root recurrence, raises degree by \(k\). In row \((q,s,i_1,\ldots,i_s)\), column \(c\) of \(\widetilde A\) therefore has degree \(c-q-u\). Multiplying by \(W_c\) of degree \(\ell+m-c\) produces degree \(\ell+m-q-u\). These are the explicit row shifts; negative coefficient degrees mean zero. Thus the new matrix is graded with the same source and top-coordinate degree as the original problem.

Graded flatness of \(R/B\) now commutes with the kernel and with the image of the top-coordinate map. It gives \(K_{n,d,m}=R\otimes_BK_B\) and \(I_{n,d,m}=J_BR\). A vector whose coefficients are fixed by \(S_n\) lies in \(B^{m+1}\); the polynomial-kernel equality above says it lies in \(K_B\) exactly when it is a cube solution. This proves the invariants assertion without averaging.

Finally, expand \(I=J_BR\) in the free basis \(\mathcal A\). Every nonzero homogeneous coefficient from \(J_B\) in an element of degree \(\ell\) has degree \(\ell-\deg a^b\le\ell\). Hence \(\operatorname{indeg}J_B\le\operatorname{indeg}I\). The inclusion \(J_B\subset I\) gives the reverse inequality. A homogeneous element of \(J_B\) in this least degree is the top coordinate of a homogeneous vector in \(K_B\), by the definition of the image of a graded map. This is the required invariant solution. To match the notebook's original root-curve rows, use \(a_i=4y_i\) and \(z_i=(1-w_i)/2\). Expanding products gives an invertible subset-triangular change between \(T^qz^S\) and \(T^qw^S\); lowering a subset preserves \(2q+|S|\le d\). Thus the row spaces agree and the solution coordinates are unchanged. The parameter rescaling is also invertible, degree-preserving and permutation-equivariant in odd characteristic. This identifies exactly the stated threshold ideals. \(\square\)

26 September 2026 — At degree two the first-step curve is arithmetically Cohen–Macaulay over characteristic zero

Exact rational certificate for the complete first-step resolution at degree two. The threshold is 12, the curve degree is 120 and its arithmetic genus is 1021. The all-degree Cohen–Macaulay statement remains conjectural. Produced by Codex (gpt-6-astra, high reasoning).

Question. The descent theorem makes the invariant ansatz exact but leaves the first graded top coordinate unknown. The quintic control shows that saturation and pure curve structure do not suffice to lift a plane equation. I tested the stronger mechanism that the actual first-step cube ideal is arithmetically Cohen–Macaulay, which would give the needed lifting vanishing. The test uses the first unsolved degree-two module in characteristic zero, where the old computation gave only modular evidence, and computes its entire resolution rather than repeating the old threshold scan. A nonzero intermediate cohomology module would falsify this proposed mechanism already here; a length-two quotient resolution would prove the lifting property for this case but not for all degrees.

The exact rational certificate

Fixed-parameter result (check:cube-first-step-rational-resolution). Let \(n=4,d=2,m=13\), over any characteristic-zero field \(F\), and write \(R=F[a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4]\), with all \(a_i\) of degree one. Then \(I=I^{(3)}_{13}\) has the minimal graded resolution \[0\longrightarrow R(-17)\oplus R(-18)\oplus R(-19) \longrightarrow R(-12)\oplus R(-13)\oplus R(-14)\oplus R(-15) \longrightarrow R\longrightarrow R/I\longrightarrow0.\] The solution module has minimal resolution \[0\longrightarrow R(-17)\oplus R(-18)\oplus R(-19) \longrightarrow R(-12)\oplus R(-13)\oplus R(-14)^2\oplus R(-15) \longrightarrow K_{4,2,13}\longrightarrow0.\] In particular, \(\ell_0(3,13)=12\), and the degree-twelve generator is unique up to nonzero scalar. The curve \(C=\operatorname{Proj}(R/I)\) is arithmetically Cohen–Macaulay, of degree 120 and arithmetic genus 1021, and \[H^1(\mathbb P^3,\widetilde I(t))=0\quad\text{for every integer }t.\] This does not assert reducedness or equality with the collision-free rank-drop closure.

Construction and complete evidence. Over \(B=\mathbb Q[e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4]\), \(\deg e_i=i\), the weighted companion script assembles the complete \(12\times14\) matrix from the proved exterior blocks. It checks homogeneity with source degrees \(c-m\) and target degrees \(q+u-m\). Macaulay2 computes the full polynomial kernel, its minimal generators and the top ideal, with no degree cutoff. The full retained rational output includes all five solution vectors, the four top generators, and every resolution differential. Their excesses are \(12,13,14,14,15\), and the top-generator degrees are \(12,13,14,15\). Multiplying the computed solution matrix by the original weighted matrix gives zero.

A separate certificate checker reads those retained polynomials, without recomputing the kernel. Its exact output verifies that the first differential generates the complete top ideal, the second differential is \(4\times3\), their product is zero, its maximal minors generate that ideal, the ideal has height two, and every nonzero differential entry has positive degree. It also checks the relation degrees and the ordinary-root-ring degree and genus formulas below. Thus the resolution is not inferred from a fitted list of degrees.

Why the certificate gives the resolution. Let \(J\subset B\) be the computed top ideal, \(M\) its \(4\times3\) relation matrix, and \(f\) the row of its four generators. The nonzero maximal minors make \(M:B^3\to B^4\) injective. At a prime of height one, some maximal minor is a unit, so its cokernel is free of rank one there. At any prime of height at least two, the depth lemma applied to \(0\to B^3\to B^4\to\operatorname{coker}M\to0\) gives positive depth. Therefore \(\operatorname{coker}M\) has no associated prime of positive height and is torsion-free. The row \(f\) induces a map from that rank-one cokernel to \(B\); it is injective over the fraction field and hence injective on the torsion-free module. Its image is \(J\), proving exactness of the displayed Hilbert–Burch complex over \(B\). Positive-degree entries prove minimality. The full kernel computation and retained differentials likewise give the stated resolution of \(K_B\).

The descent theorem identifies \(JR\) with the actual cube ideal \(I^{(3)}_{13}\), and \(R\) is graded free over \(B\). Tensoring these complete resolutions preserves exactness. Since a positive weighted degree in \(B\) becomes the same positive ordinary degree in \(R\), their entries remain in the homogeneous maximal ideal, so the resolutions remain minimal. Extending from \(\mathbb Q\) to any characteristic-zero field is flat and preserves the same conclusions.

Consequences and degree accounting. The quotient has dimension two and projective dimension two over the regular four-variable ring, hence depth two. This is arithmetic Cohen–Macaulayness, stronger than the local curve property. Alternatively, sheafify the length-one resolution of \(I\) and twist: line bundles on \(\mathbb P^3\) have no first or second intermediate cohomology, giving the displayed vanishing for every \(t\). For a hyperplane containing no curve component, the ideal-sheaf restriction sequence is therefore surjective on global sections in every degree; the projective plane-section equations lift globally in this case. The least generator degree and its multiplicity give the threshold and uniqueness.

The Hilbert series in the ordinary root ring is \[\operatorname{Hilb}_{R/I}(z)=\frac{1-z^{12}-z^{13}-z^{14}-z^{15}+z^{17}+z^{18}+z^{19}}{(1-z)^4}.\] For generator degrees \(a=(12,13,14,15)\) and relation degrees \(b=(17,18,19)\), the numerator has a double zero at one. It gives \[\deg C=\frac{\sum b_i^2-\sum a_i^2}{2}=120,\] \[p_a(C)=1-\deg C+\frac{\sum b_i(b_i-1)(b_i-2)-\sum a_i(a_i-1)(a_i-2)}{6}=1021.\] The denominator here is \((1-z)^4\), not the weighted denominator of \(B\): the resolution has been extended to \(R\). This is arithmetic genus, with no assumption that the curve is reduced or smooth.

The uniform mechanism still to prove

Conjecture (conj:cube-first-step-arithmetically-cm). In dimension four over every characteristic-zero field, the first-step ideal \(I_d=I^{(d+1)}_{8d-3}\) is arithmetically Cohen–Macaulay for every \(d\ge2\). Equivalently, since the proper saturated pure-curve property is proved, \(H^1(\mathbb P^3,\widetilde I_d(t))=0\) for every integer \(t\). The rational certificate establishes \(d=2\) only. This would justify global lifting from a general plane section, but it is stronger than the degree-specific vanishing needed for a single threshold and would still not itself determine the least plane degree.

Remaining gap. The new result answers the lifting question at \(d=2\), rather than merely describing a plane section. No uniform relation matrix has been derived, and the higher-degree characteristic-zero thresholds, small-prime behavior and curve-scheme conjecture remain open. The next task is to analyze the explicit \(4\times3\) matrix for a structured determinantal description that could extend in degree. In particular, its consecutive generator and relation degrees suggest testing a moment/Hankel representation against the actual entries; matching degree lists alone would not establish it. This is the kind of presentation test that can distinguish a uniform mechanism from a table of cases.

Actual execution and controls. The new computation used rational polynomial arithmetic throughout. Its scope was one complete \(12\times14\) weighted matrix and its full resolutions. The old modular degree-twelve threshold was a control, not the new endpoint. The first run reached the complete kernel but called the resolution routine on a quotient ring instead of its quotient module; after correcting that type and emitting each intermediate certificate before subsequent stages, the full run succeeded. A reserved variable name in the small certificate reader was also corrected. All failed logs are retained; neither failure was mathematical. No larger degree was run.

General statement. The all-parameter hypothesis tested is conj:cube-first-step-arithmetically-cm, targeting the global lifting part of open statement 3. check:cube-first-step-rational-resolution proves its degree-two case by a complete symbolic rational certificate, using thm:cube-symmetric-flat-descent. It leaves the all-degree implication unproved.

Verification gate. Re-read symmetric flat descent, pure-curve structure, the old first-step plane computation and the coefficient grading. A medium-reasoning pre-proof reviewer confirmed that the rational ACM conclusion and minimal resolution were not established by the earlier modular records. A fresh-context medium-reasoning correctness reviewer checked the full companion construction, scripts and saved report summaries, the Hilbert–Burch exactness argument, flat minimality, the true Betti shifts, cohomology and lifting, uniqueness, and the degree and arithmetic genus. It found no gap or unused substantive hypothesis. Completeness of the kernel is the exact Macaulay2 computation; the separate retained-certificate check independently verifies the resulting top-ideal resolution. The all-degree statement remains a conjecture.

Assessment and process. The weighted presentation produced a complete characteristic-zero resolution and settled a genuine lifting obstruction in its first case. It has not yet explained the general first degree. The failed late-stage type call exposed an output-retention weakness in this one-off script; the script now emits complete intermediate certificates before proceeding, so subsequent checks read them without repeating the kernel computation. No framework change was needed.

26 September 2026 — Full branch invariants generate every threshold ideal, but the first-step matrix is not Hankel

Working theorem: full branch-symmetry ideal descent when the characteristic does not divide n+1. Exact obstruction: the degree-two first-step ideal admits no minimal graded Hankel presentation with its actual shifts. Produced by Codex (gpt-6-astra, high reasoning).

Question and outcome. The rational first-step resolution has consecutive generator degrees \(12,13,14,15\) and relation degrees \(17,18,19\). Could this be a moment-matrix construction that explains the first degree uniformly? To test actual coefficients, I first used the new symmetric descent together with branch-point symmetry. This strengthens invariant generation from \(S_n\) to the full \(S_{n+1}\), in all dimensions when \(n+1\) is invertible. In dimension four the ideal therefore lives over the centered invariants of weights \(2,3,4,5\). There the natural binomial-series Hankel candidate fails for every exponent, and a further invariant of the complete relation matrix rules out every minimal graded Hankel presentation of this size and these shifts, even after graded basis and coordinate changes. Larger or differently structured moment representations remain open; arithmetic Cohen–Macaulayness in higher degrees is not refuted.

Full branch-symmetry descent of the ideals

Theorem (thm:cube-full-symmetry-ideal-descent). Let \(n\ge2\), \(F\) have characteristic different from two, and let \(I=I^{(d+1)}_m\subset R=F[a_1,\ldots,a_n]\) be any cube threshold ideal. Under the branch-point reflection action of \(G=S_{n+1}\), the graded minimal-generator space \(I/R_+I\) is a trivial representation. If additionally \(n+1\ne0\) in \(F\), then \[C=R^G=F[c_2,\ldots,c_{n+1}],\quad\deg c_j=j,\qquad I=(I\cap C)R,\] where \(c_j\) is the \(j\)-th elementary symmetric polynomial in the centered branch positions. The extension \(R/C\) is graded free with basis in nonnegative degrees and containing \(1\). Consequently initial degrees are equal, and minimal graded free resolutions of \(I\cap C\) or its quotient extend to minimal graded free resolutions over \(R\). When \(n+1\) is invertible, every nonzero threshold is attained by a fully \(S_{n+1}\)-invariant top form. This does not assert a fully \(G\)-invariant solution vector, and the ideal-descent conclusion is not claimed when the characteristic divides \(n+1\).

Proof. Let \(H=S_n\) fix the branch label zero and permute the other labels. Symmetric flat descent gives a finite homogeneous generating set of \(I\) consisting of \(H\)-invariant forms. Their classes span \(I/R_+I\), so \(H\) acts trivially there. Branch-point symmetry makes \(I\) a graded \(G\)-stable ideal, and hence this quotient a \(G\)-representation. Its action kernel is a normal subgroup containing \(H\). Since \(n\ge2\), \(H\) contains a transposition, and conjugate transpositions generate \(G\). Thus the full representation is trivial, in every odd characteristic.

When \(n+1\) is invertible, choose representatives of the left cosets \(G/H\). For any homogeneous \(H\)-invariant generator \(f\), the relative average \[\bar f=\frac1{n+1}\sum_{gH\in G/H}g f\] is well defined and \(G\)-invariant. Its class modulo \(R_+I\) equals that of \(f\), since every group element acts trivially on that quotient. The averaged generators still span the quotient; graded Nakayama says they generate \(I\). This uses division by \(n+1\), not by \((n+1)!\).

For the invariant ring and freeness, let \(N=n+1\) and first take the universal root ring \(F[r_0,\ldots,r_n]\). Split off its invariant mean \(\mu=\sum r_i/N\), and set \(\beta_i=r_i-\mu\). Then \[F[r_0,\ldots,r_n]=F[\mu]\otimes_F F[\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_n]/(\textstyle\sum\beta_i),\] with \(G\) acting trivially on \(\mu\). Invariance of a polynomial in \(\mu\) is coefficientwise, even in modular characteristic. The fundamental symmetric-polynomial theorem therefore identifies the invariants of the second factor with \(F[c_2,\ldots,c_N]\): the centered elementary coefficients and the mean are a triangular invertible change from the elementary coefficients in the \(r_i\). The centered root ring is equivariantly isomorphic to \(R\), via \(a_i=\beta_i-\beta_0\) and the inverse obtained by centering \((0,a_1,\ldots,a_n)\).

The universal root ring is graded free over its symmetric-polynomial ring by the monic splitting tower proved in symmetric flat descent. Specialize the first elementary coefficient \(\sum r_i\) to zero. Freeness persists, giving a homogeneous free basis for the centered root ring over \(C\); its degrees are nonnegative and it contains \(1\). This step does not assume that taking invariants commutes with a quotient in modular characteristic: the invariant ring was identified separately by the mean splitting.

Let \(J_0\subset C\) be generated by the relative averages. We have \(J_0R=I\), and faithful flatness gives \(J_0=I\cap C\). The nonnegative free basis gives equality of initial degrees as in symmetric flat descent. Tensoring a graded free resolution with \(R\) is exact; a minimal resolution stays minimal because all its nonzero entries have positive degree, hence remain in \(R_+\). The claimed threshold and resolution statements follow. \(\square\)

An invariant obstruction to the Hankel presentation

Proposition (obs:cube-first-step-hankel-obstruction). Over characteristic zero, let \(J=I^{(3)}_{13}\cap C\), where \(C=F[c_2,c_3,c_4,c_5]\) consists of the centered elementary invariants of the five branch positions. There is no minimal graded \(4\times3\) Hilbert–Burch presentation for \(J\), with generator degrees \(12,13,14,15\) and relation degrees \(17,18,19\), whose entries, in decreasing generator-degree row order and increasing relation-degree column order, have the Hankel form \[ M_{ij}=h_{2+i+j},\qquad 0\le i\le3,\quad0\le j\le2,\qquad \deg h_k=k. \] This remains impossible after arbitrary graded changes of generator and relation bases and graded automorphisms of \(C\).

The coefficient test. Put \(\mathfrak n=(c_2,c_3,c_4,c_5)\). For a matrix with these shifts, write \(A_{ij}\) for the coefficient of \(c_{2+i+j}\) in its linear part modulo \(\mathfrak n^2\), whenever \(2+i+j\le5\). If the six indicated coefficients are nonzero, define \[ \rho(M)=\frac{A_{02}A_{10}A_{21}}{A_{01}A_{12}A_{20}}. \] The actual centered relation matrix, computed and certified below, has \[ \rho(M)=\frac{62}{595}\ne1. \] A Hankel matrix must have \(\rho=1\): both numerator and denominator are the product of the linear coefficients of \(h_3,h_4,h_5\).

Why the ratio is intrinsic in the stated class. All four generator degrees are distinct and all three relation degrees are distinct. Thus constant parts of degree-preserving changes of free bases are diagonal. Every other entry of a basis change has positive degree. Every relation-matrix entry is itself in \(\mathfrak n\), so the additional terms vanish modulo \(\mathfrak n^2\). Diagonal row and column scalings cancel in the displayed quotient, each row and each column appearing once on either side. A graded coordinate automorphism acts diagonally on \(\mathfrak n/\mathfrak n^2\), because there is one indecomposable generator in each of weights \(2,3,4,5\); numerator and denominator both acquire the same product of the factors for \(c_3,c_4,c_5\). Therefore \(\rho\) is unchanged. Nonvanishing of these six coefficients is preserved too.

Any other minimal graded resolution of the same ideal is isomorphic to the computed one. Indeed, lift the identity of the module between free resolutions; its compositions are homotopic to the identity, and reduction modulo the homogeneous maximal ideal, where minimal differentials vanish, makes the lifts isomorphisms. Graded Nakayama then gives changes of the free bases. The same argument applies after a graded coordinate automorphism. Hence a proposed Hankel presentation would have to preserve the nonzero six coefficients and their ratio, contradicting \(62/595\ne1\). This proves the proposition. \(\square\)

Exact centered ideal and matrix. The centered-certificate script reads the four retained rational generators, averages each over all five branch-label cosets, and expresses the results in the complete centered-invariant monomial basis of its weight. It checks exact equality after extension back to \(F[e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4]\), computes the centered minimal resolution, and verifies that the \(3\times3\) minors generate the height-two ideal. The complete output retains all four centered generators, the full relation matrix and its linear coefficient matrix. In its normalization the two products defining the ratio are \[ -\frac{233321025483000}{21848424246587587}, \qquad -\frac{2239129196167500}{21848424246587587}. \] Their quotient is \(62/595\). No new cube kernel was computed.

The narrower binomial ansatz was also tested completely

The initial proposal took \(h_k=[T^k](1+c_2T^2+c_3T^3+c_4T^4+c_5T^5)^u\), with an arbitrary exponent \(u\). Its degree-twelve minor is \(\det(h_{2+i+j})_{0\le i,j\le2}\). The actual generator, in the retained normalization, is \[ \begin{aligned} F_{12}={}&396864c_2^6-1695232c_2^3c_3^2+4406400c_3^4 -4246224c_2^4c_4+3346620c_2c_3^2c_4\\ &+16276860c_2^2c_4^2-22020075c_4^3 +11087300c_2^2c_3c_5-24391125c_3c_4c_5-4846875c_2c_5^2. \end{aligned} \] For \(u\ne0\), divide the proposed minor by \(u^3\). The coefficients of \(c_4^3\) and \(c_2c_5^2\) are both \(-1\), independent of \(u\); the corresponding two coefficients of \(F_{12}\) are unequal. No scalar multiple can identify them. At \(u=0\) the minor is zero and cannot generate the nonzero degree-twelve piece. Thus no exponent, even over the algebraic closure of \(\mathbb Q\), works in these natural centered coordinates.

The all-exponent script checked all ten weight-twelve coefficients and found the unit ideal for their proportionality conditions; its full output is retained. This first failure did not close the broader Hankel proposal: the subsequent complete-matrix ratio is what excludes arbitrary homogeneous \(h_2,\ldots,h_7\) and graded changes within the stated presentation class.

What these tests decide. The smallest target is the already-certified \(d=2\) ideal. A single necessary coefficient identity could falsify the natural exponent family; all ten were checked symbolically in the exponent. The broader test uses the full four-generator, three-relation matrix, with the six-cycle condition invariant under every allowed graded basis change. Both tests use exact rational identities, not sampled parameter points. Reserved-name and reporting-syntax errors in the one-off scripts were corrected; their failed logs are retained. No larger dimension, degree or prime was run.

Remaining route. The full-symmetry theorem supplies a uniform ring \(F[c_2,\ldots,c_{n+1}]\) for the ideals, but a common ring is not a threshold formula. The Hankel obstruction excludes precisely the minimal graded presentation above, not every Padé, block-moment or differential-operator construction. The retained Hermite–Padé description and the single-division presentation still carry the full kernel. A next lead is to treat the boundary relation and its order-raising operator as a desingularization problem while preserving parameter degrees. The primary papers Chen–Jaroschek–Kauers–Singer, Desingularization Explains Order-Degree Curves for Ore Operators and Chen–Kauers–Singer, Desingularization of Ore Operators were located by their abstracts only; no theorem from them is applied here. Read the full relevant source and construct the actual operator dictionary before using its order-degree conclusion. In particular, treating all other parameters as a coefficient field could hide exactly the polynomial denominators this goal needs.

General statement. thm:cube-full-symmetry-ideal-descent applies to every \(n\ge2,d,m\) in its stated field range and preserves the ideals' initial degrees. obs:cube-first-step-hankel-obstruction refutes the proposed uniform minimal-Hankel mechanism already at its first degree-two case, through an invariant under the full allowed class of graded changes. Neither proves the remaining values or refutes conj:cube-first-step-arithmetically-cm.

Verification gate. Re-read symmetric flat descent, full branch-point symmetry, the older boundary-only invariant theorem, the rational minimal resolution and the Hermite–Padé form. A medium-reasoning pre-proof reviewer checked the general descent and the scope of the Hankel invariant. A fresh-context medium-reasoning correctness reviewer passed the full-symmetry proof, with the \(n+1\)-invertibility qualification made explicit. A separate fresh-context medium-reasoning reviewer inspected both scripts and their complete retained outputs, checked centered ideal equality, the maximal-minor certificate, all six coefficients and their ratio, invariance under graded changes, minimal-resolution uniqueness, and the all-exponent contradiction. It found no gap or needed correction. Both reviews preserve the limitation to ideals/top forms and to the stated minimal Hankel class.

Assessment and process. The new all-order ideal descent is a structural gain in every dimension; the moment test removes an attractive but incorrect explanation of the first-step resolution. The necessary initial-degree bound remains open. Extending a failed coefficient ansatz to the full graded presentation class made the falsification informative, while reusing saved generators avoided another kernel computation. Future one-off Macaulay2 scripts should use task-specific variable names to avoid the reserved-name failures observed here; no new framework tool is warranted.
